# CMF 3D-QSAR
The continuous molecular fields approach, as a program

# What this program is

CMF 3D-QSAR is a desktop application, a Python library and a command-line tool implementing the
**Continuous Molecular Fields** approach to three-dimensional structure–activity modelling. The
method was introduced by Zhokhova, Baskin and co-workers [1, 2] and extended with continuous
indicator fields [4] and co-fields [6], and the program follows
those papers closely enough that their published statistics can be reproduced from the same data —
`docs/benchmark.md` records that comparison set by set.

## The idea in one page

A molecule is represented not by a table of descriptors and not by values on a lattice, but by
**continuous functions of space**. Each field is a sum of Gaussians centred on the atoms,

$$
X_f(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_l w_{lf}\, \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\alpha_f}{2}\,|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_l|^2\right)
$$

where $w_{lf}$ is the weight of atom $l$ in field $f$ — its partial charge for the electrostatic
field, its Crippen logP contribution for the hydrophobic field, 1 for an indicator field of a
given atom type, or any number the file carries per atom — and $\alpha_f$ is the attenuation factor
that sets how far the field reaches.

Two molecules are compared by the **overlap integral** of their fields, which for Gaussians has a
closed form:

$$
K_f(A,B) = \int X_{fA}(\mathbf{r})\, X_{fB}(\mathbf{r})\, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{\alpha}\right)^{3/2} \sum_l \sum_m w_{lf} w_{mf}\, \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\alpha}{4}\,|\mathbf{r}_l-\mathbf{r}_m|^2\right)
$$

No grid is ever evaluated for this: the kernel is a sum over atom pairs, computed exactly. The
kernels of the individual fields are mixed with coefficients $h_f$ into one kernel, and that
kernel goes into a kernel method — ridge regression, a support vector machine, a Gaussian process.
Three consequences follow, and they are what distinguishes the approach from CoMFA:

- **Nothing is discretised.** There is no lattice spacing to choose, no alignment of grids, no
  variable selection among tens of thousands of columns, and no truncation at a cut-off distance.
- **The model is a function of space again.** A kernel ridge model predicts
  $y(X) = \sum_j a_j K(X, X_j) + b$, and because the kernel is an integral of a product, the whole
  sum can be rewritten as the overlap of the molecule's field with one function, the **co-field**
  $C_f(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_j a_j X_{fj}(\mathbf{r})$. The co-field is the program's map: it plays the role of CoMFA's
  coefficient contour, but it is the model rather than a projection of it.
- **The decomposition is exact.** Because the prediction is bilinear in the fields, it can be
  split without approximation into contributions of training molecules, of field types, of regions
  of space, or of individual atoms.

![The method in six steps, each computed from the steroid model of the chapter *Reading the model*. (1) The training molecules in one frame, one of them in red. (2) A field of that molecule, the electrostatic one, in the mean plane of the series: a Gaussian on every atom, red where the field is positive and blue where it is negative. (3) The kernel matrix: the overlap of the fields of every pair of training molecules, with the five field types mixed. (4) The fit gives one coefficient for every training molecule. (5) The co-field: the fields of all training molecules, each multiplied by its coefficient, summed. (6) The prediction of a molecule is the overlap of its field with the co-field, plus a constant; the points are the molecules that were held out of the fit. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/idea.png)

## What you can do with it

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| Build a 3D-QSAR regression model on an aligned congeneric series | Model panel, or `cmf_cli.py build` |
| Work without an alignment | topomer fields, the rotation-invariant autocorrelation kernel, or the pose-free count kernel |
| Classify actives against inactives, or screen with actives alone | binary (SVC, ν-SVC, Laplace GP) and one-class (1-SVM, centroid, k-NN, GP, kernel PCA) tasks |
| See what the model says about space | co-fields as isosurfaces, molecular fields, overlap maps, Gaussian-cube export |
| See what the model says about a molecule | training-molecule contributions, atom contributions, Shapley values and interaction indices |
| Turn a model into design instructions | pharmacophore extraction from co-field lobes, field-difference maps against a reference ligand |
| Use the protein | fetch or load a pocket, draw it behind the fields, score field complementarity, dock |
| Average over conformations | conformational ensembles (4D) and multi-instance learning |
| Map a data set | kernel GTM chemical-space maps with activity, class and density landscapes |
| Model crystals and layers | the periodic-structures window: the autocorrelation kernel for any cells, the overlap kernel with its co-field inside the cell for a series on one lattice, the sites coloured by their contributions; `cmf build-crystals` and `cmf predict` |

## How this manual is arranged

*How a prediction is made* follows one prediction from the atoms to the number, which is the
method in full. *Installation and first run* and *The application window* get you running and
name every part of the window. *Preparing the data*, *Before you model*, *Building a model* and
*Reading the model* are the working cycle: prepare the data, check what it can support, fit a
model, read it. *Classification and virtual screening*, *Conformations*, *Working without an
alignment* and *Protein pockets* are the specialised routes, and *Three series, worked through*
applies the tools to three series from start to finish. Then come the complete *Command-line
reference*, the library (*Using it as a library*), *The example data sets*, and *When something
goes wrong*, which collects the things that go wrong. The appendices hold the field
parameterisation, the file conventions, a glossary of the terms this manual uses in a particular
sense, and the bibliography. In the typeset manual every chapter and section carries a number;
the numbers are assigned when the PDF is built, so this text refers to chapters by their titles.

Conventions: *Menu → Item* names a menu command, `monospace` names a file, an option or a piece of
code. Equations are numbered by chapter when the PDF is built, (2.3) being the third equation
of chapter 2, and the text refers to them by that number. References are cited by their number in the
bibliography of Appendix D.

# How a prediction is made

This chapter follows one number — the activity predicted for one molecule — from the atoms it
starts in to the value that appears in the table. Nothing here is a sketch: every formula is the
one the program evaluates, and the worked example at the end was computed by running it.

The chain has six links:

1. each molecule becomes a set of **fields**, one per field type, each a sum of Gaussians on its
   atoms;
2. every pair of molecules gets a **field kernel** per field type, the overlap integral of those
   two fields, computed in closed form;
3. each field kernel is **normalised** and **scaled**;
4. the field kernels are **mixed** into one kernel matrix;
5. the learner turns that matrix and the activities into **dual coefficients**;
6. a new molecule is pushed through steps 1 to 4 against the training set, and its prediction is
   the **weighted sum of its kernel values** with those coefficients.

## The fields

Atom *l* of a molecule carries a weight $w_{lf}$ in field *f* — its partial charge in the
electrostatic field, its Crippen logP contribution in the hydrophobic field, an Abraham-type
increment in the hydrogen-bond fields, the Tripos van der Waals well depth in the steric field, 1
in an indicator field for atoms of that type and 0 elsewhere, or a number read from the file in a
`prop:` field. Appendix A lists them.

The field itself is the sum of Gaussians those weights define,

$$
X_f(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_l w_{lf}\,\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{b_{lf}}{2}|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_l|^2\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:field -->

with width $b_{lf} = \alpha_f$ for every field except the steric one, where it is scaled by the
atom's van der Waals radius, $b_{lf} = \alpha_f/R_{l}^2$, so that a large atom spreads its bulk
over a correspondingly larger region.

![The electrostatic field of cortisol in the mean plane of the steroid series at α = 0.3 and at α = 3, and its steric field at α = 1; red is positive, blue negative, and the skeleton of the molecule is drawn over the map. A small attenuation spreads the Gaussian of every atom over its neighbours, a large one keeps each atom's contribution to itself. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`, as are the other computed figures of this manual.](docs/figures/fields.png)

There is no grid. The field is never evaluated anywhere in order to make a prediction; it is
evaluated only when a map has to be *drawn*.

## The overlap integral

Two Gaussians have an overlap integral in closed form, so the inner product of two whole fields is
a double sum over atom pairs:

$$
K_f(A,B) = \int X_{fA}(\mathbf{r})X_{fB}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \sum_{l \in A}\ \sum_{m \in B} w_{lf}w_{mf}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{b_{lf}+b_{mf}}\right)^{3/2}\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{b_{lf}b_{mf}}{2(b_{lf}+b_{mf})}|\mathbf{r}_l-\mathbf{r}_m|^2\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:overlap -->

When every atom shares one width, $b_{lf} = b_{mf} = \alpha$, this collapses to the form the
papers quote,

$$
K_f(A,B) = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{\alpha}\right)^{3/2}\sum_l \sum_m w_{lf}w_{mf}\,\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\alpha}{4}\,|\mathbf{r}_l-\mathbf{r}_m|^2\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:kernel -->

and the general form is what the steric field needs, since its widths differ atom by atom. A unit
test checks both against numerical quadrature of the fields on a fine grid.

Two things follow immediately. The cost of a kernel is the number of atom pairs, not the number of
grid points, which is why a 300-molecule set takes seconds. And the attenuation $\alpha$ is the
only thing that decides how far apart two atoms may be and still contribute: large $\alpha$
demands close matching, small $\alpha$ lets distant atoms see each other, and in the limit
$\alpha \to 0$ the geometry drops out altogether and the kernel becomes a product of atom counts —
which is the alignment-free baseline of *Working without an alignment*.

![The overlap of the Gaussians of two atoms of the same width against the distance between them, relative to its value at distance zero, exp(−αd²/4), for three attenuations. At α = 3 two atoms 2 Å apart no longer see each other; at α = 0.3 their overlap is still 74 % of the maximum.](docs/figures/overlap.svg)

## Normalisation and scaling

Two corrections stand between the raw integrals and a usable kernel, and they do different jobs.

**Cosine normalisation** (*Normalise kernels*) divides each field kernel by the norms of the two
fields,

$$
\hat{K}_f(A,B) = \dfrac{K_f(A,B)}{\sqrt{K_f(A,A)\,K_f(B,B)}}
$$
<!-- #eq:normalised -->

so that every molecule has unit self-similarity in every field -- the normalised kernel of a
molecule with itself is 1 by construction -- and a large molecule cannot look important merely
for being large.

**Field scaling** (*Scale fields*) then multiplies each field kernel by a constant $c_f$ chosen so
that its mean diagonal over the training set is 1. It equalises the fields' contributions before
they are mixed, which matters when one field's raw magnitudes dwarf another's — an electrostatic
kernel built from partial charges and a steric kernel built from well depths are not naturally on
the same scale. With cosine normalisation on, every diagonal is already 1 and $c_f = 1$; the two
options are therefore alternatives in practice, and unticking both gives the raw-kernel convention
of the papers.

The scaling constants are computed **on the training set and then stored**: a prediction must not
rescale anything according to the molecules being predicted, or two test molecules would be scored
on different scales.

## Mixing the fields

The joint kernel is a weighted sum over field types,

$$
K(A,B) = \sum_f h_f\,c_f\,\hat{K}_f(A,B)
$$
<!-- #eq:joint -->

with the mixing coefficients $h_f$ left at 1 by default, edited by hand in the field table, chosen
by coordinate descent on the cross-validated error, or set by centred kernel alignment. Since each
normalised field kernel has unit diagonal, the joint self-kernel of any molecule is $\sum_f h_f
c_f$ — five, for the five default fields with unit coefficients, which is the 5 on the diagonal of
the matrix in the worked example below.

![The joint kernel as a sum of blocks, for the 21 training steroids in the order of their activity. Each of the first five panels is the normalised kernel of one field type over all pairs of molecules, times its mixing coefficient and its scale, on one colour scale. The last panel is their sum, the kernel the learner is given, on a scale of its own. The steric kernel is close to one everywhere, because the molecules of a congeneric series have nearly the same shape. Other blocks join the sum in the same way: a block of descriptors, or a block of water fields. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/blocks.png)

## Fitting: what is learned from the training set

Kernel ridge regression with a bias term solves one linear system:

$$
(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\,\mathbf{a} + b\,\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{a} = 0
$$
<!-- #eq:ridge -->

The outcome is one **dual coefficient** $a_j$ per training molecule and one bias $b$. The last row
of the system is the constraint $\sum_j a_j = 0$, which is what makes the bias meaningful: the
coefficients describe only *departures* from a constant level, and $b$ carries the level itself.
The ridge parameter $\lambda$ adds to the diagonal, which keeps the system solvable when molecules
are nearly identical — as they are in a congeneric series, where the off-diagonal kernel values
run above 0.97 — and controls how closely the model follows the training activities.

The other learners differ only in how $\mathbf{a}$ and $b$ are obtained, never in what they are:
ε-SVR and ν-SVR get them from a quadratic program in which most $a_j$ come out exactly zero,
C-SVC and ν-SVC the same for class labels, and the Laplace Gaussian-process classifier from the
posterior mode of a latent function. In every case the fitted model is the pair $(\mathbf{a}, b)$
over the training molecules.

## Predicting a new molecule

For a molecule the model has never seen, the program:

1. builds its fields **with the same field set** — the same α, the same charge model, the same
   parameterisation, the same atom typing;
2. computes the per-field overlap integrals between its atoms and the atoms of every training
   molecule, giving one row $K_f(x, j)$ per field;
3. normalises that row with the molecule's own self-kernels and the **stored** training
   self-kernels, and multiplies by the **stored** scales $c_f$;
4. mixes those normalised, scaled fields into one row $k_j(x)$ with the mixing coefficients
   $h_f$, which is the joint kernel $K(x, j)$ of *Mixing the fields* above;
5. returns

$$
\hat{y}(x) = \sum_j a_j\, k_j(x) + b = \mathbf{k}(x)^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{a} + b
$$
<!-- #eq:prediction -->

That is the whole prediction: a similarity-weighted combination of the training activities, where
"similarity" is the overlap of molecular fields and the weights were fixed when the model was
fitted. Molecules with $a_j = 0$ — most of them, after an SVM fit — contribute nothing, which is
why the *Contributions* tab can list the handful that actually make a given prediction.

## The same prediction, as a field

Because the kernel is an integral of a product and the prediction is linear in it, the sum over
training molecules can be moved inside the integral. Writing $s_j = 1/\sqrt{K_f(j,j)}$ for the
normalisation of training molecule *j*, define the **co-field**

$$
C_f(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_j a_j\, s_j X_{fj}(\mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:cofield -->

and the prediction becomes

$$
\hat{y}(x) = \sum_f \dfrac{h_f c_f}{\sqrt{K_f(x,x)}}\int X_{fx}(\mathbf{r})\,C_f(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} + b
$$
<!-- #eq:prediction-field -->

The model is therefore a *function of space*, one per field type, and a molecule is scored by how
much of its own field lies in the positive regions of that function and how much in the negative
ones. This is the identity that makes the pictures of *Reading the model* the model rather than an
illustration of it, and the division by the molecule's own field norm is the only thing the
normalisation adds to the picture. It also explains what co-fields cannot survive: a nonlinear
kernel layer, which is not an integral of a product, and the autocorrelation kernel source, which
has no frame to draw in.

## Why a kernel is enough: the feature space and the kernel trick

The chain above never builds a table of descriptors. This section explains why it does not need
one. The argument is the standard one of kernel methods [28]. What is special to CMF is that
every object in the argument is a function of space and can be drawn.

**The feature space.** A linear model needs a *feature vector* for every molecule: a list of
numbers that describes it. In CoMFA [9] the feature vector is the list of the field values at
the nodes of a grid. In CMF the feature vector of a molecule is the field itself. The rule that
gives the feature vector is called the *feature map* and is written $\Phi$:

$$
\Phi(x) \;=\; X_x(\mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:feature-map -->

A field has a value at every point of space, so this vector has infinitely many components, one
for each point. The set of all such vectors is the *feature space*. The feature space has an
inner product, which is the integral of the product of two fields. For two molecules it is the
overlap integral of Eq. (#eq:overlap):

$$
\langle \Phi(A),\, \Phi(B) \rangle \;=\; \int X_A(\mathbf{r})\, X_B(\mathbf{r})\, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \;=\; K(A,B)
$$
<!-- #eq:inner-product -->

A *kernel* is, by definition, a function of two objects that is equal to the inner product of
their feature vectors.

**A linear model in the feature space.** A linear model has a *weight vector* $w$, which is an
element of the feature space, and a bias $b$. Its prediction is the inner product of the weight
vector with the feature vector of the molecule, plus the bias:

$$
\hat{y}(x) \;=\; \langle w,\, \Phi(x) \rangle + b
$$
<!-- #eq:linear-model -->

Kernel ridge regression chooses $w$ and $b$ so that the sum of the squared errors on the
training set plus a penalty on the length of the weight vector is as small as possible:

$$
\min_{w,\,b}\;\; \sum_i\, \left( y_i - \hat{y}(x_i) \right)^2 \;+\; \lambda\, \|w\|^2
$$
<!-- #eq:ridge-objective -->

**The kernel trick.** The weight vector that minimises Eq. (#eq:ridge-objective) is always a
weighted sum of the feature vectors of the training molecules. This statement is the
representer theorem [29]:

$$
w \;=\; \sum_j\, a_j\, \Phi(x_j)
$$
<!-- #eq:representer -->

Two things follow. With Eq. (#eq:representer) inside Eq. (#eq:linear-model), the prediction is
the sum of $a_j$ times the inner product of training molecule *j* with the new molecule, plus
the bias. This is Eq. (#eq:prediction). With Eq. (#eq:representer) inside
Eq. (#eq:ridge-objective), the minimisation becomes the linear system of Eq. (#eq:ridge). In
both results the feature vectors occur only inside inner products, and every inner product is a
kernel value.

So the program never needs a feature vector. It needs the kernel values, and the kernel has a
closed form. A problem in a space of infinitely many dimensions becomes a linear system with
one unknown per training molecule. This replacement of feature vectors by kernel values is
called the *kernel trick*. The coefficients $a_j$ are called *dual* coefficients, because they
belong to the training molecules and not to the features. The weight vector $w$ is the *primal*
form of the same model.

**What is special to CMF.** For most kernels the feature space is abstract. A Gaussian kernel
on a table of descriptors has a feature space that cannot be looked at, and its weight vector
is known only through the coefficients $a_j$. In CMF the feature space consists of functions on
ordinary three-dimensional space. The weight vector of Eq. (#eq:representer) is then such a
function too, and it is the co-field of Eq. (#eq:cofield). The co-field is therefore not a
picture that is added to a fitted model. It is the weight vector of a linear model, as the
coefficient map of a CoMFA model is, but it is exact and it needs no grid.

![The feature space of the overlap kernel, on the training steroids with a kernel ridge model at α = 1. Top left: a point of the feature space is the field of a molecule. The map is the electrostatic field of the most active steroid in the mean plane of the series; its other four fields are the rest of the same point. Bottom left: a direction in the feature space is a field too. The map is the electrostatic co-field, which is the weight vector of the model. Right: a plane through the feature space, with every training molecule as a point coloured by its observed activity. The horizontal axis is the projection of the molecule on the direction of the co-field, and the upper axis converts it to the prediction. The vertical axis is the direction across it in which the training molecules spread most. The circled point is the molecule of the left panels, and the dashed line is its projection. All coordinates of the right panel are computed from the kernel matrix alone, without a feature vector. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/featurespace.png)

**Several fields, normalisation and scaling.** The joint kernel of Eq. (#eq:joint) is an inner
product too. Its feature vector is the list of the $F$ fields of the molecule, each divided by
its own length and multiplied by the square root of its mixing coefficient and of its scale:

$$
\Phi(x) \;=\; \left( \sqrt{h_f c_f}\;\dfrac{X_{fx}(\mathbf{r})}{\sqrt{K_f(x,x)}} \right)_{f\,=\,1,\ldots,F}
$$
<!-- #eq:joint-feature -->

Cosine normalisation gives every molecule the same length in each field, so a normalised kernel
value is the cosine of the angle between two feature vectors. The part of the weight vector
that belongs to field *f* is the co-field $C_f$ times the same square root, and the squared
length of the weight vector is

$$
\|w\|^2 \;=\; \sum_f\, h_f c_f \int\, C_f(\mathbf{r})^2\, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \;=\; \mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{K}\, \mathbf{a}
$$
<!-- #eq:weight-length -->

This gives the ridge parameter a direct meaning. The penalty of Eq. (#eq:ridge-objective) is
$\lambda$ times the integral of the squared co-fields, so a larger $\lambda$ gives co-fields of
smaller amplitude.

**What a function must satisfy to be a kernel.** Not every measure of similarity is an inner
product. A function of two molecules is a kernel exactly when it is symmetric and *positive
semidefinite*: for any set of molecules and any real numbers $c_i$,

$$
\sum_i\, \sum_j\, c_i\, c_j\, K(x_i, x_j) \;=\; \|u\|^2 \;\geq\; 0, \qquad u \;=\; \sum_i\, c_i\, \Phi(x_i)
$$
<!-- #eq:positive-semidefinite -->

The sum is the squared length of a vector of the feature space, and a squared length cannot be
negative. For the overlap kernel it is the integral of a squared field. The
property has practical consequences. It makes the system of Eq. (#eq:ridge) have exactly one
solution for every $\lambda > 0$, and it makes the quadratic programs of the support-vector
learners convex, so that they have one optimum. The property is kept by every operation of
this chapter: the division by the lengths, the multiplication by a positive constant, and the
sum with weights that are not negative. A negative mixing coefficient would break it. The
Gaussian and the arc-cosine layer of *Nonlinear kernel layers and multiple kernel learning*
keep the property as well. But the feature space of a kernel with such a layer is no longer a
space of functions on three-dimensional space, and this is why a model with a layer has no
single co-field.

**Distances.** The feature space has distances as well as angles, and they also need only
kernel values:

$$
d^2(A,B) \;=\; \| \Phi(A) - \Phi(B) \|^2 \;=\; K(A,A) - 2K(A,B) + K(B,B)
$$
<!-- #eq:feature-distance -->

Later chapters work in this space directly. The applicability domain of *Where does the model
apply?* uses the cosine of the angle between a molecule and its nearest training molecules. The Gaussian
layer is a function of the distance of Eq. (#eq:feature-distance). The maps of *Chemical space
maps* project the space on a plane, and the decoder of pseudo-atoms minimises a distance in it.
Those chapters call the space the *field Hilbert space*. The literature has a second name for
the same structure, seen from the side of the predictions. The functions of a molecule that
have the form of Eq. (#eq:prediction) without the bias, with the squared norm of
Eq. (#eq:weight-length), form the *reproducing kernel Hilbert space* (RKHS) of the kernel [30].
Every such function belongs to one weight vector and has the same length as it.

**The readings of the other kernels.** The same argument holds for every kernel of this
program. What changes is the feature vector, and with it the form in which the weight vector
can be read:

| kernel | feature vector of a sample | weight vector of the model |
|---|---|---|
| overlap kernel of fields | the fields, functions of space | the co-fields, *Reading the model* |
| invariant kernels: autocorrelation, surface, periodic, reciprocal | a finite list of channels | the co-pattern, *The co-pattern as a chart* |
| spectrum kernel | the broadened spectrum, a function on a line | the co-spectrum, *A spectrum as a one-dimensional field* |
| any of these under a Gaussian or arc-cosine layer | not available in closed form | none for the whole model; a local co-field per molecule |

When the feature vector is a finite list, the model can also be solved in the primal form, for
the weight vector directly. The cost then grows with the number of features and not with the
square of the number of samples. The local kernels of *Working without an alignment* offer this
as the option `--primal`.

## A worked example

Four molecules from `examples/benzamides_synthetic.sdf` as the training set, the five default
fields, α = 0.5, cosine normalisation, λ = 0.1, and the fifth molecule as the one to predict. The
numbers below are the program's own, printed from the objects it fits.

![The parent of the worked example, N-phenylbenzamide, with the positions the series substitutes marked as the molecule names of the file count them: 3 and 4 on the ring of the acid, 3' and 4' on the ring of the amine. The names in the tables below are the substituents at those positions, so 4'Cl is a chlorine para to the nitrogen and 4F a fluorine para to the carbonyl group.](docs/figures/parent.svg)

The joint kernel of the training set, the sum of the five normalised field kernels, so the diagonal is 5:

```
            parent     4F      4'F     4Cl          y
parent      5.0000  2.8362  3.2195  2.5368       5.585
4F          2.8362  5.0000  2.3310  3.9647       5.230
4'F         3.2195  2.3310  5.0000  2.8882       6.471
4Cl         2.5368  3.9647  2.8882  5.0000       5.355
```

Solving the bordered system gives

```
a = [-0.1358, -0.0581, +0.3487, -0.1549]      sum(a) = 0      b = 5.7124
```

The test molecule 4'Cl is then compared with each training molecule, field by field:

```
                      parent      4F      4'F     4Cl
electrostatic         0.0878  0.6028  0.1009  0.3915
steric                0.9793  0.9824  0.9863  0.9579
hydrophobic           0.8936  0.9412  0.9443  0.8437
H-bond acceptor       0.2600  0.9895  0.1927  0.6539
H-bond donor          0.5815  1.0000  0.4424  0.7379
                      ------  ------  ------  ------
k(x)  (their sum)     2.8022  4.5159  2.6667  3.5849
```

and the prediction is that row times the coefficients, plus the bias:

```
y(x) = 2.8022(-0.1358) + 4.5159(-0.0581) + 2.6667(0.3487) + 3.5849(-0.1549) + 5.7124
     = 5.4444
```

which is exactly what *Pred (test)* shows for that molecule. Two things can be checked directly in this
example rather than taken on trust. The steric and hydrophobic rows are nearly constant across
the training set — these molecules differ by one halogen — so almost all the discrimination comes
from the electrostatic and hydrogen-bond fields, which is visible in the spread of their rows.
And the prediction, 5.44 against an observed 7.21, is poor, because four training molecules and no
hyper-parameter search is not a model: the arithmetic is the lesson here, not the accuracy.

## What changes for the other tasks

| Model | What the prediction is |
|---|---|
| Kernel ridge | $\hat{y} = \mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{a} + b$, as above |
| Gaussian process | the same mean, plus the variance $\sigma^2(x) = K(x,x) - \mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{T}}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}$, which the *Align by prediction confidence* tool minimises |
| ε-SVR, ν-SVR | the same formula; most $a_j$ are zero |
| C-SVC, ν-SVC | the same formula, read as a decision value: its sign is the class, its magnitude the margin |
| Laplace GP classifier | the same formula gives the latent mean, which is squashed to a probability and averaged over the latent variance |
| Kernel Fisher discriminant | the same formula gives the position along the discriminant direction, in units of the within-class spread; the bias is the threshold chosen out of fold, and a logistic map turns the score into a probability |
| Kernel logistic regression | the same formula gives the latent function, and the probability is the likelihood at it, $1/(1+e^{-f})$, with no variance averaged in; the boundary is $f = 0$, which is $p = 0.5$ |
| One-class methods | a score built from the same kernel row, but also from the molecule's own self-kernel: distance to the centroid, to the k-th nearest active, to the principal subspace, or the 1-SVM decision value |
| Nonlinear kernel layer | the joint kernel is passed through $\exp(-\gamma d^2)$ or an arc-cosine function first; the prediction formula is unchanged, the co-field identity is lost; the derivative of the prediction at one molecule is still a field, the local co-field |
| Autocorrelation source | the kernel row comes from the rotation-invariant distance profiles instead of the overlap integrals; everything downstream is identical |
| Surface source | for molecules over a surface at $z = 0$: the in-plane distance profiles resolved by the heights of both atoms, invariant in the plane and to rotation about the normal only; heights and tilts are kept, no in-plane alignment is needed (command line: `--kernel surface --surface-z ZMIN ZMAX ZSTEP`) |
| Periodic source | for crystals: the distance profiles summed over the neighbour list of the cell with its images, per atom, background removed, cutoff tapered; invariant to the choice of cell, origin and orientation (command line: `build-crystals`). For layers and chains the same, with the background per unit area or repeat length and no pair across the vacuum (`--pbc ab`); a layer can be resolved by the heights of both atoms above its mean plane (`--heights`) |
| Two endpoints | the same formula once per endpoint, with coefficients tied through a task correlation; the difference of the two coefficient vectors gives the selectivity co-field |

## What has to match between fitting and predicting

Because the kernel row is computed against the stored training atoms with the stored constants, a
prediction is only meaningful if the new molecule was prepared the way the training molecules
were. The saved `.cmf` model therefore carries the field set, the α values, the charge model, the
parameterisation, the normalisation and scaling flags, the mixing coefficients, the training
atoms and the coefficients — everything in steps 1 to 5 — and reuses them. It also carries a
record of how the training molecules were prepared: the version of the program that wrote it,
the date, how many molecules, where their partial charges came from (the file, or computed),
whether they carried explicit hydrogens, and the box their atoms occupy. Before any prediction
the program compares the new molecules with that record and reports what does not match:

- **The chemistry behind the weights.** Charges read from a file for the training set and
  Gasteiger charges for the new molecules are two different electrostatic fields under one
  name. A model fitted on file charges therefore **refuses** a molecule that carries none, rather
  than falling back to Gasteiger charges silently; `cmf_cli.py predict --allow-mismatch`
  overrides the refusal, and the application asks. Supply the charges (a MOL2 charge column or a
  `partial_charge` atom property) or build the model with computed charges.
- **Explicit hydrogens.** The donor field sits on the hydrogens and the steric field counts
  them, so a set with hydrogens and a set without are two different sets of fields. A mismatch
  is a **warning**.
- **The frame.** The overlap integral is not invariant to rotation or translation, so a molecule
  predicted in a different frame from the training set scores low on every field and is predicted
  towards the mean. A molecule whose centroid lies more than 4 Å outside the box of the training
  atoms is reported as a **warning**.
- **The pose inside the frame.** A molecule can be in the right place and still be turned the
  wrong way, and a rotation about its own centre moves no centroid, so the box test above sees
  nothing. The check that does see it compares the molecule with the *shape* the training set
  occupies rather than with its box: the share of its atoms that come within 1.5 Å of some
  training atom, against the share this training set asks of its own molecules — the fifth
  percentile of the same quantity measured on each training molecule against the others, less a
  small slack, so that a series of close analogues gets a strict rule, exactly as the applicability domain's
  threshold does. Measured on the eight Sutherland sets [17], turning every held-out molecule 90° about
  its own centre is caught **95 % of the time, for a false-positive rate of 2.6 %** on the
  molecules left as they were. If the new molecules are not in the frame, align them (*Preparing
  the data*) or use a frame-free kernel source (*Working without an alignment*).
- **Per-atom property fields** that are zero on a molecule, because it carries no value of that
  property, are a warning; a file written by another version of the program, or by a version
  that recorded no provenance, is a note.

The findings appear in the log of the application and on the console of the command-line tool,
each marked `[refuse]`, `[warn]` or `[note]`. A model file written by a newer version of the
program than the one reading it is not opened.

# Installation and first run

## Where the program lives

The repository is [github.com/igbaskin/cmf-qsar](https://github.com/igbaskin/cmf-qsar) — private,
so the link asks for a GitHub account with access:

```
git clone https://github.com/igbaskin/cmf-qsar.git
cd cmf-qsar
```

Everything this manual describes is in that checkout: the `cmfqsar` package with the
command-line tool inside it (`cmfqsar/cli.py`), the two launchers (`cmf_app.py`, `cmf_cli.py`),
the example data under `examples/`, the benchmark scripts under `benchmarks/` with their recorded
results, the tests, and this manual with the script that typesets it.

## Requirements

Python 3.10 or newer. The package is declared in `pyproject.toml`, so from the checkout

```
pip install -e .[gui]
```

installs the library with RDKit (chemistry), scikit-image (marching cubes for the isosurfaces),
scikit-learn (the SVM solvers), NumPy, SciPy and joblib, and with the `gui` extra PySide6 (the
interface) and pyqtgraph with PyOpenGL (the 3D view); it also puts the commands `cmf-app` and
`cmf` on the path. The library alone, `pip install -e .`, needs no Qt. The program is pure Python
and needs no compilation step; it has been used on Windows, Linux and macOS.

Further extras, only needed for particular work:

- `docs` — reportlab and matplotlib (which supplies the DejaVu fonts) to typeset this manual;
- `dev` — pytest, for the test suite;
- `examples` — `dimorphite_dl`, protonation states when importing SMILES for a given pH;
- a local ORCA or VASP installation if you intend to compute per-atom quantum properties to use as
  fields (see *Preparing the data* and appendix A); these are programs, not packages.
- a local xtb installation to build and optimise solvation complexes (`cmfqsar/solvation.py`,
  *The ion with its shell as the molecule*). `cmfqsar/xtb.py` finds it by the `XTB_EXE`
  environment variable, on the path, or at its built-in default; it is also a program and not a
  package.

`pip install -r requirements.txt` installs the working checkout, `.[gui,docs,dev]`.
`requirements-lock.txt` pins the exact versions the benchmark tables were produced with:
`pip install -r requirements-lock.txt` and then `pip install --no-deps -e .` reproduces that
environment. `CITATION.cff` says how to cite the software and the papers.

## Starting the application

```
cmf-app
```

or `python cmf_app.py` from the checkout, which takes the same arguments; or directly with a data set,
which skips two dialogs:

```
cmf-app examples/benzamides_synthetic.sdf --activity pActivity --test-fraction 0.25
```

The command-line tool is `cmf` once installed and `python cmf_cli.py` from the checkout; the
rest of this manual writes the latter, and the two are the same program.

If the 3D view stays black, the OpenGL driver is the usual cause; see *When something goes wrong*.

## A first model in five minutes

1. *File → Open training set…* and choose `examples/benzamides_synthetic.sdf`. It holds 109
   aligned N-phenylbenzamides with a synthetic activity, so you know the answer the model should
   find. Pick `pActivity` as the activity property.
2. In the data-set table, press *Random split* and set a quarter of the molecules aside as a test
   set.
3. In the Model panel leave the five physico-chemical fields ticked, leave the method at kernel
   ridge regression, and press **Build model**.
4. Read the *Statistics* tab: q² should be about 0.87 and R²pred about 0.84 — the noise ceiling of
   that set is 0.94, so the model has recovered nearly all of the signal that was put into it.
5. Press **Compute co-field**, choose *Electrostatic*, and move the *iso level* slider. The red and
   blue lobes that appear are the pseudo-receptor zones the activity was generated from.

Nothing in that sequence is specific to the example: it is the working cycle of the program.

# The application window

![The HIF-2α series of the Merck free-energy benchmark, 38 ligands: a kernel ridge model with q² = 0.62, its electrostatic co-field drawn as ± isosurfaces, and the binding site of the reference crystal structure, which the data set brings with it and which needs no superposition.](docs/screenshot.png)

![The parts of the main window, marked on the screenshot above. The sections of this chapter describe them in turn: the Data set panel (2), the Model panel (6), the 3D view (4) with its controls (3), the Results panel (5) and the menus (1). The status line (7) says what the last action did. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/window.png)

The window is a 3D view with three dockable panels around it. The **3D view** and its control strip
occupy the centre and are always there; the **Data set** panel docks on the left, the **Model**
panel on the right inside a scroll area, and the **Results** panel across the bottom under the
view. All three are ordinary dock widgets: drag one by its title bar to another edge, drop it on
another to stack them as tabs, or pull it off entirely to float it on a second monitor. The layout
is remembered between sessions, and *View → Restore default layout* puts it back when an
experiment goes wrong.

At the bottom, the **status bar** shows what the program is doing, with a progress bar on the right
during a long task. Every long task — a grid search, a co-field, an alignment, a conformer
generation — runs in a worker thread, so the window stays responsive and the *Cancel* button in the
model panel stops the work rather than the application.

## The Data set panel

Three buttons at the top load structures: **Open training set…**, **Add test set…** and **Add
decoys…**, the same actions as the first three entries of the *File* menu. Beside them the
*Activity* selector names the SD property the activities are read from; changing it re-reads the
column without reloading the file.

The table has one row per molecule and seven columns:

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| Show | the tick that decides whether this molecule is drawn in the 3D view |
| Name | the molecule's title from the file |
| Activity | the experimental value, from the chosen property |
| Set | train, test or decoy |
| Pred (fit) | the model's prediction for the molecule it was fitted on |
| Pred (CV) | its prediction when it was in the held-out fold |
| Pred (test) | its prediction as a test molecule |
| AD | its similarity to the training set, when the applicability domain was computed |

An eighth column, **Chemotype**, appears once the chemotypes have been found. Rows are selected
singly or in blocks, and the selection drives everything else: the co-field overlap, the atom
contributions, the Shapley decomposition and the complementarity numbers all refer to the molecule
currently selected.

**Sorting.** Clicking a column header sorts by it, a second click reverses the order, and a third
restores the order of the file. Molecules with no value in that column are always placed at the bottom,
whichever direction is in force, so an unpredicted molecule never hides among the predictions. The
*Show* ticks, the selection and the 3D view follow the molecule and not the row, so sorting never
disturbs what is on screen.

**Splitting.** *Random split* assigns a fraction to the test set; the *→ train* and *→ test*
buttons move the selected rows by hand. A `subset`, `set` or `split` tag in the file is honoured on
loading, which is how the published splits of the example sets arrive without any clicking.

**Showing.** *Show all*, *Show none* and *Show selected only* control the view in bulk. With one
molecule shown, the maps in the viewer refer to it; with all of them shown, the co-field sits in
the middle of the series as it should.

A line under the table reports the state of the data set — how many molecules, how many in each
subset, which activity property — and a note in brackets records any transformation that has been
applied, for instance *[topomer substituents of …]*, so that a changed data set never passes for
the original.

## The Model panel

Everything that defines a model, in the order one normally works down it. The panel scrolls; on a
small screen nothing is hidden, it is merely below.

**Molecular fields.** Five tick boxes for the physico-chemical fields — Electrostatic, Steric,
Hydrophobic, H-bond acceptor, H-bond donor — then *Continuous indicator fields (CIF)* with its
typing scheme (`sybyl`, `element`, `element+aromatic`) and the minimum number of training molecules
an atom type must occur in to be given a field. Below them, *Per-atom property fields* lists the
per-atom properties the loaded file carries, each of which can be turned into a field of its own.

*Partial charges* chooses between Gasteiger, MMFF94 and the charges stored in the file;
*Increments* chooses the parameterisation (`rdkit`, `tripos`, `tripos-legacy`). Two tick boxes set
the kernel conventions: *Normalise kernels* for cosine-normalised field kernels, *Scale fields* to
rescale every field kernel to unit mean diagonal before mixing — untick it for the raw-kernel
convention of the papers.

*Conformations* switches between one conformation per molecule and an ensemble, with the weighting
(uniform or Boltzmann), kT, a cap on the number of conformations, and the multi-instance settings
(the softness β, and *one conformation* for the hard selection). A label beside them reports how
many conformations the data set currently holds.

A table at the foot of the group lists the fields that will actually be built, with the columns
**Use**, **Field**, **alpha**, **h (mix)** and **scale**: per-field attenuation and mixing
coefficients are editable there, which is how a field is given more or less weight than the others
without leaving the panel.

**Learning method and hyper-parameters.** A form, row by row:

| Row | What it sets |
|---|---|
| Task | regression, binary classification, or one-class (virtual screening) |
| Classes | for classification: a threshold on the activity, with *active below* for data where small is potent, or a class property from the file |
| Method | the learner; the list changes with the task — KRR, GP, ε-SVR, ν-SVR for regression; C-SVC, ν-SVC, Laplace GP for classification; 1-SVM, centroid, k-NN, one-class GP and kernel PCA for one-class work |
| Nonlinear kernel | none (the linear CMF kernel), a Gaussian layer, or one or two arc-cosine layers |
| Mixing coeff. h | fixed from the table, optimised by coordinate descent, or set by centred kernel alignment |
| Attenuation α | a single value, or the grid below |
| Kernel from | overlap integrals of the fields, which need one frame; the rotation-invariant autocorrelation, which does not; or the surface autocorrelation for poses over a surface at $z = 0$, which needs only the normal (command line) |
| α grid, λ grid, C grid, ε/ν grids | the search ranges, as comma-separated lists |
| Cross-validation | the number of folds and the shuffling seed |
| External CV | the outer folds and the number of repeats for the nested procedure |
| Probe fields | GRID-like fields for the water, methyl, carbonyl, amine and cation probes, and the number of Gaussians per atom |
| Computed descriptors | molecular weight, clogP, TPSA and rotatable bonds, computed by RDKit; all off by default |
| Descriptors (per molecule) | which numeric molecule properties enter as non-field descriptors, and the block's mixing coefficient |
| Validation | *shuffles* for y-randomisation, *bootstrap* for confidence intervals, and the *applicability domain* tick — all three off by default, all three run as part of **Build model** rather than from a button of their own |

Four buttons close the panel: **Build model** runs the grid search, the final fit, the internal
cross-validation and the test prediction; **External CV** runs the nested procedure and reports
q²ex; **Predict test set** applies the current model to the test molecules; **Cancel** stops
whatever is running.

## The 3D view

The view itself is an OpenGL scene: drag to orbit, the wheel to zoom, middle-drag (or shift-drag)
to pan. *Reset view* reframes the whole scene, *Tools → Center view on current molecule* reframes
the selected one, and *File → Save 3D view as image…* writes what you see to PNG.

The control strip above the view is five rows, and everything on it redraws immediately:

- **Molecules.** Drawing style (ball & stick, sticks, lines, space fill), *H atoms*, *Labels*
  (none, element + number, atom type, partial charge), *dark background*, *Reset view*.
- **Maps.** *Field type* chooses which field the maps refer to; **Compute co-field** evaluates the
  co-fields on a grid around the training set; then the maps themselves — *co-field C(r)*,
  *molecular field X(r)*, *overlap C·X*, *Shapley field Φ(r)*, *atom contributions*, *difference
  map*, *pharmacophore*,
  *vector co-field (arrows)* — each with its own solid-or-mesh style where that applies. After a
  two-endpoint fit an *Endpoint* box joins the row and chooses whose co-field the maps show:
  either endpoint, or their difference, the selectivity co-field.
- **Levels.** *iso level*, the isosurface threshold as a percentage of the largest absolute value
  rather than an absolute number, so the surfaces stay comparable when the field changes; and
  *opacity*.
- **Protein site.** *protein site* draws the residues within the chosen distance of the molecules
  on screen, as lines or sticks, with *H*, *waters* and residue labels optional, and
  *complementarity surface* paints the molecule's surface by how well it complements the pocket.
- **Surface slab.** *surface slab* draws a patch of a loaded or built metal surface behind the
  molecules, as balls or dots, with the *patch* radius, the *frame axes* of the surface frame and
  the *surface sites* of the top layer. The section *A metal surface behind the molecules* is
  about this row.

Co-field colours are fixed, so that maps made in different sessions can be compared at a glance:

| Field | Positive lobe | Negative lobe |
|---|---|---|
| Electrostatic | red | blue |
| Steric | green | yellow |
| Hydrophobic | orange | light blue |
| H-bond acceptor | magenta | dark red |
| H-bond donor | cyan | purple |
| Indicator field | red: an atom of that type is favoured here | blue: it is disfavoured here |

## The Results panel

Fourteen tabs, each filled by the work that produces it:

| Tab | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Statistics | every figure of merit, for the fit, the cross-validation, the test set and the external CV; the y-randomisation, bootstrap and applicability-domain results follow at the bottom, under a *Validation* heading, when they were asked for |
| Scatter plot | observed against predicted, by subset, with the molecule under the cursor named |
| ROC | the receiver-operating curves of a classification model, per subset |
| Scores | the ranked decision values or calibrated probabilities: rank, molecule, score, set, class |
| Enrichment | the enrichment curve against a decoy set, with EF at 0.5, 1, 5 and 10 %, BEDROC and RIE |
| Map | the kernel-GTM chemical-space map, with the activity, class and density landscapes, and a control for how the molecules themselves are drawn over it |
| Hyper-parameter search | the whole grid — α, the other parameters, RMSEcv and q² — so that an optimum at the edge of the grid is visible rather than hidden |
| Contributions | two tables for the selected molecule: the training molecules that make its prediction, with `a_j` and `a_j K(X, X_j)`, and its own atoms with their contributions |
| Co-pattern | the reading of a kernel that has no co-field: the channel weight against distance, for one pair of field types at a time. See *The co-pattern as a chart* |
| Surface poses | the height and the tilt of every molecule in the surface frame, filled by *Tools → Pose the molecules in the surface frame* |
| Shapley | the Shapley decomposition, over atoms, substituents of the common scaffold or field types, with second-order interactions |
| Complementarity | the field complementarity of the molecules and of the co-field with the pocket, by sign agreement, cosine or correlation |
| Chemotypes | the Murcko scaffolds found in the set, their sizes, and the leave-one-chemotype-out result beside the alignment-free baseline |
| Log | everything the program did, with timings and warnings — including the names of the molecules that fell outside the applicability domain — the first place to look when a result surprises you |

## The menus

**File** — *Open training set…* (Ctrl+O), *Add test set…*, *Add decoys (background set)…*, *Import
activities from CSV…*; *Crystals and other periodic structures…*, which opens the window of the
section below; *Load protein structure (PDB/mmCIF)…*, *Fetch protein from the PDB…*,
*Forget protein structure*; *Load a surface slab (POSCAR/CIF/XYZ)…*, *Build a bcc(110) surface
slab…*, *Forget the surface slab*; *Open project…* (Ctrl+Shift+O), *Save project* (Ctrl+Shift+S), *Save
project as…*; *Load model…* (Ctrl+L), *Save model…* (Ctrl+S); *Export predictions
(CSV)…*, *Export aligned data set (SDF)…*, *Export current co-field (Gaussian cube)…*, *Export
current Shapley field (Gaussian cube)…*, *Save 3D view as image…*; *Quit* (Ctrl+Q).

**View** — show or hide each panel, *Results panel spans full width* for when the tables and plots
matter more than the view, and *Restore default layout*.

**Tools** — *Generate conformations (4D)…*; *Dock into the pocket…*; *Align data set to
reference…*; *Pose the molecules in the surface frame…*; *Align by prediction confidence (GP variance)…* and its cross-validated form for the
training set; *Replace molecules by their topomer substituents…*; *Field difference from a
reference molecule…*; *Extract pharmacophore from the co-field…*; *Model several endpoints (selectivity co-field)…*;
*Chemical space map…*;
*Align decoys to the training set…*; *Unalign (randomise poses)…*; *Undo last alignment step*
(Ctrl+Z); *Compare two models on these molecules…*; *Center view on current
molecule*; *Quantum-chemical properties with ORCA…* and *Save the data set with its
properties (SDF)…*; and the submenu *Heterogeneous sets (several chemotypes)* with its four numbered steps.

**Help** — *About CMF 3D-QSAR / method summary*, which names the equations of the papers that each
part of the program implements.

Every *Tools* entry opens a dialog that states what it is about to do and on which molecules, and
each one runs in the background with the progress bar and the *Cancel* button live.

## Crystals and other periodic structures

Everything the program does with crystals — the periodic autocorrelation kernel, the periodic
overlap kernel with its co-field inside the cell, the split of a prediction over the sites —
lived on the command line and in the library until version 1.0. *File → Crystals and other
periodic structures…* opens a window of its own for that side of the program. It is a window
and not a mode of the main one, because a crystal is not a molecule with a box around it: it has
a lattice instead of a pose, no bond table, and half of what its kernel sees lies outside the
cell, in the periodic images. The two windows do not share a data set.

**Opening a set.** *File → Open a folder of structures…* reads every structure file in a folder
(CIF, POSCAR or CONTCAR, extended XYZ, ASE JSON, and the other formats ASE reads), one
structure per file, named after its file; this is how a set downloaded from a database arrives.
*Open one structure file…* reads a file that holds one structure or many, as `examples/sac/`
and `examples/hops/` do. Both routes read through ASE, so any format ASE reads is accepted. A
folder is searched for the file endings `.cif`, `.vasp`, `.poscar`, `.contcar`, `.extxyz`,
`.xyz`, `.json` (an ASE database), `.traj` (an ASE trajectory), `.cell` (CASTEP), `.res`
(SHELX), `.xsf` (XCrySDen) and `.pwo` (Quantum ESPRESSO output), and for files named `POSCAR`
or `CONTCAR`, which VASP writes without an ending; a file with any other ending is left
alone, so notes and tables may sit beside the structures. The file dialog lists the common
endings; a file of another ASE format is opened through *All files*. A CIF with partly
occupied sites is read with its occupancies, as the section on partial occupancy describes. The *Structures* panel lists what came back with the
measured value, the subset and the prediction of each cell, and the line under it says how many
atoms the cells have.

**The measured values.** *File → Read the measured values from a CSV…* takes a table whose first
column holds the structure names as the panel shows them. A plain `name,value` file needs no
further choice; a prepared table with one column per property asks which column is the property.
A per-structure property stored in the file itself (the `info` key of an extended-XYZ file) is
read with `--target KEY` on the command line and is not offered in the window.

**What the view draws.** The cell is drawn as the twelve edges of its box, with the first,
second and third lattice vectors in red, green and blue. Its atoms are spheres coloured by
element, with the colours the molecular view uses for the organic elements and the standard Jmol
colours for the rest. Outside the box, *Periodic images* draws every copy of the cell's atoms
within the radius beside it, as dots: these are the atoms the periodic kernel sums over, and
seeing them is how one checks that the cutoff reaches as far as it should. Once a model is
fitted the radius is set to the kernel's own cutoff — the one of the neighbour list for the
autocorrelation, the one the overlap kernel's Gaussians reach to for the overlap — and the line
under the view says so. The legend also names the cell: its atoms, its lattice lengths, and in
how many directions it is periodic. *Site numbers* writes the index and element of every site
beside it, which is how a site in the Reading table is found in the picture.

![The window for crystals with the thirteen solid electrolytes of `examples/hops/disordered` and a periodic-autocorrelation model fitted to the number of lithium sites per cubic nanometre, the target `benchmarks/run_cell_view.py` uses. On screen is the largest cell, the cubic garnet Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 with 256 atoms: the cell box with its lattice vectors, the atoms as spheres coloured by element, the periodic images out to the kernel's cutoff as dots, and over every site the sphere of its contribution to the prediction, red where the site adds to it and blue where it subtracts. The line under the view names the cell and says that the contributions sum to the prediction. Taken by `docs/make_screenshot.py --what crystal`.](docs/figures/crystal_window.png)

The images are cheap. `benchmarks/results/cell_view/table.md` measures the window on the three
example sets: a 256-atom cell of the garnet Li$_{6.5}$La$_3$Zr$_{1.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$O$_{12}$ has
6,581 image atoms within 14.9 Å, expanded in 6 ms and drawn, with the cell and its atoms, in
11 ms; the 112- to 128-atom supercells of the three solid electrolytes of the hop section take
10 to 13 ms; a 127-atom sheet of the single-atom catalysts, periodic in two directions, has
836 images and draws in 3 ms. The thirteen CIF files of `examples/hops/disordered/` are read
in half a second.

**How the atoms are drawn, and the bonds.** The *Atoms* box offers four representations. *balls*
is one sphere per atom, coloured by element and sized by its covalent radius, and *dots* is one
point per atom, which stays fast for a cell of thousands. Those two show the atoms alone, which
is the honest picture of a file that states where the atoms are and nothing about which of them
are bonded. *ball and stick* and *sticks* add the bonds.

The bonds are perceived from the distances, because no CIF or extended-XYZ file carries a bond
table: a pair is bonded when its distance is below the sum of the two covalent radii plus
0.45 Å, which is the rule the protein reader already applies, with no stick drawn longer than
2.4 Å. Two things make it work for a periodic structure. The pairs are taken over the cell **and
its periodic images**, so a ring that the file leaves split across the cell boundary is drawn as
a ring, with the sticks leaving the box and the image atoms they end on drawn beside them; a bond
that crosses the boundary is drawn from both of its ends, because both halves of it are inside
the box, and the legend states the number of bonds and the number of sticks apart. And **a metal
atom gets no bonds**: a distance rule gives every atom of a close-packed metal about twelve
neighbours, and twelve sticks per atom hide the structure they are meant to show. So a slab stays
spheres and the organic molecule adsorbed on it gets its bonds, which is the one picture an
adsorbate study cannot do without. A cell whose atoms get no bonds at all falls back to *balls*
and the legend says why rather than showing an empty box.

This perception is **for drawing only**. No bond order is assigned, no molecule is sanitised and
no charge is perceived from it; a stick on screen never reaches a field, a kernel or a
prediction. Turning a periodic structure into a molecule is a different job (plan item M8) and
this is not it.

**What a metal gets instead: coordination polyhedra.** *Coordination polyhedra* draws the first
coordination shell of every metal atom as a translucent polyhedron. The shell is found without
any chemistry: the nearest neighbour of the atom sets a distance, and every neighbour within
1.3 times that distance is a vertex, with the non-metal neighbours preferred where the atom has
any, so the vertices of an ionic structure are its anions. Neighbours are taken over the periodic
images, so a polyhedron at the edge of the cell is whole. A flat shell -- square-planar,
trigonal-planar -- has no volume, so it is drawn as a polygon and the legend says how many were.
A shell of fewer than three neighbours is not a shape and gets nothing, and the legend counts
those atoms too: on a disordered conductor whose lithium sites are partly occupied, the nearest
oxygen of a site can be more than 1.3 times closer than the next one, and then the rule leaves a
shell of one atom. Widening the ratio would draw those and inflate every well-behaved shell as
well, so the convention stays and the number is stated instead.
This is how an inorganic structure is read: a chain of corner-sharing octahedra says more than
any number of sticks would, and it is the reading the bonds deliberately do not offer for a
metal.

What the polyhedra are *not* for is a metal slab. Every atom of a close-packed metal has twelve
or fourteen neighbours, so its polyhedron says only that the metal is close-packed, which the
spheres already showed; and on a slab with an adsorbate the few iron atoms under the molecule
take its carbon and nitrogen atoms as their vertices, because non-metal neighbours are preferred,
which is the rule working as written and not a reading worth having. The option is for an ionic
or framework structure -- an oxide, a garnet, a zeolite -- and it is off until it is asked for.

**What the drawing is worth, measured.** `benchmarks/results/surface_view/table.md` checks the
perception against a bond table that was not perceived. The molecules of the two Fe(110) sets
came from SDF files, which do carry one, so there is a ground truth on 138 real molecules with
their hydrogens: in the open the rule returns the molecule's own bonds for 72 of 73 and 63 of 65
of them, the misses being long bonds in a relaxed pose that the radii plus 0.45 Å do not reach
across. Put each molecule on the Fe(110) slab in its 16.68 x 11.79 Å cell and wrap it so that the
box cuts it in two, and the perception over the images returns the molecule's own bonds for
**65 of the 65** and **57 of the 58** molecules that fit inside that cell. The ones it gets wrong
are almost exactly the molecules longer than a cell edge: those touch their own periodic image,
so two atoms far apart in the molecule become neighbours across the boundary and the rule joins
them. That is a property of the cell and not of the rule, and it is the one caution to carry into
a picture: a long inhibitor in a small surface cell needs a wider cell, or sticks read with care.
No bond ever reaches the 144-atom slab, which the benchmark asserts rather than reports.
Perceiving the bonds of one molecule costs 0.1 ms in the open and about 1 ms in a cell; on the
largest cells of `examples/hops/disordered/`, 192 and 256 atoms, the bonds take 2 ms and the
polyhedra 29 to 59 ms, so neither option makes the window wait. Those garnets are also the case
the two options were built as a pair for: only their oxygen is a bonding element and no two
oxygen atoms are within 2.4 A, so the distance rule gives them no bonds at all and the polyhedra
are the whole of their reading.

**An organic molecule on a surface, in the window.** This is the case the representations exist
for, and the repository ships the file to open:

```bash
cmf-app                 # File -> Crystals and other periodic structures -> Open one structure file
#   examples/corrosion_fe110/benzimidazole_on_fe110.extxyz
#   Periodic in: ab: a layer      Atoms: ball and stick
```

It holds eight of the benzimidazoles of the Fe(110) study on the slab they were relaxed on: the
6 x 6 x 4 Fe(110) slab of 144 atoms with one molecule at its relaxed pose, periodic in the two
surface directions and open along the normal, with the adsorption energy of each in an info
field, so *Read the measured values* is not even needed -- `--target E_ads_kJmol` on the command
line reads it. With *ball and stick* the molecule comes out with its rings while the 144 iron
atoms stay spheres, because a metal atom gets no perceived bonds. That picture is the whole point
of the two representations.

`examples/corrosion_fe110/make_adsorbate_cell.py` writes that file from the two halves the
repository already had -- the relaxed poses in `157_benzimidazole_uma.sdf`, which hold the
molecules alone, and `cmfqsar.slab.bcc110_slab` -- because a data set of adsorbates keeps the
molecules alone and leaves out the slab every one of them shares. Two of its options matter here:
`--count` writes more molecules, and `--place corner` keeps each pose where the SDF has it, which
is about x = y = 0 and therefore at the corner of the slab's cell, so the molecule straddles the
boundary. That is the file to open to see a bond drawn across the cell boundary with the image
atoms it ends on beside it; the shipped file uses `--place centre`, a translation by half a cell
that changes no distance and leaves the molecule in the middle of the picture.

Your own relaxed state needs no script: one file holding a slab and an adsorbate is what a
relaxation writes, so open its `CONTCAR`, CIF or extended-XYZ file directly.

**Fitting a model.** The *Model* panel is the crystal form of the main window's: the fields
(electrostatic, steric, electronegativity, mass, and one indicator field per element that occurs
in at least the stated number of cells, plus one for the rest), where the electrostatic weights
come from (the oxidation-state guess, the electronegativity proxy, or the charges a calculation
wrote into the file; the guess is exact for a small ionic cell and slow for a large cell of many
elements), in how many directions the cells are periodic (a layer is summed only in its own
plane, and the uniform background is taken per unit area), and the kernel:

- **periodic field autocorrelation (any cells)** — the distance descriptor of the section
  *Crystals: the periodic autocorrelation kernel*, with its cutoff, channel width, taper and
  background switch. It needs no common frame, so it is the kernel for a set of different
  structures, such as the thirteen conductors of the example folder.
- **periodic overlap (cells on one lattice)** — the overlap integral over one cell with the
  images summed in, from the section *A series on one lattice*. It compares two cells point by
  point, so it is for a doped, substituted or defective series on one parent lattice, such as
  the single-atom sheets of `examples/sac/`, and it is the kernel that has a co-field.

The attenuation and the ridge are grids, as in the main window; *Build model* runs the search
and the final fit in the background with the progress bar live, and the *Statistics* tab shows
the summary. The fitted model is saved with *File → Save model…* and is the same file
`build-crystals` writes, so `cmf predict` applies it to new cells.

**Reading the model.** Which reading applies depends on the kernel, and the window offers the
one that exists rather than both:

- The **co-field inside the cell** exists for the overlap kernel. *Compute co-field* evaluates
  $C_f(\mathbf{r})$ of the chosen field on a grid over the box of the selected cell (the grid is
  cut to the atoms along a direction with vacuum, so a layer does not spend its points on empty
  space), and the two isosurfaces are drawn in the fixed colours of the field at the chosen
  percentage of the largest value, as the main window draws them: a positive lobe is a place
  where more of that field raises the property, a negative lobe a place where it lowers it. The
  co-field of a periodic model is a sum over the images of the training cells out to the
  kernel's cutoff; the benchmark doubles that cutoff and finds that the images beyond it change
  the co-field inside the cell by $8 \times 10^{-15}$ of its peak, so the sum is complete. On
  twenty sheets of 127 atoms the steric co-field on 30,744 points at 0.5 Å takes 1.4 s. The
  autocorrelation has no co-field, because a distribution of distances cannot say *where*; the
  box is disabled for it, and clicking the button says why.
- The **site contributions** exist for both kernels and are the same decomposition seen from two
  sides. *Site contributions* draws one translucent sphere per site, red where the site adds to
  the prediction and blue where it subtracts, its radius growing with the square root of the
  magnitude so that the area on screen follows the value, and the colour scale on the control
  strip states the value the largest sphere stands for, in the units of the property. For the
  overlap kernel the numbers are the atom contributions of decomposition rule 3; for the
  autocorrelation they are the split of the descriptor over the sites of plan item M5. In both
  cases they sum to the prediction less the bias, and the legend says whether they do: for the
  autocorrelation the residual is rounding ($6 \times 10^{-14}$ on the thirteen conductors);
  for the overlap kernel the integral runs over the cell of one structure and the images of the
  other, so the two orders agree only on exactly one lattice, and on the relaxed sheets, whose
  lattice vectors differ by 0.4 %, the sum misses the prediction by 0.007 on a property whose
  spread is 0.34. The legend reports that difference whenever it exceeds a tenth of a per cent
  of the prediction, with the reason.
- The **Reading** tab holds the same numbers as a table: for the autocorrelation the co-pattern
  of the model — the channels (a pair of fields at a distance) that move the prediction most,
  with the weight, its spread over the training set and their product, which is what
  `build-crystals` prints — and for either kernel the sites of the selected cell, largest
  magnitude first, with their positions. Beside that table the same co-pattern is drawn as a
  curve of weight against distance, one pair of field types at a time, so that the table says
  which channel and the chart says what the profile over distance is; the section
  *The co-pattern as a chart* is about it.

A check the reading passes on its own: the property of the single-atom sheets used by the
benchmark is the height of the metal above the sheet, and the largest per-site contribution of
the first cell is the metal itself, at −0.39 Å against a largest sphere of ±0.39. The colouring
points at the atom the property belongs to.

**A worked example.** Open `examples/hops/disordered/` with *Open a folder of structures…*,
leave the periodic directions *as the files say*, choose the autocorrelation kernel, and build:
the thirteen conductors have no common lattice and a measured property of your own goes in from
a CSV. Then open `examples/sac/substrates.extxyz` with *Open one structure file…*, set the
periodic directions to *ab: a layer*, read `examples/sac/sac_hoer.csv` and pick the column
`height`, choose the overlap kernel, set the charges to *electronegativity* (a sheet of carbon
with one metal has no oxidation states worth guessing), and build; then *Compute co-field* on
any sheet and tick *Site contributions*. The benchmark's twenty sheets fit in 2 s with
$q^2 = 0.99$ on three folds, which says only that the height of a metal above a sheet is an
easy property for a field that sees the metal; the kernel costs grow with the square of the
number of cells.

**`cmf predict` on a crystal.** A model fitted with `build-crystals`, or saved from this window,
is applied from the command line like any other:

```bash
python cmf_cli.py predict cells.cmf new_cells/ --activity-file values.csv --activity-column dG
python cmf_cli.py predict sheets.cmf more_sheets.extxyz --pbc ab --out predictions.csv
```

The structures are read the way `build-crystals` reads them — one file or a folder of files,
`--pbc` for the periodic directions — and the model decides the path: a periodic model takes
crystals, a molecular model takes molecules, and the options that only mean something for a
molecule (`--align-variance` and the rest) are refused for a crystal rather than ignored. The
contract check of the section *What has to match between fitting and predicting* asks the
questions a crystal raises instead of the ones a molecule raises: a structure without a lattice
is refused; an element the field set has no indicator field for is reported, as a warning when
it falls into the `cif:other` field and as a refusal when no field collects it; an element the
training cells never contained is named as an extrapolation; electrostatic weights from another
source than the training cells' are a warning; a cell whose lattice vectors differ from the
training lattice by more than the training set's own spread, or 10 %, is a warning for the
overlap kernel, which compares cells point by point; and partly occupied sites in a set fitted
on ordered cells, or the reverse, are reported. A model fitted on sites of a cell (plan item M5)
is not a crystal model, and `predict` says so instead of guessing.

**What the window does not do.** It fits the two whole-cell kernels and nothing else: no
site-resolved model, no difference fields of a defect series, no three-body or reciprocal-space
channels, which stay in the library and the benchmarks. It draws one cell at a time. The images
are dots and not spheres, because a cell with its images is thousands of atoms, and only the
image atoms a bond ends on are drawn as atoms. The bonds it draws are perceived for the picture
and are not a bond table the program will use for anything else. And it keeps no
project file: the model is saved, the structures are the files they came from.

## A metal surface behind the molecules

The 3D view draws a protein pocket behind a ligand. An electrode is the same problem with a
different receptor: a slab, periodic in the two directions of the surface, with no residues and
no edge. The section *A metal surface as the receptor* is about what such a receptor is worth;
this one is about seeing it.

**Loading one.** *File → Load a surface slab (POSCAR/CIF/XYZ)…* reads a slab from any structure
file ASE reads and shifts it along $z$ so that its highest atom sits at $z = 0$. *Build a
bcc(110) surface slab…* builds one instead, and its defaults are the slab the Fe(110) adsorption
energies of `examples/corrosion_fe110` were relaxed on: iron, a $6 \times 6$ orthogonal surface
cell, four layers, $a = 2.78$ Å, which is the minimum of the UMA potential for body-centred cubic
iron rather than the experimental 2.87. *Forget the surface slab* takes it away. The slab is not
part of a project file: it is the file it came from, or four numbers in a dialog.

**The frame.** The surface frame of this program is the normal along $z$ with the top atomic
layer at $z = 0$, which is the frame `examples/uma_fe110_adsorption.py` writes its poses in and
the frame `cmfqsar/planealign.py` poses a molecule in. A frame that is not drawn is a frame the
reader has to take on trust, so *frame axes* draws the three axes at the origin, red for $x$ and
green for $y$ in the surface and blue for $z$ along the normal, the same colours the lattice
vectors of a cell carry in the crystal window. If the molecules on screen reach below the top
layer they are not in this frame, and the log says so when the slab is installed.

**The patch.** A surface has no edge, so there is no cell to draw. What is drawn is the top two
layers repeated over the surface lattice and then cut to the atoms whose distance to a molecule
is at most the *patch* radius — measured **in the plane**, not in space, so the surface stays a
surface under a molecule that sits high above it instead of thinning out to nothing. A small
radius shows the patch under the molecule and a large one shows that the surface continues.
`benchmarks/results/surface_view/table.md` measures the cost on both Fe(110) sets: on the
benzimidazole set a 6 Å patch is 93 surface atoms and a 24 Å patch 845, chosen in 1 ms either
way, and the whole view — the patch, the molecule, the frame — is drawn in 3 ms and 11 ms. Every
drawn atom lies at or below $z = 0$, and all of them are atoms of the complementarity receptor
`cmfqsar.slab.slab_receptor` builds, so the picture shows what a score against the surface is
computed from and not something that merely looks like it.

**The sites.** *surface sites* marks the top, bridge and hollow sites of the top layer as small
spheres, yellow, cyan and magenta. They come from a Delaunay triangulation of the top layer, so
they are found for any surface and not only for the lattice the program can build, and what a
molecule sits over is the surface's answer to a residue profile.

**The pose, in two numbers.** A molecule in the surface frame has four free motions and the
surface kernel sees two of them: how high it sits and how far it is tilted. Where it sits in the
plane and how it is turned about the normal are what that kernel is invariant to. So the line
under the view states the two the kernel sees, for the selected molecule: the height of its
lowest heavy atom above the surface, the height of its heavy-atom centroid, and the tilt — the
angle between the molecule's own plane, spanned by its two longest principal axes, and the
surface, so $0°$ is a molecule lying flat and $90°$ one standing on edge. A molecule with no
plane to speak of is told apart rather than given a meaningless angle: the line then says how
thick it is, and the *Surface poses* tab has a column for it.

*Tools → Pose the molecules in the surface frame…* puts every molecule on $z = 0$ by rule — the
rules of the section *Posed by rule: the surface frame without the slab* — and fills that tab
with one row per molecule. The step moves the molecules rigidly, so it joins the pose history and
*Undo last alignment step* takes it back.

The two numbers are checked against something the window never reads. The relaxation that
produced the Fe(110) poses wrote the height of each one into the data set as a column of its own;
the window computes it from the coordinates, and on all 138 molecules of the two sets the two
agree to 0.005 Å. The same measurement says what the poses are: the relaxed heights run from
1.23 to 4.83 Å, the median tilt is 18° on the benzimidazole set and 27° on the quinoline set, and
only 29 % and 14 % of the molecules have a flat plane at all. A molecule relaxed on iron is
therefore not lying flat, and the flat rule pose differs from the relaxed tilt by that same
median — which is the honest form of what the section on the rule poses says about them.

**What this does not do.** It does not dock: the pose search constrained to a surface is
`cmfqsar.slab.dock_on_surface` and is measured in the slab benchmark, not offered in a dialog.
It draws one slab at a time. And the drawing says nothing about the fields: on a one-element
metal four of the five physicochemical fields are identically zero, so a complementarity score
against a clean metal is a shape score, and the section *What a clean metal surface offers*
states why.

## The vector co-field: a direction instead of a value

Every field of this program is a scalar except one. The electric-field kind of the section
*The field a reaction centre feels* carries the same charges as the electrostatic field and pairs
