*statistic* given these predictions, which is exactly what decides whether two settings differ.
On the 21 training steroids, q² = 0.768 carries a 95 % interval of [0.47, 0.89] — wide enough to
show that a difference of a hundredth means nothing.

`--bootstrap-refit N` adds Cramer's bootstrap [26] as well: resample the training set with replacement,
refit, and score the molecules that were left out of the bag. That one measures the variability of
the fit rather than of the statistic, and it is the more pessimistic of the two. The kernel is
never recomputed — a resample is an index into the matrix — so a hundred refits cost about as much
as one cross-validation.

## How certain is *one* prediction? Conformal intervals

The bootstrap says how firm a figure of merit is. It says nothing about the molecule in front of
you, and neither does anything else the program has offered so far: the Gaussian-process posterior
spread is the spread of a model that believes its own kernel, which for molecular fields it should
not.

Conformal prediction supplies the missing guarantee and requires almost nothing in return. Take the
absolute errors the model makes on molecules it did not fit, let $q$ be their $(1-\alpha)$ quantile
— the $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$-th smallest, the $+1$ being what makes the result
finite-sample rather than asymptotic — and report $\hat{y} \pm q$. Then, as long as the
calibration molecules and the new one are exchangeable, the truth lies inside at least
$(1-\alpha)$ of the time, **whatever the learner, whatever the kernel, however wrong the model
is**. A badly specified model does not lose its coverage; it pays with a wider interval
instead.

```bash
python cmf_cli.py build data.sdf --charges file --conformal 0.9 --save model.cmf
python cmf_cli.py predict model.cmf new.sdf --out predictions.csv
```

`--conformal` calibrates on the errors of the cross-validation the program is running anyway, so
it costs nothing and adds no step, prints the half width, and — when there is a test set — the
coverage it actually achieved on molecules that were never part of the calibration. The rule is
stored in the `.cmf` file, so `predict` prints an interval beside every number and writes `lower`
and `upper` columns into the CSV. `--conformal LEVEL` on `predict` re-reads the stored errors at a
different level; the errors are kept, not just the width.

### What it costs, measured

Calibrating on out-of-fold errors and then predicting with the model refitted on everything is
not exactly exchangeable — the errors come from models fitted on nine tenths of the training set
and the predictions from a model fitted on all of it — so the guarantee becomes an approximation,
and the size of the gap is an empirical question. `benchmarks/run_conformal.py` answers it on the
eight Sutherland sets, ten random 70/30 splits each, with the width in units of the activity
(whose standard deviation averages 1.36):

| nominal | out-of-fold (`cv`) | held-out third (`split`) | GP posterior |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 80 % | **80.3 %**, width 2.28 | 80.1 %, width 2.59 | 77.7 %, width 3.00 |
| 90 % | **89.9 %**, width 3.10 | 90.1 %, width 3.61 | 83.1 %, width 3.85 |
| 95 % | **95.1 %**, width 4.09 | 94.9 %, width 4.04 | 86.9 %, width 4.59 |

The cheap variant holds its level to a few tenths of a per cent at every level, and is **narrower**
than the exact split version, which loses accuracy because it fits on less data after holding a third out. The
Gaussian-process interval, which is what one would otherwise reach for, misses its level at all
three — and misses it unpredictably: across the eight sets its 90 % coverage ranges from 63 % to
99 %, while every conformal rule stays between 89 and 96 %.

**Normalised conformal** — dividing each error by the distance of its molecule from the training
set, so that the interval widens where the model extrapolates — is available as
`--conformal-normalise`, and on these sets it gains nothing: it over-covers (93.4 % at a nominal
90 %) and is a third wider. Softening it until it stops over-covering turns it back into the plain
rule. The error on these series simply does not grow with distance from the training set strongly
enough for the normalisation to be useful, which is itself worth knowing about one's data.

Two limits worth stating. The guarantee is **marginal**, not conditional: 90 % of molecules are
covered, not 90 % of *every kind* of molecule, so a subclass the model handles badly can be
covered less often than that while the overall figure holds. And a level needs molecules to support
it — 19 calibration errors for 95 %, 9 for 90 % — below which the program says the level is not
reachable rather than returning its widest error and calling it an interval.

Regression only: conformal classification produces prediction *sets* rather than intervals, and is
not implemented.

### When the scale of the activity is the problem: a warped process

The interval above, and the standard deviation of the chapter after this one, assume one thing
about the activity: that what the kernel does not explain is Gaussian noise on one scale. A pIC50
series is often not like that. The scale is skewed, a floor of inactive compounds sits at one
value, a handful of very active ones stretch the top. A Gaussian process on such a series spends
its noise on the shape of the scale instead of on the chemistry, and its interval is too wide at
one end and too narrow at the other.

The remedy of Snelson, Ghahramani and Rasmussen (NIPS 2003) is to learn a monotone transform of
the response *together with* the process, so that the transformed activity is what the GP models
and every prediction is carried back through the inverse. `cmfqsar.warp` does this (plan item
ND11). With $u = (y - \text{centre}) / \text{width}$ the standardised activity,

$$
g(y) = u + \sum_{i=1}^{I} a_i \tanh(b_i (u + c_i)), \qquad a_i > 0, \; b_i > 0,
$$
<!-- #eq:warp -->

a straight line plus a few smooth steps, each of which stretches the scale around one place and
compresses it far away. Two terms are the default, six parameters, so it fits thirty molecules.
The parameters maximise the log marginal likelihood of the warped activities under the kernel --
with the amplitude profiled out and the constant mean marginalised, as the evidence of
*Choosing the attenuation and the ridge by the evidence* is computed -- plus the Jacobian
$\sum_i \log g'(y_i)$ that makes it the likelihood of the *original* activities. Because the
amplitude is profiled, the objective does not change when the transform is scaled, so what is
fitted is only its shape.

**A series close to normal is left alone.** Six free parameters gain a few nats of evidence on
any series. The transform is therefore kept only if it beats the penalty of the Bayesian
information criterion for its parameters, half their number times $\log n$ -- about twelve nats
on sixty molecules, where a Gaussian series gains four -- and the identity is used otherwise.
The output says which happened and by how much.

**What comes back.** The GP gives a mean and a deviation in the warped units. The prediction in
the original units is the *median*, $g^{-1}(\text{mean})$, and an interval is
$[g^{-1}(\text{mean} - k\,\text{sd}),\; g^{-1}(\text{mean} + k\,\text{sd})]$, which is no
longer symmetric about the prediction -- that asymmetry is the point. The model stays linear in
the field in the warped units: the co-field and the atom contributions are read there, and the
output says so.

```python
model = CMFModel(fieldset=fs, method="krr", params={"lam": 0.1}, warp=2)
model.fit(table, y)                                 # the transform is learned with the fit
print(model.warp_.describe())                        # or "the identity", and why
pred = model.predict(test)                           # the median, in the original units
median, lo, hi = model.predict_warped_interval(test, level=0.9)
```

On the command line it is `cmf build --warp 2`; the transform travels with the saved model, so
`predict` and the conformal interval report in the original units without being told.

**Measured** on the eight Sutherland sets and on the 38 sets of the Mittal collection, five
random 70/30 splits each, with alpha and lambda chosen by the evidence on the training part: the
central 90 % interval of the warped process against the plain process's and the conformal
interval calibrated on the plain fit's folds, on the held-out molecules
(`benchmarks/run_warped.py`, `benchmarks/results/warped/table.md` and
`benchmarks/results/warped_mittal/table.md`). Two of the collection's 38 sets are not in the table, APZ and RYR, which have 16 and 17 molecules, too few for a 70/30 split with an interval.

| collection | sets | warp kept | q2, plain | q2, warped | coverage, plain GP | coverage, conformal | coverage, warped | width, plain GP | width, conformal | width, warped |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sutherland | 8 | 32% of splits | +0.484 | +0.482 | 88% | 89% | 88% | 3.00 | 3.17 | 2.96 |
| Mittal | 36 | 41% of splits | +0.102 | +0.057 | 88% | 90% | 87% | 4.93 | 5.73 | 4.83 |

The last column of each coverage group is what the gate reads. Over the 44 series the warped interval is closer to the promised 90% than the plain process's on 8 and further on 14 (1 and 2 on the Sutherland sets, 7 and 12 on the collection). The paired differences over the sets, with their 95 % bootstrap intervals: on the Sutherland sets coverage -0.2% [-0.5%, -0.0%] against the plain GP and -1.8% [-3.6%, +0.3%] against the conformal interval, width -0.044 [-0.133, +0.013] and -0.213 [-0.345, -0.080], q2 -0.002 [-0.012, +0.007]; on the collection coverage -1.1% [-2.1%, -0.2%] and -3.1% [-4.6%, -1.8%], width -0.099 [-0.170, -0.041] and -0.904 [-2.107, -0.242], q2 -0.045 [-0.086, -0.016]. The transform was kept on 32% of the Sutherland splits and 41% of the collection's, gaining +10.3 and +16.3 nats of evidence over the identity on average; where it was kept, q2 moved by -0.004 [-0.024, +0.013] on the 4 Sutherland sets concerned and -0.065 [-0.122, -0.025] on the 25 of the collection, and coverage by -0.5% [-0.8%, -0.1%] and -1.6% [-2.9%, -0.3%]. Coverage does not improve on more series than it worsens, so the warp stays an option (`--warp`) and not a default, as the item's own rule says.

**What writing it found.** Three sets of the collection -- PTC, DIAZEPAM and EV71 -- have no hydrogen-bond donor on any molecule, so the donor field is zero throughout. The choice of attenuation and ridge by the evidence that the error benchmarks share divided each field by the mean of its training diagonal, which is zero for such a field, so the kernel filled with NaN and the evidence was finite for nothing. The model's own rule, a scale of zero for a field that is zero everywhere, is now used there too; the Sutherland sets all have donors, so no stored number changed.

## Three estimates of the error, compared

The program now offers three answers to *should I believe this number*, and they come from three
different places: the **Gaussian-process posterior variance**, which is the kernel's own statement
about how much of this molecule lies in the span of the training set; the **applicability domain**,
which is a geometric statement about how far it is from its nearest training neighbours; and the
**conformal interval**, whose normalised form widens where the model is extrapolating. They are in
three different units — a variance, a distance in field space, a width in log units of activity —
so they cannot be compared by their numbers. What can be compared is the order they put the
molecules in, because that is what they are used for: which prediction do I act on, which do I
measure first.

```bash
python cmf_cli.py build data.sdf --test-file test.sdf --domain \
       --conformal 0.8 --conformal-normalise --error-predictors
```

Each estimate is scored against the absolute error actually made on the test molecules, three ways.
**Spearman's ρ** asks whether the order is right at all. The **risk–coverage efficiency** asks what
is gained by acting on it: trust the most confident fraction, measure the RMSE of that fraction, and compare
the area under that curve with two references — the *oracle*, which orders the molecules by the
error they really made, and the flat curve of ignoring the estimate. One means the oracle, zero
means no better than ignoring it, and a negative number means actively misleading. The **halves**
are the crudest and most practical: the RMSE of the half it trusts against the half it doubts.

**Measured, the three are indistinguishable.** Eight Sutherland sets, five 70/30 splits each,
α and λ chosen by the evidence on the training part, the conformal rule calibrated on that part's
own out-of-fold errors:

| estimate | ρ | efficiency | RMSE trusted | RMSE doubted | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GP variance | +0.142 | **+0.198** | 0.835 | 1.024 | 1.38 |
| distance to the training set | +0.125 | +0.186 | 0.853 | 1.009 | 1.31 |
| domain dissimilarity | +0.133 | +0.181 | 0.841 | 1.022 | 1.36 |
| normalised conformal width | +0.133 | +0.181 | 0.841 | 1.022 | 1.36 |

The GP variance is ahead by +0.011 in efficiency over the distance, with a 95 % interval of
[−0.021, +0.044] — zero is inside it, and the choice between the three does not matter.

![The risk–coverage efficiency of the three estimates on each of the eight Sutherland sets, mean over five splits. One would be the oracle that knows the error of every molecule, zero an estimate that carries no information. The three move together from set to set, and on THER all three are below zero.](docs/figures/errorpred.svg)

Two things in that table deserve more attention than the ranking. The first is that the **normalised
conformal width and the domain measure score identically, and must**: the normalisation divides the
interval by the molecule's difficulty, which *is* its distance from the training set, so the width
is a monotone function of the domain and cannot order the molecules differently. The conformal rule
is justified by being calibrated — it covers what it says it covers, which neither of the others
claims — and not by ordering. There are three estimates here, not four.

And the remaining two are nearly the same. Over the same splits the estimates agree with each other at a
mean Spearman ρ of **+0.80 to +0.86** — the GP variance against the distance to the training set at
+0.799, against the domain dissimilarity at +0.853 — while the conformal width against the domain
measure is **+1.000**, exactly as the algebra says it must be. That is why the efficiencies in the
table are indistinguishable: these are not three independent opinions about a molecule but one
geometric fact, how far it sits from the training set, expressed in three sets of units.

The second is the size of all of them. The best captures about a fifth of what the oracle would,
and the half it trusts has an RMSE of 0.84 against 1.02 for the half it doubts. That ratio of about
1.4 is real and useful — it is exactly the gain from measuring the confident half first — and it is
nothing like a per-molecule error bar. On one of the eight sets (THER) every estimate comes out
negative: an estimate of error is itself a model, and it can be wrong about a series. Use them to
order molecules, and quote the conformal interval when a number has to be attached to one.

## The model as the fast level of a hierarchy: a standard deviation in the units of the activity

A multiscale scheme puts a CMF model between an electronic-structure method and a coarser model:
the fine level labels a few hundred structures, the model answers for the thousands the coarse
model needs, and the coarse model turns them into a material property. For that the model must say,
per structure, whether its answer can be used. The posterior variance of the Gaussian process (the
*Gaussian process* row of the learner table) is the right quantity, but as it stands it is not
usable for the purpose, for three reasons.

**It is in the units of the kernel.** The Gaussian process that matches the ridge fit has the prior
covariance $s\,\mathbf{K}$ and the noise $s\lambda$, where $s$ is the one amplitude the evidence
profiles out in closed form (the section *Choosing α and λ by the evidence*): the mean squared
whitened residual of the training set, $s = \mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{T}}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{r}/(n-1)$
with $\mathbf{r}$ the residual about the fitted constant. The predictive variance of a new
*measurement* at $x$ is then

$$\sigma^2(x) = s\left[K(x,x) - \mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{T}}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k} + \frac{(1-\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{T}}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{1})^2}{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{1}} + \lambda\right]$$

and its square root is in the units of the activity. The third term inside the bracket is the
uncertainty of the constant mean that the ridge fits as its bias, marginalised under a flat prior
(Rasmussen and Williams 2006, eq. 2.42 with one basis function); it is what makes a structure far
from every training one uncertain about the *level* of the activity and not only about its shape.
Without the last term, $\lambda$, the deviation is that of the underlying value rather than of a
measurement, which is what two predictions of the same structure share.

**Nobody had checked that it means what it says.** On the folds, the standardised out-of-fold
residual $z = (y - \hat y)/\sigma$ should have a root mean square of one, and the interval of two
standard deviations should hold about 95 % of the activities. The program reports both, and the
factor that would make the root mean square one. A factor well above one says the model is surer
than it should be, which is the usual finding when the kernel misses a part of the chemistry. The
factor is reported and not applied.

**A number is not a decision.** A tolerance in the units of the activity turns it into one: every
structure whose standard deviation exceeds the tolerance is marked as one to pass to the fine level
(a DFT calculation, a measurement) instead of using the model's answer. The share the fine level
can afford goes the other way, to the tolerance that sends it that many.

![The tolerance rule on the test molecules of the ACE set. Left: the error of every prediction, with the molecules in the order of their standard deviation and the band of two standard deviations. At the tolerance that passes three tenths of the molecules to the fine level, the model answers the blue ones and passes the red ones on. Right: the error of the molecules that the model answers, as the share that is passed on grows; the dashed line is the error when the molecules to pass on are drawn at random. On a congeneric series the gain is modest, as the measurements below say. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/tolerance.svg)

```bash
python cmf_cli.py build data.sdf --charges file --test-fraction 0.3 --calibration --save model.cmf
python cmf_cli.py predict model.cmf new.sdf --sd --tolerance 0.7 --out predictions.csv
```

`--calibration` prints the check on the folds and, when there is a test set, on it. `--sd` prints
the prediction with its standard deviation and writes it to the CSV as `predicted_sd`;
`--tolerance` adds the marks (`-> fine level` on the screen, a `defer` column of 0 and 1 in the
CSV) and a line saying how many structures the model answers and, where the activities are known,
the error on each side. In Python the same three things are `model.predict_with_sd(test)`,
`model.calibration()` and `cmfqsar.surrogate.Handoff.of(sd, tolerance, y, mean)`; the deviation
needs the linear kernel and the ridge learner, and a low-rank model refuses it, because the term of
the mean needs the full training kernel.

**Measured, the deviation is calibrated as it stands.** Eight Sutherland sets, five random 70/30
splits each, α and λ by the evidence on the training part (`benchmarks/run_surrogate.py`):

| set | n | test RMSE | mean σ | z rms, folds | z rms, test | inside 2σ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DHFR | 361 | 0.751 | 0.679 | 1.10 | 1.08 | 93 % |
| COX2 | 282 | 0.811 | 0.825 | 0.97 | 0.99 | 93 % |
| BZR | 147 | 0.610 | 0.620 | 1.03 | 0.98 | 94 % |
| ACE | 114 | 1.512 | 1.378 | 0.99 | 1.15 | 89 % |
| AChE | 111 | 0.809 | 0.830 | 1.05 | 0.96 | 94 % |
| THR | 88 | 0.672 | 0.641 | 0.96 | 1.02 | 94 % |
| THER | 76 | 1.635 | 1.605 | 1.03 | 1.07 | 93 % |
| GPB | 66 | 0.767 | 0.722 | 0.99 | 1.10 | 92 % |
| **mean** | | 0.946 | 0.912 | **1.02** | **1.05** | **93 %** |

The root mean square of $z$ is 1.02 on the folds and 1.05 on the held-out molecules, and two
standard deviations hold 93 % of them against the 95 % of a Gaussian. The mean deviation is within
4 % of the error actually made on every set. So the scale that the evidence profiles out *is* the
noise level of the series, and the correction factor, though reported, is not needed on these sets;
applied to the held-out molecules it moves the root mean square from 1.05 to 1.03.

**The tolerance rule does what it promises, and no more.** With the tolerance set to the
cross-validated RMSE of the training part, the error the model claims for a typical molecule, the
model answers **61 %** of the held-out molecules at an RMSE of **0.90** and defers the rest, whose
RMSE is **1.03**; the mean tolerance is 0.92, so the answered share's error sits where the rule
said it would. Sending a fixed quarter of the molecules to the fine level gives 0.88 against 1.08.
The separation is modest, and it must be: the section above showed that the posterior variance is
the distance to the training set in other units and captures about a fifth of what an oracle would.
On THER the deferred molecules are *better* predicted than the answered ones, as every estimate of
the error was on that set. What calibration adds is not a better ordering but a fair size: the
error the fast level reports for the structures it answers is the error it makes, which is what a
coarse model needs in order to carry it forward.

**On a hop set, where the hierarchy is real, the rule earns more.** The sample of LiTraj used
in the external check of the hop model — 1,801 hops of lithium ions in 393 crystals, each labelled
by a bond-valence calculation, which is the fine level here — with ten folds that hold out whole
structures and the ridge and the width of a Gaussian kernel chosen on an inner split of the same
kind (`benchmarks/run_surrogate.py --hops`):

| kernel | q² | held-out RMSE (eV) | mean σ (eV) | z rms, inner folds | z rms, held out | inside 2σ | σ against the error (ρ) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| linear, invariant local | +0.572 | 1.246 | 1.136 | 1.04 | 1.05 | 95 % | +0.20 |
| Gaussian on the same rows | +0.623 | 1.169 | 1.053 | 1.01 | 0.99 | 96 % | +0.35 |

| kernel | tolerance (eV) | answered | RMSE answered | RMSE deferred | answered at 25 % deferred | RMSE of that 25 % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| linear | 1.242 | 87 % | 1.123 | 1.856 | 1.063 | 1.681 |
| Gaussian | 1.207 | 82 % | 0.998 | 1.752 | 0.840 | 1.830 |

The deviation is calibrated here as well, for both kernels, which is what the scale absorbing the
units of the kernel promises: the root mean square of $z$ is 1.05 and 0.99, and two standard
deviations hold 95 % and 96 % of the barriers. The rule now separates by a factor of 1.8 rather
than 1.1: with the Gaussian kernel the model answers 82 % of the hops at an RMSE of 1.00 eV and
sends back 18 % whose RMSE would have been 1.75 eV, and a fixed quarter sent back leaves 0.84 eV
against 1.83 eV for the quarter. The reason is the data and not the method. A Sutherland series is
congeneric, so every held-out molecule has close relatives in the training part and the deviations
are all alike; the collection behind the hop sample covers every chemistry that holds lithium, so
a held-out structure is often the only one of its chemical system, and the deviation says so. That
is the situation a hierarchy is in, and it is where a calibrated deviation does its work: the hops
the fast level keeps carry the error it claims, and the ones it returns are the ones the
calculation was needed for.

### The same deviation without the n by n kernel

Everything above needs the training kernel, factorised once. A set of a hundred thousand
structures has no such kernel -- that is why the low-rank path of *Large training sets* fits in
the space of a few hundred landmarks instead -- and until now that path could predict but could
not say how sure it was: `surrogate()` refused it in those words. Plan item MS6 removes the
refusal, and nothing of size $n$ is built to do it.

The kernel of a low-rank model is $\Phi\Phi^T$, with $\Phi$
the $n \times m$ matrix of features against the landmarks, and every quantity the surrogate
computes has an $m \times m$ form through the Woodbury identity. With
$\mathbf{A} = \Phi^T\Phi + \lambda\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{r}$ the
residual about the fitted constant,

$$
\mathbf{r}^T(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{r}
= \frac{\mathbf{r}^T\mathbf{r} - (\Phi^T\mathbf{r})^T\mathbf{A}^{-1}(\Phi^T\mathbf{r})}{\lambda},
\qquad
\mathbf{1}^T(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{1}
= \frac{n - (\Phi^T\mathbf{1})^T\mathbf{A}^{-1}(\Phi^T\mathbf{1})}{\lambda},
$$
<!-- #eq:lowrank-scale -->

so the scale $s$ is the same mean squared whitened residual as before, the term of the unknown
mean is $(1 - \boldsymbol{\phi}^T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\Phi^T\mathbf{1})^2$
over the second quantity, and the posterior variance is the one the low-rank path already had,
with the exact self-kernel kept so that it does not fall to zero where the landmarks span
nothing. The Gram the fit stores -- $\Phi^T\Phi$,
$\Phi^T\mathbf{y}$, $\Phi^T\mathbf{1}$, $n$, $\sum y$ and
$\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y}$ -- holds everything these expressions need, which is why a
model read back from a file can give its deviation without its training set.

```python
model.fit_low_rank(train, y, landmarks, lam=0.1)
mean, sd = model.predict_with_sd(test)     # the same call as for the exact model
model.calibration(folds=10)                # on the same folds the exact path uses
```

`LowRankSurrogate` in `cmfqsar.surrogate` is the object behind it; `lowrank.cross_validate`
returns the out-of-fold deviation with `with_sd=True`, and `lowrank.LowRank.joint_self` is the
exact self-kernel of a table. The tests fix the claim the way the low-rank tests fix the fit:
with the training molecules as the landmarks the kernel is reproduced exactly, so the scale, the
mean, the deviation and the calibration must equal the exact path's to round-off, and they do.

**Measured** on the stored splits of the eight Sutherland sets -- the same five 70/30 splits, the
same attenuation and ridge as the table at the start of this chapter, so the only thing that
differs is the path -- with three landmark sets: every training molecule (the exact kernel
computed another way), half of them and a quarter of them, drawn at random
(`benchmarks/run_surrogate.py --low-rank`, `benchmarks/results/surrogate/table.md`).

| landmarks | rank | z rms, folds | exact | z rms, test | exact | inside 2 sd | largest difference from the exact path |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| molecules | 497 | 1.02 | 1.02 | 1.05 | 1.05 | 93% | 1.1e-08 |
| half | 253 | 0.95 | 1.02 | 0.94 | 1.05 | 95% | 6.0e-01 |
| quarter | 129 | 0.86 | 1.02 | 0.82 | 1.05 | 97% | 1.2e+00 |

The averages are over the eight sets and five splits. The last column is what the gate reads: the largest difference from the exact path over every set and split, which is 1.1e-08 with the molecules as landmarks -- the same kernel computed another way, so round-off -- and 6.0e-01 and 1.2e+00 with half and a quarter of them. So the gate holds where the landmarks span the data, which is the reading's own claim, and the approximation loosens it in one direction: with half the molecules as landmarks the root mean square of z falls below the exact path's on every split, by 0.07 on the folds and 0.11 on the held-out molecules on average, and with a quarter by 0.16 and 0.23 -- the deviation of the approximate model is larger than its error. That is the term which keeps the variance from falling to zero where the landmarks span nothing being conservative by construction, not an error in reading it; the largest single-split differences, 0.60 and 1.20, are both GPB, where 46 training molecules leave a quarter at twelve landmarks.

**What writing it found.** Two faults of the low-rank path, both older than this item and both
invisible on a set where every molecule carries every field. The exact fit scales each field by one
over the mean of its normalised training diagonal; that diagonal is 1 for a molecule whose field is
not identically zero and 0 for one whose field is -- no donor, no acceptor, no charge -- so on a set
that holds such molecules the scale is above one. The low-rank path took one, which made it another
model on exactly those sets: with the training molecules themselves as landmarks its kernel missed
the exact one by 1 % on the ACE set, where 13 of 80 training molecules have no hydrogen-bond donor.
And the self-kernel it kept for the variance counted every field as one for every molecule, where
the normalisation leaves a zero field at zero, so a molecule without a donor had its deviation
inflated by that field's whole share. Both are repaired -- the scale is now the exact path's, and
`LowRank.joint_self` is the one definition of the self-kernel -- and the test that would have caught
them, a series with esters and a nitrile among the acids, is in `tests/test_lowrank_surrogate.py`.
The repair also reaches `cmf build --low-rank`, which had used a scale of one for choosing its ridge,
and which passed over `--calibration` without a word; it reports the calibration now.

What this does not do is train on a hundred thousand structures. The path can -- its memory is
the rank squared whatever the number of molecules, as *Large training sets* measured -- but the
test case the plan names, the full LiTraj collection, is held in this repository as a sample of
1,801 hops, and the hop model of that sample is the rotation-invariant local kernel, which has
explicit features and does not go through this path at all. The deviation at that scale is
therefore shown to be *computable* here and not yet *measured*; the measurement needs the
overlap kernel on a large set in one frame, and it is recorded as open.

## What the model thinks the groups are: clustering the kernel

Every grouped validation in this manual splits the molecules by their Bemis–Murcko scaffold, and
the reasoning is sound: random folds put a molecule's own scaffold-mates in the training part and
greatly overstate the quality of a mixed series. But it rests on an assumption nobody checks — that a scaffold is
what makes two molecules alike *to the model*. The model does not see scaffolds. It sees fields,
and its notion of similarity is the kernel.

*Spectral clustering* partitions that similarity directly. The kernel is already a similarity
matrix, so there is nothing to build: form the normalised Laplacian, take the eigenvectors
belonging to its smallest eigenvalues, put the rows on the unit sphere and run k-means there [27]. Groups that are not linearly separable in field space are separable in those
coordinates, which is the point of the construction. How many groups is decided by the **eigengap**
unless it is given, and the gap is reported beside the answer so that a weak one can be seen for
what it is.

```bash
python cmf_cli.py cluster data.sdf --charges file
python cmf_cli.py cluster data.sdf --clusters 5 --out clusters.csv
```

The command prints the clusters, the spectrum they came from, the activity of each, and the
**adjusted Rand index** between them and the scaffold groups — the number that says whether the
usual grouping groups by what the model actually responds to.

### The two partitions do not agree, and it matters

Measured on the eight Sutherland sets, with both partitions cut into the same number of groups —
holding out one of two clusters removes half the training set and holding out one of nine does
not, so a difference in granularity would be read as a difference in difficulty:

| | q² |
|---|---:|
| random 10-fold | +0.508 |
| leave one **scaffold group** out | +0.271 |
| leave one **field cluster** out | +0.057 |

and the adjusted Rand index between the two partitions averages **+0.140**, which is weak
agreement: what the chemist calls a series and what the kernel finds similar are largely different
things. On BZR they are different enough that holding out a field cluster takes q² to −0.740.

The consequence is uncomfortable and worth stating. This manual recommends the
leave-one-chemotype-out figure as the more reliable one, and against random folds it is — 0.271 against
0.508. But it is not the hardest reliable test available: holding out a group of the model's own
similarity costs another 0.214, because a scaffold group leaves molecules the kernel still
considers close in the training part. Quote the scaffold figure, by all means; just do not read it
as the worst case.

## Where the validation appears

The three checks of *Building a model* — y-randomisation, the bootstrap intervals and the
applicability domain — are set in one place and reported in another, which is worth stating
plainly because there is no button and no separate window for them.

**Setting them**: the *Validation* row at the foot of the model panel's second group, directly
under *External CV*. Three controls: **shuffles** (0 = off), **bootstrap** (0 = off), and the
**applicability domain** tick. They are settings, not actions — choose them before pressing
**Build model**, and they run as part of that build, after the fit and the test prediction.

**Reading them**: the *Statistics* tab of the results panel, where they are appended below the
usual figures under a heading *Validation*. The names of the molecules that fell outside the
applicability domain go to the *Log* tab instead, with their similarity values, so that the
statistics stay a summary and the list of molecules outside the domain stays with the rest of the log.

Three cases produce no validation block at all, and each says why rather than leaving a blank:

- all three controls at their defaults — nothing was asked for;
- a classification or one-class model — y-randomisation and the bootstrap are implemented for
  regression only, and the block says so;
- the autocorrelation kernel source — the applicability domain is measured in the field kernel,
  which that source does not provide.

## Statistics reported

Regression: r² and RMSE for the fit, q² and RMSEcv for the cross-validation, R²pred and RMSEpred
for the test set in both variance conventions, q²ex and RMSEcvex for the external CV.
Classification: accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation, AUC
and the ROC curve, each for the fit, the cross-validation and the test set. Screening: AUC,
enrichment factors at 0.5, 1, 5 and 10 %, the best achievable enrichment at each of those
fractions, BEDROC and RIE.

![Observed against predicted for the kernel ridge model of the steroid set at the best point of the grid of *Attenuation, regularisation and the grids*: the cross-validated predictions of the training molecules and the predictions of the ten test molecules, with the line of a perfect prediction. The two values of R²pred are the two conventions, against the variance of the test set and against the training mean; the test affinities span a narrow range, so the first is negative while the second is not. The molecule named is the only one with a fluorine, an atom the training set does not contain. The *Scatter plot* tab shows the same points and names the molecule under the cursor.](docs/figures/scatter.svg)

## Saving and reusing

*File → Save model…* writes a `.cmf` file (joblib) holding the field set, the kernels' definition,
the fitted coefficients, the training molecules, every setting needed to predict later, and the
record of how the training set was prepared that *What has to match between fitting and
predicting* describes. `cmf_cli.py predict model.cmf new.sdf --out predictions.csv` applies it,
after checking the new molecules against that record; the GUI loads it with *File → Load model…*
and writes the record's summary to the log.
## A report to hand to a colleague

A `.cmf` file is for the program. The person who has to judge the model — a colleague, a reviewer,
a supervisor — will never start the application, and what they need is one file they can open.

```bash
python cmf_cli.py report model.cmf --out model.html
```

That writes a single self-contained HTML page: every picture is inside it, so it survives being
emailed, attached or put on a share, and it opens in any browser and prints to PDF. It has seven
sections, in the order a sceptical reader asks for them.

- **What this model is** — fields, α, learner, kernel, how the charges were made.
- **How well it fits and predicts** — the statistics with the observed-against-predicted plots
  beside them, because a q² is a summary of that picture and not a substitute for it.
- **Whether to believe that** — the validation that was actually run: y-randomisation, the
  bootstrap intervals, the applicability domain, the conformal level, the comparison of error
  predictors. **A check that was not run is reported as not run**, never silently omitted, which
  is the difference between a report and an advertisement.
- **What the model rests on** — the mean absolute contribution of each field, which is what
  separates a model standing on its geometry from one standing on a single field.
- **The co-fields**, projected onto the three coordinate planes from fixed viewpoints: the
  strongest signed value along each viewing axis, with the training atoms as grey dots for scale.
  A projection rather than an isosurface, because a report has no camera and its reader has no
  mouse.
- **The extremes of the series** — the most and least active training molecules, each decomposed
  over the fields by exact Shapley values and over its own atoms by the contribution rule.
- **The pharmacophore** read out of the co-fields, and the provenance of the model file.

Everything comes out of the model file, so a report costs no refitting and **cannot disagree with
the model it describes**. Missing parts are reported rather than causing a failure: a nonlinear kernel has no
co-fields, no atom contributions and no pharmacophore, and the report says so in place of each and
keeps the rest; a model fitted without a test set reports no R²pred.

`--no-cofields` leaves out the pictures, which are the slow part — a report of a 50-molecule model
takes about three seconds with them and under one without — and `--spacing` sets how finely they
and the pharmacophore are computed. `--open` shows it in the browser straight away.

# Reading the model

A CMF model is readable in a way a grid model is not, because the prediction can be taken apart
exactly. Reference [6] states three decomposition rules, and the program implements all three.

## The three decomposition rules

Every model the program fits is a sum of kernel values with the training molecules, and the three rules below follow from that one fact. Reference [6] states them for the kernel of overlap integrals. The program keeps them for every model that is still such a sum, and it says so when a model is not: a nonlinear kernel layer keeps rule 2 and loses rules 1 and 3.

**Rule 1: the co-field is a weighted sum of the fields of the training molecules.**

$$
C_f(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_j a_j\, s_j\, X_{fj}(\mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:rule1 -->

This is Eq. (#eq:cofield) restated. The weights are the fitted dual coefficients $a_j$, one per training molecule, times the normalisation $s_j$ of its field when the kernels are normalised. Every lobe of a co-field therefore comes from named molecules: a positive lobe is where the fields of the molecules with a positive weight are strong and the fields of the molecules with a negative weight are weak. The scheme below draws the three terms of the largest weight for the electrostatic co-field of the steroid model, and the co-field that they and the other eighteen terms add up to. In the program the co-field is the **Compute co-field** button, described in *Co-fields* below; the weights are `model.coef` in the library, and the *Contributions* tab lists them beside the products of rule 2.

![Rule 1 for the electrostatic co-field of the steroid model of this chapter: the three training molecules of the largest weight, each field drawn times its weight with the skeleton of the molecule over it, and the co-field that all 21 terms add up to, on one colour scale. The weight of a training molecule is its dual coefficient times the normalisation of its field, and the sign of the weight, not the activity itself, decides whether its field is added or subtracted.](docs/figures/rule1.png)

**Rule 2: a prediction is the bias plus one contribution per training molecule.**

$$
\hat{y} = b + \sum_j a_j\, K(X, X_j)
$$
<!-- #eq:rule2 -->

This is Eq. (#eq:prediction) restated. $K(X, X_j)$ is the kernel between the molecule and training molecule $j$, so the contribution of a training molecule is its similarity to the molecule times its weight, which is why the rule is also called the similarity decomposition. The rule holds for every kernel, a nonlinear layer included, because the layer changes the kernel and not the form of the sum. It is the first thing to read when a prediction surprises you: a prediction resting on one or two training molecules is a warning, and a support vector machine makes the sum short on purpose, since most of its coefficients are zero. The scheme shows the contributions of the 21 training molecules to one test molecule of the steroid set, sorted: the molecules the fit weighted positively and that resemble the test molecule pull the prediction up, the others pull it down. The *Contributions* tab lists them, `cmf report` prints the largest, and `model.training_contributions(mol)` returns them.

![Rule 2 for one test molecule of the steroid set, the one the model of this chapter predicts highest: the contribution of each of the 21 training molecules, sorted, with the observed affinity of the training molecule in brackets; the bias and the sum of the bars are in the title. The bars are not an activity ranking of the training set, because the similarity to the test molecule is a factor in every term.](docs/figures/rule2.svg)

**Rule 3: a prediction is a sum over the atoms of the molecule.**

$$
\hat{y} = b + \sum_k y_k
$$
<!-- #eq:rule3 -->

The field of a molecule is a sum of Gaussians centred on its atoms, and the overlap kernel is a sum over pairs of atoms, so the contribution of every training molecule splits further into one term $y_k$ per atom $k$ of the molecule being predicted, the overlap of that atom's own Gaussians with the co-fields:

$$
y_k = \sum_f \dfrac{h_f c_f}{\sqrt{K_f(x,x)}} \int X_{fk}(\mathbf{r})\, C_f(\mathbf{r})\, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}, \qquad X_{fx}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_k X_{fk}(\mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:atom -->

Here $X_{fk}$ is the part of the field of the molecule that atom $k$ carries, and the rest is Eq. (#eq:prediction-field) with the sum over the atoms taken outside the integral. The contribution of a substituent or a fragment is the sum over its atoms. This is the rule for design, because it says which part of a molecule helps and which part does not. It needs a kernel that is a sum over atom pairs, which the overlap kernel and the rotation-invariant autocorrelation kernel are and a nonlinear layer is not; under a layer the Shapley values of *Shapley values* below take its place. The scheme draws the atom contributions of the two test molecules the steroid model predicts highest and lowest, as Figure 3 of [6] draws them: red spheres raise the predicted affinity, blue ones lower it, and the area is the magnitude. The 3D view draws the same spheres for the selected molecule, and `model.atom_contributions(mol)` returns the values, per field with `per_field=True`.

![Rule 3 for the two test molecules of the steroid set that the model of this chapter predicts highest and lowest, drawn as Figure 3 of [6]: one circle per atom, hydrogens included, red for a positive contribution and blue for a negative one, with an area proportional to the magnitude and the three largest values written out. The sums in the titles are the predictions minus the bias. The largest contributions sit on oxygen atoms, where the electrostatic co-field has its lobes.](docs/figures/rule3.svg)

**What to do with the map.** An atom with a negative contribution is a candidate for removal or for replacement, an atom with a positive one is what to keep, and the sum over a substituent is what the model says that substituent is worth at its position. The predicted effect of exchanging one group for another at a position is the difference of the two sums, one integral per pair of groups and no refit: that is the measure behind the table of *Which groups are interchangeable: a bioisostere table*, `cmf design` in *Designing the next compound* ranks candidate groups by the prediction for the whole molecule, and on a series without a common frame the invariant route of that chapter reports how much of a candidate's prediction comes from the group that was put in. One caution: the contributions describe the molecule as it is posed in the model's frame. Taking a group away changes the normalisation of the field and may change the conformation, the alignment and the charges of what is left, so the map says where to act, and the prediction for the edited molecule says whether the action worked. The same split written as a file for another program to read is *A map as an output mode* in *A site of the cell as the sample* below, which covers molecules and cells alike.

The two sums are the same number: the contributions of the training molecules and the contributions of the atoms both add up to the prediction minus the bias, and a test asserts it. For a classification model the coefficients carry the sign of the class, $a_j = \alpha_j y_j$, and the three rules read the same way with the active class in place of the higher activity.

## Co-fields

The co-field of Eq. (#eq:cofield), restated above as rule 1, is the model as a function of
space: a weighted sum of the training molecules' fields with the fitted dual coefficients as weights,
each divided by the norm $s_j = K_f(j,j)^{-1/2}$ of its own field when the kernels are
normalised, which they are by default. The
prediction of any molecule is then the overlap of its own field with the co-field, field type by
field type. Press **Compute co-field** and the program evaluates it on a grid around the training
set; choose the field with the *Field* selector and set the *iso level* slider, which is a
percentage of the largest absolute value rather than an absolute number, so the surfaces stay
meaningful when you change field.

What the lobes mean: a positive co-field lobe is a region where *more* of that field raises the
predicted activity. For the electrostatic field that means positive charge is favoured there, for
the steric field bulk, for the hydrophobic field lipophilicity, and for an indicator field it means
an atom of that type is favoured at that position.

![The electrostatic and the steric co-field of a model of the steroid training set (α = 1, λ = 1, q² = 0.79), cut in the mean plane of the series, with corticosterone, the most active training molecule, drawn over them. Red marks a region where more of that field raises the predicted affinity: positive charge for the electrostatic field, bulk for the steric one. The lobes sit at the two ends of the skeleton, which is where the series varies.](docs/figures/cofield.png)

**Isosurfaces and plane cuts.** The 3D view, like the figures of the papers, draws a field as two closed surfaces, the places where it equals plus and minus the iso level, and everything weaker than that level is left invisible. The maps of this manual cut the same function with one plane and colour every point of the plane by its value, so weak regions are visible and anything off the plane is not. The two are the same object drawn two ways; the figure below shows the electrostatic co-field of the previous figure both ways, and the dashed lines on the map are where the two isosurfaces cross the plane. A weak but wide lobe that a map shows may fall below the iso level in the 3D view, and lowering the level with the slider brings it back.

![The same electrostatic co-field as the previous figure, drawn as the application draws it and as this manual draws it. Left: the isosurfaces at plus and minus 30 per cent of the largest absolute value, red positive and blue negative, with corticosterone inside them and the mean plane of the series marked; the lobes are the regions the iso level encloses, and nothing weaker is shown. Right: the cut of that plane through the same function, coloured by value, with the dashed lines where the two isosurfaces meet the plane. The map shows the whole plane, the surfaces show the whole space above one level.](docs/figures/isosurface.png)

Two further maps use the same grid, for the molecule currently shown:

- the **molecular field** $X_f(\mathbf{r})$ of that molecule, in the same colours. The two share a
  colour scale, so only the drawing style tells them apart: the style box is `auto` by default,
  which draws this one as a mesh while a co-field is on screen and solid when it is the only
  surface shown;
- the **overlap** $C_f(\mathbf{r})\,X_f(\mathbf{r})$, whose integral *is* that field's contribution to the prediction
  by Eq. (#eq:prediction-field), so the map shows where the prediction comes from.

![The prediction as an overlap, for the electrostatic field of one test molecule of the steroid set and the model of the previous figure: the co-field of the model, times the molecule's own field, gives the product whose integral over space, with the field's scale and mixing coefficient, is that field's contribution to the predicted affinity. The prediction is the sum of these contributions over the fields plus the bias. This is Fig. 1 of [2] drawn with the program's own maps; the application shows the same three maps in 3D for the molecule on screen.](docs/figures/overlapmap.png)

*File → Export current co-field (Gaussian cube)* writes a cube file readable by PyMOL, VMD or
Jmol, which is the way to put a co-field into a publication figure.

### How much of it is noise

A co-field is read as a fact about the chemistry. It is a linear map of the measured activities, so
part of its shape is a fact about the measurement error instead, and the program can say which part
in closed form.

The dual coefficients are a linear map of the activities — with a bias, the bordered system of Eq. (#eq:ridge), whose inverse's top-left block is the matrix below — so activities carrying independent
noise of variance $\sigma^2$ give coefficients carrying covariance $\sigma^2 \mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\mathrm{T}}$, and
the co-field, being linear in them, carries

$$
\mathrm{Var}\,[C_f(\mathbf{r})] = \sigma^2 \left\| \mathbf{G}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{x}_f(\mathbf{r}) \right\|^2, \qquad x_{fj}(\mathbf{r}) = s_{fj} X_{fj}(\mathbf{r})
$$

— one matrix product per block of grid points, no resampling and no refitting. The **hide noise**
tick of the 3D view then draws only what lies more than two standard deviations from zero, and
`pharmacophore --min-z 2` reads features off the same masked map, so that a lobe the noise could
have produced never becomes a feature. The report (`report`) does both by default.

The noise level $\sigma$ is the model's own out-of-fold error, RMSEcv, which is the assay's noise
and the model's error together; `--sigma` sets it directly.

**What this is, precisely.** It is not the Bayesian posterior variance of the co-field, and the
difference is worth stating. Under the Gaussian process whose kernel this is, the prior on the
field weight function is white noise on $L^2$: its value at a point is not a random variable at
all, and the pointwise posterior variance is infinite everywhere. What the prior does allow is the
variance of $\langle w, g\rangle$ for a probe field $g$ of non-zero width — which is exactly the
GP variance of a prediction for a one-atom molecule placed there, and the program already computes
that. The quantity above is the other half of the question: the molecules and the kernel are held
fixed, and the noise in the activities is propagated. It answers *how much of this lobe would
survive the error in the measurements*, which is the question a co-field picture provokes.

**Measured, the mask keeps about a third of the picture, and that third is the part that is stable.**
Eight Sutherland sets, co-fields on a 0.8 Å grid
(`benchmarks/results/cofield_error/table.md`); the training set is then resampled with replacement
thirty times and refitted, and a voxel counts as stable when the sign of its co-field survives
that — a harder perturbation than the formula models, since it moves the molecules too:

| | |
|---|---|
| kept by the mask, of what would have been drawn | **30 %** |
| of the kept part, holds its sign under resampling | **97.8 %** |
| of the cut part | **90.6 %** |
| difference | **+0.072**, 95 % interval [+0.064, +0.083], in the same direction on 8 of 8 sets |

One more figure, for completeness: the bootstrap moves the co-field only about 0.6 times as
far as the closed form allows for, so cutting at two standard deviations is really cutting at
about 3.2 of the bootstrap's — the threshold is conservative, which follows from taking σ to be the
out-of-fold error. What it gets right is *where* the uncertainty is, and the two orderings agree
across the grid at a rank correlation of +0.82. That is what a mask needs, since a mask is an
ordering with a cut-off.

**A co-field at a point, and what an atom there would do.** A co-field is a value per unit
of field, which is not a number anyone can check against anything: a field is not something one
can put somewhere. An atom is. `cofields.atom_effect` gives the overlap of the co-field with one
atom's own Gaussian, which is the same closed-form integral the kernel sums over atom pairs, so
the answer is in the units of the activity -- ppm for a shift, log units for an affinity -- and
says what adding that atom there would add to the prediction. For a continuous indicator field the
atom of its type carries a weight of one, so the number is directly "what one oxygen here does";
for the electrostatic field the weight is a partial charge and has to be given.
`cofield_at_points` reads the co-field itself at a list of places, `cofield_covariance_at` and
`atom_effect_covariance` give the error that the noise in the activities allows, and `contrast_at`
compares two places with the covariance between them taken into account, which matters because two
points a few angstrom apart are built from the same training fields and their errors are far from
independent. Plan item LP3 uses all of this to read a co-field at the ortho, meta and para
positions of a ring; nothing in it is specific to that use.

### The co-field of a nonlinear model: one per molecule

A model with a kernel layer (*Nonlinear kernel layers and multiple kernel learning*) predicts

$$
y(X) = \sum_j a_j\, g\left(K(X, X_j),\, K(X, X),\, K(X_j, X_j)\right) + b,
$$

where $K$ is the linear joint kernel of Eq. (#eq:prediction) and $g$ is the layer: the
identity for the linear model, $\exp(-\gamma d^2)$ for the Gaussian layer, the arc-cosine
function for the arc-cosine layers. The prediction is no longer the overlap of the field with
one fixed co-field, which is why the program refuses to draw one. It is still a differentiable
function of the field, and its derivative with respect to the normalised field of type $f$,
taken at molecule $X$, is a field:

$$
C_{f,X}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_j a_j\, g_s(X, X_j)\, s_{fj} X_{fj}(\mathbf{r}) \;+\; 2 \left[ \sum_j a_j\, g_n(X, X_j) \right] s_{fX} X_f(\mathbf{r}),
$$
<!-- #eq:localcofield -->

with $g_s = \partial g / \partial K(X, X_j)$ and $g_n = \partial g / \partial K(X, X)$. This is the
**local co-field**: the co-field of the linear model tangent to the nonlinear one at $X$. The
prediction of a molecule close to $X$ changes by the overlap of $C_{f,X}$ with the change of
its normalised field, summed over the field types with the usual factors $h_f c_f$, and nothing
else. The two derivatives are closed forms:

| layer | $g_s$ | $g_n$ |
|---|---|---|
| linear | 1 | 0 |
| Gaussian, $g = e^{-\gamma d^2}$ | $2\gamma g$ | $-\gamma g$ |
| arc-cosine, $\cos\theta = K(X,X_j)/\sqrt{K(X,X)K(X_j,X_j)}$ | $(\pi - \theta)/\pi$ | $\sqrt{K(X_j,X_j)/K(X,X)}\,\sin\theta / 2\pi$ |

For the linear layer Eq. (#eq:localcofield) is the ordinary co-field whatever $X$ is. For the
Gaussian layer it is the ordinary co-field with every training molecule weighted by its kernel
similarity to $X$, and with the field taken relative to $X$'s own: the model reads a molecule
through the training molecules that resemble it. The second term lies along $X$'s own field.
With cosine-normalised kernels, which are the default, $K(X, X)$ does not change when the
normalised field moves, so the term has no effect on any prediction and is left out, as the
ordinary co-field leaves out the dependence of the normalisation on the field; without
normalisation it is kept. The unit test moves one atom's weight by a small amount and checks
that the prediction moves by the overlap of Eq. (#eq:localcofield) with the change of the
normalised field, for every layer and both conventions.

Two things are built on the local co-fields of the training molecules:

- **the spread.** Their mean, point by point, is the one co-field to draw for a nonlinear
  model; their standard deviation is a map of where the effect of field depends on the rest of
  the molecule. It is zero everywhere for a linear model and large where the model is not
  additive. Both are read off the same matrix the noise band of the previous section uses, the
  normalised fields of the training molecules at the grid points, so the cost is that of one
  co-field with a matrix product per block of points;
- **the non-linearity index** of a field type,

$$
\nu_f = 1 - \frac{\| \bar{C}_f \|^2}{\frac{1}{n} \sum_X \| C_{f,X} \|^2},
$$

  the share of the mean squared norm of the local co-fields that their spread around the mean
  makes up: 0 for a linear model, 1 when the local co-fields have nothing in common. The norms
  are overlap integrals, and the local co-fields are combinations of the training fields, so
  the index is read off the Gram matrix $\mathbf{B} \mathbf{K}_f \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{T}}$ with
  $\mathbf{B}$ the coefficient matrix of Eq. (#eq:localcofield) and $\mathbf{K}_f$ the training
  kernel of the field, which the model keeps; nothing is evaluated on a grid. The mean cosine
  between the local co-fields of two training molecules is reported beside it, and a joint
  index takes all the fields together, weighted as the joint kernel weighs them.

`cmf cofield --kind local --molecule FILE` writes the local co-field at that molecule as cube
files, and `--kind spread` writes the spread and the mean (`<prefix>_spread_<field>.cube` and
`<prefix>_spreadmean_<field>.cube`) and prints the index of every field; in Python the three
are `cmfqsar.nonlinearity.local_cofield_coefficients`, `cofield_spread` and
`nonlinearity_indices`. The application does not draw them yet.

**What it measures, and what it does not.** The maps describe the tangent models, not the
chemistry by themselves. The Gaussian layer makes every model nonlinear to a degree set by its
bandwidth, so the spread is nonzero even when the measured relation is additive, as long as
$\gamma$ is finite. Three checks go with the maps: the linear model's $q^2$ beside the layered
one (if the linear kernel predicts as well, the spread is a property of the kernel), the
stability of the maps under refitting on part of the set, and a target made non-additive on
purpose, whose index must come out higher. Second derivatives, how the effect of field at one
place depends on the field at another, are a function of two points and not a field; they are
not drawn here.

**Measured** (`benchmarks/run_nonlinearity.py`, `results/nonlinearity/`), on the Hammett set of
`benchmarks/run_hammett.py`, the substituted benzenes in one frame: one conformer per
substituent, Gasteiger charges, the five
physicochemical fields, $\alpha$, $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ by 10-fold cross-validation. The fourth
target is $\sigma_p \cdot \pi$ on the 69 substituents that have both, a product of two constants
and therefore quadratic in the fields if each factor is linear in them.

| target | n | q² linear | q² Gaussian layer | γ | index, joint | index, electrostatic | spread map, stability | mean map, stability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| σm | 95 | 0.70 | 0.80 | 1 | 0.20 | 0.18 | 1.00 | 0.99 |
| σp | 95 | 0.66 | 0.78 | 0.5 | 0.10 | 0.08 | 0.99 | 0.99 |
| π | 69 | 0.72 | 0.88 | 1 | 0.32 | 0.41 | 0.87 | 0.54 |
| σp · π | 69 | 0.19 | 0.44 | 1 | 0.41 | 0.42 | 0.96 | 0.80 |

Stability is the mean correlation between the maps of five refits on random four-fifths of the
set. Four things follow. The index orders the targets as it should: the product made
non-additive on purpose has the largest index, 0.41, and $\sigma_p$ the smallest, 0.10, with a
mean cosine of 0.94 between its local co-fields, so its model is close to additive and its mean
local co-field is the linear co-field with slightly sharper lobes (figure). The constants
themselves are not linear in the *normalised* field: the Gaussian layer gains 0.10 to 0.16 in
$q^2$ on all three, most on $\pi$. One likely reason, not tested here, is that $\pi$ grows with
the size of the substituent while a cosine-normalised kernel does not see size. The spread maps
survive refitting on three of the four targets at a correlation of 0.96 or better; on $\pi$ the
chosen $\lambda$ is $10^{-4}$, the fit is close to interpolation and the mean map changes from
refit to refit (0.54), which is the stability check doing its job: that map should not be read.
And the spread of $\sigma_p$ sits at the ipso carbon and the first atom of the substituent,
which says that the effect of charge there depends on what the rest of the substituent is, while
for the product it covers the whole substituent region.

![The electrostatic field in the ring plane, for σp (top) and for the product σp · π (bottom): the co-field of the linear model, the mean of the local co-fields of the Gaussian layer, and their spread over the 95 (69) training molecules. For σp the mean local co-field is the linear co-field, slightly sharpened, and the spread is confined to the ipso position; for the target made non-additive on purpose the mean map differs from the linear one and the spread covers the substituent.](docs/figures/nonlinearity_maps.png)

### Second derivatives: the pair-interaction field and the interaction modes

The local co-field says what more field at one place does. Whether that depends on the field
at another place is a second derivative. Taken with respect to the field at two points it is a
function of two points, not a field, and on its diagonal it carries a Dirac delta; so the program
takes it with respect to the amplitudes of **probe atoms** instead: Gaussians of the field's own
width added to the molecule's raw field, one at each place, with amplitudes $\varepsilon_k$.
With $X_f + \sum_k \varepsilon_k p_k$ in place of the field, the prediction is an ordinary
function of the amplitudes, and the chain rule through the layer gives

$$
\frac{\partial y}{\partial \varepsilon_k} = \sum_j a_j \left[ g_s S_{jk} + g_n n_k \right],
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial \varepsilon_k \, \partial \varepsilon_l} = \sum_j a_j \left[ g_{ss} S_{jk} S_{jl} + g_{sn} \left( S_{jk} n_l + n_k S_{jl} \right) + g_{nn} n_k n_l + g_s S_{jkl} + g_n n_{kl} \right],
$$
<!-- #eq:probehessian -->

where $S_{jk}$ and $S_{jkl}$ are the derivatives of the linear joint kernel $K(X, X_j)$ with
respect to the amplitudes, $n_k$ and $n_{kl}$ those of the self-kernel $K(X, X)$, and the
$g$'s the derivatives of the layer. All of them are closed forms in three overlap integrals: the
probe with the molecule's own field, the probe with each training field, and probe with probe
(the docstring of `cmfqsar/nonlinearity.py` writes them out). The normalisation of the kernels
is differentiated exactly rather than argued away, and the unit tests check the result against
second differences of the prediction, with the probes on the molecule's own atoms and at
arbitrary points in space, for both conventions. Three things follow from the formula. A linear
model without normalisation has no second derivative at all. With cosine normalisation even
the linear model has one, because a normalised field cannot grow without bound: that is a
non-additivity of the kernel, not of the data, and the maps show it. The arc-cosine layers are
refused: their kernel has a cusp where a molecule meets a training molecule, and the second
derivative diverges there.

Three readings of Eq. (#eq:probehessian) are implemented:

- the **pair-interaction field** (`cmf cofield --kind pair --molecule FILE --probe-atom K`,
  `nonlinearity.pair_interaction_field`): one probe fixed on atom $K$ of the molecule, carrying
  that atom's weight in the field, the other scanned over the grid. The value at $\mathbf{r}$ is
  how much adding field there changes what the fixed atom does: positive where the two reinforce
  each other, negative where one undoes part of the other, zero where the model treats the two
  places additively. `--probe-field` puts the fixed probe in another field type than the one
  drawn;
- the **curvature field** (`--kind curvature`, `nonlinearity.curvature_field`), the diagonal:
  the second derivative along one probe, negative where the model saturates and positive where
  it accelerates. Its first-derivative companion `nonlinearity.gradient_field` is what one unit
  of a probe adds, the `atom_effect` of a linear model generalised to a layer;
- the **atom interaction matrix** and its **modes** (`--kind modes`,
  `nonlinearity.atom_interactions`, `nonlinearity.interaction_modes`): the second derivatives
  with respect to the weights of every pair of the molecule's own atoms -- two partial charges,
  say -- beside the first derivatives, which under a layer take the place of the atom
  contributions. The eigenvectors of the matrix are patterns of atoms whose weights the model
  reads together; the eigenvalue is the curvature along the pattern, positive when the changes
  in it reinforce one another, negative when they saturate. The command prints the leading
  modes with the atoms that carry them and writes the matrix with `--csv`.

All three are in the units of the activity per unit of amplitude squared, so a pair term is
judged by multiplying it by two realistic amplitudes -- two partial charges, two indicator
weights of one -- and comparing the product with what the first derivatives give for the same
changes. Where the product is small against that, the model is additive there for every
practical purpose, whatever the map looks like.

**Measured** (`benchmarks/run_interactions.py`, `results/interactions/`). No measured set in the
repository has a known non-additive pair, so the benchmark makes one: 105 para-disubstituted
benzenes X-C$_6$H$_4$-Y from 14 substituents, built in the frame of the Hammett example, with an
additive activity $\sigma_p(X) + \sigma_p(Y)$ and an interacting one that adds
$1.5\,\sigma_p(X)\,\sigma_p(Y)$, both with 0.02 units of noise; five fields, unnormalised
kernels, the Gaussian layer, $\alpha$, $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ by 10-fold cross-validation. The
pair term costs the linear kernel 0.17 in $q^2$ (0.99 to 0.82) and the layer recovers most of it
(0.95). The interacting activity has an exact second derivative: with $c_k$ the sensitivity of
$\sigma$ to the charge of atom $k$, the cross derivative between an atom of X and an atom of Y
is $1.5\,c_k c_l$ and there is none within a group; the additive activity has none anywhere.
Reading $c_k$ off the additive model's first derivatives, every cross pair of every molecule
(78 molecules with X and Y both other than H and different) has a designed value, and the
fitted values are regressed on it through the origin:

| model | slope, atom pairs | correlation | slope, pair field near Y | correlation | within-group RMS over the designed cross RMS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| additive | 0.06 | 0.30 | 0.08 | 0.42 | 0.35 |
| interacting | 1.87 | 0.73 | 1.43 | 0.67 | 2.39 |

The pair field near Y is the field with the probe fixed on the first heavy atom of X, within 2 Å
of the Y group, against its designed shape, $1.5\,c_k$ times the fixed atom's charge times the
additive model's first-derivative field there. Three things follow. The designed pair term is
recovered where there is one and absent where there is none: slopes of 1.9 and 1.4 against 0.06
and 0.08, correlations of 0.7 against 0.3 to 0.4, and the pair field of one molecule is stable
under refitting on four-fifths of the set (correlation 0.97). The size is overstated by a factor
of 1.4 to 1.9, and the within-group block of the interacting model, which should be zero, is
2.4 times the designed cross block in root mean square: a Gaussian layer that has learnt a pair
term is curved within the groups too. And *where* the curvature sits does not tell the two
models apart: the share of the atom matrix between the two groups is 0.10 for the additive model
and 0.09 for the interacting one (0.07 for the share of pairs), and the share of the pair field
near Y is 0.32 against 0.28 (0.08 of the volume) -- the layer puts curvature where the training
fields are, whatever the target. The signal of a pair term is the *size* of the second
derivative, which is why the figure draws the two models on one colour scale and why the advice
above is to judge a pair term by its product with realistic amplitudes. Between two sites the
sign and the order of magnitude can be read; within one site the values are mostly the kernel's
own curvature, and a reference model of an additive quantity, when one exists, is the right thing
to subtract.

![The pair-interaction field of the electrostatic field in the ring plane for OCH3-C6H4-NO2, the fixed probe (green ring) on the oxygen of the methoxy group, the nitro group on the far side: the model of the additive activity, the model of the interacting one, and their difference, on one colour scale. The additive model's field is small everywhere; the interacting model's is large, negative over the nitro group and around the probe, positive beyond the methoxy group.](docs/figures/pair_fields.png)

## Shapley values

The *Shapley* tab decomposes a single prediction into additive contributions by the Shapley
construction, over **atoms**, over **substituents of the common scaffold**, or over **field
types**, with second-order interaction indices available. It serves two purposes. With the linear
kernel it reproduces the atom contributions exactly, which is a useful check. With a nonlinear
kernel layer, where co-fields do not exist, it is the only decomposition left — and it still works,
because it needs nothing but the ability to evaluate the model on subsets.

## A pharmacophore out of the co-field

*Tools → Extract pharmacophore from the co-field…* turns the co-field into a discrete, typed
pharmacophore: the favourable lobes of each field become feature points of the matching kind
(positive and negative centres, hydrophobe, donor, acceptor), each with a tolerance radius taken
from the size of its lobe, and the unfavourable steric lobes — or the pocket, when a protein is
loaded — become exclusion volumes. The result is a table and a PDB-style file of feature spheres
that other software can read, and it draws in the 3D view; untick *pharmacophore* in the viewer
controls to clear it.

This is the bridge from a CMF model to a screening query: the model is continuous and needs an
alignment, the pharmacophore is discrete and does not.

![The pharmacophore extracted from the steroid model of chapter 8 at half height, drawn over the electrostatic and the steric co-field in the mean plane with the most active training molecule: each feature is a circle of its tolerance radius at its centre, fainter the further it lies from the plane, coloured by its kind, and an exclusion volume is dashed. The favourable lobes of each field have become typed points, the unfavourable steric lobes exclusion volumes, and that set of spheres is what the query files of the next part carry.](docs/figures/pharmacophore.png)

### Taking the query out of the program

```bash
python cmf_cli.py pharmacophore model.cmf --min-z 2 --query query.json
python cmf_cli.py pharmacophore model.cmf --min-z 2 --query query.pml --enable-top 3
```

`.json` writes a **Pharmit** session and `.pml` the **LigandScout-style XML**; both are written
to the documented shape of those formats, which is as far as this program can go — it cannot
test any particular viewer. Three things about the file are worth knowing before it is opened
somewhere else.

**A query is a conjunction**, so a dozen features at once matches nothing. The strongest
`--enable-top` features are written switched on and the rest switched off, for the user to choose
among in their own program; exclusion spheres are always on, since they only forbid.

**Hydrogen-bond features have no direction.** A co-field says that a donor *here* raises the
activity; it says nothing about where the hydrogen points, so the features are written as
isotropic points rather than as the vectors those formats usually carry.

**Three of this program's feature types cannot be expressed at all** and are reported rather than
quietly dropped. `bulk` asks for atoms of any kind, which no query language expresses. The
disfavoured `polar`, `acceptor_bad` and `donor_bad` say that one *particular* kind of group is
unwelcome; the only negative a query has is an exclusion sphere, and that would forbid every
atom, which is a much stronger claim than the co-field makes.

### Is the query any good, measured

Eight Sutherland sets, five 70/30 splits each. The pharmacophore is read out of the
training model's co-fields — masked at two standard deviations first, so that a lobe the
measurement error could have produced never becomes a feature — and its strongest four features
are matched against the molecules held out, by the simple rule a screening program uses: an atom
of the right kind inside the sphere. The actives are the most active quarter.

| set | n | features | AUC query | AUC random centres | AUC the model |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DHFR | 361 | 7.4 | 0.573 | 0.498 | 0.901 |
| COX2 | 282 | 8.4 | 0.662 | 0.478 | 0.867 |
| BZR | 147 | 7.8 | 0.518 | 0.514 | 0.797 |
| ACE | 114 | 7.0 | 0.789 | 0.552 | 0.927 |
| AChE | 111 | 7.8 | 0.631 | 0.484 | 0.903 |
| THR | 88 | 8.4 | 0.595 | 0.468 | 0.780 |
| THER | 76 | 7.2 | 0.711 | 0.482 | 0.812 |
| GPB | 66 | 6.8 | 0.838 | 0.484 | 0.902 |
| **mean** |  |  | **0.665** | **0.495** | **0.861** |

The query separates the active quarter at an AUC of 0.665, against
0.495 for the same features moved to random places in the same box — a paired
difference of +0.170 with a 95 % interval of [+0.102, +0.238], so the places the co-field picked are doing the work, and
ahead on 36 of 40 splits. Over every split together the top tenth by the
query holds 1.77 times as many actives as chance would put there.

**The model it was read from reaches 0.861 on the same molecules**, and that gap
is the price of the summary: a pharmacophore is four spheres and a rule for counting them, while
the model is every training molecule's field weighed by a fitted coefficient. What the query gains
is that it can leave this program — it goes into a screening tool and runs over libraries no kernel
method here could hold.



## What a candidate is missing

*Tools → Field difference from a reference molecule…* subtracts two molecules' fields on the
co-field grid and reports, per field type, the cosine between them, the distance, and how much of
the reference's field the candidate **fails to reproduce** against how much it **adds**. The
difference map draws as its own isosurface, and the table ranks the whole data set by field
similarity to the reference. In a lead-optimisation reading: the "missing" column is what to put
back, the "added" column is what may be causing trouble.

## Several endpoints at once: the selectivity co-field

A separation problem, or any selectivity, is not one property but two: an extractant has an
affinity for americium and an affinity for europium, and what matters is the difference. A model
of the ratio works, but it throws information away. Each affinity has its own measurements, often
on partly different compounds; a ligand that binds both metals strongly looks, to a model of the
ratio, exactly like one that binds neither; and the ratio cannot say *which* of the two affinities
a substituent moved.

*Tools → Model several endpoints (selectivity co-field)…* fits every endpoint you tick on the
kernel of the model you have already built, with one bias per endpoint and a task covariance that
lets them share information with each other:

$$
y_t(X) = \sum_j c_{jt}\,K(X, X_j) + b_t ,
$$

where the coefficients of the two endpoints are tied through a single correlation $\rho$. At
$\rho = 0$ the endpoints are modelled separately and share only the kernel; as $\rho$ rises they
share information; at $\rho = 1$ the two sets of coefficients coincide and the model could
only predict a *constant* selectivity, so 1 is excluded (and $\rho$ may be negative, for endpoints
that move in opposite directions). The dialog searches $\rho$ and the ridge by cross-validation,
and the cross-validation holds out whole **molecules**, never single measurements: with a
molecule's first endpoint in the training set and its second in the test set, the correlation would
reveal the answer.

Because each endpoint's prediction is linear in the field with its own coefficients, each endpoint
has a co-field, and so does their difference — the **selectivity co-field**

$$
C_A(\mathbf{r}) - C_B(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_j (c_{jA} - c_{jB})\, X_j(\mathbf{r}) ,
$$

a map of where more of a field raises the first endpoint more than the second. Only a model
linear in the field can produce it; it is available here for the same reason co-fields are
available at all, and it is refused for a model with a nonlinear kernel layer.

![The selectivity co-field of the 57 AMPA / glycine-NMDA antagonists of `examples/selectivity`, AMPA minus glycine, in the plane of the tricyclic core, with the most AMPA-selective compound drawn over it. A red lobe is a place where more of that field shifts the preference towards the AMPA receptor, a blue one towards the glycine site. The two-endpoint fit has its correlation and ridge chosen by cross-validation.](docs/figures/selectivity.png)

Once the fit is made, an **Endpoint** box appears in the *Maps* row of the control strip with one
entry per endpoint and one for the difference of the pair you named — and every map, export and
contribution table then refers to the chosen one; a cube exported while the selectivity is chosen
carries it in its file name. The endpoints are numeric properties of the data set, so the ones
beyond the first are imported with *File → Import activities from CSV…* or read from columns of
