field of the cell is the field of the host plus the field of that change: a vacancy is the host
atom with its weights negated, a substitution is that row and the new species on the same site
(`periodic.defect_fields`, `periodic.defect_table`; `periodic.match_sites` finds the site of
every atom at the nearest image). The kernel is bilinear, so the kernel of two difference fields
is the kernel of the two whole cells minus terms that are the same for every pair, and a model
with a bias on the differences is the model on the whole cells -- the tests check it to 1e-7 on
real cells. The differences are small tables, a few rows per cell instead of two hundred, and
they are not normalised: the pristine cell is the empty difference, and its norm is zero.

**The host symmetry.** Two arrangements of the same defects that differ by a symmetry operation
of the host -- the same vacancy pair two sites along -- have the same energy, but in a fixed
frame their fields do not overlap at all. The kernel is therefore averaged over the space group
of the host, read from spglib (`periodic.host_symmetry`; 768 operations for an 8 x 8 supercell
of a monolayer, 64 translations times 12 point operations):

$$
\bar{K}(P, Q) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} K(P, gQ)
$$

which is the kernel of the orbit-averaged fields and so a kernel in its own right. Averaged this
way, the **linear** overlap turns out to be a count kernel: the orbit mean of a defect's field is
the same wherever the defect sits, so the average is additive over the defects and blind to their
arrangement. That is a useful baseline and not the kernel the series needs. The arrangement
survives when the **Gaussian layer** is averaged over the group instead,

$$
\bar{K}_{\gamma}(P, Q) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \exp\!\left(-\gamma\,[K(P,P) + K(Q,Q) - 2K(P, gQ)]\right),
$$

which is the orbit mean in the layer's feature space, positive semidefinite for the same reason
(`periodic.symmetry_averaged_kernels`; `CMFModel(..., pbc_overlap=True, pbc_symmetry=...)`). A
compiled loop (`fastkernel.defect_kernels`) takes every atom pair at its nearest image in
fractional coordinates, with the cutoff capped at half the cell, and sums both averages at once:
125 s for 2,000 cells and 768 operations, against hours for the image-expanded reference, which
the tests keep for agreement. The per-atom contributions of rule 3 go through the same loop.

**Measured** on 2DMD (Huang et al. 2023): one to three vacancies and substitutions on the 8 x 8
supercell of MoS2 and of WSe2, the DFT formation energy of the cell, 2,000 random cells per
material and then all 5,933, five random folds with the attenuation, the bandwidth and the ridge
chosen inside each training
part (`benchmarks/run_2dmd.py`, `benchmarks/results/2dmd/table.md`). All 5,933 cells of each
material are distinct under the host group, so every test cell is an arrangement the model has
not seen. The error per defect site, which is what the literature on this set reports:

| kernel | MoS2, 2,000 cells | WSe2, 2,000 cells | MoS2, all 5,933 | WSe2, all 5,933 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fixed frame, no symmetry | 60 | 57 | 42 | 42 |
| counts (the linear symmetry average) | 41 | 42 | 41 | 41 |
| periodic autocorrelation | 8.3 | 15.7 | 3.0 | 6.0 |
| **arrangement** (the symmetry-averaged layer) | **1.8** | **5.2** | **1.9** | **4.4** |

On 2,000 cells the arrangement kernel beats the autocorrelation by 6.5 [5.3, 7.7] and 10.5 [9.1,
12.1] meV per site (paired bootstrap over the cells, 95 %) -- the half of the gate of the previous
section that the perovskites could not test -- and the fixed frame and the counts lose to it by 26
to 52 meV: the symmetry average is what makes the overlap kernel work on a series, and the layer
is what makes it see the arrangement. On all 5,933 cells the autocorrelation gains most from the
extra training cells and the lead of the arrangement kernel shrinks to 1.0 [0.8, 1.2] and 1.5
[1.3, 1.9] meV per site, still with intervals that exclude zero; the fixed frame reaches the
counts, because with enough cells it learns the orbit from the data. The published errors on this
set, on the authors' own split of all 5,933 cells, are 2.6 and 4.8 meV for a sparse graph network
and 11.8 and 14.7 for gradient boosting on descriptors (Kazeev et al. 2023). Trained on the 131
cells with one or two defects and predicting those with three (1,869 in the 2,000-cell sample,
5,802 in the full set), the arrangement kernel reaches 4.3 and 4.7 meV per site on MoS2 and 54 and
38 on WSe2, where the additive count kernel gives 38 on both; the autocorrelation does not
extrapolate at all (R² near zero), and the fixed frame reaches R² 0.6 to 0.8.

**What each kind of defect costs.** The per-defect contributions of the symmetry-averaged linear
model (rule 3) are one number per kind of defect, the same to four decimals in every cell, as the
symmetry requires -- and they are the chemistry the data hold. In MoS2 a sulfur vacancy costs
2.59 eV, a molybdenum vacancy 6.98, selenium for sulfur 0.31 and tungsten for molybdenum 0.19,
against the four single-defect cells of the set at 2.65, 7.12, 0.28 and 0.17 eV; in WSe2 a
selenium vacancy 2.62, a tungsten vacancy 5.09, sulfur for selenium -0.41 and molybdenum for
tungsten -0.42, against 2.70, 5.30, -0.38 and -0.41. The difference is the mean interaction of
the three defects in the cells the model was fitted on. The co-field is not the reading for this
series: averaged over the host group it is one value per site type and says which species, not
where, and the arrangement model has a layer, so rule 3 does not apply to it.

## A site of the cell as the sample: the split of the autocorrelation

The pair histogram $P_{fg}$ of the periodic autocorrelation above is a sum over ordered pairs of
atoms of one cell, and such a sum can be grouped by the atom that stands first in each pair. The
grouping is exact and costs nothing: the same neighbour list, read one row at a time. Writing
$G_k(r)$ for the Gaussian of channel $d_k$ times the taper,

$$
\Phi_{fg}(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{l\,\in\,\mathrm{cell}} s_l(f,g,d_k),
\qquad
s_l(f,g,d_k) = w_{lf}\sum_{m}\;\sum_{\mathbf{T}} w_{mg}\,G_k\!\left(|\mathbf{r}_l-\mathbf{r}_m-\mathbf{T}|\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:site-split -->

with the second order $s_l(g,f,d_k)$ added for a pair of different field types, the $l=m$ term
where the spec keeps it, and the uniform background of that site subtracted, exactly as the whole
cell has them. The row $s_l$ is the **profile of site $l$**: which field type stands how far from
it, with the periodic images summed in. It is the periodic counterpart of the atom-centred
environment of the next section, with two differences. Nothing is cut out of the solid, so a site
deep in a crystal is described as it is and not as the middle of a cluster; and the profile is
one-centred -- pairs that start at the site -- rather than all pairs inside an envelope.

`cmfqsar/sites.py` (plan item M5) holds it. `site_autocorrelation` returns the rows, and their
mean is the descriptor of the cell to machine precision, which is the property the module is
tested on. The rows are not divided by the number of atoms, so a site profile does not change
when the same site is written in a larger supercell.

**A site is a sample.** `site_fields(crystal, site)` returns the cell with that site as its
centre, and the periodic autocorrelation of such a record is that site's row. Everything else
follows without new machinery: `site_table` builds the table, `CMFModel(kernel_source="periodic")`
fits it, and the targets are the ones `cmfqsar/atomtargets.py` already holds -- one array per
structure, *not a number* where a site was not measured. The folds hold out whole **structures**:
two sites of one cell, one in the training set and one in the test set, would let the model see
the cell it is being tested on.

The descriptor needs no alignment, because it is built from distances. Its pair term is local --
only neighbours inside the cutoff enter it -- but its background is not, being the mean field of
the whole cell times the shell integral, so two cells of different composition have different
backgrounds at the same site. With `background=False` the profile depends on nothing beyond the
cutoff.

**What a site profile is worth.** The first set is the single-atom catalysts of the EC8 pilot
(`benchmarks/run_sac.py`, which cuts the site out of the sheet and is the thing to be level
with): the metal site of 139 M@C(4-x)Nx sheets, with the binding energies of H, O and OH on 104
of them and of OOH on 91. Six bare sheets have been recomputed with plain PBE since the pilot
ran and more are being recomputed, so these numbers are not comparable with the pilot's own and
every reference here is recomputed on the same catalysts. Three designs of folds, as the pilot
used: random catalysts, a whole metal held out, a whole motif held out. Every descriptor is a
family -- three field sets by three cutoffs for the site profile and for the whole cell, the
widths and attenuations of the pilot for the cut cluster -- and each family chooses inside an
inner cross-validation of the same kind as the outer folds, so the comparison favours none. Mean
q² over the four endpoints:

| Descriptor | Random catalysts | One metal held out | One motif held out |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **site profile of the cell (M5)** | **+0.792** | **+0.721** | **+0.755** |
| the cut cluster, invariant (LP2) | +0.801 | +0.739 | +0.712 |
| the cut cluster, overlap kernel (EC8) | +0.782 | +0.695 | +0.724 |
| the whole cell, autocorrelation | +0.794 | +0.756 | +0.744 |
| counts in shells around the site | +0.758 | +0.096 | +0.749 |

**The site profile does what cutting the site out of the sheet does, without cutting it, and
nothing more.** Of the twelve paired comparisons (four endpoints by three designs, the catalysts
resampled) it is level with everything built from fields: against the cut cluster better in two
and worse in one for the overlap kernel, better in one and worse in none for the invariant one;
against the whole cell better in one (the OH binding with a motif held out, +0.066) and worse in
two (the O and OOH binding with a metal held out, -0.046 and -0.085). It is clearly better only
than the counts, in five of the twelve, never losing to them. So the site resolution saves the
cut and the termination of a cluster, which is worth having on a site that cannot be cut out
cleanly, and it buys no accuracy on this set. The counts are the other reading of that table:
they hold their own when the metals are known and collapse to +0.096 when a metal is new, which
is what a descriptor made of element labels does, while every descriptor built from fields keeps
most of its accuracy. The set is small enough to move: the recomputed sheet added between two
runs of this benchmark took every method's OOH q² from about +0.93 to about +0.77, so the
differences between the methods are worth reading and their absolute values are not. The full
table is in `benchmarks/results/sites/table.md` (`benchmarks/run_sites.py`).

**Many sites in one cell.** The second set is the bond-valence site energy of every lithium site
of the three solid electrolytes of `examples/hops`: 104 sites in beta-Li3PO4, Li3BP2O8 and
alpha-LiBO2, where a fold is a whole compound the model has never seen. There the site profile
**fails as an absolute predictor and works as a ranking**. It cannot place a compound it has not
seen on the energy scale: the offsets are -0.12, +0.04 and +0.13 eV and the overall q² is
negative for every method, the counts and the mean of the other compounds included, because with
three compounds almost all of the variance is between them. Inside a compound it orders the sites
-- Spearman +0.78, +0.84 and +0.55, and q² about the compound's own mean +0.60 for the phosphate
and +0.77 for the borophosphate. The borate is the third case: its sites differ by 0.007 eV,
which is nothing to predict.

**A whole-cell model read site by site.** The split works in the other direction as well. A model
on the whole-cell descriptor is linear in the channels, the channels of a cell are the mean of
its site profiles, so the prediction minus the bias is a sum of one number per site:

$$
\hat{y}(i) - b = \sum_{l\,\in\,\mathrm{cell}\,i} c_l,
\qquad
c_l = \frac{1}{N}\;\frac{\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\mathbf{s}_l\right)\cdot\mathbf{w}}{\|\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\mathbf{x}_i\|}
$$
<!-- #eq:site-contrib -->

with $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ the channel scale, $\mathbf{x}_i$ the cell's channels and $\mathbf{w}$
the co-pattern of the fitted linear model (`periodic.channel_weights`). Nothing is attributed:
this is rule 3 for the autocorrelation kernel, and `sites.site_contributions` returns the
numbers. That is the local reading the autocorrelation could not give. A distance distribution
says which pair of field types at which distance raises the property; the split says **which site
of the cell** carries it.

On a model of the OH binding energy over the 104 catalysts (q² +0.893 in five folds, 0.51 eV) the
weight falls where a chemist would put it: the metal site carries 8.9 % of it, which is 11.3
times what an even spread over the 127 sites of the sheet would put there, and the metal with its
four neighbours carries 16.0 % against 3.9 %. Beyond 5 Å from the metal every site carries about
half of an even share. The channels of the metal site say what the model reads there: for Pt@C4
the d electron count at the site itself, for Fe@N4 the electrostatic field at 2.0 Å, which is the
first shell.

![What each site of the sheet adds to the predicted OH binding energy of a whole-cell model, for Fe@N4 and Pt@C4: red raises the binding energy, blue lowers it, the circled atom is the metal and the labelled ones its four neighbours. The right panel is the weight per site by distance from the metal, divided by the weight an even spread over the sites would give; the dashed line is that even spread. The metal site carries eleven times its share and everything beyond 5 Å about half. Drawn by `benchmarks/run_sites.py`.](benchmarks/results/sites/contributions.png)

**The limits.** The height channels of a layer have no site split in this version: a site profile
of a slab is taken with `z_max = 0` and does not tell a neighbour above the plane from one below
it at the same distance. The contributions are defined for the linear kernel layer, as the
co-pattern is. And the background of a site profile is a property of the whole cell, so a set of
unrelated cells carries their compositions in it; a series on one host lattice does not have that
difficulty.

### A map as an output mode

The split above is a reading for a person: red and blue spheres on a molecule, a number per site of
a cell. A coarser model needs the same numbers as data — a barrier per site, a reactivity per
surface site, a growth rate per patch — and that is an output mode rather than a figure. It is
`cmfqsar.sitemap` (plan item MS2), and it holds two different maps behind one entry.

**The split of one prediction.** `site_map(model, structure)` returns a `SiteMap`: one number per
place, where each place is, the fitted constant as a place of its own, and the prediction the model
itself made. A molecule is split over its atoms by rule 3 and a periodic cell over its sites by
Eq. (#eq:site-contrib), so the caller does not have to know which kernel the model carries. The
constant is kept apart because it belongs to no place, and with it the column adds up to the
prediction exactly: `SiteMap.check()` verifies that, and the entry runs it by default.

```python
from cmfqsar.sitemap import by_element, region_map, site_map

m = site_map(model, mol, units="log units")
print(m.prediction, m.total, m.bias)    # the second is the first, to round-off
m.write_table("map.csv")                # one row per place, with x, y, z
region_map(m, by_element(mol))          # the same map, grouped
```

**Regions.** A place of a coarse model is rarely one atom. `region_map` groups the places and sums
their numbers, which needs no new mathematics because a split is additive: `by_element` collects
each element, `shells_around` collects them by distance from one place, measured through the images
when the structure is periodic, and any grouping of indices can be given directly. A place may
belong to one region at most, because a split is shared out and not copied, and the places left
over are collected into one region so that the total still holds; dropping them instead is allowed
and the map then says in a note that it no longer adds up.

**A prediction per site.** The second map is not a split. A site model (the first part of this
chapter) takes one site of a cell as its sample, so it can be asked about every site of a cell:
`site_predictions(model, crystal)` returns one answer per site, in the units of the property. The
two must not be confused, and a map says which it holds in its `quantity` field. A contribution is
a share of one structure's answer; a prediction is an answer of its own. `SiteMap.check` refuses a
map of predictions for exactly that reason: there is no total for it to check.

**On the command line.** `cmf sites MODEL STRUCTURES --out map.csv` writes either map, choosing by
what the model was fitted on, and `--regions elements` or `--regions shells --centre I` group the
places first. The table has one row per place with the columns `structure, place, label, atoms, x,
y, z, quantity, value`: a reader that steps on places keeps the rows it needs, and a reader that
wants the structure's own answer back adds the `value` column of one structure, constant included.
`--json` writes the same maps with every number.

**What has no map.** Four kernels are refused by name, with the reason: the in-plane surface
channels, whose places are columns of a slab rather than atoms; the reciprocal-space structure
factors, which are sums over the cell as a whole; the three-body channels, whose shares belong to
triangles and not to single atoms; and the periodic overlap kernel, where a place of one cell
overlaps places of every image of the other. A nonlinear kernel layer is refused as well, as rule 3
is, and the Shapley values take its place.

**Does the map rank the sites as a site model ranks them?** This is the gate of item MS2 and the
answer is in two parts. The arithmetic half holds exactly: on the single-atom catalyst set the sum
of the places and the constant differs from the prediction by at most 3.5e-13, which is round-off.
The ranking half does not hold, and the measurement says why. Both models are fitted on the same
catalysts with the same kernel, the same cutoff and the same ridge value — only the sample differs,
a cell for one and the measured site of a cell for the other — and everything below is out of
fold. The catalyst set has grown since the numbers earlier in this chapter were computed, so the
counts differ between the two; the comparison here is internal to it.

| Target | Catalysts | The metal is the largest place | Weight on the metal | Within a cell, mean rho | At the measured site, across cells |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| dE_H | 133 | 72 % | 11.7 % | +0.465 | +0.219 |
| dE_O | 133 | 62 % | 9.0 % | +0.476 | +0.743 |
| dE_OH | 133 | 77 % | 8.1 % | +0.350 | +0.600 |
| dE_OOH | 119 | 69 % | 8.6 % | +0.025 | -0.001 |

The split locates the property. The binding energy of these catalysts belongs to the metal site,
and the split puts its largest number there in 62 to 77 % of the cells -- its median rank is 1 on
every target -- giving it 8.1 to 11.7 % of the weight where an even spread over the 127 sites of
the sheet would give it 0.8 %, ten to fifteen times its share. What the split does not do is
reproduce the site model's ordering of all the sites of a cell: the mean rank correlation inside a
cell is +0.025 to +0.476 and it passes +0.7 on at most 13 % of the cells. Across the cells, at the
one site of each cell that was measured, it is -0.001 to +0.743, which passes +0.7 on one target of
the four.

Two reasons, and neither is a fault in either model. The quantities differ: a contribution says how
much of this cell's answer came from this place, and a prediction says what would be measured at
that place, so the sites a cell model leans on need not be the sites that bind most strongly. And
the site model was fitted on the metal site of every cell and on no other site, so its answers at
the carbon and nitrogen sites are extrapolation — the gate compares the split against a model that
was never shown the places the comparison runs over. The reading that stays inside both models'
training data is the two predictions themselves, and there they agree closely:

| Target | Cell model against site model | Cell model against the measurement | Site model against the measurement |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| dE_H | +0.968 | +0.771 | +0.762 |
| dE_O | +0.987 | +0.927 | +0.927 |
| dE_OH | +0.992 | +0.952 | +0.956 |
| dE_OOH | +0.971 | +0.883 | +0.862 |

So the map is usable as an output mode — that is the first half of the gate, and the weight it puts
on the metal — while the ordering it gives inside a cell is a statement about the cell model and
not a site-level prediction. For a number per site to hand to a coarser model, fit a site model and
use `site_predictions`; the split says which places the cell model read, which is what interpreting
it needs. The full table is in `benchmarks/results/sites/table.md`
(`benchmarks/run_sites.py --agreement`).

## Order the cutoff cannot reach: the reciprocal-space channels

Everything above is a sum over a neighbour list, so a crystal is described out to $r_{\max}$ and
no further. A superstructure with a long repeat, a modulation, the long-range part of the
electrostatic interaction: none of them reaches the descriptor. The channels that do cost nothing
for the distance, because they are sums over the atoms of **one cell** with no neighbour list at
all (plan item M6, `cmfqsar/reciprocal.py`).

For a field $f$ and a vector $\mathbf{G}$ of the reciprocal lattice -- the lattice of vectors with
$\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{T} = 2\pi n$ for every lattice translation $\mathbf{T}$ -- the **typed
structure factor** is

$$
S_f(\mathbf{G}) = \sum_{l\,\in\,\mathrm{cell}} w_{lf}\, \exp\!\left(i\,\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}_l\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:structure-factor -->

It is the Fourier transform of the field of the whole infinite crystal at $\mathbf{G}$, and it is
what a diffraction experiment measures: $|S_f(\mathbf{G})|^2$ is the intensity of the Bragg
reflection at $\mathbf{G}$ when field $f$ is the scattering power. One value of $S_f$ already
holds information about the whole structure, however far the order extends, which is why these
channels have no cutoff radius.

The channel at the reciprocal length $q_k$ for a pair of field types is the intensity of that
pair, averaged over the directions of $\mathbf{G}$:

$$
\Psi_{fg}(q_k) = \dfrac{1}{N}\left[\, \dfrac{(2\pi)^3}{V\,I_k} \sum_{\mathbf{G} \neq 0} A_{fg}(\mathbf{G})\, F(|\mathbf{G}|)\, B_k(|\mathbf{G}|) \;+\; \left(e_{fg} - c_{fg}\right) \langle F \rangle_k \,\right]
$$
<!-- #eq:reciprocal-channel -->

with $A_{fg} = |S_f|^2$ for one field type and $2\,\mathrm{Re}\,[S_f \overline{S_g}]$ for two,
which counts a pair of different types in both orders as the real-space descriptor does;
$B_k(q) = \omega(q)\exp(-(q-q_k)^2/2\sigma^2)$ the channel with the same tapered window as the
real-space cutoff; $I_k = \int 4\pi q^2 B_k(q)\,\mathrm{d}q$ its shell integral, which is how
many reciprocal-lattice points the channel is expected to hold; $V$ the volume of the cell and
$N$ its atoms. The term outside the sum is the part of $A_{fg}$ that comes from an atom with
itself, $c_{fg} = \sum_l w_{lf} w_{lg}$ from the weights and $e_{fg}$ the same sum of the second
moments of a disordered site. The two are equal for an ordered structure, so that term vanishes
there; where they differ it is the correction partial occupancy asks for. Neither is summed over
the lattice: a quantity that does not depend on $\mathbf{G}$ contributes $\langle F \rangle_k$,
the mean of the form factor over the channel, and taking it from that integral instead of from
the grid is what makes the descriptor independent of the choice of cell **exactly** -- a cell with
few atoms holds few reciprocal-lattice points per channel, and a sum would estimate a constant
differently in a supercell of the same structure.

**The width of the field is a resolution.** $F(q) = \exp(-a^2 q^2)$ is the form factor: the two
fields are Gaussians of width $a$, so their product in reciprocal space carries this factor. It
falls with $q$, so $a$ decides how much fine detail reaches the descriptor -- a wide field sees
only the first few reflections. This is the same width the real-space descriptor uses along the
distance axis, read in reciprocal space, and it is a resolution and not a cutoff: every atom of
the cell enters every channel whatever the distances in the structure. A channel at $q$ describes
the structure on the scale $2\pi/q$, which is how these channels are compared with a cutoff
radius.

**Two things the real-space form has only as approximations.** The uniform background is the
$\mathbf{G} = 0$ term, $A_{fg}(0) = (\sum_l w_{lf})(\sum_l w_{lg})$, the forward scattering: here
it is one term of the sum, left out, with no integral to approximate. And the two descriptions are
one object. Summing the field in real space and summing it over the reciprocal lattice give the
same number -- Poisson summation, the identity an Ewald sum is built on -- so for any width $u$,

$$
\sum_{l,m}\sum_{\mathbf{T}} w_{lf} w_{mg} \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{|\mathbf{r}_l - \mathbf{r}_m - \mathbf{T}|^2}{2u^2}\right) = \dfrac{(2\pi u^2)^{3/2}}{V} \sum_{\mathbf{G}} A_{fg}(\mathbf{G})\, \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{u^2 |\mathbf{G}|^2}{2}\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:parseval -->

`parseval_residual` computes both sides. The left side is this program's neighbour list and the
right side is the sum over the reciprocal lattice, so the identity tests the two pieces of code
against each other, and it is the statement that the reciprocal channels are the same descriptor
at a different resolution rather than a second one.

![What a reciprocal-space channel adds. (a) Two cells of a silicon host with two substituted sites, 5.4 angstrom apart in one and 10.9 in the other: the same composition and the same local environment around every atom. (b) The real-space channel of the substituted pair. Everything that separates the two structures lies outside a 4 angstrom cutoff, so the descriptor with that cutoff gives them a kernel of 1.000000 -- for it they are one structure -- while a 12 angstrom cutoff reaches the first peak and gives 0.947. (c) The reciprocal channels of the same pair, which have no cutoff: the two profiles differ from the lowest reciprocal length upwards, and the kernel is 0.955. The dotted curves are the form factor for three widths of the field, which is the resolution; the second axis gives the length 2 pi / q that each channel describes. (d) The identity of equation (#eq:parseval): the lattice sum over the images and the sum over the reciprocal lattice, as the width of the Gaussian is varied, agree to one part in 1e13. Drawn by `benchmarks/run_reciprocal.py`.](benchmarks/results/reciprocal/concept.png)

**Using them.** `reciprocal_feature_matrix` builds the channels of a set and
`CMFModel(kernel_source="reciprocal")` fits them with the machinery the periodic autocorrelation
already uses -- the per-block scaling, the cosine normalisation, the learners, the file format.
`joint_features` puts the two descriptions side by side in one matrix, and
`reciprocal_pattern` reads a fitted model the way the co-pattern reads the real-space one: which
pair of field types at which reciprocal length, that is, at which spacing of planes.

**What it measured.** Three Matbench tasks, 1,200 structures of each, the five published folds,
the setting of the descriptor and the ridge chosen inside every training fold
(`benchmarks/run_reciprocal.py`; the table is `benchmarks/results/reciprocal/table.md`). The
reciprocal channels were measured alone and added to the real-space descriptor as a second
kernel, `K = (1-t) K_real + t K_reciprocal`, with the weight $t$ chosen in the training fold.
Three things came out of it.

**They carry as much as the real-space descriptor, with no neighbour list.** Alone they reach
R² +0.518 on the formation energy of the perovskites against +0.528 for the best real-space
cutoff, +0.778 against +0.773 on the bulk modulus and +0.728 against +0.735 on the shear
modulus. All three differences have an interval that contains zero. A descriptor built only from
sums over the atoms of one cell is level with a tuned pair-distance descriptor, which is the
first thing worth knowing about it.

**Added to the real-space descriptor they gain on one task of the three.** Against the best
real-space cutoff: +0.066 [+0.045, +0.090] on the formation energy, +0.015 [+0.002, +0.027] on
the shear modulus and +0.008 [-0.005, +0.022] on the bulk modulus, the intervals from 2,000
bootstrap resamples of the structures. So the gain is clear on one set, small on the second and
absent on the third. The mixing weight the folds chose is 0.25 to 0.55, so the training sets do
put real weight there.

**Reaching further in real space costs accuracy; reaching further in reciprocal space does
not.** On both moduli, taking the real-space cutoff from 4 to 10 Å *loses* about 0.10 of R²
(+0.773 to +0.671 and +0.735 to +0.635): the longer sum adds many weakly informative distance
channels that dilute the kernel. Adding the reciprocal channels to that 10 Å descriptor gives
back +0.102 [+0.052, +0.172] and +0.076 [+0.051, +0.103]. Long-range information is worth
having, and this is the cheap way to carry it: the number of reciprocal channels does not grow
with the range at all.

**The width of the field is the resolution, and the cutoff in q is not a parameter.** On the
bulk modulus the accuracy of the reciprocal channels falls steadily as the field widens, R²
+0.785 at $a$ = 0.15 Å down to +0.587 at 0.7 Å, and changes by at most 0.002 when the sum over
$\mathbf{G}$ is taken to 12 Å⁻¹ instead of 8. Once the form factor has decided what is visible,
summing further changes nothing, which is what the word resolution means here.

**The identity holds on real structures.** Over 120 crystals of the three tasks the two sides of
equation (#eq:parseval) agree to about one part in $10^{13}$, worst case $2\times10^{-11}$.

**What a model reads there.** On the bulk modulus the channels that move the prediction most sit
at $q$ = 2 to 3.5 Å⁻¹, which is a spacing of 1.8 to 3.1 Å -- the nearest-neighbour scale that
sets an elastic constant -- with the electronegativity and inverse-square-root-mass fields and
their products carrying them. Neighbouring channels are strongly correlated, so single weights
alternate in sign and it is the envelope over $q$ that carries the reading;
`benchmarks/results/reciprocal/pattern.png` draws it.

**The limits.** The channels need a structure periodic in all three directions; a layer or a
chain has a reciprocal lattice of lower dimension, and the intensity then depends on the
direction across the vacuum, which these channels do not resolve. There is no site split of them
(a structure factor is a sum over the whole cell, so the intensity cannot be divided among the
sites the way the pair sum can), and a site record is refused for that reason. And the intensity
of a reflection is the same for a structure and its mirror image, so these channels share the one
blindness of every two-point descriptor.

## A measured curve as the sample: the untyped descriptor

A diffraction experiment on a powder, a glass or a nanoparticle gives one curve and no
coordinates. That curve is not a different object from the descriptors above. It is the
**untyped** one (plan item M12, `cmfqsar/scattering.py`).

Every descriptor so far is *typed*: one channel block per pair of field types. An experiment
cannot separate the types, because every atom scatters into the same detector. What it measures
is the single block of one field whose weight is the atom's **scattering length** -- the neutron
value $b$, or for X-rays the atomic number $Z$. Writing $\rho_0$ for the number density and
$\langle b \rangle$ for the mean scattering length, the reduced pair distribution function is

$$
G(r) \;=\; \dfrac{\Phi_{bb}(r)}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\; r \; \langle b \rangle^{2}}
$$
<!-- #eq:pair-distribution -->

where $\Phi_{bb}$ is the periodic autocorrelation of that one field with the uniform background
kept and the self term dropped. Every piece of the standard definition is already there: the
background term of the descriptor *is* the $-4\pi r \rho_0$ that the definition subtracts, and
$\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}$ is the integral of the channel's Gaussian. The identity is exact as the
channel narrows, and `pair_distribution_residual` measures the difference against a direct sum
over the neighbour list.

The same holds in reciprocal space, which is the other thing an experiment reports. The
Faber-Ziman total structure factor is the one-field channel of the previous section divided by
$\langle b \rangle^2$, and $F(Q) = Q\,[S(Q) - 1]$ and $G(r)$ are a sine transform apart. The
*distinct* scattering is what enters: the term an atom gives with itself is taken out, so that
$S$ approaches 1 and $F$ approaches zero at large $Q$. Leaving it in would add a straight line
$(\langle b^2\rangle/\langle b\rangle^2 - 1)\,Q$ to the curve of every structure with more than
one element.

**What this gains.** A sample where there is no structure. `read_curve` reads the two-column text
the common measurement programs write, `resample` puts it on the grid a model uses, and
`curve_kernel` compares it with computed curves -- so a model fitted on structures can be asked
about a measurement, and materials whose atomic structure nobody knows become describable.

**What it costs: the typing.** That cost is a question about data and not about code, and
`benchmarks/run_scattering.py` measures it on the three Matbench tasks of the previous section,
with the same folds.

**What a measurement is not.** A computed curve is sharper and cleaner than any measurement.
Four things separate them, and `measured_like` applies all four so that a model can be tested
against them before any experiment is trusted: a finite range in $Q$, which puts ripples of
period $2\pi/Q_{\max}$ around every peak; counting noise on $F(Q)$; an error in the number
density, which adds a straight line to $G(r)$ because $\rho_0$ is what the baseline is drawn
from; and a limited range in $r$.

![What a detector sums away. One cell of cubic BaTiO3, five atoms, described three ways by `benchmarks/run_scattering.py --stage concept`. (a) What the program computes: 15 typed channel blocks, one per pair of field types, of which the six with the largest values are drawn. (b) What a detector can measure: the reduced pair distribution function G(r), one curve, with the types summed away by the weighting that scattering applies. (c) The same curve as an instrument would report it, from a transform cut at Q = 20 angstrom^-1, with 5 % counting noise and the number density wrong by 5 %. The kernel between the computed curve and the measured one is 0.8543: the gap in (c) is what the measurement section below measures the cost of.](benchmarks/results/scattering/concept.png)

**What the measurement says.** `benchmarks/run_scattering.py` ran the three Matbench tasks of the
previous section, 600 structures of each, with the same five published folds; the numbers are in
`benchmarks/results/scattering/table.md`. It reports five things.

*The identity holds to the accuracy the derivation promises.* The curve from the descriptor and
the curve summed over the neighbour list differ by 8.2e-05 of the curve at a channel width of
0.05 Å (median over 30 structures of each task; worst case 3.2e-04) and by 5.5e-06 at 0.02 Å. The
difference falls with the channel width, as it must.

*Summing away the types costs most of the accuracy.* The typed descriptor reaches R² +0.771 on the
bulk modulus, +0.684 on the shear modulus and +0.418 on the perovskite formation energies. The one
X-ray curve of the same structures reaches +0.303, +0.192 and +0.012: a difference of -0.469
[-0.560, -0.389], -0.492 [-0.579, -0.414] and -0.406 [-0.498, -0.311], with the interval from
2,000 bootstrap resamples of the structures. On the formation energies the curve alone is no
better than predicting the mean. The neutron curve is worse than the X-ray one on the structures
its table covers, +0.093, +0.086 and +0.101 (78 % of the elasticity sets and 96.5 % of the
perovskites have a tabulated scattering length for every element). The likely reason is that the
X-ray weight, the atomic number, orders the elements, while the neutron scattering lengths of
neighbouring elements are irregular and change sign, so one weighted sum separates the structures
less well. Both curves were offered at two ranges, 10 and 20 Å, and all 30 folds chose the
shorter one.

*A computed curve is too sharp to compare, and what an instrument does to it is what makes the
kernel work.* As computed, with a channel 0.05 Å wide, the 20 Å curve predicts nothing: R² +0.003
on the bulk modulus, -0.050 on the shear modulus and -0.001 on the formation energies. Cutting
the transform at $Q_{\max} = 20$ Å⁻¹, which broadens every peak by about $\pi/Q_{\max} = 0.16$ Å,
raises the same curve to +0.327, +0.235 and +0.030, and at $Q_{\max} = 10$ Å⁻¹ to +0.432, +0.344
and +0.050. Two Gaussians 0.05 Å wide and 0.2 Å apart barely overlap, so a kernel over sharp
curves sees two structures as unrelated however their peaks moved; the resolution of the
instrument is a width the comparison needs.

*Of the other instrument effects, counting noise is the one that matters.* Noise of 2 % leaves the
bulk modulus at +0.324 against +0.327 without it, and 10 % cuts it to +0.150 and the shear modulus
to +0.040. An error of 10 % in the number density costs nothing measurable (+0.336), because it
adds a straight line that the kernel largely ignores. Dropping the curve below 2 Å costs a little
(+0.260), and dropping it above 10 Å gains (+0.438), which is the same reading as the fit stage's
choice of the shorter range.

*A model must be fitted at the resolution of the measurement.* Fitting on the computed curves and
then predicting the degraded ones -- what someone with a structure database and one measurement in
hand would do -- never reaches R² +0.06 in any of the 36 settings tried and is negative in 15 of
them, against +0.327 for the same curves when the model is fitted on curves degraded alike. The
two are not the same object: one is sharp and the other is broad. The remedy is `measured_like`:
put the computed curves through the instrument's $Q_{\max}$ and noise first, and fit on those.

*A curve written to a file finds its structure again.* 25 curves of the bulk modulus set, written
in the two-column form with a header, degraded as above and read back, all match the structure
they came from best; the kernel with their own structure is 0.891 and with the others 0.001.

**The limits.** No experimental data is used in any of this and none is implied: there is no
public set of measured curves with measured properties to fit, so what the measurement reports
is how good an instrument would have to be, not that an instrument worked. A disordered cell is
refused, because the mean over the species is right for the pair term and not for the self term
that the total curve keeps. The X-ray weight is the atomic number, the $Q \to 0$ limit of the
form factor, rather than the form factor itself. And a neutron scattering length is taken from a
table that leaves out the elements whose value depends strongly on the wavelength; a structure
containing one of those is refused rather than guessed at.

## A microstructure as the sample: the field on a voxel grid

A micrograph has no atoms. A two-phase microstructure on a voxel grid is nevertheless a field --
the indicator of each phase, one value per voxel, is one channel -- and the kernel of this program,
the overlap integral of two fields, applies to it as it stands. What changes is only how the field
is made: not from atom-centred Gaussians but from the voxels themselves, with the fast Fourier
transform doing the overlaps on the periodic grid. This is the way into the hierarchical
materials informatics of the Materials Knowledge Systems (MKS) of Kalidindi and co-workers, whose
descriptor is the **two-point statistics** of the microstructure: the probability that two
voxels a vector $r$ apart are in phases $a$ and $b$. That statistic is the translation-averaged
self-overlap of the phase field with its own translate, which is to say the periodic
autocorrelation of the chapter above with voxels in place of atoms. `benchmarks/run_microstructure.py`
measures what the field kernels are worth against that workflow, on the smallest fair benchmark.

**The phase field and its co-field.** The *phase field* of a cell is the set of the indicator
functions of its phases: $m_a(\mathbf{x})$ is 1 where voxel $\mathbf{x}$ belongs to phase $a$
and 0 elsewhere. A Gaussian of a chosen width may smooth it, as the attenuation does for an
atom. The two-point statistics of two phases $a$ and $b$ are the mean of the product of the two
indicators a lag vector $\mathbf{r}$ apart, over the $N$ voxels of the periodic cell:

$$
S_{ab}(\mathbf{r}) \;=\; \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{\mathbf{x}}\, m_a(\mathbf{x})\, m_b(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:two-point -->

The cells of a set share a grid and no frame, so a co-field over the positions of the grid
would say nothing: a grain is at a different place in every cell. The statistics of
Eq. (#eq:two-point) do not depend on where a grain is. A linear model on them has a weight for
every pair of phases and every lag vector, and its prediction is

$$
\hat{y} \;=\; b + \sum_{a,b}\, \sum_{\mathbf{r}}\, w_{ab}(\mathbf{r})\, S_{ab}(\mathbf{r})
$$
<!-- #eq:lag-cofield -->

The weight $w_{ab}(\mathbf{r})$ is the co-field of this model. It is a field over the lag vector
and not over the position: it says at which separation, and in which direction, finding phase
$b$ again from phase $a$ raises the property. It is the weight vector of the section *Why a
kernel is enough*, read from the dual coefficients as a co-field or a co-pattern is. The fourth
test below reads it for two properties.

![The phase field of a microstructure and the co-field of a model on it, on the 400 synthetic two-phase cells of `benchmarks/run_microstructure.py` in which phase 1 conducts 100 times better than phase 0. The property is the effective conductivity along x. Cells A and B are the two cells with a phase fraction between 0.45 and 0.55 that have the largest and the smallest conductivity. Left column: the cell. Middle column: its phase field, the indicator of phase 1 on the voxel grid. It is drawn smoothed with a Gaussian of 2 voxels to show what the width setting does; the model of this figure uses the indicator without smoothing, which is what cross-validation chooses for this kernel. Right column: its two-point statistics for phase 1 with phase 1, drawn over the lag vector. A streak along x says that the conductor continues along x. Bottom left: the co-field of the kernel ridge model, a weight for every lag vector, red where the statistics raise the predicted conductivity and blue where they lower it. Bottom middle and right: weight times statistics of the two cells, lag by lag, summed over the two phase pairs. The line above the panels writes the sums out. The model is linear in the statistics, and it reproduces cell A better than cell B. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/phasefield.png)

**The data.** 400 synthetic two-phase cells on a periodic 51 x 51 grid (and 400 on a 21^3 grid),
by the recipe of the `pymks` generator: Gaussian-filtered white noise cut at the quantile that
gives the phase fraction. The fraction, the grain size, the elongation of the grains and their
direction all vary from sample to sample. The label is the effective thermal conductivity of
the cell from a finite-volume solver written in the script (`pymks` does not build on Python
3.13, and its elastic solver needs a finite-element package); phase 0 conducts 1, phase 1
conducts 10 or 100. Two labels: the component along $x$, which depends on the direction of the
grains, and the mean over the directions, which does not.

**The descriptions.** The plain kernel of this program -- the overlap of the smoothed phase
fields at zero shift, in the frame the samples were generated in; the same averaged over the
point group of the grid; the overlap of two samples' two-point autocorrelations, which is the
invariant route and is also the overlap of their power spectra, raw and in the cosine form of
the autocorrelation kernel, averaged over the point group, and binned by the length of $r$; and
the MKS baseline, two-point statistics, principal components fitted on the training part and a
polynomial of the scores. Every kernel is tried linear and under the Gaussian layer, with the
Gaussian smoothing width of the field (0 to 5 voxels), the layer and the ridge chosen by
cross-validation inside the training part. Training sets of 20, 50, 100 and 200 samples are
drawn five times each and the rest of the set is held out.

**What it says** (`benchmarks/results/microstructure/table.md`, with the notes beside it). On
the direction-dependent label at contrast 10 the overlap of the autocorrelations reaches q2
0.89 at 20 training samples, 0.97 at 100 and 0.98 at 200; the MKS baseline 0.93, 0.965 and 0.97;
at contrast 100 the two are 0.81 against 0.81 at 20 samples and 0.90 against 0.88 at 200; on the
3D cells 0.97 against 0.96 at 20 and 0.989 against 0.987 at 200. So the field-overlap kernel on
the two-point statistics matches the baseline at 20 to 50 samples and is a little better from
100 on, and the gain holds where the contrast makes the arrangement matter.
The zero-shift overlap in the generating frame is poor, and should be: these samples share a
grid and nothing else, so it compares two structures at a random relative shift, and what it
keeps as the smoothing grows is the phase fractions. A rotation average loses the direction of
the grains and with it the direction-dependent label, and recovers everything on the
direction-free one. The phase fraction alone explains 0.87 to 0.98 of the variance, as it does
in the published homogenisation examples, which is why the arrangement is a second-order
signal here.

**The length scale.** The smoothing width is the knob a multi-scale kernel would turn. The
inner cross-validation sets it to zero for the autocorrelation kernels on the
direction-dependent label -- the statistic wants its full resolution -- and to the widest
width tried, 5 voxels, close to the grain size, for the zero-shift overlap and for the
direction-free label, where the kernel then sees little beyond the fractions. A hierarchical
model would therefore carry the fine width for the arrangement and the coarse one for the
composition, which is what two field types with their own widths already do in this program.

**The gate: the current baseline, a real micrograph set, two scales, and the map.** The pilot's
margin over polynomial ridge regression on principal components was small and that baseline is
old, so four more tests were run, reported in the notes beside the table. *First*, every method
was given the same budget of 40 settings, twenty draws per training size, and the current MKS
baseline was added: a Gaussian process on the principal-component scores with one length scale
per score, fitted by the marginal likelihood; and the label of the published MKS benchmark,
the effective elastic stiffness from the finite-element solver of PyMKS, was computed beside the
conductivity (PyMKS needed three patches to run on a current Python and `sfepy`;
`benchmarks/prepare_elastic.py` lists them). The two labels correlate at 0.98 to 0.995, so the
pilot's conductivity was a fair stand-in. Read this way, the overlap of the two-point
autocorrelations and the Gaussian process are the same model to within the noise of the draws
from 100 samples on,
and below 100 samples the kernel is the steadier of the two, ahead in 14 to 17 of 20 draws by
0.02 to 0.15 in q2, where the GP's fit of twenty length scales on 16 to 40 points is the
unstable step. *Second*, a real micrograph set, the 961 ultrahigh-carbon steel micrographs of DeCost and co-workers (2017) with seven microconstituent classes and the heat treatment of 598 of them: here the autocorrelation kernel of the grey level, computed with zero padding because a micrograph is one window on a medium that does not repeat, is the best of the second-order descriptions (accuracy 0.61 at 500 training images against 0.55 for the polynomial and 0.51 for the GP on the principal components) and is far behind the published route, features of a convolutional network with a linear model on top (0.87), in 0 of 20 draws ahead at any training size, because the classes are named after shapes that a second-order statistic does not carry; and when whole specimens are held out, every method loses 0.1 to 0.2 in accuracy and none predicts the treatment of a specimen it never saw. *Third*, a property that depends on two scales: phase 1 was
given a defect concentration that sets its conductivity by a known law, and the cells were
solved again. Each scale alone explains a third of the variance; the sum of an arrangement
kernel and a descriptor kernel reaches 0.74; their product reaches 0.97, ahead of the MKS
baseline with the descriptor appended in 19 or 20 of 20 draws. The kernel across scales is the
product, because an effective property is close to the property of the conducting phase times
a factor of the arrangement -- as two molecular fields that act together, not in turn. A second
width of the same arrangement adds nothing. *Fourth*, the interpretation map: for the linear
autocorrelation kernel the model is a linear function of the two-point statistics and its
coefficient field over the lag vector is read straight from the dual coefficients
(`benchmarks/results/microstructure/map_2d51_n400_c100.png`). For the conductivity along $x$
it is a four-lobed figure that credits phase 1 found again 2 to 8 voxels away along the
gradient, peaking at 3 to 4 voxels, and debits the same lags across it; for the direction-free
mean it is a ring that credits every direction at the grain size, 5 voxels, and nothing larger.
A principal-component regression has no such map, because its coefficients do not live on
lags. The conclusion of the whole is scope rather than victory: a method built for molecules
reaches microstructure informatics through its invariant route, lands on the established
statistic with the same accuracy as the current baseline, is steadier below 100 samples,
combines scales by a product, carries a continuous interpretation map, and shares the limit
of that statistic on real micrographs, where a trained network sees more.

## Three atoms at a time: what a histogram of distances cannot see

Every descriptor of a crystal above is a **two-point** one. It counts how much field weight sits
at each distance from how much other field weight, and that is all it knows. Two limitations
follow, and both belong to the description and not to the data (plan item M10,
`cmfqsar/threebody.py`).

The first is that two structures can have exactly the same multiset of distances and not be the
same structure. Such a pair is called **homometric**. It is not a curiosity of mathematics: a
defect series on one lattice holds many arrangements whose distance histograms are equal or very
nearly so, and the two-point kernel then gives them a kernel of one and the model cannot tell
them apart. The second is that a mirror image has the same distances as the structure it
reflects, so no two-point descriptor can tell a left-handed crystal from a right-handed one.

**The three-body block.** Take every atom of the cell as a centre in turn. Two neighbours and the
centre form a triangle, and a triangle is fixed by its three sides: the two distances from the
centre and the distance between the two neighbours. Writing $r_a$ for the distance of neighbour
$a$ from the centre, $d_{ab}$ for the distance between two neighbours and $N$ for the atoms in
the cell,

$$
\Phi_{fg}(k, k', m) \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{l} \sum_{a, b \in \mathcal{N}(l)}
   w_{af}\, w_{bg}\, R_k(r_a)\, R_{k'}(r_b)\, D_m(d_{ab})
$$
<!-- #eq:threebody -->

with $R_k$ a Gaussian window on a grid of radii from the centre and $D_m$ one on a grid of
distances between neighbours. The neighbourhood $\mathcal{N}(l)$ holds the centre itself, at
radius zero, so its own field types enter the channels, and every atom of every periodic image
within the cutoff. Dividing by $N$ makes a supercell give exactly the same channels as the cell
it repeats, as it does for the two-point descriptor. The channel layout is the one of the
triangle block that `cmfqsar/triangles.py` builds around one atom of a molecule: one block per
pair of field types, and inside a block one column per pair of radial windows and distance
window.

**The handedness block.** Three distances fix a triangle only up to its mirror image, so the
block above is still blind to a reflection. The signed quantity that is not is the triple product
of three vectors. About each centre,

$$
X_{fgh}(s) \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{l} \det[\, A_f(l, s),\; A_g(l, s),\; A_h(l, s) \,],
\qquad A_f(l, s) \;=\; \sum_{a \in \mathcal{N}(l)} w_{af}\, G_s(r_a)\, (\mathbf{r}_a -
\mathbf{r}_l)
$$
<!-- #eq:handedness -->

with $G_s$ a Gaussian window on a grid of radii, which keeps the handedness resolved by distance
from the centre instead of reduced to one number for the whole structure. Under a proper rotation
all three vectors turn together and the determinant does not change; under a reflection it
changes sign; a centrosymmetric neighbourhood gives zero, as an achiral environment must.

**The cost, and a correction to what the plan expected.** The development plan assumed this block
would need a sum over triples of atoms, because the factorisation that the molecular chirality
block uses needs an origin and a periodic structure has no centroid to use. With the centre atom
as that origin the factorisation survives in full: a determinant is linear in each of its three
arguments, so the sum over triples of neighbours **is** the determinant of three summed vectors.
Both blocks therefore cost one pass over the pairs of neighbours of each atom, and nothing cubic
is summed.

**When the handedness block is empty**, which is a property of the block and not a fault. A
determinant of three vectors is zero whenever they lie in a plane. A field weight that depends
only on the species of the atom makes every $A_f$ a combination of one vector per species, so a
structure of two species gives vectors in a plane at most and every channel is zero; three
species are the minimum. A site with a rotation axis through it also gives zero, because a sum
that the rotation leaves unchanged can only lie along the axis. The block is a sharp test for
handedness rather than a general descriptor, and it is off by default.

![The two blind spots of a two-point descriptor, drawn by `benchmarks/run_threebody.py --stage concept`. (a) Two cells of five atoms on a ring of twelve sites, at 0, 1, 2, 4, 7 and at 0, 1, 3, 5, 6: every distance occurs as often in one as in the other. (b) Every two-point channel of structure A against the same channel of structure B. Every point lies on the line, so for that descriptor the two cells are one structure: kernel 1.00000000. (c) The same plot for the three-body channels. The points leave the line and the kernel falls to 0.9372, so the arrangement is resolved and not only the distances. (d) The handedness channels of a cell of four species with no symmetry against those of its mirror image: the same size and the opposite sign, kernel -1.000000, while the three-body channels of that same pair agree to 6.9e-16 of the largest channel.](benchmarks/results/threebody/concept.png)

**What the measurement says.** `benchmarks/run_threebody.py` ran three stages: the two blind spots
on constructed structures, three Matbench tasks of 600 structures each with the same five
published folds as the sections above, and the defect series of plan item M14. The numbers are in
`benchmarks/results/threebody/table.md`.

*Both blind spots are real, and the two blocks close them.* Two cells of five atoms on a ring of
twelve sites, at positions 0, 1, 2, 4, 7 and at 0, 1, 3, 5, 6, have the same multiset of
distances. The two-point channels give them a kernel of 1.00000000: for that description they are
one structure. The three-body channels give 0.9372. A cell of four species with no symmetry and
its mirror image agree in the three-body channels to 6.9e-16 of the largest channel, as every
description built from distances must, while their handedness channels have the same size and the
opposite sign (kernel -1.000000). Rocksalt, which is centrosymmetric, gives 2.5e-45 in every
handedness channel.

*On a property, the triangles gain where an angle is the signal.* The three Matbench tasks were
run with the two descriptions alone and with their kernels mixed as
$K = (1-t)\,K_\text{two-point} + t\,K_\text{three-body}$, with $t$ chosen inside every training
fold. R² over the five folds:

| Descriptor | formation energy | bulk modulus | shear modulus |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| the two-point descriptor | +0.453 | +0.781 | +0.699 |
| the three-body channels | +0.542 | +0.789 | +0.727 |
| the two kernels mixed | +0.515 | +0.799 | +0.721 |

The perovskite set is compounds of one composition type whose cells differ mainly by how the
octahedra tilt, which is an angle and not a distance. There the three-body channels gain +0.089,
with a 95 % interval of [+0.041, +0.140] from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the structures. On the
two elastic moduli the gains are +0.009 [-0.022, +0.041] and +0.028 [-0.003, +0.065]: both
intervals include zero, so on those tasks the two descriptions are level. The mixture is the best
of the three on the bulk modulus, but its gain there is +0.018 [-0.006, +0.044], which includes
zero as well, and on the formation energies the mixture is worse than the three-body channels
alone. Mixing adds a setting to choose and, on these three tasks, no accuracy.

*On a set where the arrangement is the whole signal, the triangles do what a two-point description
cannot.* The 2DMD defect series (plan item M14) is one host lattice and one supercell with one to
three point defects placed differently in every cell. Two splits were run over 2,000 cells of each
of two hosts, with the same folds, the same ridge grid and the same Gaussian layers as the
two-point rows. Energies are given as the mean absolute error per site of the 191-atom cell.

| The set | Descriptor | random folds: R² | meV per site | one and two defects to three: R² | meV per site |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MoS2 | two-point, 10 Å | +0.9997 | 8.3 | -0.015 | 1222 |
| MoS2 | overlap of M14, 10 Å | +1.0000 | 1.8 | +1.000 | 4 |
| MoS2 | three-body, 4 to 5 Å | +0.9972 | 36.0 | +0.940 | 240 |
| MoS2 | the two kernels mixed | +0.9988 | 25.6 | +0.021 | 1201 |
| WSe2 | two-point, 10 Å | +0.9989 | 15.7 | +0.060 | 1096 |
| WSe2 | overlap of M14, 10 Å | +0.9998 | 5.2 | +0.996 | 54 |
| WSe2 | three-body, 4 to 5 Å | +0.9861 | 38.3 | +0.954 | 198 |
| WSe2 | the two kernels mixed | +0.9977 | 23.8 | +0.091 | 1078 |

On random folds, where the training set holds arrangements much like the tested one, the
two-point description is the better of the two, because it reaches 10 Å and the three-body
channels only four to five. The second split is the one the item was built for: it trains on the
131 cells with one or two defects and predicts the cells with three, so every tested arrangement
is new. There the two-point description fails -- R² -0.015 on MoS2, an error of 1,222 meV per site,
which is no better than predicting the mean -- and the three-body channels hold, at +0.940 and 240
meV per site. The overlap kernel of M14 is better still, but it needs every cell to share one
lattice and one supercell, which is what it uses to put two cells in a common frame; the
three-body channels assume nothing about the set and work on structures that have nothing in
common.

*A mixed kernel does not inherit what the three-body one can do.* The mixture lies between the two
descriptions on random folds and fails with the two-point one on the extrapolation split, at R²
+0.021 and +0.091. Its weight is chosen inside the training fold: on the random folds every fold
gave the three-body kernel a quarter of the weight, and on the extrapolation split the choice
fell on three quarters, so the mixture failed even where the three-body kernel carried most of
it. The likely reason is that the two-point kernel is close to one for every pair of these cells,
which share a lattice and differ in a few sites, so what it adds to the mixture is nearly
constant and compresses the differences that the three-body part supplies. A second reading is
about model selection and not about this descriptor: the weight and the kernel layer were chosen
on a random inner split, where both descriptions look nearly perfect, so the choice could not see
the failure that the outer split tests for. A model that is meant to extrapolate needs an inner
split that extrapolates too.

*The cost.* A cell of 191 atoms takes 0.26 s for the 14,112 channels of the first setting, so the
2,000 cells of one host take about nine minutes, and their feature matrix is 0.11 GB; the second
setting has 29,120 channels and 0.23 GB. The whole three-body row of one host -- the features of
both settings, then twelve kernels over five folds and the second split -- took 35 minutes, and
the mixed row eleven.

**The limits.** A disordered cell is refused: a three-body channel is a product of three weights,
and the mean of that product over the species sharing a site is not the product of their means,
which is all the module has. No uniform background is subtracted, unlike the two-point
descriptor, so these channels carry how dense the structure is as well as how it is arranged; a
cosine-normalised kernel removes most of that, and the two-point channels are there to carry the
density properly. The number of channels grows as the square of (fields times radii), so the
radial grid is coarse and the cutoff short -- four to five angstrom, against the ten a two-point
descriptor reaches cheaply. The two are complements and not alternatives, which is what the
measurement says as well.

## Designing a crystal: a prototype, a budget and a loop

Every section above asks how well a model predicts. A design study asks the other question: with
a budget of calculations, can the model find a better structure than the ones it was fitted on?
For molecules that question has the sections on which compound to make next; for crystals it
needs a way to propose candidates, because there is no parent molecule to substitute on (plan
item M11, `cmfqsar/prototypes.py`).

**A prototype is a cell with site classes.** One cell, its sites grouped into classes, and a
list of the elements each class may take. Two modes cover what a materials study asks for. In
*composition* mode every site of a class takes the same element, which is the ABO3 case: one
prototype, many compositions. In *arrangement* mode a fixed number of the sites of a class take
a substituent and the rest keep what the prototype has, which is the point-defect case: one
composition, many arrangements. The element name `vac` removes the atom instead of replacing it,
so a vacancy series is an arrangement series.

The number of candidates is a product of the choices and grows quickly, so nothing is built
until it is asked for. `Prototype.n_candidates` counts them, `candidate_at` builds the one with
a given index, and `candidates` either walks the enumeration or draws a sample from it without
replacement. A pool of a few thousand can therefore be taken from an enumeration of millions
without building the candidates that are left out.

**Two candidates can be one structure.** Any symmetry operation of the prototype that maps the
substituted sites onto each other gives the same structure a second index. `site_permutations`
reads those operations from spglib and turns them into permutations of the substitutable sites,
and `unique` keeps one candidate per orbit. The other test is the descriptor itself:
`channel_keys` gives each candidate the key of its channels, and two candidates with the same key
are one structure *for the model*, whatever their coordinates say. The two tests do not agree, and
the measurement below says what that costs.

**An oracle is what computes the property.** A design loop has to evaluate what it proposes.
`LookupOracle` reads the value from a table, which is how the loop is measured on a published
set, and it counts the calls, because a budget is counted in calls. `CalculatorOracle` runs any
ASE calculator and relaxes the cell first if asked; the same interface takes a machine-learned
potential or a VASP calculator, and what changes is the cost of a call, not the loop.

**The loop.** `design_loop` is given a pool, an oracle, a start set and a budget. At every step
it fits the kernel model on what the oracle has answered so far, chooses the ridge by the
evidence of plan item B4, scores every candidate that is left by one of the rules of
`cmfqsar/active.py`, and asks the oracle about the best-scoring one. It never looks at a value
it has not asked for and never asks twice about the same candidate, so the budget it reports is
the budget a study would pay. A formation energy is to be made small and every rule in that
module prefers a large score, so `maximise=False` negates the target inside the loop; with that,
`ucb` reads as the lower confidence bound of the section on which molecule to make next -- a
candidate is proposed only when the model is both optimistic and sure.

![Designing a crystal. Top left: a prototype, the cubic ABO3 cell with its three site classes, and the size of the space it spans. Top right: the loop. Below: the loop measured on 4,000 perovskite cells with the three-body kernel, as the gate below reports it: the lowest formation energy that each rule found within its budget, one point for each start set. The rule that takes the best prediction reaches the best cell of the pool in most runs. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py` from the stored results.](docs/figures/crystaldesign.svg)

**How large a design space is, and how much of it is already computed.** The five-atom cubic ABO3
prototype with the 52 A elements and 52 B elements of `matbench_perovskites` allows 2,704
candidates, and that set already holds a computed formation energy for 2,661 of them: 98.4 % of the
space, with 43 candidates left. One more site class changes that. The doubled cell with its two B
sites free of each other (A2BB'O6) allows 140,608 candidates, and the repository holds a computed
formation energy for none of them. Counting the space is therefore the first step of a design
study, and it is what tells a materials project whether the generator is needed at all.

**Which candidates are one structure.** On the 16 sites of an fcc supercell, one substituted site
gives 16 placements and 1 arrangement, two give 120 and 5, and three give 560 and 10. The
descriptor's own test is the weaker of the two: of those 10 arrangements, both descriptors give 8
channel sets at every reach tried -- the two-point channels at 6 and at 14 Å, the three-body
channels at 5 and at 9 Å. The two merged pairs are not the same structure. ASE's symmetry
comparator separates them, their space groups are 25 and 25 with different Wyckoff positions in
one pair and 25 and 65 in the other, and an EMT calculation on the unrelaxed cells puts the two
energies of each pair 0.6 meV per atom apart. That difference is an error no model built on these
channels can avoid, and it is the limit of the whole family: a loop can be told that two
candidates are one structure only as far as its channels see.

**The gate.** The pool is 4,000 cells of `matbench_perovskites`, the target is the formation
energy and is to be made small, the oracle reads the tabulated value, and the budget is 100 calls
after the start set. Ten start sets are drawn, every rule begins from the same ones, and two
start sizes are run, because the model is what ranks the candidates. Two rules meet the gate,
and both of them act on the prediction. With the three-body kernel and 100 computed cells the
greedy rule reaches the best cell of the 4,000 (median rank 1) and improves on its start set in 7 of the 10 runs -- one of the ten start sets
already held the best cell of the pool, so 9 runs could improve at all -- and it enters the best
one per cent of the pool in 8 of 10 runs after a median of 8 calls; the lower confidence bound
improves on its start set in 7 of 10 runs as well and reaches median rank 9. With 25 computed
cells it
still reaches median rank 1 with the three-body kernel, and only rank 15 with the two-point
kernel: this is the one place in the study where the three-body channels of plan item M10 decide
the outcome. Random choice reaches median rank 27 with 125 computed cells and 14 with 200, which
is what chance gives (the median best rank of 125 and 200 draws from 4,000 is 22 and 14), and the
rules that explore do no better here -- median rank 28 to 82 for `variance` and `maxmin` and 28
to 40 for `ei`, and they improve on their start set in 1 to 4 of the 10 runs against 5 of 10 for
random choice.

**Where the arrangement is the signal.** The second measurement is the question a defect study
asks: of 2,000 arrangements of one to three point defects on the 8 x 8 supercell of MoS2 and of
WSe2 (the data of plan item M14), which arrangement is the most stable. The kernels are the ones
items M14 and M10 already cached, so this stage costs minutes. On WSe2 the loop does what a
design study hopes for: `greedy` and the lower confidence bound reach median rank 1 of 2,000 and
enter the best one per cent in 10 of 10 runs after 20 to 38 calls, with either descriptor and
either start size. On MoS2 the same two rules fail: median rank 10 of 2,000 with 100 computed
cells and 37 with 25, and the best one per cent reached in 0 of 10 runs, while random choice
reaches median rank 5 and enters the best one per cent in 6 of 10. There the rules that explore
are the ones that work: on the three-body kernel with 100 computed cells `ei` reaches median rank
1 and `maxmin` enters the best one per cent in 10 of 10 runs.

**A model that predicts well can still be useless for design.** The stage that explains this
(`--stage ordering`) fits the same model on the same start sets and asks where it puts the best
candidate of the pool. On MoS2 the model is accurate: rank correlation +0.87 and R² +0.84 on the
cells it has not computed, which is far above anything the perovskite pool reaches (+0.53 and +0.31
with 100 computed cells). Yet it puts the best candidate of the pool at place 894 of the 1,900 left
out, so a rule that proposes the best-predicted candidate does not come near it. On WSe2 the same
model at the same accuracy (+0.93 and +0.88) puts the best candidate at place 59. The difference is
in the pools and not in the models. On WSe2 the best one per cent of the arrangements lies within
0.002 eV of the best one, so a rule that lands anywhere in that group has found what the study
wants. On MoS2 the best arrangement lies 0.41 eV below the boundary of the best one per cent: it is
an isolated candidate, and a kernel ridge model shrinks an isolated value toward the mean along
with everything else. Two things follow. The number to report for a design loop is not the accuracy
of the model but the place it gives the best candidate, and that place is measured before the loop
starts, while the loop refits after every answer -- on the perovskites the best cell starts at
place 227 of 3,900 and `greedy` still reaches it, because each answer improves a model that began
weak, while on MoS2 the model is already as good as it will get and the 100 further answers do not
move the best candidate forward. Three pools are too few for a general rule, but they are enough to
show that the accuracy of a model does not say whether a design loop will work.

**A closed loop, with a calculator instead of a table.** The last stage computes
every value inside the loop, so that nothing is read from a table anywhere. Eight of the 32 sites
of an fcc copper cell take gold: one composition and 10,518,300 arrangements. A sample of 3,000
placements leaves 2,459 distinct candidates after the symmetry reduction, and 400 of those are
the pool. The oracle is an ASE EMT calculator that relaxes the cell in every call, at 0.22 s per
call, which is cheap enough to compute the whole pool exhaustively as well (88 s) and make the
rank of what the loop found exact. The energies run from +0.0480 to +0.0805 eV per atom, a spread
of 33 meV per atom. With 10 computed candidates to start, a budget of 100 calls and five start
sets, every rule that uses the model -- `greedy`, `ucb`, `ei`, `variance` and `maxmin` -- finds
the best candidate of the 400 in 5 of 5 runs, the greedy rule already at its first call, while
random choice reaches median rank 3 and finds the best candidate in 1 of 5 runs. The budget is a
quarter of the pool here, so this stage shows that the loop runs from end to end with a
calculator and that using the model is better than not using it; it is too easy a search to say
by how much. Replacing EMT with a machine-learned potential or with VASP changes the cost of a
call and nothing else in the loop, and that is the step this item has not measured.

**The limits.** The generator substitutes on a fixed cell: it does not relax what it proposes, so
the structure the model sees is the prototype's geometry with other elements on it, and the
relaxation is the oracle's business. That is how a screening study works, but it means the
descriptor of a candidate is not the descriptor of the relaxed structure the oracle returns, and
the difference grows as the substituted ions differ more in size. The loop takes one pool and does not
grow it, so a space too large to enumerate must be sampled first; a generator that proposes near
what the model likes, rather than from a fixed pool, is not built. The gate above is met by the
two rules that act on the prediction and by none of the three that only explore, and the defect
series shows those same two rules failing on one of two materials, so the rule has to be chosen
for the pool and not once for the program. And the loop is only as good as
the model that ranks for it, which is the measurement this section ends with.

## An atom instead of a molecule: the local invariant kernel

Every model so far predicts one number per molecule. A carbon shift, an acidity, a local
reactivity or a site's energy belongs to an **atom in a molecule**, so the sample has to be the
atom and its surroundings (plan item LP2). The section on per-atom targets above holds the targets
of that shape (`cmfqsar/atomtargets.py`); `cmfqsar/localenv.py` builds the samples that go with
them.

**The sample is the field under an envelope.** The environment of atom $a$ of molecule $A$ is the
molecule's own field, for every field type $f$, multiplied by a Gaussian envelope centred on
that atom:

$$
X_{fa}(\mathbf{r}) = X_{fA}(\mathbf{r})\,\exp\!\left(-\rho\,|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_a|^2\right)
$$

Here $\mathbf{r}_a$ is the position of the atom and $\rho$ sets the width of the envelope, in
Å$^{-2}$. An atom near the centre keeps its weight and one far away loses it. A CMF field is a sum of
atom-centred Gaussians and the envelope keeps that form, which is the point: an environment **is**
a field of the same class as a molecule's, so the kernels, the regression, the variance and the
atom decomposition all apply to it unchanged. The centre is the first atom of the environment, and
`member_atom_map` records which atom of the molecule each atom of the environment came from, so a
per-atom quantity can be put back where it belongs.

**$\rho$ says how far the model looks**, and it is a hyper-parameter like $\alpha$ (the option is
`rho`): the envelope falls to $1/e$ of its height at a distance $1/\sqrt{\rho}$ from the centre,
which `envelope_width` reports. The default $\rho = 0.5$ Å$^{-2}$ is a width of 1.4 Å, which is a
first-shell view; $\rho = 0.1$ Å$^{-2}$ is 3.2 Å and takes in most of a small molecule. It
has to be chosen for the property, and the measurement below shows that it decides everything.
Atoms whose envelope factor falls below 1e-4 are left out, which costs nothing measurable and
saves carrying them; `kept_share` says what share of the enveloped weight that dropped.

**The kernel needs no alignment.** The kernel to use on an environment first is the
rotation-invariant field autocorrelation of the sections above, taken from the centre instead of
over a whole molecule: two environments of two different molecules need not be superimposed for
their autocorrelations to be compared. That matters here more than anywhere else, because a common
frame for carbons of unrelated molecules does not exist. On an environment the autocorrelation
becomes a double sum over atom pairs in which each atom carries its envelope factor, and the
distance axis is shorter -- `LOCAL_SPEC` runs to 8 Å in steps of 0.5 Å, because the envelope has
already removed everything beyond a few Å.

**An acidity is the field of a change.** A pKa is the free energy of losing a proton, so the sample
for it is not the acid but the **difference field** of the acid and its anion, which
`difference_field` builds: a kernel on CMF fields is bilinear, so a difference of two fields is
again a field, whose atoms are the atoms of both molecules with the second one's weights negated.
That is the signed counterpart of the ensemble builder of the protonation section, which averages
members and therefore needs non-negative weights. The two molecules have to be in one frame for
the difference to mean anything, which is why the anion is built on the geometry of the acid.

**The reference is an atom-centred count.** What such a model has to beat is the simplest thing
that could work: the type of the centre itself plus the counts of atom types in distance shells
around it, which is what a per-atom increment scheme is. `count_features` builds it from the same
molecules, the same samples and the same folds, so the only difference between the two numbers is
the descriptor.

**The folds hold out whole molecules.** `AtomTargets.folds` splits molecules, never atoms. Two
carbons of one molecule, one in the training set and one in the test set, would let the model see
the molecule it is being tested on. For the same reason the bootstrap interval resamples
molecules, with every measured atom of a drawn molecule going in with it.

```bash
cmf atoms examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --list        # what could be a target here
cmf local examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --target shift --reference
cmf local examples/local/carboxylic_pka.sdf --target pka --rho 0.1 0.5 --reference \
    --out with_predictions.sdf
```

`cmf local` fits the local kernel on the per-atom target, searches the ridge on the folds that hold
out whole molecules, and with `--reference` fits the count model on the same folds and bootstraps
the difference over molecules. `--out` writes an SDF carrying the measured value and the
out-of-fold prediction on the atom each belongs to.
