### What it is worth, measured

`benchmarks/run_local.py` measures the two properties the plan names, against the count reference
on the same folds. Both sets are prepared by `examples/make_local_examples.py` from free
downloads and are in `examples/local/`, with their origin, their licences and every filter in
`examples/local/README.md`. The last column but one is the mean kernel value between two different
samples: a cosine-normalised kernel of 1 says the descriptor cannot tell two samples apart,
whatever the regression does with it afterwards.

**13C shifts in chloroform, 5096 assigned carbons in 400 molecules.**

| descriptor | envelope width rho | q2 | error (ppm) | mean kernel between two samples | difference in q2 against the counts |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| atom-centred counts (18 atom types in 6 shells) | -- | +0.853 | 20.464 | 0.566 | -- |
| local field | 0.25 | +0.902 | 16.731 | 0.462 | +0.049 [+0.030, +0.067] |
| local field | 0.5 | +0.962 | 10.404 | 0.486 | +0.109 [+0.097, +0.123] |
| local field | 1 | +0.973 | 8.824 | 0.537 | +0.120 [+0.107, +0.133] |
| local field | 2 | +0.969 | 9.460 | 0.562 | +0.116 [+0.103, +0.130] |

**The field around a carbon predicts its shift better than a count around it does, and the
envelope width decides how much.** At a width of 1.0 Å the error is 8.8 ppm against
20.5 ppm for the counts, a difference in q2 of +0.120 [+0.107, +0.133], which is far outside
the interval. At the module's default width of 1.4 Å, which was fixed before either set here was
measured, it is +0.109 [+0.097, +0.123]. A wider envelope
is worse (+0.902 at a width of 2.0 Å) and so is a narrower one (+0.969 at 0.7 Å), so the best view
of a carbon is about one angstrom across, which is what a shift should ask for: it is a property of
the atom, its bonds and the next shell.

What these numbers are **not** is a shift predictor. Programs built for that task reach one to
three ppm on 13C by using tens of thousands of spectra and often a calculated geometry; this model
has 400 molecules and one force-field conformation each. The question the item asks is
narrower, and the measurement answers it.

**Carboxylic acid pKa, 912 acids with the value on the carboxyl carbon.**

| descriptor | envelope width rho | q2 | error (pKa units) | mean kernel between two samples | difference in q2 against the counts |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| atom-centred counts (20 atom types in 6 shells) | -- | +0.541 | 0.563 | 0.577 | -- |
| local field | 0.05 | +0.570 | 0.545 | 0.716 | +0.029 [-0.030, +0.086] |
| local difference field | 0.05 | +0.045 | 0.811 | 1.000 | -0.495 [-0.718, -0.356] |
| local field | 0.1 | +0.582 | 0.537 | 0.775 | +0.041 [-0.013, +0.094] |
| local difference field | 0.1 | +0.028 | 0.818 | 1.000 | -0.512 [-0.570, -0.451] |
| local field | 0.25 | +0.553 | 0.555 | 0.877 | +0.013 [-0.052, +0.075] |
| local difference field | 0.25 | +0.014 | 0.824 | 1.000 | -0.526 [-0.579, -0.468] |
| local field | 0.5 | +0.526 | 0.571 | 0.957 | -0.014 [-0.079, +0.051] |
| local difference field | 0.5 | +0.315 | 0.687 | 1.000 | -0.226 [-0.383, -0.113] |
| local field | 1 | +0.470 | 0.604 | 0.990 | -0.070 [-0.126, -0.006] |
| local difference field | 1 | +0.020 | 0.822 | 0.999 | -0.520 [-0.610, -0.445] |
| local field | 2 | +0.395 | 0.646 | 0.997 | -0.146 [-0.207, -0.081] |
| local difference field | 2 | +0.033 | 0.816 | 0.998 | -0.508 [-0.561, -0.449] |

**Here the local kernel is no better than the count, and the difference field, which the plan
proposed as the sample, is far worse.** The best of the plain environments is a width of 3.2 Å,
+0.582 against +0.541 for the counts, a difference of +0.041 [-0.013, +0.094] -- inside the
interval, so by rule 4 it is not a result. The direction the plan expected is right, though: an
acidity wants a **wider** envelope than a shift, and a tight one fails: +0.526 at a width of
1.4 Å and +0.395 at 0.7 Å, both below the count.

The mean-kernel column says why, and it is the useful part of this measurement. For the difference
field it is 0.998 or more at every width, and 0.9999 at the three widest: **every carboxylic
acid loses its proton in nearly the same way**, so the difference of the two fields is nearly the same pattern for all 912 of them, and
after the cosine normalisation the samples are indistinguishable. The free energy of deprotonation
is indeed a response to that change, but what distinguishes one acid from another is not in the
change itself -- it is in what surrounds it, which is exactly what the difference removes. The same
column explains the plain environments: at a width of 1.4 Å the mean kernel is already
0.957, because the first shell of a carboxyl group is the same group in every molecule,
and the model only starts to see the substituent as the envelope widens.

![q² against the envelope width 1/√ρ for the two per-atom targets, with the atom-centred counts as the dotted line. Left: a ¹³C shift wants a narrow envelope of about 1 Å. Middle: an acidity wants a wide one, and the difference field fails at every width. Right: the gain of the pKa models over the counts with its 95 % bootstrap interval; only an interval that excludes zero is a result.](docs/figures/envelope.svg)

**The conformations the molecule visits.** A measured shift is an average over the
conformations a molecule visits, and so is an acidity; the single geometry that distance geometry
returns is a stand-in for that average, and both measurements above named it as their weakest
part. Plan item LP4 is the test of what it costs. It needs no new kernel: an environment is a
field, so the mean of the per-conformation environments is a field too and the kernel on it is the
mean-map kernel (`localenv.ensemble_environment`). What it cannot be is the environment of the
mean field of the molecule: the atom sits in a different place in every conformation, so each
conformation has its own environment, centred on its own copy of the atom, and it is those that
are averaged. With a frame the same order applies -- pose each conformation, then average
(`localalign.posed_ensemble`) -- because the site moves with the conformation.

`benchmarks/run_local.py` asks for 5 conformations per molecule from the distance-geometry
generator with a force-field refinement, keeps the prepared geometry as the first of them, and
measures four samples: that geometry alone, the lowest in energy of the pool alone, and the
ensemble weighed equally and by the force field's energies.

**On the shifts, averaging costs, and the control says it is the averaging.**

| conformations | q2 | error (ppm) | atoms per sample | difference in q2 against the prepared one |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| one, as prepared | +0.973 | 8.824 | 13 | -- |
| one, lowest in energy | +0.972 | 8.880 | 13 | -0.000 [-0.001, +0.000] |
| the ensemble, weighed equally | +0.952 | 11.632 | 71 | -0.020 [-0.024, -0.017] |
| the ensemble, weighed by energy | +0.956 | 11.149 | 71 | -0.016 [-0.019, -0.014] |

The prepared geometry gives q2 +0.973 and 8.82 ppm. Averaging over the ensemble gives 11.63 ppm weighed equally and 11.15 ppm weighed by energy, which is -0.020 [-0.024, -0.017] and -0.016 [-0.019, -0.014] in q2 -- both outside their intervals, so both are real losses. The second row is the control: a different single conformation, the lowest in energy of the same pool, which differs from the prepared one for 285 of the 400 molecules and costs -0.000 [-0.001, +0.000] -- nothing. So the loss is not that the generated geometries are worse than the prepared one. It is the averaging.

The reading is that the mean field smears every atom over the positions it takes in the conformations. At an envelope width of 1.0 Å what is left inside the envelope is the first shells, and those are the same in every conformation: the averaging adds blur and no information. The atom count per sample says the same thing from the other side -- 13 atoms become 71 and the model gets worse.

**On the acidities, it neither helps nor costs.**

| conformations | q2 | error (pKa units) | atoms per sample | difference in q2 against the prepared one |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| one, as prepared | +0.582 | 0.537 | 25 | -- |
| one, lowest in energy | +0.576 | 0.540 | 25 | -0.005 [-0.043, +0.035] |
| the ensemble, weighed equally | +0.562 | 0.550 | 127 | -0.020 [-0.061, +0.025] |
| the ensemble, weighed by energy | +0.549 | 0.557 | 127 | -0.032 [-0.070, +0.013] |

The prepared geometry gives q2 +0.582, the ensemble +0.562 weighed equally and +0.549 weighed by energy, which is -0.020 [-0.061, +0.025] and -0.032 [-0.070, +0.013]. The control costs -0.005 [-0.043, +0.035]. Both ensemble intervals include zero, so by rule 4 this is not a measurable loss; what it is not is a gain. The envelope here is wider, 3.2 Å, and does reach the parts of a molecule that move between conformations, which is the case where averaging had the best chance of paying. It did not take it.

```bash
cmf local examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --target shift --conformers 5 \
    --conformer-weighting boltzmann
```

The option is there because the question is a fair one to ask of another set, not because it helps
on these two.

**Many atoms at once.** A per-atom target is a large problem where a per-molecule one is a
small one: the 400 molecules in `examples/local/` are 5096 carbons, and the free NMR databases
hold hundreds of thousands. An exact kernel over samples costs the square of their number in
memory and the cube in time, so plan item LP5 asks for a Nyström or inducing-point approximation.
For this kernel none is needed, and that is the first thing `benchmarks/run_local_scale.py`
measures.

The rotation-invariant local kernel is a **linear kernel on a finite feature map**. The field
autocorrelation of an environment is a fixed number of channels -- 255 for the five
physico-chemical fields -- scaled per block and cosine-normalised, and the kernel is the inner
product of those rows. So the ridge regression can be solved in the space of the 255
coefficients instead of the space of the samples (`cmfqsar/locallarge.py`), which is the same
model and not an approximation of it:

| route | q2 | error (ppm) | memory | the folds |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| dual, an n by n kernel | +0.972645 | 8.8240 | 0.19 GB | 13 s |
| primal, n by d rows | +0.972645 | 8.8240 | 10 MB | 0.1 s |

The predictions of the two differ by 2e-06 ppm, which is round-off. What differs is the cost, and
it is the memory that decides: the kernel grows with the square of the samples and the rows grow
with the samples. At twenty times these 5096 carbons the kernel would be 77 GB and the rows 198 MB.

**More data does not help.** With the primal route a much larger set becomes easy, so the question
the item really asks can be put: is the error of the sections above the method's or the data
set's? The set is 58705 carbons in 6000 molecules, built from the whole nmrshiftdb2 dump rather than from its chloroform spectra alone, so it is noisier by about a ppm and far larger. An exact kernel over it would be 25.7 GB; the primal route cross-validates it in 7 seconds. Each size is a subset of the next.

| molecules | carbons | q2 | error (ppm) | the folds |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100 | 1105 | +0.953 | 10.84 | 0.2 s |
| 200 | 2131 | +0.961 | 10.13 | 0.3 s |
| 400 | 4113 | +0.964 | 9.73 | 0.4 s |
| 800 | 8079 | +0.965 | 9.61 | 1.0 s |
| 1600 | 15780 | +0.965 | 9.70 | 1.7 s |
| 3200 | 31221 | +0.964 | 9.83 | 3.2 s |
| 6000 | 58705 | +0.965 | 9.75 | 6.8 s |

From 100 molecules to 6000 the error goes from 10.84 to 9.75 ppm, and from eight hundred molecules onwards it does not move at all. Sixty times the data is worth 1.23 ppm, nearly all of it spent before the first thousand molecules.

**A finer descriptor helps more than sixty times the data.** A flat curve says the error is not the data's. What is left is the descriptor, and the cheapest test of that is a finer one on the same samples: the distance axis of the autocorrelation at 0.5 A per bin against two finer spacings, everything else unchanged.

| distance bins | channels | q2 | error (ppm) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| every 0.5 A | 255 | +0.965 | 9.75 |
| every 0.25 A | 495 | +0.974 | 8.35 |
| every 0.125 A | 975 | +0.978 | 7.76 |

Halving the bin width gains 1.40 ppm and halving again gains 1.99 ppm in all -- against the 1.23 ppm that sixty times the data gave. **The error of this model is set by what the descriptor can tell apart, not by how many carbons it has seen.** The route to the shift predictors this item names runs through a richer descriptor, which is plan item C5, rather than through a larger training set. What the scale work gives is that the question could be asked at all: the whole curve above, every fold and every ridge, is a few minutes of arithmetic.

![The learning curve of the local shift model on the 6000-molecule nmrshiftdb2 set, cross-validated error against the number of training molecules, each size a subset of the next, and the same error at the full size when the distance bins of the descriptor are halved twice. Sixty times the data gains about one ppm and stops gaining after eight hundred molecules; two halvings of the bin width gain two. Drawn from benchmarks/results/local_scale/curve.json.](docs/figures/scale.svg)

**The kernel that does need landmarks.** The posed overlap kernel of the next section has no finite
feature map -- its features are the field itself, a function on space -- so there the dual form is
the only exact one and the Nyström approximation is the route the plan names.
`locallarge.nystrom_kernel` builds it from landmark environments, and on the 1225
aromatic carbons of that section it works very well: 200 landmarks of 1225 samples, 16 per cent of the rank, reproduce the exact q2 of +0.899, and 100 already give a relative kernel error of 0.001, while 25 give 0.072. The environments of one site are alike, which is why so few span them.

| landmarks | relative error of the kernel | q2 | error (ppm) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| all 1225 (exact) | 0.000 | +0.899 | 4.217 |
| 25 | 0.072 | +0.801 | 5.908 |
| 50 | 0.031 | +0.859 | 4.970 |
| 100 | 0.001 | +0.883 | 4.539 |
| 200 | 0.000 | +0.899 | 4.203 |
| 400 | 0.000 | +0.898 | 4.231 |
| 800 | 0.000 | +0.899 | 4.217 |

**What the descriptor still lacks, measured with SOAP.** The learning curve above said the
local model is limited by its descriptor. `benchmarks/run_soap_gate.py` asks which part is
missing, by computing a descriptor that has it on the same carbons, with the same ridge and
the same folds: SOAP (Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions), the power spectrum of one Gaussian
density per element around the atom, from the dscribe package. The autocorrelation of this
section is a two-point quantity. It resolves the distance between two neighbours of the
centre and not their distances from it, so the triangle the three atoms form stays open.
SOAP at angular order 0 resolves the distances from the centre alone and is two-body as
well; each higher order adds the angle at the centre.

| descriptor | 5096 carbons, error (ppm) | 1225 aromatic carbons, error (ppm) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| atom-centred counts | 20.46 | 6.38 |
| field autocorrelation, best envelope width | 8.82 | 5.19 |
| posed overlap kernel (next section) | -- | 4.22 |
| SOAP, angular order 0 | 8.15 | 4.94 |
| SOAP, angular order 8, same density width and kernel exponent | 6.62 | 3.81 |
| SOAP, angular order 8, best density width and kernel exponent | 5.72 | 3.50 |

The two-body SOAP matches the autocorrelation (+0.004 [-0.001, +0.008] in q2 on the 5096
carbons, bootstrapped over molecules). The angular orders are what lowers the error:
+0.008 [+0.006, +0.011] there and +0.057 [+0.045, +0.070] on the aromatic carbons. On the
aromatic carbons the best SOAP is better than the posed overlap kernel of the next section
(+0.031 [+0.015, +0.052]), with no frame at all. So the part the local descriptor lacks is
the angle at the centre. A CMF form of it would resolve each neighbour pair over its two
distances from the centre as well as the distance between them, with the field weights as
the channels in place of the elements. The next section builds that form and measures it.

**The three-distance autocorrelation: the angle at the centre, with the fields as channels.**
`cmfqsar/triangles.py` resolves every pair of atoms in the environment over three distances:
the distance of each atom from the centre and the distance between the two. Three sides fix a
triangle, so this carries what the SOAP power spectrum carries, in a different basis, and it
keeps the closed pair sum of the two-point descriptor: for every pair of fields, every pair of
radial windows and every distance window, the sum over atom pairs of the two field weights
times the three windows. Its channels are the fields. Where SOAP has one density per element,
this descriptor has one weight per field, so a channel says which two atomic properties, at
which two distances from the centre and how far apart, the model reads. An element indicator is
itself a field, so SOAP's channels are one setting of the same code, and the two kinds of
channel can be mixed. `cmf local --triangles` selects it; `--r-max` is the cutoff and the reach
of the radial grid, `--grid-step` the spacing of both grids, `--grid-sigma` the window width,
`--scaling` how the channel blocks are scaled before the kernel (per field, per pair of fields
as the two-point kernel does, or not at all) and `--power` an integer exponent on the
cosine-normalised kernel, which is what SOAP calls zeta. It works with `--primal` too, at
power 1. An environment and its mirror image give the same channels: three distances fix a
triangle up to reflection, which is the blind spot measured on whole molecules under plan item
C5, and it is unchanged here.

`benchmarks/run_triangles.py` measures it on the carbons, ridge grid and folds of the SOAP
gate above, with the element indicators of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as a second
set of channels through the same code, and both sets together. The settings below were chosen
on the sets: cutoff 5 Å, grid step 0.5 Å, window 0.35 Å, kernel power 1, envelope width
parameter 0.5 on the 5096 carbons and 0.1 on the aromatic carbons. Errors are root-mean-square
out of fold, in ppm.

| descriptor and channels | 5096 carbons | 1225 aromatic carbons |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| two-point field autocorrelation, best envelope width | 8.82 | 5.19 |
| SOAP, best of the gate | 5.72 | 3.50 |
| three-distance, five fields, scaled per field | 5.45 | 4.13 |
| three-distance, four elements, scaled per field | 5.47 | 3.93 |
| three-distance, four elements, no scaling | 5.58 | 3.67 |
| three-distance, fields and elements, scaled per field | 4.96 | 3.86 |
| three-distance, fields and elements, no scaling | 4.83 | 3.81 |

Three things follow, each with its interval in q2, bootstrapped over molecules. **The basis
reproduces SOAP.** With the element channels the three-distance descriptor is SOAP within the
interval on both sets (+0.001 [-0.001, +0.003] on the 5096 carbons, -0.007 [-0.015, +0.001]
on the aromatic ones), so the angular term the gate asked for is in the program. **The fields
are a good set of channels on the broad set.** The five fields alone match SOAP there (+0.001
[-0.001, +0.003]) and improve on the two-point kernel by +0.017 [+0.014, +0.020]; put together
with the elements they give 4.83 ppm, better than SOAP (+0.003 [+0.002, +0.005]) and than
either set of channels on its own (+0.002 [+0.001, +0.004] against each). **On the aromatic
carbons the fields carry less than the elements.** They improve on the two-point kernel by
more (+0.056 [+0.033, +0.079]) but stay behind SOAP (-0.027 [-0.050, -0.010]) and behind the
element channels in the same basis (-0.020 [-0.042, -0.001]), and adding them to the elements
gains nothing (-0.006 [-0.035, +0.011]). The aromatic shift follows the substitution pattern
of the ring, and the element channels state that pattern more directly than the field weights,
which are smooth functions of it, do; on the broad set, where the carbons differ in
hybridisation and neighbours, the field weights add information the elements do not have.

The smaller choices: a window of 0.35 Å is better than 0.5 or 0.7 Å on both sets; a kernel
power above one, which SOAP needs, gains nothing here (5.46 ppm at power 2 against 5.45);
scaling the channel blocks per field is best for the field channels and no scaling is best for
the element channels, which is why the option exists. The cost is in the channel count, which
grows as the square of fields times radii: 32 340 channels for five fields at the 5 Å cutoff
and 128 205 for ten, and ten to twenty-five minutes per ten-fold cross-validation on the 5096
carbons against one minute for the two-point kernel. The default cutoff is 4 Å, which halves
the count and loses 0.02 ppm on the shift set and nothing on the aromatic carbons. The command
of the best shift model is

```
cmf local examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --target shift --rho 0.5 --triangles --r-max 5 --reference
```

The element channels of the benchmark are built in Python with `element_weights` of the
module; the command line offers the fields. Results in `benchmarks/results/triangles/`.

## A co-field around one atom: the local alignment

The local kernel of the previous section needs no frame, and that is also its limit: with no
frame there is no co-field, so it cannot say **where** around the atom, and in which field, a
feature raises or lowers the property. For one site a frame costs nothing, and plan item LP3 is
that frame (`cmfqsar/localalign.py`).

**The rule.** The centre is already the origin and the first atom of the environment, so what is
left is the rotation, and two of the centre's bonded neighbours fix it: the first gives the x
axis, the second the xy plane. Which two is decided by the **atom type and nothing else**. A bond
length would make a poor rule -- the two ring bonds of an aromatic carbon differ by hundredths of
an angstrom, and by which of them is longer in one conformation -- so neighbours of the same type
are treated as interchangeable. When that leaves the choice open, as it does for the two ring
neighbours of an aromatic carbon or the three hydrogens of a methyl group, **every pose is kept
and averaged**: the environment becomes the mean field of its poses, which is a mean-map kernel
over the frames the site allows. That is the device the symmetrised Hammett set uses for the four
images of a monosubstituted benzene, applied to one atom instead of one molecule.

**The ring site.** `ring_frames` is the site the plan names: an aromatic carbon of a six-membered
ring, with the bond that leaves the ring on +x, the ring in the xy plane, the ring normal on z,
and the two mirror images kept. In that frame the positions a substituent occupies on the ring are
fixed numbers, which `RING_POSITIONS` holds: ipso at 1.4 A on +x, then ortho at 2.4 A, meta at
3.7 A and para at 4.2 A from the centre. A carbon where two rings meet has three aromatic
neighbours and no such frame, and the rule refuses it rather than posing it anyway.

**Then everything applies.** The posed environments are in one frame, so the ordinary overlap
kernel of this program works on them exactly as it works on molecules, and so does the co-field:
`overlap_kernel` builds the `AtomTable` and the kernel, and `CMFModel.cofield_coefficients` gives
the co-field around the atom. `cofields.cofield_at_points` reads it at places a chemist can name,
`cofield_covariance_at` says how far the noise in the measured values moves it, and `contrast_at`
compares two places with the right error bar: the co-field at two positions a few angstrom apart
is built from the same training fields, so the two values are correlated and the error of their
difference is not the two error bars added.

```bash
cmf local examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --target shift --align --site ring --rho 0.25 \
    --cofield cofield.cube
```

`--align` replaces the rotation-invariant kernel by the posed overlap kernel, `--site ring` uses
the ring rule and leaves out every atom it does not fit, and `--cofield` writes the co-field
around the centre as a cube file in the frame of the pose, which any molecular viewer draws.

### What it is worth, measured

`benchmarks/run_local_cofield.py` measures two things on the aromatic carbons of the shift set:
1225 carbons of six-membered aromatic rings in 170 molecules, with folds that
hold out whole molecules, and the atom-centred count of the previous section as the reference.

**The frame gains where the envelope is wide, and nothing where it is narrow.**

| descriptor | envelope width rho | width (A) | q2 | error (ppm) | ridge | difference in q2 against the counts |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| atom-centred counts (18 atom types in 6 shells) | -- | -- | +0.768 | 6.383 | 0.01 | -- |
| posed overlap | 0.05 | 4.5 | +0.872 | 4.745 | 0.1 | +0.104 [+0.070, +0.144] |
| invariant local | 0.05 | 4.5 | +0.116 | 12.461 | 0.1 | -0.652 [-0.695, -0.594] |
| posed overlap | 0.1 | 3.2 | +0.887 | 4.448 | 0.01 | +0.119 [+0.086, +0.158] |
| invariant local | 0.1 | 3.2 | +0.366 | 10.554 | 0.1 | -0.402 [-0.457, -0.344] |
| posed overlap | 0.25 | 2.0 | +0.899 | 4.217 | 0.01 | +0.131 [+0.098, +0.170] |
| invariant local | 0.25 | 2.0 | +0.803 | 5.882 | 0.001 | +0.035 [+0.003, +0.068] |
| posed overlap | 0.5 | 1.4 | +0.889 | 4.425 | 0.0001 | +0.121 [+0.083, +0.162] |
| invariant local | 0.5 | 1.4 | +0.847 | 5.187 | 0.01 | +0.079 [+0.048, +0.116] |
| posed overlap | 1 | 1.0 | +0.861 | 4.935 | 1e-06 | +0.093 [+0.046, +0.143] |
| invariant local | 1 | 1.0 | +0.836 | 5.361 | 0.01 | +0.068 [+0.036, +0.105] |

At the same envelope width the posed kernel is ahead of the invariant one by +0.756 [+0.718, +0.791] at a width of 4.5 A; +0.522 [+0.477, +0.572] at a width of 3.2 A; +0.096 [+0.069, +0.124] at a width of 2.0 A; +0.042 [+0.022, +0.061] at a width of 1.4 A; +0.025 [-0.015, +0.060] at a width of 1.0 A. The last of those is inside its interval, so at a width of 1 A the frame adds nothing that can be measured. Each at its own best width -- posed at rho 0.25 (+0.899) against invariant at rho 0.5 (+0.847) -- the difference is +0.052 [+0.033, +0.071].

That is what a frame is and is not for. An invariant descriptor of a wide environment has only
distances, and at a width of 4.5 A the surroundings of an aromatic carbon are nearly the same
distances in every molecule; the pose keeps the directions, so the ortho position and the meta
position are two places rather than two atoms at similar distances. Squeeze the envelope down to
1 A and there is little left but the first shell, which distances alone describe perfectly well,
and the frame adds nothing that can be measured.

**Where the co-field sits, and what it does not say.**

| field | ipso | ortho | meta | para | \|para\| - \|meta\| |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| electrostatic | -16.7 +- 20.3 | +33.0 +- 15.4 | -28.5 +- 15.0 | -10.0 +- 20.0 | -18.5 +- 24.7 |
| steric | +15.5 +- 1.3 | -2.6 +- 1.0 | -2.7 +- 0.9 | -4.2 +- 1.2 | +1.5 +- 1.5 |
| hydrophobic | +1.4 +- 4.5 | -2.0 +- 3.4 | +6.6 +- 3.3 | +2.2 +- 4.7 | -4.4 +- 5.9 |
| hba | -57.4 +- 21.4 | +17.8 +- 15.0 | +29.6 +- 13.4 | -41.1 +- 18.8 | +11.5 +- 25.2 |
| hbd | +7.1 +- 33.6 | +58.4 +- 25.4 | -0.2 +- 23.7 | +62.6 +- 30.4 | +62.4 +- 39.2 |

**The co-field says the large thing and not the subtle one.** The numbers above are the co-field at the four positions with the error the noise in the shifts allows, and one feature stands far above everything else: the **steric field at the ipso position**, +15.5 +- 1.3, 12 standard deviations from zero where nothing else reaches four. It says that putting anything bulkier than hydrogen on the measured carbon raises its shift, which is the dominant term of the 13C substituent effect and true of nearly every group: methyl +9 ppm, chlorine +6, nitro +20, methoxy +31.

**What it does not reproduce is the alternation around the ring, and that is the half of this item that fails.** The question the plan asks is whether the co-field puts more at the para position than at the meta one. The para position is further from the measured carbon (4.2 A) than the meta one (3.7 A), so the envelope and the overlap both favour meta, and a co-field that still came out larger at para would be saying what the geometry does not. None does. For the electrostatic field the difference is -18.5 +- 24.7, the wrong sign and inside the error. The closest any field comes is the hydrogen-bond-donor one, +62.4 +- 39.2 (z +1.6), which is the right sign and the right field -- a hydroxyl or an amino group is where the ortho and para effects on an aromatic shift are largest -- and still short of two standard deviations.

Read the five co-fields together rather than one at a time. The fields overlap in what they describe -- an oxygen is a heavy atom, an acceptor and a negative charge at once -- so a co-field per field is a decomposition of one effect over five bases, not five independent statements, and the hydrogen-bond-acceptor co-field correcting the steric one at the ipso position is that decomposition at work rather than a claim about acceptors.

The signs are the more interesting half, and they are not nothing. The electrostatic co-field comes out -16.7 at ipso, +33.0 at ortho, -28.5 at meta and -10.0 at para, and a negative value means that negative charge at that place raises the shift of the carbon at the origin. A methoxy group raises the shift of the carbon it sits on by 31 ppm and lowers the ortho and para carbons by 14 and 8 ppm, and its oxygen is negatively charged, so a co-field that had learned that effect would be negative at ipso and positive at ortho and para. This one agrees at 3 of the four positions, with a correlation of +0.55 over them, but the y-scramble null for that correlation is wide (z +1.2): a correlation over four points cannot be sharp, and this one is not.

There is a reason to expect no better from these fields. A nitro group, whose nitrogen is **positively** charged, also raises the ipso carbon, by 20 ppm, and raises the para carbon where methoxy lowers it. No model linear in fragment charges can follow both groups, because what separates them is resonance and fragment charges do not carry it. That is the same wall the Hammett co-fields of this program met for sigma_p, and the remedy there was quantum charges computed on the whole molecule, which carry the polarisation of the ring by the substituent (`examples/orca_atom_properties.py` and the `prop:` fields). The shift set here has no such charges. The other way round the wall is to stop asking the charge and ask the atom type, which is what the next part does and what settles the question.

![The co-fields of the Hammett constants $\sigma_m$ and $\sigma_p$, from the Hammett benchmark: the electrostatic and the steric co-field in the ring plane and 1.7 Å above it, with the ring and the substituent position X marked. Red raises the constant per unit of field. The electrostatic map of $\sigma_p$ has lobes of both signs around the substituent position, a pattern that fragment charges cannot deliver for a nitro group and a methoxy group at once. Drawn by `benchmarks/run_hammett.py`.](benchmarks/results/hammett/cofields.png)

![The electrostatic and the steric co-field of the shift model around the measured carbon, at the origin, in the ring plane, with the ring and its four positions marked. Red raises the shift of that carbon per unit of field. The steric lobe at the ipso position is the feature twelve standard deviations from zero; the electrostatic map alternates in sign around the ring. Drawn by `benchmarks/run_local_cofield.py`.](benchmarks/results/local_cofield/cofield.png)

**The same co-field, read from the indicator fields.** A partial charge cannot tell a
pi-donor from a pi-acceptor, which is why the electrostatic co-field above could not reproduce the
ring picture. A continuous indicator field carries the atom **type** instead: there is one field
per Sybyl type, so an ether oxygen at the ortho position and a carbonyl carbon at the ortho
position are different features with co-fields of their own. That is how a table of substituent
effects is written, and the second part of `benchmarks/run_local_cofield.py` asks whether the
model writes the same table. It uses 17 types beside the five physico-chemical fields, at
an envelope width of 4.5 A -- wider than the co-field above, because an envelope that damps
the para position to nothing cannot be asked what sits there -- and predicts about as well
(q2 +0.882, 4.55 ppm out of fold).

Two things make this a comparison of numbers rather than of pictures. First,
`cofields.atom_effect` turns a co-field into **what one atom placed at a point would add to the
prediction**, in ppm: the co-field is a sum of Gaussians and so is the atom, the overlap of two
Gaussians is the closed-form integral the kernel itself sums over atom pairs, and the test suite
checks the result against what the model's own prediction does when that atom is added. Second,
the atom enters with the weight the envelope gives it at that distance (ipso 0.91, ortho 0.75, meta 0.50, para 0.41), so the number
is what a real substituent at that ring position contributes rather than what an undamped one
would.

| type | ipso | ortho | meta | para | measured, for the group named |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H | -1.6 +- 0.6 (n 774) | +0.2 +- 0.4 (n 1483) | +0.5 +- 0.3 (n 1448) | -0.1 +- 0.3 (n 733) | -- |
| O.3 | +5.4 +- 1.6 (n 170) | -6.4 +- 1.1 (n 342) | -1.3 +- 0.8 (n 334) | -1.5 +- 0.9 (n 157) | +31.4, -14.4, +1.0, -7.7 (methoxy (anisole)) |
| C.3 | +13.6 +- 0.8 (n 126) | +0.5 +- 0.5 (n 242) | -1.1 +- 0.4 (n 239) | -0.5 +- 0.5 (n 120) | +9.3, +0.7, -0.1, -2.9 (methyl (toluene)) |
| C.2 | +9.0 +- 1.1 (n 87) | -0.2 +- 0.7 (n 172) | -0.7 +- 0.5 (n 168) | +0.7 +- 0.7 (n 84) | +9.3, +0.2, +0.2, +4.2 (acetyl (acetophenone)) |
| C.ar | +1.0 +- 0.2 (n 0) | -0.3 +- 0.2 (n 68) | -0.1 +- 0.1 (n 108) | -0.1 +- 0.2 (n 56) | -- |
| N.pl3 | +3.1 +- 2.0 (n 25) | -9.1 +- 1.4 (n 50) | -2.2 +- 1.1 (n 50) | -5.9 +- 1.4 (n 25) | +18.0, -13.3, +0.9, -9.8 (amino (aniline)) |
| Cl | +7.4 +- 2.2 (n 16) | +0.1 +- 1.5 (n 32) | +1.7 +- 1.3 (n 32) | -2.4 +- 1.7 (n 16) | +6.2, +0.4, +1.3, -1.9 (chlorine (chlorobenzene)) |

**The pattern comes out right.** Over the 15 (type, ring position) pairs that have a measured value -- the ipso position left out, because it is the largest effect in every row and would carry the comparison by itself -- the correlation with the measured table is +0.89. Including the ipso position it is +0.72. The sharpest of these is the question the electrostatic field could not answer at all: a pi-donor lowers the para carbon and a pi-acceptor raises it, although the first atom of the donor is negatively charged and that of the acceptor is positive. Here the amino nitrogen gives -5.9 +- 1.4 ppm at the para position, 4 standard deviations from zero, against -9.8 measured, while the sp2 carbon gives +0.7 +- 0.7 against +4.2 measured. The signs are opposite, and the ether oxygen sits on the donor side as well (-1.5 +- 0.9). That is the resonance distinction no model linear in fragment charges can make.

**The sizes are compressed.** A straight line through those 15 pairs has a slope of 0.46, so the model reproduces the shape of the table and about 46 per cent of its size. The root mean square difference from the measured row, per type, is Cl 0.7, C.2 1.8, C.3 2.5, N.pl3 8.1, O.3 14.0 ppm: the halogen and the two carbons come within a few ppm and the two strong donors are the ones held back. Three things pull that way: the ridge, which shrinks every coefficient; the envelope, which lets a para atom in at 0.41 of itself; and the set, where most rings carry several substituents whose effects the model shares out, while the table is measured on rings carrying one. The type labels are coarser than the table's groups too -- O.3 is every ether and hydroxyl oxygen, not only a methoxy, and C.2 is every sp2 carbon, not only an acetyl -- so the measured column is the nearest published row rather than the same quantity.

The same field set is a flag on the command, so the table above can be read off any per-atom
target without the benchmark:

```bash
cmf local examples/local/shifts_cdcl3.sdf --target shift --align --site ring \
    --rho 0.05 --cif --cofield cofield.cube
```

`benchmarks/results/local_cofield/indicator.png` draws the two co-fields in the ring plane side by side. Both are positive where a substituent sits on the measured carbon and negative at the ortho positions, which is the large part of the effect; what separates the donor from the acceptor is the weaker pattern further out, and that is read off at the points in the table rather than by eye.

**The other site the plan names, the carboxyl carbon, is not rescued by the frame either.**
The previous section found no signal on the 912 carboxylic acids: the invariant local kernel was no better than an atom-centred count there, and the difference field of the acid and its anion was far worse. A carboxyl carbon has two oxygens and a carbon of its own, which the atom types separate, so its pose is unique and nothing has to be averaged -- and with it the model loses to the count, -0.101 [-0.164, -0.037], and differs from the invariant kernel by -0.142 [-0.198, -0.088]. The frame was not what was missing. Only the model is measured there: a co-field read off a model that does not predict would be an interpretation of noise, which is why the pKa co-field of the substituted benzoic acids that this item's gate asks for is not drawn.

**What is not done.** The plan asks for a panel in the application that shows the environment with
its co-field instead of the molecule. There is none: the co-field comes out of `cmf local
--cofield` as a cube file, which a viewer draws, and the application still knows only models whose
sample is a molecule.

## A vibrational band as the local target: the carbonyl stretch of the benzoic acids

A shift and an acidity were the first two local targets. A vibrational band is a third. It
belongs to a bond. It is computed here and not measured, so its noise is the numerical noise of
the quantum program. And the series is the one Hammett defined his constants on. Plan item SP2
asks two questions. Does the field around an atom predict such a band better than a count of what
is around the atom? And does the co-field around the atom say where the substituent acts?

The answer in short. On the geometries that the quantum program optimised, the field predicts the
band almost exactly, and this result does not count: the field reads the length of the carbonyl
bond, and that length comes from the same calculation as the band. On the force-field
geometries the field predicts the band as well as a linear regression on the Hammett constant
and a little better than the count, and only with an envelope wide enough to reach the
substituent.

**The series and the band.** The 95 substituents of the Hammett set (`examples/hammett/`), each
placed meta and para to the carboxyl group of benzoic acid, give 189 acids
(`examples/make_band_examples.py`, `examples/spectra/`). Each is optimised and its harmonic
frequencies are computed with ORCA at r2SCAN-3c; the carbonyl stretch is the normal mode between
1600 and 1900 cm$^{-1}$ that moves the carbonyl carbon and oxygen apart most, which is how a band
is assigned by its motion and not by its position alone (`orca.bond_stretch_mode`), and it is
multiplied by the conventional scaling factor of the level (`orca.FREQUENCY_SCALE`). The band
sits on the carbonyl carbon as `atom.dprop.co_stretch`, one number per acid, so `cmf local` and
the benchmark read it as they read a shift. The frequency run itself is `orca.run_band`: the same
cached job, the same status file and the same rule that a failed molecule is reported and never
fatal as the property runs of the quantum stage.

**A stationary point that is not a minimum.** An optimisation stops where the forces vanish, and
that point can be a saddle point: a methyl group eclipsed with the ring, for example. The
frequency run shows it as an imaginary frequency. `orca.retry_band` moves such a molecule along
the mode of its lowest frequency (`orca.displaced_along_mode`; the atom that moves most moves
0.2 A) and optimises it once more, in a job directory of its own. The second result replaces the
first when it has fewer imaginary frequencies, or as many and a lower energy, and it keeps the
first band as the property `co_stretch_retry`, so the size of the correction can be read.
In this series 13 of the 189 acids ended the first optimisation with one imaginary frequency.
Eleven of them took the result of the second optimisation: eight became minima, and three (meta-
vinyl, para-SPh and meta-SPh) keep one imaginary frequency at a lower energy. For the two acids
with an N=NPh group the second optimisation was not better, and the first result is kept. So 5
acids keep one imaginary frequency, of 8 to 17 cm$^{-1}$. The second optimisation moved the band
by 0.26 cm$^{-1}$ at the median and by 3.3 cm$^{-1}$ at most (para-OSO2CH3, from 1724.8 to
1728.1), which is small beside the spread of the series (4.5 cm$^{-1}$).

**A start geometry that is not the molecule.** The two acids with an SF5 group failed in the
first run, and the reason was the start geometry. UFF, the only force field of RDKit with
parameters for this group, left it far from an octahedron: S-F lengths from 1.25 to 2.17 A and
F-S-F angles down to 25 degrees. The quantum optimisation then broke the group apart (one of the
two acids kept one fluorine on the sulfur) and stopped at its limit of cycles. Two changes
follow. The data script sets an SF5 group to a regular octahedron after the force field
(`regular_sf5`; S-F 1.59 A, C-S 1.80 A, the four equatorial fluorines turned by 45 degrees from
the ring plane). And a geometry is checked against the bond table: `orca.bond_length_ratios`
divides every bond length by the sum of the covalent radii of its two atoms, and
`orca.changed_bonds` lists the bonds outside 0.6 to 1.5. `run_band` reports a molecule whose
optimised geometry has such a bond as a failure, because its band would be the band of another
molecule. In the 187 acids without SF5 every ratio is between 0.79 and 1.03, before and after
the optimisation. `run_band` can also continue an optimisation that stopped at the limit of
cycles from its last geometry, with a computed Hessian (job `freq_more`); this helps a molecule
with a very soft motion and does not help a wrong start geometry, and no acid of this series
needed it.

**One acid with two carboxyl groups.** In terephthalic acid (the substituent COOH in para) the two
carbonyl stretches couple into two modes less than 2 cm$^{-1}$ apart, and each mode has about a
third of its motion on the bond that is the target. The rule takes the mode with the larger
share. The error of this choice is below 1 cm$^{-1}$, and no other acid of the series has it.

```
python examples/make_band_examples.py                    # the 189 acids, from SMILES
python examples/make_band_examples.py --orca --jobs 10   # optimisation and frequencies, cached
python examples/make_band_examples.py --xtb --jobs 8     # GFN2-xTB charges, 13 seconds
python benchmarks/run_band.py                            # the measurement below, 8 minutes
python benchmarks/run_band.py --only indicator           # part 7 alone, 1 to 2 minutes
python benchmarks/run_band.py --only charges             # part 8 alone, 4 to 5 minutes
```

**What is measured** (`benchmarks/run_band.py`, `benchmarks/results/band/table.md`). The
benchmark has eight parts.

1. The computed band against the Hammett constant sigma, as a linear regression: the straight
   line band = a + b sigma, fitted by least squares. This is the plot of a physical organic
   chemist. Fitted inside each fold, the regression is also a reference beside the count. It
   has two forms: one equation for all acids, called the Hammett regression below, and two
   equations, one for the meta and one for the para acids, called the separate Hammett
   regressions.
2. The invariant local kernel (section *An atom instead of a molecule*) and the posed overlap
   kernel (the previous section), at eight envelope widths from 0.7 to 10 A, against the
   atom-centred shell count. Ten folds hold out whole molecules, and the ridge is chosen on the
   same folds for every descriptor.
3. The co-field at the ring positions in the frame of the carbonyl carbon, at three envelope
   widths. The positions are read from the posed geometries themselves (ipso, ortho, meta and
   para; the two ortho and the two meta carbons are told apart by the side of the carboxyl group
   they lie on). Each value has the error that the noise in the bands allows and a y-scramble
   null (the same reading on models fitted to bands in random order). A carbonyl carbon has one
   carbon and two oxygens of different types bonded to it, so its frame is unique and nothing is
   averaged.
4. A linear regression of the band on the length of the C=O bond, called the bond-length
   regression below, as one more reference.
5. Parts 2 to 4 a second time, on the start geometries: the force-field structures of
   `examples/spectra/benzoic_acids.sdf`, from which the quantum optimisation started. The partial
   charges of both runs are Gasteiger charges, which depend on the bond graph only, so the two
   runs differ in the coordinates and in nothing else.
6. The differences in q2 with their 95 % bootstrap intervals over the molecules.
7. The indicator fields of the previous section on the start geometries: one Gaussian field
   per Sybyl atom type, alone and together with the five physico-chemical fields. This part
   repeats the cross-validation ten times with other folds. It gives every number a second
   time for folds that hold out whole substituents, because the series holds each substituent
   twice. It writes `indicator.json`, and the table gains a part from it.
8. Quantum charges in the electrostatic field, on the start geometries. The charge of every
   atom comes from one GFN2-xTB calculation without a geometry optimisation
   (`examples/spectra/benzoic_acids_xtb.sdf`). The field sets are the electrostatic field
   alone, the five fields, the five fields with one field for each of the two Fukui indices,
   and the five fields with the indicator fields. The envelope width and the ridge are chosen
   inside the folds. The references gain two regressions on the quantum charges of the
   carboxyl group. This part writes `charges.json`, and the table gains a part from it.

**The band follows the Hammett constant.** The 189 bands lie between 1710.6 and
1737.1 cm$^{-1}$, with a spread (standard deviation) of 4.5 cm$^{-1}$. A
substituent that withdraws electrons raises the band, by about 11.5 cm$^{-1}$ per unit of sigma, and
the slope is the same for the meta and the para acids. Benzoic acid itself is counted in the
meta and in the para regression.

| acids | number | slope, cm$^{-1}$ per unit of sigma | correlation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| all | 189 | +11.7 | +0.866 |
| meta | 95 | +11.3 | +0.817 |
| para | 95 | +11.5 | +0.910 |

**The references.** A descriptor has to be compared with what is known without it. The Hammett
regressions need no geometry. The count and the bond-length regression are given on both
geometry sets.

| reference | geometries it uses | q2 | error (RMSE), cm$^{-1}$ |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hammett regression, band = a + b sigma, one equation for all acids | none | +0.740 | 2.28 |
| separate Hammett regressions, one equation for meta and one for para | none | +0.781 | 2.09 |
| atom-centred count | optimised | +0.662 | 2.60 |
| atom-centred count | start | +0.616 | 2.77 |
| linear regression on the length of the C=O bond | optimised | +0.973 | 0.74 |
| linear regression on the length of the C=O bond | start | -0.014 | 4.50 |

**On the optimised geometries the narrow field reads one bond length.** On the geometries of the
quantum optimisation both kernels improve as the envelope gets narrower. They are best at a width
of 1 A: q2 +0.976 for the invariant kernel and +0.978 for
the posed overlap, against +0.662 for the count.

| envelope width, A | invariant kernel, q2 | invariant against the count | posed overlap, q2 | posed against the count | posed against the bond-length regression |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10.00 | +0.743 | +0.081 [-0.000, +0.152] | +0.725 | +0.063 [-0.006, +0.132] | -0.248 [-0.312, -0.204] |
| 7.07 | +0.750 | +0.088 [+0.012, +0.158] | +0.719 | +0.058 [-0.008, +0.124] | -0.253 [-0.307, -0.212] |
| 4.47 | +0.770 | +0.108 [+0.031, +0.182] | +0.733 | +0.072 [+0.005, +0.139] | -0.239 [-0.309, -0.193] |
| 3.16 | +0.863 | +0.202 [+0.131, +0.276] | +0.869 | +0.208 [+0.147, +0.274] | -0.103 [-0.142, -0.076] |
| 2.00 | +0.929 | +0.268 [+0.147, +0.373] | +0.903 | +0.241 [+0.153, +0.331] | -0.070 [-0.145, -0.031] |
| 1.41 | +0.960 | +0.298 [+0.240, +0.374] | +0.963 | +0.301 [+0.243, +0.377] | -0.010 [-0.032, +0.003] |
| 1.00 | +0.976 | +0.314 [+0.257, +0.388] | +0.978 | +0.316 [+0.259, +0.390] | +0.005 [+0.002, +0.009] |
| 0.71 | +0.974 | +0.312 [+0.254, +0.386] | +0.974 | +0.312 [+0.255, +0.386] | +0.001 [-0.000, +0.003] |

This looks like the result the plan expected. It is not a prediction from the structure. The C=O
bond of the optimised acids is between 1.2088 and 1.2160 A long, with a spread of 0.0012 A. A
linear regression on this one length, fitted in each fold, predicts the band with q2
+0.973; the correlation of the length with the band is -0.987. This is
Badger's rule: a shorter bond is stiffer and has a higher stretching frequency. The field at 1 A
is above that regression by +0.003 [+0.001, +0.006] (invariant kernel) and by
+0.005 [+0.002, +0.009] (posed overlap). So nearly all of what the narrow field
predicts is one bond length, read to a thousandth of an angstrom. That length is a result of the
quantum optimisation, and the optimisation is the first half of the calculation that gives the
band. A user who wants the band of a new acid does not have this length before the calculation
is done.

The force-field geometries confirm this. Their C=O lengths (1.2162 to 1.2683 A) have a
correlation of -0.006 with the band, and the regression on them predicts nothing
(q2 -0.014).

**From the structure alone the field equals the Hammett regression.** The start geometries hold
nothing from the quantum calculation.

| envelope width, A | invariant kernel, q2 | invariant against the count | invariant against the Hammett regression | posed overlap, q2 | posed against the count |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10.00 | +0.746 | +0.130 [+0.043, +0.209] | +0.006 [-0.065, +0.077] | +0.702 | +0.087 [+0.002, +0.168] |
| 7.07 | +0.742 | +0.126 [+0.046, +0.202] | +0.002 [-0.068, +0.074] | +0.698 | +0.082 [+0.004, +0.163] |
| 4.47 | +0.707 | +0.092 [+0.000, +0.176] | -0.033 [-0.114, +0.040] | +0.691 | +0.075 [-0.004, +0.150] |
| 3.16 | +0.650 | +0.034 [-0.063, +0.121] | -0.091 [-0.173, -0.011] | +0.663 | +0.047 [-0.033, +0.121] |
| 2.00 | +0.254 | -0.362 [-0.485, -0.242] | -0.486 [-0.594, -0.381] | +0.326 | -0.290 [-0.399, -0.173] |
| 1.41 | +0.279 | -0.336 [-0.478, -0.203] | -0.461 [-0.595, -0.331] | +0.259 | -0.357 [-0.444, -0.244] |
| 1.00 | +0.191 | -0.425 [-0.719, -0.231] | -0.550 [-0.829, -0.363] | +0.231 | -0.385 [-0.523, -0.248] |
| 0.71 | +0.218 | -0.398 [-0.533, -0.270] | -0.522 [-0.653, -0.399] | +0.191 | -0.424 [-0.723, -0.229] |

At a width of 2 A or less both kernels are between q2 +0.191 and +0.326, far below the
count (+0.616). A narrow envelope sees the carboxyl group and the nearest ring
carbons, and these are the same atoms in every acid. From 4.5 A on the invariant kernel reaches
+0.707 to +0.746. At 7 and 10 A it is above the count by
+0.126 [+0.046, +0.202] and +0.130 [+0.043, +0.209]. Against
the Hammett regression the difference is +0.002 [-0.068, +0.074] and
+0.006 [-0.065, +0.077]: the two are equal. The separate Hammett regressions
(q2 +0.781) are above every field model of this table. The posed overlap is
a little lower than the invariant kernel (+0.691 to +0.702 at the three wide widths),
and the lower end of its interval against the count is at zero.

The Hammett constant is a measured quantity: it was defined from the ionisation of these same
acids in water. A model that uses only the structure and equals the Hammett regression has
therefore recovered from the structure what the constant holds, and no more than that.

Three cautions belong to the margin over the count. First, it is read at the best of eight
widths. The neighbouring wide widths agree (+0.092 to +0.130), so the choice of
the width does not make the result, but the lower end of the interval is close to zero. Second,
the posed overlap has a smaller margin (+0.075 to +0.087). Third, the margin depends
on a few acids. A control without the five acids that keep an imaginary frequency (184 acids;
run once, not stored among the results) gave +0.092 [-0.005, +0.174] for the invariant kernel and
+0.090 [+0.015, +0.162] for the posed overlap at 10 A. The fair summary is a margin of about +0.1
in q2 whose interval begins at zero.

At the wide widths the two geometry sets agree: on the optimised geometries the invariant kernel
is at +0.743 to +0.770 there. The quantum geometry adds something only where the envelope
is narrow enough to resolve the bond length.

**The width that works is the distance to the substituent.** The plan expected a best width near
1 A, as for the shift. That expectation was wrong for this band. In the shift set the measured
carbon is a ring carbon, and the substituents sit on it or next to it. Here the measured carbon is
outside the ring. The ring carbons are 1.48 (ipso), 2.19 (ortho),
3.58 (meta) and 4.29 A (para) from it. The first atom of the
substituent is 5.0 A away in a meta acid (4.8 to
5.5 A over the series) and 5.8 A in a para acid
(5.6 to 6.4 A). The envelope gives an atom at the distance r
the weight exp(-rho r$^2$), and the width is the distance at which this weight is 1/e:

| envelope width, A | weight of the first atom of a meta substituent (5.0 A) | weight of the first atom of a para substituent (5.8 A) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10.00 | 0.78 | 0.71 |
| 7.07 | 0.61 | 0.51 |
| 4.47 | 0.29 | 0.19 |
| 3.16 | 0.08 | 0.03 |
| 2.00 | 0.002 | below 0.001 |
| 1.00 | below 0.001 | below 0.001 |

A local target is local in where the property is. Its cause can be further away, and the envelope
has to reach the cause.

**The co-field.** The table gives the electrostatic co-field at the four ring positions: what one
unit of the electrostatic field at that place adds to the band, in cm$^{-1}$, with the standard
deviation that the noise in the bands allows. A positive value means that positive charge at that
place raises the band. *Para minus meta* is the difference of the absolute values. *Para over
meta* is that difference divided by the sum, with the mean and the standard deviation of the
y-scramble null. The table of the benchmark has the other four fields.

| geometries | envelope width, A | posed overlap, q2 | ipso | ortho | meta | para | para minus meta, with its z against the noise | para over meta, with the scramble null and its z |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| optimised | 10.00 | +0.725 | +0.277 +- 0.17 | +1.23 +- 0.26 | +3.58 +- 0.58 | +4.91 +- 0.59 | +1.33 +- 0.31 (z +4.3) | +0.16 (null +0.02 +- 0.46, z +0.3) |
| optimised | 4.47 | +0.733 | -1.09 +- 1.1 | +3.24 +- 1.2 | +4.47 +- 2 | +6.5 +- 2.4 | +2.03 +- 1.3 (z +1.6) | +0.18 (null +0.10 +- 0.50, z +0.2) |
| optimised | 3.16 | +0.869 | -3.39 +- 10 | +53.2 +- 8.2 | +2 +- 11 | -18 +- 12 | +16 +- 22 (z +0.7) | +0.80 (null +0.04 +- 0.44, z +1.7) |
| start | 10.00 | +0.702 | +0.268 +- 0.18 | +1.11 +- 0.27 | +3.68 +- 0.59 | +5.01 +- 0.61 | +1.33 +- 0.31 (z +4.3) | +0.15 (null +0.03 +- 0.42, z +0.3) |
| start | 4.47 | +0.691 | -0.45 +- 1.2 | +2.41 +- 1.3 | +5.32 +- 2.2 | +8.03 +- 2.6 | +2.71 +- 1.4 (z +1.9) | +0.20 (null +0.05 +- 0.49, z +0.3) |
| start | 3.16 | +0.663 | -5.54 +- 6.1 | +7.19 +- 4.4 | -9.4 +- 6.7 | -8.86 +- 8.5 | -0.547 +- 5 (z -0.1) | -0.03 (null -0.00 +- 0.48, z -0.1) |

At a width of 10 A the two geometry sets give the same map: +3.58 and
+3.68 at the meta carbon, +4.91 and
+5.01 at the para carbon, which is 6 and 8
standard deviations from zero on the start geometries, and small values at ipso and ortho.
Positive charge on the far side of the ring raises the band. That is the direction of the Hammett
slope: a substituent that withdraws electrons raises the band. The para value is above the meta
value by +1.33 +- 0.31,
4.3 standard deviations of the noise. Against the y-scramble null this
is not resolved (z +0.3): the ratio lies well inside the spread of the
ratios that models fitted to scrambled bands give. At 4.5 A the signs are the same and the
difference is 1.6 to 1.9 standard
deviations. At 3.2 A, the width that the shift co-field of the previous section used, the map
cannot be read. At the ipso, meta and para carbons the errors are as large as the values, and the
two geometry sets give different maps (at the ortho carbon +53.2 +- 8.2 against
+7.19 +- 4.4). An envelope that gives the substituent a weight below 0.1 cannot say where
the substituent acts.

![The electrostatic and the steric co-field of the band model around the carbonyl carbon, at the origin, in the plane of the ring, on the start geometries at an envelope width of 10 A. The ring carbons are marked. Red raises the band per unit of field. The electrostatic co-field is positive at the meta and para carbons and beyond them, where the substituents are. Drawn by `benchmarks/run_band.py`.](benchmarks/results/band/start_cofield_rho_0p01.png)

Two limits of this reading. The co-field gives the place (the meta and the para carbon and the
space beyond them) and one sign. It does not separate a substituent that donates electrons by
resonance from one that withdraws them, for the reason the previous section gave: fragment charges
do not carry resonance. And the Hammett regressions themselves give no strong reason to expect para
above meta here: the two slopes are equal (+11.3 and
+11.5), so one unit of sigma moves the band by the same
amount from either position.

**One field per atom type: the indicator fields.** The separate Hammett regressions are above
every field model of the tables above. The five physico-chemical fields do not name the atom
types, and fragment charges do not carry resonance. A continuous indicator field of an atom type
is one Gaussian on every atom of that type, so a model with such fields can give every type an
effect of its own. The previous section read the ring picture of the shifts with these fields.
Part 7 of the benchmark measures them on the start geometries, at an envelope width of 10 A. The
width was fixed before this measurement, as the width where the five fields were best. 15 Sybyl
types occur in at least 10 acids, and each gets a field. A control gives a field to every type
that occurs in at least 2 acids (25 types).

Two things differ from the tables above. First, the cross-validation is repeated ten times with
other folds. A q2 is the mean over the ten repeats, and the number in brackets is its standard
deviation over the repeats. Second, every number is given for two kinds of folds. The series
holds each substituent twice, meta and para to the carboxyl group. Over the 94 substituents that
occur twice, the band of the meta acid and the band of the para acid correlate with r +0.80. A
fold that holds out one acid therefore usually keeps the other acid of the same substituent in
the training set. The second kind of fold holds out both acids of a substituent together (95
substituents). The differences carry 95 % bootstrap intervals over the acids for the first kind
of fold and over the substituents for the second. The table is for the invariant local kernel;
the table of the benchmark has the posed overlap and three more widths.

| descriptor | q2, whole acids held out | difference from the separate Hammett regressions, whole acids held out | q2, whole substituents held out | difference from the separate Hammett regressions, whole substituents held out |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| atom-centred count | +0.650 (0.017) | | +0.623 (0.009) | |
| Hammett regression | +0.742 (0.002) | | +0.742 (0.002) | |
| separate Hammett regressions | +0.782 (0.002) | | +0.782 (0.002) | |
| the five fields | +0.741 (0.026) | -0.041 [-0.110, +0.022] | +0.676 (0.015) | -0.106 [-0.243, -0.011] |
| 15 indicator fields | +0.749 (0.022) | -0.033 [-0.122, +0.046] | +0.675 (0.014) | -0.106 [-0.262, +0.005] |
| the five fields and 15 indicator fields | +0.776 (0.017) | -0.005 [-0.090, +0.072] | +0.705 (0.015) | -0.076 [-0.229, +0.033] |
| the five fields and 25 indicator fields | +0.784 (0.018) | +0.003 [-0.086, +0.080] | +0.709 (0.015) | -0.073 [-0.238, +0.042] |

With whole acids held out, the indicator fields alone equal the five fields (+0.749 and +0.741),
and both together reach +0.776. The gain over the five fields is +0.036 [-0.047, +0.116], which
is not resolved. The difference from the separate Hammett regressions is
-0.005 [-0.090, +0.072]. So the field model reaches these regressions and does not pass them.
The control with 25 types gives the same result (+0.784).

With whole substituents held out, every field model loses about 0.07 in q2 (the five fields
+0.676, both field sets +0.705), and the Hammett regressions do not change. The reason is what a
Hammett constant is: a measured value of the substituent. The regression receives this value for
the acid that is held out. A field model has to learn a substituent from the other substituents.
On these folds the five fields are below the separate Hammett regressions
(-0.106 [-0.243, -0.011]), and both field sets are -0.076 [-0.229, +0.033] from them.

The two descriptions are different ones. The correlation between the off-diagonal elements of
the kernel of the indicator fields and of the kernel of the five fields, each centred first, is
+0.33 for the invariant kernel and +0.38 for the posed overlap at 10 A (+0.12 and +0.13 at
3.2 A). Two descriptions that order the pairs of acids so differently reach the same q2, and
together they add about +0.03. The posed overlap does not gain from the indicator fields: +0.718
with both field sets against +0.707 with the five fields, whole acids held out
(+0.011 [-0.088, +0.083]).

The ten repeats also correct the margin of the five fields over the count. The tables above were
read on one set of folds, and on those folds the count has its lowest q2 of the ten repeats
(+0.616; the ten values lie between +0.616 and +0.666, with a mean of +0.650). Over the ten
repeats the five fields are above the count by +0.091 [+0.017, +0.162] with whole acids held
out, where the tables above gave +0.130. With whole substituents held out the margin is
+0.053 [-0.097, +0.168], which does not exclude zero.

The posed model with both field sets also says what it has stored. For one atom of a type at a
place, the atom effect of the previous section is what this atom adds to the band. The places
are the mean positions of the first atom of the substituent: para (5.8 A from the carbonyl
carbon) and meta on either side of the carboxyl group (5.0 and 5.1 A). The table gives the
effects at the para place for the types with which at least six para substituents begin.

| atom type of the first atom of the substituent | para acids | effect of one such atom at the para place, cm$^{-1}$ | mean band of these acids minus the band of benzoic acid, cm$^{-1}$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C.3 | 26 | -0.78 +- 0.51 | -1.2 |
| C.2 | 11 | -0.53 +- 0.61 | +1.5 |
| O.3 | 9 | -0.47 +- 0.54 | -4.7 |
| N.am | 8 | -1.12 +- 1.07 | -3.9 |
| S.3 | 8 | -3.97 +- 1.15 | -2.6 |
| N.pl3 | 7 | -4.94 +- 1.05 | -9.0 |
| S.O2 | 6 | +0.93 +- 1.49 | +5.3 |

Over the 22 pairs of a type and a place with at least 2 acids, the effects correlate with the
mean observed shifts with r +0.85. The model was fitted on these bands, so this is a check of
what the model has stored and not a prediction. The effect of the first atom is smaller than the
mean shift in five of the seven rows, because the other atoms of the substituent carry the rest
(the oxygens of a sulfonyl group, for example: one O.2 oxygen at the para place adds
+2.71 +- 1.38).

**Quantum charges in the electrostatic field.** The electrostatic field of the five fields is
built from Gasteiger charges. That scheme computes the charges from the bond graph and moves
charge along the sigma bonds only. The charges of the four atoms of the carboxyl group are then
the same in every acid (their standard deviation over the series is at most 0.0001 e), and the
field holds a substituent only at the place of the substituent. The effect of a substituent
through the pi electrons of the ring (resonance) is not in these charges. Part 8 takes the
charge of every atom from one calculation with the semi-empirical quantum method GFN2-xTB on
the start geometry (section *A cheap quantum stage: GFN2-xTB*; the field set is built with
`charge_model="file"`). The geometry is not optimised, so the description still
holds nothing about the geometry of the ORCA run that gives the band. The quantum charge of the
carbonyl oxygen varies over the acids (mean -0.418 e, standard deviation 0.0083 e). It
correlates with the band with r +0.875 and with the Hammett constant with r +0.909.

Three things were added to the protocol of part 7.

- *Two more references.* The charges of the carboxyl group are computed numbers that could hold
  the whole answer, as the bond length did on the optimised geometries. The references
  therefore include a linear regression on the quantum charge of the carbonyl oxygen, and a
  multiple linear regression on the quantum charges of the four atoms of the carboxyl group
  (one equation with four slopes). Both are fitted inside the folds. A field with quantum
  charges that is no better than these regressions has read the charges of the carboxyl group
  and not the field of the acid.
- *The width and the ridge are chosen inside the folds.* The quantum calculation carries the
  effect of the substituent to the atoms of the carboxyl group, and a narrow field reads it
  there. With Gasteiger charges the electrostatic field alone reaches q2 +0.355 at 2 A and
  +0.547 at 10 A. With quantum charges it reaches +0.825 at 2 A and +0.612 at 10 A (whole
  acids held out, ridge chosen by the q2). The width therefore decides the result, and a width
  chosen by the result would overstate it. Every training part is divided again into five
  inner folds. The width (one of 10, 4.47, 2 and 1 A) and the ridge are the pair with the best
  q2 on these inner folds, so the held-out acids take no part in the choice. This is a nested
  cross-validation.
- *The difference between the para acid and the meta acid of one substituent.* Resonance is the
  part of a substituent effect that differs between the para and the meta position. Over the
  94 substituents that occur twice, the band of the para acid minus the band of the meta acid
  has a mean of -2.6 cm$^{-1}$ and a standard deviation of 2.9 cm$^{-1}$. The second table
  below gives the q2 of this difference, computed from the out-of-fold predictions of the two
  acids. A q2 below zero means that the description predicts the difference worse than its
  mean does.

The first table is for the invariant local kernel, with the width and the ridge chosen inside
the folds and ten repeats of the folds. A difference carries its 95 % bootstrap interval over
the units that the folds hold out.

| descriptor | q2, whole acids held out | difference from the separate Hammett regressions, whole acids held out | q2, whole substituents held out | difference from the separate Hammett regressions, whole substituents held out |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| atom-centred counts | +0.650 | | +0.623 | |
| Hammett regression (one equation) | +0.742 | | +0.742 | |
| separate Hammett regressions (two equations) | +0.782 | 0 | +0.782 | 0 |
| linear regression on the quantum charge of the carbonyl oxygen | +0.758 | | +0.760 | |
| multiple linear regression on the four quantum charges of the carboxyl group | +0.786 | | +0.783 | |
| the five fields, Gasteiger charges | +0.718 | -0.064 [-0.135, +0.000] | +0.640 | -0.141 [-0.278, -0.043] |
| the electrostatic field alone, Gasteiger charges | +0.562 | -0.220 [-0.358, -0.117] | +0.130 | -0.652 [-1.447, -0.173] |
| the electrostatic field alone, quantum charges | +0.824 | +0.042 [-0.005, +0.093] | +0.799 | +0.017 [-0.038, +0.074] |
| the five fields, quantum charges | +0.651 | -0.130 [-0.487, +0.064] | +0.361 | -0.420 [-1.577, +0.089] |
| the five fields with quantum charges and the two Fukui fields | +0.837 | +0.056 [-0.006, +0.120] | +0.823 | +0.042 [-0.050, +0.115] |
| the five fields with quantum charges and the 15 indicator fields | +0.692 | -0.090 [-0.261, +0.034] | +0.611 | -0.170 [-0.622, +0.054] |

*No field set with quantum charges passes the separate Hammett regressions on both kinds of
folds.* The electrostatic field alone with quantum charges, and the five fields with quantum
charges and the two Fukui fields, reach them: their differences are positive and every interval
holds zero. The same two sets are not separated from the regression on the four charges of the
carboxyl group either (+0.038 [-0.001, +0.084] and +0.052 [-0.003, +0.108] with whole acids
held out, +0.016 [-0.014, +0.056] and +0.040 [-0.013, +0.088] with whole substituents held
out). So most of what these fields predict is already in the four charges.

*Quantum charges are clearly better than Gasteiger charges.* The electrostatic field alone
gains +0.262 [+0.166, +0.396] with whole acids held out and +0.669 [+0.203, +1.461] with whole
substituents held out. The set with the two Fukui fields is above the five fields with
Gasteiger charges by +0.120 [+0.063, +0.184] and +0.183 [+0.090, +0.316]. The inner folds
choose 2 A for the electrostatic field with quantum charges in 100 of 100 folds with whole
acids held out and in 86 of 100 with whole substituents held out. For the two sets with
Gasteiger charges they choose 10 A or 4.47 A in every fold.

*What a choice by the result adds.* At a fixed width of 2 A, with the ridge chosen by the q2
of the outer folds, the set with the two Fukui fields is +0.080 [+0.025, +0.146] and
+0.078 [+0.028, +0.131] above the separate Hammett regressions, and both intervals exclude
zero. With the width and the ridge chosen inside the folds the same set is +0.056 and +0.042
above them, and both intervals hold zero. The choice by the result adds 0.02 to 0.04 in q2,
and that is enough to change the conclusion. The same check on part 7: with the
width chosen inside the folds, the five fields with Gasteiger charges give +0.718 and +0.640
(+0.741 and +0.676 at the fixed width of 10 A). With whole substituents held out they are below
the separate Hammett regressions.

| descriptor | q2 of the predicted difference between the para and the meta acid, whole acids held out | q2 of the predicted difference between the para and the meta acid, whole substituents held out |
|---|---:|---:|
| atom-centred counts | -0.27 | -0.17 |
| Hammett regression (one equation) | +0.02 | +0.05 |
| separate Hammett regressions (two equations) | +0.42 | +0.42 |
| linear regression on the quantum charge of the carbonyl oxygen | -0.09 | -0.06 |
| multiple linear regression on the four quantum charges of the carboxyl group | +0.22 | +0.27 |
| the five fields, Gasteiger charges | -0.30 | +0.18 |
| the electrostatic field alone, Gasteiger charges | -0.41 | -0.10 |
| the electrostatic field alone, quantum charges | +0.41 | +0.44 |
| the five fields, quantum charges | +0.08 | +0.14 |
| the five fields with quantum charges and the two Fukui fields | +0.42 | +0.60 |
| the five fields with quantum charges and the 15 indicator fields | +0.01 | -0.49 |

*Resonance.* The fields with Gasteiger charges do not predict the difference between the para
and the meta acid, and the electrostatic field with quantum charges predicts it as well as the
separate Hammett regressions do. The separate Hammett regressions are given a measured constant
for each position. The field gets the difference from one quantum calculation on a geometry of
a force field. The set with the two Fukui fields is the only row above the separate Hammett
regressions on folds over substituents (+0.60 against +0.42). These q2 have no intervals, so
that difference is a reading and not a result.

*One substituent decides the result of the five fields with quantum charges.* The row has a
standard deviation over the repeats of 0.238 and 0.324. The two acids of the substituent SF5
hold 73 % of its squared error with whole substituents held out, and meta-SF5 has a root mean
square error of 37.7 cm$^{-1}$ over the repeats. The quantum charge of the sulfur atom is
+2.05 e. The largest charge of an atom in all other acids is +1.40 e (meta-SO2F). When both
SF5 acids are held out, the training part holds no acid like them. The inner folds then choose
a narrow width with a small ridge, and that model extrapolates far. Scored without these two
acids, the same predictions give q2 +0.815 and +0.825. The substituent was found by its error,
after the result was known, so these two scores describe the failure and are not results. The
failure is one of the applicability domain, which is the range of descriptions that the
training set covers and inside which a model can be trusted. A fixed width with the ridge
chosen by the q2 does not show it, because there the ridge is chosen with the SF5 acids among
the held-out ones.

*One caution about the target.* The band is itself a computed number (ORCA, r2SCAN-3c), and
the charges come from another quantum calculation on the same molecule. Part 8 therefore says
that a calculation of less than one second on a geometry of a force field carries most of what
an optimisation and a frequency run of 14 to 100 minutes give for this band. Whether the same
holds for a measured band is not known.

**The gate.** The plan set two conditions. The first is that the local field beats the count by
more than the interval. On the optimised geometries it does so by +0.316,
and this does not count, because the field reads the bond length. On the start geometries the
invariant kernel at 7 and 10 A is above the count with an interval that excludes zero, so the
condition is met, narrowly and with the three cautions above. Over ten repeats of the folds
the margin is +0.091 [+0.017, +0.162]. On folds that hold out whole substituents it is
+0.053 [-0.097, +0.168], and there the condition is not met. The second condition is that the
co-field reproduces the meta and para picture of the Hammett co-fields. It is met in part: at the
widths that keep the substituent the co-field has the place and the sign, and para above meta
against the noise at 10 A; it is not resolved against the scramble, and at 3.2 A there is no
readable map.

**What follows for other items.** A local target that a quantum program computes on its own
optimised geometry has to be predicted from geometries the program did not make. Otherwise the
bond lengths at the target carry the answer, and a narrow field will find them. The control costs
nothing, because the start geometries are stored, and `run_band.py` now runs it by default
(`--structures none` leaves it out) and gives the bond-length regression as a reference. The
shift set of the two previous sections is not affected: its shifts are measured and its
geometries come from a force field.

A second rule comes from part 7. A series that holds each substituent at more than one
position has to be validated on folds that hold out whole substituents as well. On folds over
single acids the model sees the same substituent at the other position, and its q2 is higher
by about 0.07 here. A reference that is given a measured constant of the substituent, as the
Hammett regressions are, does not have this difference.

A third rule comes from part 8. When the description holds a number that the target follows at
one place, as the quantum charges of the carboxyl group are here, the width of the envelope
decides the result. The width and the ridge are then chosen inside the folds, and the
regression on that number is given as a reference. A fourth rule comes from the same part. A
field built from quantum charges needs a check, before a prediction, that the charges of the
new molecule lie inside the range of the charges of the training molecules.

**What is not done.** Measured carbonyl bands were not collected; with them the computed band
would become a second column beside the measured one. The indicator fields and the fields with
quantum charges reached the separate Hammett regressions and did not pass them. The check of
the range of the charges is described above and is not written: the program does not yet mark
a molecule whose charges lie outside the range of the training set. The q2 of the difference
between the para and the meta acid has no intervals. The quantum charges come from one method,
GFN2-xTB; the charges of another method were not compared. And a field of the quantum electron
density or of the quantum electrostatic potential itself, in place of charges on the atoms, was
not tried on this series.

## A spectrum as a one-dimensional field: the kernel and the co-spectrum

A spectrum is a function of one variable: an intensity over a wavenumber, over a diffraction
angle, over a binding energy or over a chemical shift. The module `cmfqsar/spectrum.py` (plan
item SP1) treats it as the rest of the program treats a molecule: as a field, here a field on a
line. Two spectra have a kernel, and a fitted model gives back a weight over the line.

**Two forms of a spectrum.** A *stick spectrum* is a list of positions and intensities. A
quantum program writes a vibrational spectrum in this form, one stick per normal mode, and a
calculated powder diffraction pattern has this form, one stick per reflection. A *measured
curve* is a list of intensities on the grid of an instrument. The class `Spectrum` holds both;
its `kind` is `"sticks"` or `"curve"`, and its `axis` names what the positions are
(`wavenumber`, `two_theta`, `q`, `binding_energy`, `shift` and others).

**The kernel.** Every stick is replaced by a Gaussian of standard deviation $\sigma$, the
*width*. For two spectra with sticks $(x_i, a_i)$ and $(y_j, b_j)$ the overlap of the two
broadened spectra has a closed form:

$$
k(A, B) \;=\; \sum_i \sum_j a_i\, b_j\, \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{(x_i - y_j)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)
$$
<!-- #eq:spectrum-kernel -->

This is the steric kernel of the molecular fields in one dimension: an atom becomes a stick,
and the weight of the atom becomes the intensity. A measured curve enters as the same sum over
its grid points, each point with the weight of its intensity times the part of the axis that it
stands for. `stick_overlap` computes the sum directly. For a set of spectra it is cheaper to
put every broadened spectrum on one grid (`feature_matrix`) and to take dot products of the
rows (`spectrum_kernel`). With 2.5 grid points in one $\sigma$ the two ways agree to one part
in a million, and a test checks it.

The default is the cosine form: the kernel is divided by the square roots of the two
self-overlaps. The total intensity of a spectrum depends on the amount of sample and on the
