instrument, and the cosine form removes it.

The width says how far apart two lines may be and still count as the same line. Two single
lines that are $d$ apart have the kernel $\exp(-d^2/4\sigma^2)$. The width is a hyper-parameter
and is chosen by cross-validation. `multi_width_kernel` takes the mean of the kernels of several
widths. A second hyper-parameter is the power of the intensity: 1 keeps the intensities, and 0.5
takes their square root, which lowers the share of the strongest line.

**The co-spectrum.** A kernel ridge model on the cosine kernel is linear in the normalised
broadened spectrum $z(x)$. Its prediction for a spectrum is

$$
\hat y \;=\; b + \int w(x)\, z(x)\, \mathrm{d}x
$$
<!-- #eq:co-spectrum -->

The weight $w(x)$ is the **co-spectrum** (`co_spectrum`). It is the analogue of the co-field in
one dimension: a curve over the axis that is positive where intensity raises the predicted
property and negative where it lowers it. `co_spectrum_effect` multiplies the weight by the
standard deviation of the intensity over the set, because a large weight at a place where no
spectrum has intensity moves no prediction.

![The concept of the co-spectrum, on the calculated infrared spectra of the 189 benzoic acids with the Hammett constant as the property, the model of `benchmarks/run_spectra_ir.py`. The two acids shown are the ones with the largest and the smallest constant. Top left: a spectrum is a field on a line. Every stick becomes a Gaussian, and the broadened spectrum is divided by its norm. The region shown holds the carbonyl stretch and the ring stretch below it. Top right: the co-spectrum is the weight of the model over the same line, dark where it is positive and light where it is negative. Bottom left: weight times intensity is what each place of the axis adds to the prediction. Bottom right: the running sum of these products along the whole axis, from high wavenumbers to low ones, starts at the bias, which is the dashed line, and ends at the prediction; the grey band marks the region of the other three panels. The line above the panels writes the sum out for both acids. The figure shows how the reading is built. How far it can be trusted is measured in the section on these acids. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/cospectrum.svg)

**Readers.** `read_sticks` and `read_measured` read two-column text. `orca_sticks` takes the
infrared spectrum from an ORCA frequency job: one stick per normal mode with a positive
frequency, at the wavenumber times the scaling factor of the level. `powder_sticks` calculates
the powder diffraction pattern of a crystal with pymatgen, for X-rays or for neutrons, as sticks
over the diffraction angle 2-theta.

```python
from cmfqsar import spectrum as SP

a = SP.orca_sticks("acid_1/freq.out", scale=0.97)       # infrared sticks of an ORCA job
b = SP.read_measured("sample.txt", axis="wavenumber")   # a measured curve
K = SP.kernel([a, b], 400.0, 4000.0, sigma=10.0)        # cosine kernel, width 10 cm^-1

pattern = SP.powder_sticks(atoms)                       # ASE Atoms or a pymatgen Structure
```

```
python benchmarks/run_spectra.py                    # the measurement below, then the table
python benchmarks/run_spectra.py --stage patterns   # the powder patterns alone, 6 minutes
python benchmarks/run_spectra.py --report
```

**What is measured** (`benchmarks/run_spectra.py`, `benchmarks/results/spectra/table.md`). The
item has two halves. This is the half that needs no new data: a calculated spectrum as the
sample. The set is the Matbench phonons task of section *Crystals: the periodic autocorrelation
kernel*: 1,265 inorganic crystals with the frequency of the highest peak of the phonon density
of states (standard deviation 494 cm$^{-1}$). The powder diffraction pattern of every crystal
is calculated from its structure, for X-rays (Cu K-alpha) and for neutrons of the same
wavelength, between 5 and 90 degrees of 2-theta. A crystal has 48 reflections at the median.
No measured pattern is used. A powder pattern is what a diffraction experiment gives when no
structure is known, so the question is the one of section *A measured curve as the sample*, put
in reciprocal space: what does the pattern say about a property without the types of the atoms?

The protocol is the one of the phonon benchmark: the five Matbench folds, and inside every
training part the settings are chosen by 10-fold cross-validation. For a pattern the settings
are the width (0.05 to 10 degrees, eight values), the power of the intensity and the ridge. A
difference in the mean absolute error (MAE) carries a 95 % bootstrap interval over the
crystals. The references are the structural kernel with the lowest error in the phonon
benchmark (the three physico-chemical fields and the mass field), the composition (a Gaussian
kernel on the fractions of the elements), a linear regression on the inverse square root of the
mass of the lightest atom, and the pair distribution function $G(r)$ of the previous sections,
which holds the same untyped distances in real space.

| description | MAE, cm$^{-1}$ (sd over the five folds) | R2 | MAE of the 62 crystals with hydrogen, cm$^{-1}$ | MAE of the crystals without hydrogen, cm$^{-1}$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| mean of the training part | 324.0 (17.7) | -0.001 | 1297.1 | 273.8 |
| linear regression on the mass of the lightest atom | 226.5 (12.2) | +0.481 | 799.9 | 197.0 |
| composition: the fractions of the elements | 97.6 (16.7) | +0.833 | 403.0 | 81.9 |
| structure: the periodic autocorrelation kernel | 92.7 (4.5) | +0.918 | 273.3 | 83.4 |
| pair distribution function $G(r)$, X-ray weights | 287.6 (17.3) | -0.119 | 1233.8 | 238.9 |
| X-ray powder pattern | 294.2 (14.8) | +0.107 | 1193.1 | 247.9 |
| neutron powder pattern | 278.3 (14.8) | +0.116 | 1252.7 | 228.0 |
| X-ray powder pattern, Gaussian kernel on top | 257.4 (9.7) | +0.212 | 1164.6 | 210.6 |
| neutron powder pattern, Gaussian kernel on top | 196.1 (13.7) | +0.466 | 878.8 | 160.9 |
| composition and X-ray powder pattern | 97.0 (17.1) | +0.831 | 424.6 | 80.1 |
| structure and X-ray powder pattern | 93.0 (4.8) | +0.916 | 266.7 | 84.1 |
| structure, X-ray and neutron powder patterns | 92.1 (3.7) | +0.918 | 261.6 | 83.3 |

**The kernels are compared first.** The gate of the item asks for the correlation of the kernel
of the patterns with the structural kernel before any fit. It is +0.047 at the width that the
folds choose and +0.203 at most, so the pattern is a different description. The useful number
is another one: the correlation of a kernel with the products of the centred targets, which
says how far crystals that the description finds alike have alike frequencies. It is +0.181 for
the structural kernel, +0.140 for the composition, and +0.009 for the X-ray pattern (+0.020 at
most over the widths). This number needs no fit, and it predicts the table.

**The pattern alone predicts little.** The X-ray pattern has an MAE of 294.2 cm$^{-1}$, which is
-29.8 [-37.7, -22.1] against the mean of the training part and +196.6 [+179.4, +214.8] against
the composition. The neutron pattern is -16.0 [-23.9, -8.1] against the X-ray pattern. The pair
distribution function gives 287.6, and the X-ray pattern is not separated from it
(+6.6 [-12.1, +22.0]): the same information in real space and in reciprocal space predicts
equally little. In every fold the choice inside the folds takes the widest broadening tried,
10 degrees. A pattern broadened that far holds only how the intensity is spread over the angle,
so the places of the single reflections give the model nothing that it can use. A Gaussian
kernel on top of the pattern kernel, which makes the model nonlinear in the spectrum, lowers
the error to 257.4 (X-ray) and 196.1 (neutron). The neutron pattern is then still
+98.4 [+84.2, +113.1] above the composition.

**Why.** The 62 crystals with hydrogen have a median frequency of 1754 cm$^{-1}$, and the others
443 cm$^{-1}$, and X-rays show hydrogen weakly. But hydrogen is not the whole reason. For the
crystals without hydrogen the X-ray pattern has an MAE of 247.9, the mean of the training part
273.8 and the composition 81.9. The frequency of the highest phonon peak depends on which
elements the crystal holds, most of all on their masses: the regression on the mass of the
lightest atom alone reaches R2 +0.481. A powder pattern holds the geometry of the lattice and
the contrast of the scattering strengths. It does not name the elements.

**The pattern beside another description adds nothing.** The kernel of the pattern joins the
structural kernel as one more kernel in the mixing of `cmfqsar/mixing.py` (`with_views`), with
weights that maximise the marginal likelihood of the training part. The MAE is then 93.0, which
is +0.3 [-1.2, +1.7] against the structural kernel alone, and the pattern gets a share of 0.00.
With equal weights the difference is +0.2 [-1.3, +1.6]. Beside the composition the pattern
gives 97.0 (-0.6 [-2.5, +1.3] against the composition alone). A user who knows the composition
of a sample and has its powder pattern gains nothing from the pattern for this property.

**A fault that this run found in `mixing.drop_one`.** On all crystals the log Bayes factor
against *the pattern adds nothing* is -1.4, and against *the structure adds nothing* it is
+1156.3. The first run of this benchmark gave +53.9 for the pattern, although the pattern had
a share of 0.00. That number was not evidence for the pattern. `drop_one` then took the best of
five fixed ridges, the lowest of them 0.001, and the best ridge of the structural kernel here
is 2.1e-05. A joined kernel of two has twice the scale of one kernel, which acts as half the
ridge, so the joined kernel was nearer to the best ridge and gained from that alone. `drop_one`
now searches the ridge relative to the scale of the kernel (section *Which fields does this
series need?*). The benchmark keeps both numbers, the old one as the record of the fault.

**The co-spectrum of this model cannot be read.** The model on all X-ray patterns reproduces the
targets it was fitted on with R2 +0.120. Its largest effect at a grid point is 206 cm$^{-1}$,
against at most 144 in 20 models fitted to the targets in random order, and the intensity of no
band of 10 degrees correlates with the target above 0.20 in size. The weights of neighbouring
grid points have opposite signs and cancel, because at a width of 10 degrees neighbouring
points hold nearly the same intensity. The function is tested on a made series, in which one
line carries the property and three lines carry nothing: there the largest effect is at that
line.

![The X-ray powder patterns of the 1,265 crystals at the width that the folds choose (10 degrees). Top: the mean normalised pattern. Middle: the co-spectrum, the weight of the model over the diffraction angle. Bottom: the weight times the standard deviation of the intensity; the dashed lines are the largest value found in 20 models fitted to the targets in random order.](benchmarks/results/spectra/cospectrum.png)

**The gate.** The item is a result when the structural kernel with the spectrum has a lower
error than the structural kernel alone by more than the interval, or when the spectrum alone
reaches the composition. Neither condition is met. The plan expected that losing the types of
the atoms costs accuracy, as section *A measured curve as the sample* found for the elastic
moduli. Here the cost is nearly everything: without the types a calculated pattern predicts
this property little better than the mean does.

**A side result.** The structural kernel (92.7) is not separated from the Gaussian kernel on the
fractions of the elements (97.6; the difference is -4.9 [-14.0, +3.5]). On this task the
composition carries most of what the structural kernel predicts. The structural kernel differs
by 0.6 cm$^{-1}$ from the 92.1 of the stored table of the phonon benchmark; the fields are
computed again here with the present code.

**What follows for other items.** Before a spectrum is used as the sample for a property, the
correlation of its kernel with the products of the centred targets is computed. It costs no
fit, and here it said what the fit then found. The second half of the item, a set of measured
spectra with a measured property, has to be a pair in which the experiment shows what decides
the property: a vibrational spectrum for a property of the bonds is such a pair, and a powder
pattern for a phonon frequency is not. The second measurement below takes such a pair, and
items SP3 and SP6 use the same vibrational spectra with the reader of this section.

**What is not done.** No measured spectrum is used; the search for a public set of measured
spectra with a measured property is the second half of the item. Only one division into folds
is run, the published one; the differences are either far from zero or within 3 cm$^{-1}$ of
it, so other divisions would not change a conclusion. The patterns are compared on the angle
axis of one wavelength, and not on the axis of the scattering vector. The run takes 3.5 hours
on the author's machine while other jobs run on it; more than half of that are the two rows
with the Gaussian kernel on top.

### The second measurement: an infrared spectrum against the Hammett constant

The powder pattern failed because a diffraction pattern does not show what decides a phonon
frequency. The second measurement takes a pair in which the experiment should show it
(`benchmarks/run_spectra_ir.py`, `benchmarks/results/spectra_ir/table.md`). The sample is the
infrared spectrum of a substituted benzoic acid. The target is the Hammett constant of its
substituent at its position.

**The data.** The ORCA frequency jobs of the previous section give every normal mode of the
189 acids with its infrared intensity, and that section kept one of them, the carbonyl stretch.
Stage `--ir` of `examples/make_band_examples.py` writes all of them to
`examples/spectra/benzoic_acids_ir.json` as stick spectra: the harmonic wavenumbers times the
scaling factor of the level, and the intensities in km/mol. An acid has 43 sticks between 400
and 4000 cm$^{-1}$ at the median. The Hammett constant is a measured number: for most
substituents it is the measured shift of the pKa of this very acid against benzoic acid. So the
spectrum is computed, the target is measured, and the calculation is not told the target.

```
python examples/make_band_examples.py --ir   # the stick spectra, from the ORCA outputs
python benchmarks/run_spectra_ir.py          # the measurement, 50 minutes
```

**The protocol** is the one of parts 7 and 8 of the previous section: ten repeats of ten folds,
with whole acids held out and with whole substituents held out. The second kind of folds
matters more here than there. A spectrum shows the bands of the substituent itself, so with
whole acids held out a model can recognise the substituent from the other acid of the pair.
The numbers below are for whole substituents held out. The width of the broadening (2 to
50 cm$^{-1}$), the power of the intensity and the ridge are chosen on five folds inside every
training part.

**A control with a known answer comes first.** The length of the C=O bond of the optimised
geometry follows the carbonyl band (r -0.987), so a kernel that can read the position of a line
has to predict it from the spectrum. It does, with q2 +0.858. A linear regression on the
position of the band itself reaches +0.973, and the spectrum is -0.114 [-0.154, -0.084] below
it. The lengths differ by a tenth of a picometre and the band moves by a few cm$^{-1}$; the
kernel sees such a shift only as a small change of the overlap of two broadened lines. So the
kernel reads the position of a line, but less exactly than a regression on the position does.

| description | q2, whole substituents held out | q2, whole acids held out | q2 of the difference between the para and the meta acid, whole substituents held out |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| atom-centred counts around the carbonyl carbon | +0.629 | +0.683 | -0.07 |
| linear regression on the position of the carbonyl band | +0.742 | +0.743 | -0.03 |
| the same regression, meta and para separately (two equations; it is told the position) | +0.771 | +0.771 | +0.32 |
| structure: the five fields, Gasteiger charges | +0.697 | +0.778 | +0.08 |
| structure: the electrostatic field alone, quantum charges | +0.798 | +0.835 | +0.47 |
| infrared spectrum, 400 to 4000 cm$^{-1}$ | +0.809 | +0.847 | +0.37 |
| infrared spectrum, Gaussian kernel on top | +0.808 | +0.860 | +0.46 |
| infrared spectrum, the region of the carbonyl stretch alone | +0.737 | +0.753 | -0.07 |
| infrared spectrum without the region of the carbonyl stretch | +0.661 | +0.735 | -0.03 |
| structure (five fields) and infrared spectrum, joined | +0.831 | +0.875 | +0.48 |
| structure (quantum charges) and infrared spectrum, joined | +0.791 | +0.824 | +0.40 |

**The spectrum predicts the constant.** The kernel of the spectra reaches q2 +0.809. That is
+0.179 [+0.086, +0.293] above the atom-centred counts and +0.111 [+0.023, +0.244] above the
five fields. It is not separated from the electrostatic field with quantum charges
(+0.010 [-0.063, +0.111]), the best structural description of this series in the previous
section. The number that needs no fit said so again: the correlation of the kernel with the
products of the centred constants is +0.438 for the spectrum and +0.432 for the field with
quantum charges, against +0.199 for the five fields and +0.228 for the counts. For the powder
pattern it was +0.009.

**The whole spectrum says more than its one known band.** A chemist would read the carbonyl
stretch, and the linear regression on the position of that band reaches +0.742. The spectrum
is +0.067 [+0.015, +0.130] above it. Against the two regressions for meta and para, which are
told the position of the substituent, it is +0.037 [-0.015, +0.098], not separated. The region
of the carbonyl stretch alone gives +0.737, the same as the regression on the band
(-0.005 [-0.046, +0.031]). The spectrum without that region gives +0.661, which is
-0.148 [-0.202, -0.101] below the whole spectrum and not separated from the counts. So the
carbonyl band carries the largest part, the rest of the spectrum carries about what a count of
the atoms carries, and the two together are worth more than either. The difference between the
para and the meta acid of one substituent, the part of the constant that resonance decides,
shows the same: the carbonyl region alone and the rest alone do not predict it (q2 -0.07 and
-0.03), and the whole spectrum does (+0.37).

**Beside the structure.** Joined with the five fields, with the share of the spectrum chosen
inside the folds, the q2 is +0.831: +0.134 [+0.056, +0.253] above the five fields alone and
+0.022 [-0.003, +0.047] against the spectrum alone. Joined with the field with quantum
charges, the spectrum adds nothing (-0.007 [-0.071, +0.066]).

**The co-spectrum, read by region.** The place with the largest effect is at 1736 cm$^{-1}$
with a positive sign, and below 1730 cm$^{-1}$ the sign is negative: intensity at the upper side
of the carbonyl band raises the predicted constant, as the band itself rises with the constant.
No single grid point is above the largest effect of models fitted to the constants in random
order (0.028 against 0.057), so the co-spectrum cannot be read point by point. It can be read by
region. The model is fitted without the substituent of an acid, the sum of weight times
intensity inside a region is computed for that acid, and the sums of all acids are correlated
with the constant:

| region | cm$^{-1}$ | held-out correlation of what the region adds with the Hammett constant | the largest value in 50 models on constants in random order |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| O-H stretch | 3450 to 3800 | +0.82 | +0.13 |
| C-H stretch | 2800 to 3200 | +0.44 | +0.18 |
| C=O stretch | 1650 to 1800 | +0.79 | +0.20 |
| ring stretch | 1550 to 1650 | +0.67 | +0.15 |
| C-O stretch, O-H bend and ring modes | 1000 to 1550 | +0.55 | +0.19 |
| out-of-plane bends and ring deformations | 400 to 1000 | +0.20 | +0.16 |

The stretch of the O-H bond, which is the bond that an acid breaks, carries as much as the
carbonyl stretch, and the model was not told either of them.

![The infrared spectra of the 189 benzoic acids against the Hammett constant, at a width of 5 cm$^{-1}$. Top: the mean normalised spectrum. Middle: the weight of the model times the standard deviation of the intensity; the dashed lines are the largest value in 50 models fitted to the constants in random order. Bottom: the region of the carbonyl stretch, with the mean spectrum as a dotted line. The weight is positive on the upper side of the band and negative on the lower side.](benchmarks/results/spectra_ir/cospectrum.png)

**The gate.** With whole substituents held out, the structural kernel with the spectrum is above
the structural kernel alone by more than the interval when the structural kernel is the five
fields, and it is not when it is the field with quantum charges. The spectrum alone is above
the counts. The gate of the item is met on this pair.

**What the result does and does not say.** The spectrum of this measurement is computed with a
quantum program on a geometry that the program optimised, 33 minutes per acid. The five fields
are built on a geometry of a force field with charges from the bond graph. The gain of the
spectrum over the five fields is therefore what a quantum calculation knows about the acid, and
the field with charges from one calculation of less than a second holds the same. What the
result does say is that the kernel takes a property out of a spectrum that holds it: more than
a regression on the one band that a chemist would read, and as much as the best structural
description of this series. With the first measurement it also says when not to try: the
correlation of the kernel with the target, computed before any fit, was +0.438 here and +0.009
for the powder pattern. A measured spectrum would be the experiment itself and not a
calculation, and none is used. That is the second half of the item, and this result is the
reason to look for the data.

## The spectrum as the bridge: which acid fits a spectrum, and what moves a band

The two sections above used a spectrum as a target and as a sample. This one uses it as the
link between two things that are known for the same molecule (plan item SP3,
`benchmarks/run_spectra_bridge.py`, `benchmarks/results/spectra_bridge/table.md`). It has two
parts. Part (b) carries the gate of the item and is given first.

**A second spectrum of every acid.** The item needs a spectrum at a second level of theory. The
driver of section *A cheap quantum stage: GFN2-xTB* has a route for it: `xtb.run_vibrations`
optimises a molecule with GFN2-xTB and computes its harmonic frequencies and infrared
intensities in one call of the program (`xtb --ohess`), and `xtb.read_vibspectrum` reads the
file that xtb writes. When the optimisation ends on a saddle point, the job is run once more
from the geometry that xtb moves along the imaginary mode. Stage `--xtb-ir` of
`examples/make_band_examples.py` does this for the 189 acids in less than a minute and writes
`examples/spectra/benzoic_acids_ir_xtb.json`. Ten acids keep one imaginary mode.

GFN2-xTB is a rough second level. A second density functional is a nearer one. Stage
`--orca-ir` of the same script optimises every acid again with ORCA at B97-3c, from the
geometry of the first functional, computes its frequencies and writes
`examples/spectra/benzoic_acids_ir_b97-3c.json` (wavenumbers times 0.98, the scaling factor of
that level). The 189 acids took 4.6 hours with 16 jobs at a time, and none failed.

```
python examples/make_band_examples.py --xtb-ir --jobs 8    # the GFN2-xTB spectra, 1 minute
python examples/make_band_examples.py --orca-ir --jobs 16  # the B97-3c spectra, hours, cached
python benchmarks/run_spectra_bridge.py                    # all parts, 15 minutes
```

No two levels put the lines at the same places, as a measured and a computed spectrum do not.
The carbonyl band of the GFN2-xTB spectrum is 29.3 cm$^{-1}$ above that of the library
spectrum (standard deviation 4.4), and its highest line, the O-H stretch in most acids, is
182 cm$^{-1}$ below (standard deviation 18.7). For B97-3c the two numbers are 4.8 cm$^{-1}$
below (3.0) and 26.6 cm$^{-1}$ below (1.5), and the lines of the two functionals, taken in
order, are 5.0 cm$^{-1}$ apart at the median.

![Which acid fits a spectrum. Top left: benzoic acid at three levels of theory, the level of the library and the two levels of the queries. Top right and bottom left: the kernel of every query with every library spectrum, for the queries of the second density functional and of GFN2-xTB; the right acid is on the diagonal. Bottom right: the share of the queries whose acid stands among the first places of the ranking. The figure uses one width of 20 cm$^{-1}$ and the axis as it is, and it takes the mean spectrum of each level off before the comparison. Part (b) below chooses the width, the power of the intensity and a map of the axis on calibration acids, and its numbers are the ones to quote. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/bridge.png)

### Part (b): which acid fits a spectrum

The spectra of the first functional (ORCA, r2SCAN-3c) are the library: one spectrum for every
candidate acid. A spectrum of a second level is the query, first from GFN2-xTB and then from
B97-3c. The 189 candidates are ranked by the kernel between the query and their library
spectra, and the question is where the acid of the query stands. Three things are chosen
before a query is ranked, all on the acids of half of the substituents, for which the right
answer is used (the *calibration acids*):

- the width of the broadening (5 to 200 cm$^{-1}$) and the power of the intensity;
- a map of the axis of the query onto the axis of the library: none, one factor for the whole
  axis, or one factor below 2300 cm$^{-1}$ and another above it, where no acid has a line;
- whether the spectra are *centred*. All acids share the bands of benzoic acid. Centring takes
  the mean normalised spectrum of each level from its spectra, which leaves what an acid has
  beyond those bands. The mean of the queries is taken over the calibration queries only.

The queries of the other half of the substituents are then ranked. The split is repeated ten
times. A map with more factors fits the calibration acids better whether or not it is better,
so the map itself is chosen inside the calibration acids: they are divided in two, every map
is fitted on one half and scored on the other.

| how the candidates are ranked | first, % of the queries | among the first three, % | median rank | the right isomer above the other isomer of the same substituent, % | first among the candidates with the composition of the query, % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| by chance | 0.5 | | 95 | 50.0 | |
| by the composition (the molecular formula) | 45.0 | | 1.5 | 50.0 | 45.0 |
| the position of the carbonyl band alone | 2.7 | 7.8 | 26.2 | 70.5 | |
| spectrum kernel, the axis as it is | 27.0 | 49.5 | 3.8 | 66.2 | 63.7 |
| centred spectra, the axis as it is | 42.8 | 67.7 | 2.0 | 74.0 | 69.8 |
| centred spectra, the axis times one factor | 43.3 | 68.8 | 2.0 | 74.8 | 71.0 |
| centred spectra, one factor below and one above 2300 cm$^{-1}$ | 36.0 | 61.3 | 2.4 | 75.6 | 71.8 |
| centred spectra, the map chosen inside the calibration acids | 42.3 | 66.9 | 2.1 | 74.9 | 70.6 |
| the same, the query as a measured-like curve | 37.8 | 60.1 | 2.4 | 82.9 | 78.1 |
| the same in the other direction (an ORCA query, the GFN2-xTB library) | 48.2 | 74.4 | 1.6 | 85.6 | 81.8 |

The rows above are for GFN2-xTB as the second level. With B97-3c as the second level, in the
same protocol:

| how the candidates are ranked | first, % of the queries | among the first three, % | median rank | the right isomer above the other isomer of the same substituent, % | first among the candidates with the composition of the query, % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| the position of the carbonyl band alone | 6.4 | 17.2 | 13.1 | 83.1 | |
| spectrum kernel, the axis as it is | 98.6 | 99.7 | 1.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| centred spectra, the map chosen inside the calibration acids | 99.6 | 99.7 | 1.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| the same, the query as a measured-like curve | 96.3 | 100.0 | 1.0 | 99.8 | 99.7 |
| the same in the other direction (an r2SCAN-3c query, the B97-3c library) | 97.8 | 99.6 | 1.0 | 99.2 | 99.2 |

**With a second density functional the gate is met.** The gate asks that a spectrum of a second
level ranks its own acid first among the series in most cases. A B97-3c spectrum does so in
99.6 % of the queries (standard deviation over the splits 0.5), and it never confuses the two
isomers of a substituent. The position of the carbonyl band alone gives 6.4 %, so it is the
whole spectrum that finds the acid and not one band. Nothing has to be repaired first: without
a map of the axis and without centring the share is already 98.6 %, the calibration chooses no
map in ten of ten splits, and the width it chooses is 10 to 20 cm$^{-1}$, at which single
lines are compared.

**With GFN2-xTB it is not met for the whole series.** A GFN2-xTB spectrum ranks its own acid
first in 42.3 % of the queries (standard deviation over the splits 3.2), and among the first
three in 66.9 %; the median rank is 2. That is far above chance (0.5 %) and above the position
of the carbonyl band alone (2.7 %), but it is not most cases. So the 42 % is a limit of that
method and not of the kernel.

**The start geometry does not explain the difference.** The B97-3c spectra start from the
geometries of the library, and the GFN2-xTB spectra start from the force-field geometries. As
a control, GFN2-xTB is run from the geometries of the library as well. The same protocol then
gives 43.3 % of first places, against 42.3 %.

**Among the isomers GFN2-xTB is enough.** The composition narrows the candidates to a few: 99 % of
the acids share their formula with at least one other acid, mostly the meta and the para acid
of one substituent, and the composition alone is right in 45.0 % of the cases by drawing among
them. This is the part that the gate names, because the composition cannot tell isomers apart.
When only the candidates with the composition of the query are ranked, the spectrum puts the
right acid first in 70.6 % of the queries, and it puts the right isomer above the other isomer
of the same substituent in 74.9 %.

**Three readings for the rough level.** Centring matters most: without it the share of first
places is 27.0 %,
because the shared bands of benzoic acid fill the comparison. A map of the axis does not help:
one factor gives the same as none, and two factors give less (36.0 %) although they fit the
calibration acids better. And the calibration chooses a width of 50 or 100 cm$^{-1}$, at which
regions of the spectrum are compared and not single lines. GFN2-xTB and the density functional
do not agree line by line. A map can move the carbonyl band and the O-H stretch onto their
places, but the other lines stay tens of cm$^{-1}$ apart in a way that no smooth map repairs.

**A measured-like query.** The same query as a curve on a grid of 4 cm$^{-1}$, with every line
broadened to a standard deviation of 4 cm$^{-1}$ and noise of 2 % of the largest value, gives
96.3 % of first places for B97-3c and 37.8 % for GFN2-xTB (78.1 % among the isomers). The
resolution and the noise of an instrument are not what limits the result. How near the level
of the library is to the level of the query is.

### Part (a): which part of the structure moves which part of the spectrum

A kernel canonical correlation analysis (section *What the field sees that another view does not*,
`cmfqsar/kcca.py`) takes a structural kernel as one description and the kernel of the ORCA
spectra as the other. It finds pairs of directions, one in each description, whose values over
the acids correlate most. A pair is judged on held-out acids, with whole substituents held
out, against 100 analyses in which the pairing of the two descriptions is shuffled. The
structural kernel is the invariant local kernel around the carbonyl carbon, and no target is
used anywhere.

| structural kernel | pair | correlation on held-out acids | shuffled pairing, 95 % | what the pair follows (r of its structural variate) | regions of the spectrum that carry it |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| the five fields, Gasteiger charges, 10 A | 1 | +0.822 | +0.190 | the Hammett constant (-0.79) | O-H stretch (+0.74), C=O stretch (+0.74) |
| | 2 | +0.804 | +0.202 | para or meta (+0.86) | C-O stretch, O-H bend and ring modes (+0.66), out-of-plane bends (+0.66) |
| the electrostatic field alone, quantum charges, 1 A | 1 | +0.893 | +0.169 | the Hammett constant (-0.92) | C=O stretch (+0.80), O-H stretch (+0.79) |

With the five fields all four leading pairs are above the shuffled pairing. The first pair is
the electronic effect of the substituent: both of its variates follow the Hammett constant,
and the regions of the spectrum that carry it are the O-H stretch and the C=O stretch. The
second pair is the position of the substituent: its variates tell para from meta with
r +0.86 and +0.84, and it is carried by the region below 1550 cm$^{-1}$, where the bending
modes of the ring hydrogens lie. A chemist reads the substitution pattern of a benzene ring in
the same region. Neither the constant nor the position was given to the analysis.

**Where the first pair lives.** The plan expected the first structural direction on the
neighbourhood of the carbonyl group and the first spectral direction on the carbonyl band. On
the spectral side it is carried by the carbonyl stretch and the O-H stretch about equally. On
the structural side the answer depends on the charges. With quantum charges the held-out
correlation of the first pair rises as the envelope around the carbonyl carbon narrows, from
+0.700 at 10 A to +0.893 at 1 A, which holds little beyond the carboxyl group: the quantum
calculation has carried the effect of the substituent to that group. With Gasteiger charges,
which are the same on the carboxyl group of every acid, it falls from +0.822 at 10 A to +0.105
at 1 A: the direction has to reach the substituent. This is the finding of section *A
vibrational band as the local target*, reached here without a target.

**What is not done.** No measured spectrum is used. The two functionals compute the same
object: the harmonic spectrum of one molecule in the gas phase, in the same conformer. A
measured spectrum of a carboxylic acid differs from that in more than the places of the lines.
In a solid or in a solution the acid forms hydrogen-bonded pairs, which moves the carbonyl
band and makes the O-H band broad, and real bands are not harmonic. So the 99.6 % says that
the kernel finds the right structure when the library is computed at a level near the query,
and it does not say how near a computed library is to a measurement. The pairs of part (a) are
read against five properties and six regions; a co-field of a structural direction in space,
which needs the posed kernel, is not drawn. And the candidates are the acids of the series only:
ranking against a large library of other compounds is another question. The section that
follows makes the first step with measured spectra.

## A measured spectrum against other measured spectra of the same compounds

The two sections above used computed spectra only. This section is the first measurement on
measured spectra (`benchmarks/run_spectra_measured.py`,
`benchmarks/results/spectra_measured/table.md`). It asks the simplest question that measured
spectra allow: does a measured spectrum of a compound find another measured spectrum of the
same compound among the spectra of many other compounds? Nothing is computed from a structure.
The answer is therefore a ceiling for the identification of the section above with a measured
query. Against a computed library, the difference between a calculation and a measurement is
added to the difference between two samples.

**The set.** Chemotion IR (Jung, Tremouilhac, Punjabi et al., Karlsruhe Institute of
Technology, 2024, https://doi.org/10.22000/OGoEQGlsZGElrgst) holds infrared spectra that
chemists of research laboratories measured of their own compounds and stored in the Chemotion
repository, with the SMILES of every compound: 2,116 measurements of 1,926 compounds in 4,183
JCAMP-DX files. Its licence is CC BY-SA 4.0, which asks that a copy is passed on under the same
licence. No file of the set is in this repository. `benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_ir.py`
downloads the archive (47.5 MB) into `benchmarks/cache/chemotion_ir`, checks the SHA-256 sums
of its two data files, reads the files in memory and writes the spectra on one grid.

```
python benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_ir.py     # once: downloads 47.5 MB
python benchmarks/run_spectra_measured.py     # 10 seconds
```

**Reading a measured spectrum.** JCAMP-DX is the text format in which instruments and
repositories store a spectrum. A file holds labelled entries (the units of the two axes, the
first and the last position, a factor for the intensities) and a table of intensities. The
table is often compressed: a letter stands for the sign and the first digit of a number, a
second set of letters gives the difference from the value before, and a third set repeats a
value. `spectrum.parse_jcamp` reads every block of a file with these forms,
`spectrum.read_jcamp` gives the first measured curve of a file as a `Spectrum`, and
`spectrum.absorbance` turns a transmittance $T$ into the absorbance $-\log_{10} T$. The kernel
needs the absorbance. The absorbance of every band is proportional to the amount of substance
in the beam, so the cosine form of the kernel removes that amount; a transmittance has no such
property.

A spectrum of the set has about 2,560 points from 4000 to 374 cm$^{-1}$, one every
1.4 cm$^{-1}$, and nearly all files give the transmittance. The prepared spectra are
absorbances from 650 to 3900 cm$^{-1}$ in steps of 2 cm$^{-1}$, a range that every infrared
spectrum of the set covers. One measurement has no curve in its file and one is not an infrared
spectrum, so 2,114 spectra of 1,925 compounds are prepared. The metadata name attenuated total
reflectance (ATR, a measurement on the neat solid or liquid pressed onto a crystal) for 2,085
of them, and most instruments are of one type.

**Copies in the set.** The prepared curves were compared with each other before any kernel was
computed. Some curves are the same point by point. In 19 cases one file is attached to two
samples of one compound. Such a copy would be found at once and without any merit of the
kernel, so one of the two is left out. In 8 cases one file is attached to the samples of two
different compounds. At least one of the two structures is then not the one that was measured,
so both are left out; the result file lists the sample numbers. After that the set has 2,079
spectra of 1,912 compounds. 138 compounds have spectra of two or more samples (120 have two,
13 have three, 5 have four to six), which gives 430 pairs of a query and a library spectrum.
Two spectra of one compound are measurements of their own: their correlation coefficient is
0.943 at the median and below 0.784 for a tenth of the pairs.

**The slope of a spectrum.** A measured curve stands on a baseline: an offset or a slow drift
that comes from the instrument and from the contact with the sample, and not from the
compound. The kernel of equation (#eq:spectrum-kernel) counts a baseline as intensity. A
computed stick spectrum has no baseline, so the two sections above did not meet the problem.
`spectrum.slope` takes the derivative of every broadened spectrum along the axis. A constant
baseline has no slope, and a slow drift has a small one. The kernel of the slopes has a closed
form of the same kind, with one more factor:

$$
k'(A, B) \;=\; \dfrac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_i \sum_j a_i\, b_j
\left(1 - \dfrac{d_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{d_{ij}^2}{4\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad d_{ij} = x_i - y_j
$$
<!-- #eq:spectrum-slope-kernel -->

Two lines at the same place count as before. Two lines $1.41\,\sigma$ apart count as nothing,
and two lines further apart count against each other. `spectrum.slope_overlap` computes this
sum, and a test checks it against the dot product of the slopes on a grid. Comparing the
derivatives of two spectra is a standard step of a library search in spectroscopy. What this
module adds is only that the step is a kernel of the same family, with a closed form for stick
spectra, so that a measured curve and a computed stick spectrum can be compared in it.

**The test.** One measured spectrum is the query. The library holds one spectrum of every
compound: for the compound of the query a spectrum of another sample, and for every other
compound its first spectrum. The 1,912 compounds are ranked by the kernel between the query
and their library spectra. A compound counts once, whatever its number of spectra. Three forms
of the kernel are compared: the plain kernel of the absorbance; the same after the mean of
every spectrum is taken off, which makes the cosine of two spectra their correlation
coefficient and removes a constant baseline; and the kernel of the slopes. Each form has a
width (not broadened, 4, 8 or 16 cm$^{-1}$). The form and the width are chosen on half of the
138 compounds and scored on the other half, in 50 random splits. The number in brackets is the
standard deviation over the splits.

| how the spectra are compared | compound is first, % of the queries | among the first three, % | among the first ten, % |
|---|---|---|---|
| chance, one of 1,912 compounds | 0.05 | 0.16 | 0.5 |
| plain kernel of the absorbance, width chosen | 59.9 (3.4) | 71.1 (3.2) | 78.7 (2.7) |
| mean of every spectrum taken off, width chosen | 77.2 (3.5) | 84.7 (3.0) | 90.0 (2.5) |
| kernel of the slopes, width chosen | 87.6 (2.5) | 93.2 (2.1) | 95.4 (1.9) |
| form and width chosen | 87.6 (2.5) | 93.2 (2.1) | 95.4 (1.9) |
| slopes, 4 cm$^{-1}$, the region 700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ alone (all compounds) | 87.9 | 92.8 | 95.2 |
| slopes, 4 cm$^{-1}$, the region 1800 to 3850 cm$^{-1}$ alone (all compounds) | 58.6 | 66.1 | 70.2 |

**What the table says.** A measured spectrum finds the other sample of its compound among
1,912 compounds in 87.6 % of the queries and puts it among the first ten in 95.4 %. The form of
the kernel matters more than anything else. The choice took the slopes in every split. The
slopes find 27.9 points more than the plain kernel (95 % bootstrap interval over the compounds
+21.8 to +34.4) and 10.3 points more than the spectra with their mean taken off (+5.7 to
+14.9). The baseline of a measured curve is not a constant, and only the slope removes most of
it.

The width that is chosen is 4 cm$^{-1}$ (in 40 of the 50 splits; 8 cm$^{-1}$ in 7). For the
plain kernel every broadening costs: 59.4 % without it and 44.2 % at 16 cm$^{-1}$. Two samples
of one compound have their bands at the same places, so there is no difference in position
that a width would have to bridge. Between two levels of theory the chosen width was 10 to
20 cm$^{-1}$, and with GFN2-xTB 50 to 100 cm$^{-1}$.

The region from 700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ alone gives the same result as the whole spectrum
(87.9 %), and the region above it gives 58.6 %. This matters for the next test. The O-H and
N-H stretch bands lie above 1800 cm$^{-1}$, and they are where a spectrum computed for one
molecule in the gas phase differs most from a measurement on a solid. Between two measured
spectra that region can be left out at no cost. The next section shows that this does not
carry over to a GFN2-xTB library.

**The wrong answers.** In 76 of the 430 pairs the kernel names another compound. That compound
is a relative of the right one. Its Tanimoto similarity to the right compound (Morgan
fingerprints of radius 2; the number of shared bits over the number of bits that either has) is
0.59 on average, against 0.10 for a compound drawn at random from the library, and in 26 % of
these pairs it is an isomer of the right compound. The library is made of series of analogues
from synthesis projects: over all 1,912 compounds, the other compound with the most similar
spectrum has a similarity of 0.5 or more in 59.6 % of the cases, against 0.5 % for a pairing at
random. So the similarity of two measured spectra in this kernel follows the similarity of the
two structures, which is the condition for a property model on measured spectra.

The 15 pairs in which the compound is not among the first ten belong to 7 compounds. The two
spectra of such a pair have a correlation coefficient of 0.49 at the median and of 0.72 at
most, against 0.94 for all pairs. The two samples did not give the same spectrum. The set does
not say why (another solid form, a solvent that was left in the sample, or a structure that is
attached to the wrong sample), and no kernel can repair it.

The molecular formula alone would name the compound in 82.1 % of the queries, because few
compounds of this library share a formula. A spectrum does not give the formula, so this is a
statement about the library and not a rival of the kernel.

**What is not done.** No computed spectrum is compared with a measured one here: that is the
next section, and its ceiling is now known. No property is predicted; the set has no measured
property. Nearly all spectra come from instruments of one type and from one way of measuring,
so the test does not say what a change of the instrument costs. The library holds one spectrum
of every compound, and 1,912 compounds are few against a commercial library. A correction of
the ATR intensities, which depend on the wavelength, was not applied; it is the same for both
spectra of a pair here, and it will not be for a computed library.

## A measured spectrum against a library of computed spectra

This section asks the question of plan item SP3 with a measured query
(`benchmarks/run_spectra_computed.py`, `benchmarks/results/spectra_computed/table.md`). The
queries are the measured spectra of the section above. The library holds one computed
spectrum for every candidate compound, made from the structure alone. The candidates are
ranked by the kernel between the measured curve and their computed stick spectra. The section
above gives the ceiling: 87.6 % when the library spectrum is a measurement of another sample.

**The computed library.** `benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_xtb.py` computes a GFN2-xTB spectrum
for every compound whose SMILES is one neutral molecule without unpaired electrons, of the
elements H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, Br, I and Se, with at most 100 atoms. Of the 1,925
compounds of the prepared set 1,645 pass. Left out are 133 salts, solvates and complexes
(more than one molecule in the SMILES), 92 molecules with more than 100 atoms, 49 compounds
with another element, which is a metal in most cases, 4 radicals, one ion and one SMILES
that is not read. For every compound that passes:

1. RDKit makes up to ten conformers from the SMILES and relaxes each with the MMFF94 force
   field. The conformer of lowest force-field energy is kept. This is a cheap choice of one
   conformer and not a search.
2. xtb optimises that geometry with GFN2-xTB and computes the harmonic wavenumbers and the
   infrared intensities of one molecule in the gas phase (`xtb.run_vibrations`).

The 1,645 jobs took 81 minutes with 14 jobs at a time, and none failed. 227 compounds keep an
imaginary mode after the one repeated optimisation that the driver makes. The file of the
library stays in the cache, because its structures come from a set with a share-alike
licence.

One fault was met on the way. The set holds many [2.2]paracyclophanes, in which two benzene
rings are bent towards each other. The standard embedding of RDKit, which knows that a
benzene ring is flat, tried for more than two minutes on each of them and then gave no
geometry. The script now limits the number of attempts and then uses plain distance geometry
without that knowledge; the force field and xtb relax the result.

```
python benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_xtb.py --jobs 14   # once: the library, 81 minutes
python benchmarks/run_spectra_computed.py              # 17 minutes
```

**What is chosen.** A computed and a measured spectrum differ in more ways than two measured
spectra do, so more is chosen than in the section above: the form of the kernel (plain, the
mean of every spectrum taken off, or the slopes); the width (4 to 64 cm$^{-1}$); one factor on
the computed wavenumbers (0.95 to 1.01), because a harmonic calculation puts the lines too
high; the region (the whole range, or 700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ alone); the power of the
intensities; whether the spectra are centred as in section *The spectrum as the bridge*; and
whether the computed intensities are divided by the wavenumber. The last option belongs to
the way these spectra were measured. In attenuated total reflectance the depth that the beam
reaches in the sample grows with the wavelength, so a band at a low wavenumber is stronger
than the same band in a transmission spectrum. These are 1,680 settings. They are chosen on
half of the compounds, for which the right answer is used, and scored on the queries of the
other half, in 20 random splits. The library always holds all 1,645 candidates, and a
compound with several measured spectra counts once.

| what is open to the choice | compound is first, % of the queries | among the first three, % | among the first ten, % |
|---|---|---|---|
| chance, one of 1,645 compounds | 0.06 | 0.18 | 0.6 |
| all settings | 5.6 (0.6) | 11.9 (0.8) | 24.5 (1.3) |
| only the kernel of the slopes | 5.7 (0.7) | 11.9 (0.8) | 24.6 (1.4) |
| only the spectra with their mean taken off | 6.0 (0.7) | 12.6 (1.1) | 24.3 (1.1) |
| only the plain kernel | 4.3 (0.5) | 10.2 (1.0) | 21.6 (1.2) |
| only the region 700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ | 2.8 (0.6) | 7.0 (0.6) | 16.7 (1.1) |
| for comparison: a measured spectrum of another sample in the library (section above, 1,912 compounds) | 87.6 | | 95.4 |

**What the table says.** With a GFN2-xTB library the measured spectrum finds its compound
first in 5.6 % of the queries and among the first ten in 24.5 %. Chance gives 0.06 %, so the
computed spectrum carries information about the measured one: at the setting chosen most
often, the right compound is in the best one per cent of the library (16 compounds of 1,645)
for 31.4 % of the queries, and its median rank is 56. But this is a coarse filter and not an
identification. The gate of plan item SP3, a query that ranks its own structure first in most
cases, is not met for a measured query with a GFN2-xTB library. The distance to the ceiling
is 82 points.

**The settings say what kind of agreement there is.** The width that is chosen is 64 cm$^{-1}$
for the slopes (in 15 of the 20 splits) and 32 cm$^{-1}$ for the spectra with their mean
taken off. Between two measured samples the width was 4 cm$^{-1}$, and between two density
functionals 10 to 20 cm$^{-1}$. A GFN2-xTB spectrum against a density-functional library
needed 50 to 100 cm$^{-1}$. So a GFN2-xTB spectrum and a measured one agree on the regions
that hold intensity and not line by line, as the two computed levels of section *The spectrum
as the bridge* did. The factor on the wavenumbers is 0.97. Dividing the computed intensities
by the wavenumber is chosen in every split (the best setting with it finds 6.5 % on all
compounds, the best without it 5.2 %), and so is centring (6.5 % against 5.3 %).

The form of the kernel matters less than between two measured spectra. The slopes and the
spectra with their mean taken off are equal within the intervals, and the plain kernel loses
1.5 points (95 % bootstrap interval over the compounds +0.7 to +2.4). At a width of
64 cm$^{-1}$ little of a baseline is left to remove.

**The region: an expectation that was wrong.** The section above found that the region from
700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ alone identifies a compound as well as the whole spectrum, and expected
the same here. It is not so. With that region alone the compound is first in 2.8 % of the
queries, 3.0 points fewer than with the whole range (+2.2 to +3.7). At this width the lines of
the lower region have merged, and what is compared is where the intensity lies. The region of
the O-H, N-H and C-H stretch bands adds whether such bands are there at all. On all compounds
the lower region alone gives 3.0 %, the upper region alone 1.0 %, and the two together 6.5 %.

**What does not explain the distance.** One conformer was computed, and one molecule in the
gas phase. Neither shows as the main limit. Compounds with at most two rotatable bonds are
found first in 7.0 % of the cases, those with three to five in 6.1 % and those with six or
more in 6.3 %. Compounds without a hydrogen-bond donor are found in 7.6 % and those with one
in 4.8 %, so hydrogen bonds cost something, but a compound that cannot form them is found no
better than one in thirteen. The 226 compounds whose computed geometry keeps an imaginary
mode are found in 3.5 %.

**The wrong answers are not relatives.** When the kernel names another compound, its Tanimoto
similarity to the right one is 0.18 on average, against 0.11 for a compound drawn at random.
Between two measured spectra it was 0.59. At a width of 64 cm$^{-1}$ the kernel compares
coarse shapes, and two compounds with the same coarse shape need not be related.

**What was tried on all compounds and gave nothing more.** Widths of 96 and 128 cm$^{-1}$
(5.6 % and 4.3 % against 6.5 % at 64 cm$^{-1}$); a second factor for the lines above
2500 cm$^{-1}$ (0.97 is the best there too); another width for the query than for the
library; and the sum of the kernels of two widths. These numbers are a look at all compounds
without a split, and they are not part of the result file.

**Reading.** The limit is most probably the level of theory, and not the conformer or the gas
phase. Three things point there: the wide width that is chosen, which is the signature that
GFN2-xTB showed against a density functional in section *The spectrum as the bridge*, where
it found 42 % of the acids against 99.6 % for a second density functional; the absence of any
loss with the number of rotatable bonds; and the modest loss with hydrogen-bond donors. This
is a reading and not a measurement. The measurement follows.

**The measurement: two levels of theory on the same small compounds.**
`benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_dft.py` takes the 231 compounds of the library that have at most
25 atoms. ORCA optimises each of them at B97-3c, the density functional of section *The
spectrum as the bridge*, and computes the harmonic wavenumbers and the infrared intensities
of one molecule in the gas phase. Every job starts from the geometry that xtb found, so both
levels describe the same conformer. 230 compounds have a spectrum. The jobs took 13.5 hours
with 14 jobs at a time, which is 164 hours of one processor core or 43 minutes for a compound
on average; GFN2-xTB needed 81 minutes for all 1,645 compounds. One compound, a diyne (two
triple bonds in a row), had no converged geometry after 190 steps of the optimisation and
was stopped by hand. Two compounds keep an imaginary mode, against 13 of the same 230
compounds with GFN2-xTB.

`run_spectra_computed.py --subset` then makes the test of this section twice, once with the
GFN2-xTB spectra and once with the B97-3c spectra. The candidates are the same 230 compounds,
the queries are the same 255 measured spectra of 228 of them, and the 20 splits are the same.
All settings are chosen again for each level.

```
python benchmarks/prepare_chemotion_dft.py --jobs 14   # once: 231 compounds at B97-3c, 13.5 hours
python benchmarks/run_spectra_computed.py --subset     # less than a minute
```

| library of the 230 small compounds | compound is first, % of the queries | among the first three, % | among the first ten, % | median rank of the right compound |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chance, one of 230 compounds | 0.4 | 1.3 | 4.3 | 115.5 |
| GFN2-xTB | 11.3 (2.4) | 22.3 (3.7) | 37.2 (3.4) | 20 |
| B97-3c | 32.3 (3.4) | 51.4 (3.5) | 71.9 (4.2) | 3 |

Only the rows of this table can be compared with each other. The table above has 1,645
candidates, and a shorter list is easier: GFN2-xTB finds 11.3 % here and 5.6 % there.

**What the comparison says.** With the B97-3c library the measured spectrum finds its
compound first in 32.3 % of the queries, and with the GFN2-xTB library in 11.3 %. The
difference is 21.2 points (95 % bootstrap interval over the compounds +16.5 to +26.2). The
median rank of the right compound falls from 20 to 3, and the compound is among the first ten
in 72 % of the queries against 37 %. So the level of theory is a large part of the distance,
as the reading above said. It is not the whole distance. Also with B97-3c the compound is
first in one query of three and not in most, so the gate of plan item SP3 is not met for a
measured query at this level either. What a B97-3c library gives is a short list: the right
compound is among ten of 230 in nearly three queries of four.

At the setting chosen most often for each level, 87 of the 228 compounds have a first place
with B97-3c and 35 with GFN2-xTB. 23 compounds have it at both levels, 64 only with B97-3c
and 12 only with GFN2-xTB.

**The settings change with the level.** With B97-3c the best share of first places on all
compounds is nearly the same for every width from 4 to 32 cm$^{-1}$ (36.5, 36.4, 36.2 and
37.4 %) and lower at 64 cm$^{-1}$ (34.8 %). With GFN2-xTB it grows with the width, from 8.6 %
at 4 cm$^{-1}$ to 14.8 % at 64 cm$^{-1}$. The lines of B97-3c are close enough to the measured
bands to be compared at the width of a band, and the lines of GFN2-xTB are not. The region
from 700 to 1800 cm$^{-1}$ alone is chosen in 15 of the 20 splits with B97-3c and gives as
much as the whole range (37.4 % against 36.4 %). The expectation that was wrong for GFN2-xTB
holds for the density functional. The factor on the wavenumbers is 0.97 for both levels. It
matters more for B97-3c: without a factor the best setting finds 15.1 % in place of 37.4 %
(GFN2-xTB: 8.9 % in place of 14.8 %). Dividing the computed intensities by the wavenumber
does not help B97-3c (36.4 % with it, 37.4 % without).

**What still limits the density functional.** The groups are read for each level at the
setting chosen most often, on all compounds.

| compounds | number | first with GFN2-xTB, % | first with B97-3c, % | among the first ten with GFN2-xTB, % | among the first ten with B97-3c, % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no hydrogen-bond donor | 112 | 18.0 | 46.1 | 43.8 | 75.9 |
| one or more hydrogen-bond donors | 116 | 11.6 | 28.9 | 33.2 | 63.8 |
| at most 2 rotatable bonds | 188 | 13.1 | 35.7 | 36.4 | 67.0 |
| 3 to 5 rotatable bonds | 40 | 22.5 | 45.0 | 47.5 | 82.5 |

A compound without a hydrogen-bond donor is found first in 46 % of the cases and a compound
with a donor in 29 %. The computed molecule is alone in the gas phase and has no hydrogen
bond to another molecule; most samples of the set are solids or liquids. With GFN2-xTB the
two groups differ by 6 points and with B97-3c by 17: when the lines are at the right places,
the missing hydrogen bond is what shows. The flexible compounds are not found less often
than the rigid ones (there are only 40 of them), so the one conformer is not the limit for
molecules of this size. For the compounds without a donor more than half of the first places
are still missing. The harmonic approximation with one factor, the computed intensities and
the state of the sample can all take part in that, and this benchmark does not separate
them.

**What is not done.** A density-functional spectrum is computed only for the 230 small
compounds, so nothing is measured for a molecule with more than 25 atoms, and the cost grows
quickly with the size (the longest job, a molecule of 24 atoms, took 4.8 hours). No model of
the hydrogen bonds was tried: a pair of molecules, a cluster or a periodic calculation. No
correction of the harmonic approximation was tried other than one factor. No
conformer search is made, and no spectrum is averaged over conformers. The 280 compounds
without a computed spectrum are not candidates, so the library is smaller than the set. A
measured spectrum of a salt or of a metal complex has no computed partner at all.

## Mixtures and quantification: the spectrum of a mixture as a sum of fields

This section is the first half of plan item SP6 (`benchmarks/run_mixtures.py`,
`benchmarks/results/mixtures/table.md`). It uses no new data and no quantum calculation.

**The identity.** By the Beer-Lambert law the absorbance spectrum of a mixture is the sum of
the spectra of its components, each times its amount. The kernel of equation
(#eq:spectrum-kernel) is linear in each of its two spectra. So the kernel of two mixtures $M$
and $M'$ with the amounts $w_a$ and $w'_b$ of the components $A_a$ is the same weighted sum
over the kernels of the components:

$$
k(M, M') \;=\; \sum_a \sum_b w_a\, w'_b\; k(A_a, A_b)
$$
<!-- #eq:mixture-kernel -->

`spectrum.mix` makes the spectrum of a mixture, and `spectrum.mixture_kernel` computes this
product from the kernel of the components. A test checks that the two ways agree; in the
benchmark they differ by $6\times10^{-16}$ of the largest element. This is the identity that
`fields.combine_members` uses for an ensemble of conformers, with one difference: the weights
of an ensemble are scaled to a sum of one, and the amounts of a mixture are not. The identity
holds for the kernel that is not normalised. The cosine kernel of the components must not be
put into it, because the length of a mixture is not the sum of the lengths of its components.

**What is made.** Mixtures are synthesised. Every repeat draws four components and makes 120
mixtures to fit and 120 to test. The fractions are drawn evenly from all compositions, and the
total amount is between 0.5 and 2. Every mixture has a baseline of its own (an offset up to 0.2
and a straight rise or fall up to 0.1 over the axis) and noise of standard deviation 0.005,
all in units of the strongest band of a pure component. Two kinds of components are used.
The computed spectra of the 189 benzoic acids of section *A vibrational band as the local
target* are close relatives, whose spectra overlap strongly. The measured Chemotion IR spectra
(2,060 of them) carry real band shapes and real baselines; this part is left out when the set
was not fetched. There are 20 repeats of each case.

![The spectrum of a mixture as a sum of fields. Top left: four components, the computed spectra of four benzoic acids, each scaled to its strongest band. Top right: one mixture, made by the recipe of the benchmark: the components times their amounts, summed, with a baseline of its own and noise. Bottom left: a ridge model on the linear kernel of the spectra, fitted on 120 mixtures of known composition, gives the amounts of 120 new mixtures; there is one colour for each component. Bottom right: the fractions, as the predicted amounts divided by their sum. The model is not told the spectra of the pure components. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/mixture.svg)

**What is asked, and of which model.** The amount of every component, and the fraction of
every component, which does not depend on the total amount. The model is kernel ridge
regression on the linear kernel of the rows of a description. The rows are the broadened
curves as they are (*plain*) or their slopes, and they are either not normalised or divided
by their length (the cosine form). The width of the broadening and the ridge are chosen by
cross-validation inside the mixtures to fit. A second model puts a Gaussian layer on the
distance of the linear kernel. Two references are given:

- *Partial least squares regression* (PLS) on the same rows, with the number of components
  chosen in the same way. This is how quantification is done in practice.
- *The floor*: a least-squares fit of every test mixture with the known spectra of the pure
  components and a baseline. With a linear response and white noise no estimate is better,
  and a model that has to learn from mixtures cannot pass it.

The numbers are root-mean-square errors on the test mixtures, means over the 20 repeats.

| question | rows of the description | computed components: linear kernel | PLS | linear kernel over the floor | measured components: linear kernel | PLS | linear kernel over the floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| amount | the floor | 0.0022 | | 1 | 0.0013 | | 1 |
| amount | plain, not normalised | 0.0024 | 0.0024 | 1.09 | 0.0014 | 0.0014 | 1.11 |
| amount | slopes, not normalised | 0.0027 | 0.0027 | 1.19 | 0.0020 | 0.0020 | 1.57 |
| amount | slopes, cosine | 0.135 | 0.136 | 65 | 0.137 | 0.139 | 112 |
| fraction | the floor | 0.0022 | | 1 | 0.0012 | | 1 |
| fraction | plain, not normalised: the predicted amounts divided by their sum | 0.0024 | 0.0023 | 1.07 | 0.0014 | 0.0013 | 1.10 |
| fraction | slopes, cosine | 0.0140 | 0.0139 | 7.3 | 0.0227 | 0.0227 | 18.9 |
| fraction | slopes, cosine, with the Gaussian layer | 0.0049 | | 2.2 | 0.0048 | | 4.0 |

**The gate of this half is met.** The model finds the amounts with an error 9 % above the
floor for the computed components and 11 % above it for the measured ones. So the weights are
recovered to within the noise. The model equals PLS: the two errors differ by less than
0.0001 in every row of the linear cases. The plan expected this. In a linear problem the
field adds no accuracy over PLS, and what it adds is the reading that follows.

**A fraction is not what the cosine form gives.** The plan named the cosine form for
fractions, because it divides the total amount out. That is half of the answer, and the half
that is missing costs a factor of 7 to 19 in the error. The cosine form divides the spectrum by
its length, and the length of a mixture is not proportional to its total amount: it depends on
which components are in it. The amount of a component over the length of the spectrum is a
linear function of the normalised spectrum, but the fraction is the ratio of two such
functions. The Gaussian layer learns a part of this ratio (2.2 and 4.0 times the floor). The
direct way is better and needs nothing new: predict the amounts with the kernel that is not
normalised and divide them by their sum, which gives 1.07 and 1.10 times the floor. The rule
for the use of the two forms is therefore: the form that is not normalised for amounts and for
fractions, and the cosine form only when nothing else than the shape of the spectrum is known,
as in the identification of the sections above.

**The slope costs when the baseline is in the fit, and saves the model when it is not.** With
slopes in place of plain rows the error of the amounts rises from 1.09 to 1.19 times the floor
for the computed components and from 1.11 to 1.57 for the measured ones. A derivative makes
noise larger, and the plain rows do not need it here: the mixtures to fit show the baseline,
and the model learns to ignore it. A fourth case takes the baseline out of the mixtures to fit
and leaves it in the test mixtures, which is what a new instrument or a new sample holder
does:

| rows of the description | error of the amounts, linear kernel | PLS | linear kernel over the floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain, not normalised | 0.179 | 0.182 | 80 |
| slopes, not normalised | 0.0029 | 0.0029 | 1.25 |

The plain rows fail, for the kernel and for PLS alike, and the slopes lose almost nothing.
The offset has no slope. The straight rise has a constant slope, and it does no harm for
another reason: every row of the fit is the slope of a spectrum whose bands return to the
baseline, so it sums to nearly zero over the axis; the weight of the model is a combination of
these rows and sums to nearly zero too, and a constant added to a row then changes no
prediction.

**A bent calibration curve.** A third case adds stray light: 2 % of the light reaches the
detector without passing the sample, and the strongest band of a pure component is 1.5, so
the measured absorbance stops rising at about 1.7. The least-squares fit with the pure spectra
takes the response as linear, and its error for the amounts is 0.054. The models that learn
from mixtures reach 0.0040, because they learn to read the bands that are not saturated. The
Gaussian layer adds nothing clear to the linear kernel for the amounts (difference 0.0000,
95 % bootstrap interval over the repeats $-0.0002$ to $+0.0002$), and 0.0003 for the fractions
that are made from them (0.0032 against 0.0035, interval $-0.0004$ to $-0.0002$). The linear
kernel is 0.0008 better than PLS on the plain rows ($-0.0017$ to $-0.0002$). So this case
does not show the gain that the plan allows the nonlinear layer where the calibration is not
linear. A case in which every band of a component is saturated was not made.

**The co-spectrum is the net signal of the component.** Chemometrics calls the part of the
spectrum of a component that no combination of the other components and of the baseline can
make its *net analyte signal*; it is the only part from which the amount of that component can
be read. The co-spectrum of the model for an amount, which is the weight of the model over the
axis, has a cosine of 0.99 with the net signal for the computed components and of 0.97 for
the measured ones. So the co-spectrum of a quantification model can be read as a spectrum: it
shows the bands of the component that the others do not cover, with a negative weight where
another component has to be taken off. PLS gives a regression vector of the same kind; the
kernel model gives it in the form that the other sections use.

The width that is chosen is 8 cm$^{-1}$ for the computed components (18 of 20 repeats) and
16 cm$^{-1}$ for the measured ones (15 of 20). The run takes 11 minutes.

```
python benchmarks/run_mixtures.py     # 11 minutes; the measured part needs prepare_chemotion_ir.py
```

**What is not done.** No measured mixture is used: that is the second half of the item, and no
public set of mixtures with known composition was looked for yet. The mixtures are ideal:
the bands of a component do not move or widen with the composition, which they do in real
solutions, and that is the other place where the plan expects the nonlinear layer to matter.
Four components are few, and all of them are known to be present.

## Two instruments: a model fitted on one instrument reads the spectra of another

This section is plan item SP5 (`benchmarks/run_calibration_transfer.py`,
`benchmarks/results/calibration_transfer/table.md`). A model that predicts a property from a
spectrum is fitted on the spectra of one instrument, the *source*. Later the same model has
to read spectra from a second instrument, the *target*. The standard remedy uses *transfer
standards*: a few samples that are measured on both instruments, from which a map between
the two instruments is fitted. The question of the item is how far the spectrum kernel comes
without such standards.

**The idea of the item.** A spectrometer broadens every line by its resolution. Two Gaussian
broadenings add as the squares of their widths. If instrument $k$ has already put the width
$r_k$ on its spectra, and the kernel broadens the spectra of that instrument by

$$
s_k \;=\; \sqrt{\sigma^2 + r_{\max}^2 - r_k^2}\,,
$$
<!-- #eq:matched-widths -->

then the spectra of all instruments end at the one width $\sqrt{\sigma^2 + r_{\max}^2}$, and a
model fitted on the rows of one instrument reads the rows of another
(`spectrum.matched_widths`). The instrument with the coarsest resolution gets the width
$\sigma$ of the kernel, and a sharper one gets more. `spectrum.fit_width` finds the
difference $r_{\max}^2 - r_k^2$ from the mean spectra of two instruments, and
`spectrum.fit_shift` finds a shift of the axis between them. Both compare the slopes of the
two mean spectra, and neither needs a sample that was measured on both instruments.

**The data.** The plan names the two sets on which the methods of calibration transfer are
compared in the literature. Both are near-infrared sets from the data archive of Eigenvector
Research. The archive states no licence, so the files are fetched into the cache and are not
in the repository (`benchmarks/prepare_calibration_transfer.py`, 6.5 MB).

- *Corn.* 80 samples of corn on three spectrometers, named `m5`, `mp5` and `mp6`, from 1100 to
  2498 nm in steps of 2 nm, with the moisture, oil, protein and starch of every sample.
- *Tablets.* 655 pharmaceutical tablets on two spectrometers, from 600 to 1898 nm in steps of
  2 nm, with the content of the active ingredient. Above 1600 nm the absorbance passes 5 and
  the two instruments differ by noise, so the benchmark uses 600 to 1600 nm.

```
python benchmarks/prepare_calibration_transfer.py   # once: downloads 6.5 MB
python benchmarks/run_calibration_transfer.py       # 33 minutes
```

**Part 1: what differs between the instruments.** Before any model, the two spectra of the
same sample are compared. The difference is taken apart step by step. Every number is a root
mean square of absorbance over the samples and the axis.

| pair of instruments | spread of the samples on the first | difference between the instruments | after the mean difference is taken off | after an offset, a gain and a sloping baseline per sample | fitted shift, nm | fitted difference in resolution, nm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corn, `m5` and `mp5` | 0.0357 | 0.0450 | 0.0077 | 0.0010 | 0.50 | 0 |
| corn, `m5` and `mp6` | 0.0357 | 0.0565 | 0.0076 | 0.0011 | 0.80 | 0 |
| corn, `mp5` and `mp6` | 0.0337 | 0.0122 | 0.0026 | 0.0003 | 0.40 | 0 |
| tablets, 1 and 2 | 0.1852 | 0.0618 | 0.0266 | 0.0085 | 0.10 | 0 |

Three things follow. First, the instruments do not differ in resolution: for no pair does a
broadening of one mean spectrum make it more like the other. The plan expected a difference
in resolution and named this case as possible. Second, the difference is large and nearly
all of it is the same for every sample. Between `m5` and `mp5` the two spectra of one sample
differ by more than two samples differ on one instrument (0.045 against 0.036), and 97 % of
the squared difference is the mean difference. Third, the shift of the wavelength axis is
0.1 to 0.8 nm, less than half a step of the grid, and removing it changes the fourth column
by less than 0.0001.

**How the models are compared.** Two models get the same rows. The reference is partial
least squares regression (PLS) with up to 30 components. The other is kernel ridge
regression on the linear spectrum kernel. The rows are the spectra as measured ("plain") or
their slopes along the axis, both after a broadening whose width (0, 4, 8 or 16 nm) is
chosen with the number of components, or with the ridge, by cross-validation inside the
samples of the fit, on the source alone. A split has 60 corn samples to fit and 20 to test,
or 155 tablets to fit and 500 to test, and there are 20 random splits. An error below is a
root-mean-square error divided by the standard deviation of the property, and for corn the
mean over the four properties; a model that predicts the mean has about 1.

A first run limited PLS to 15 components. On instrument `m5`, whose spectra carry very
little noise, PLS chooses 19 to 27 components when it may, and the limit made its error for
oil twice as large (0.058 against 0.028). The limit is 30 now, and a limit of 45 gives the
same numbers.

**Within one instrument.**

| instrument | PLS, plain spectra | PLS, slopes | kernel ridge, plain spectra | kernel ridge, slopes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| corn, `m5` | 0.120 | 0.105 | 0.115 | 0.100 |
| corn, `mp5` | 0.440 | 0.426 | 0.425 | 0.425 |
| corn, `mp6` | 0.454 | 0.415 | 0.431 | 0.398 |
| tablets, 1 | 0.245 | 0.241 | 0.239 | 0.236 |
| tablets, 2 | 0.246 | 0.245 | 0.242 | 0.240 |

The two models are close. Of the 14 pairs of an instrument and a property, kernel ridge on
the slopes is below PLS on the slopes in 6, above it in 1 and within the interval over the
splits in 7; the largest difference is 7 % of the error. Instrument `m5` is four times as
precise as the other two. These are the first models of the sections on spectra that predict a
measured property from measured spectra.

**The crossing.** A model fitted on the source reads the spectra of the test samples from
the target. What is done to the target spectra first:

- nothing ("as measured");
- *each instrument centred*: the mean spectrum of the target spectra is taken off, and the
  mean spectrum of the source spectra of the fit is put in its place. This uses the target
  spectra of the test samples and not their measured properties, and no standard;
- *shift fitted*: the shift between the two mean spectra is fitted and removed; also
  together with the centring;
- with standards, as the reference. The standards are 8 samples of the fit, chosen by the
  Kennard-Stone rule (the two spectra furthest apart, then again and again the spectrum
  furthest from those chosen). *Mean difference of the standards* adds the mean difference
  of their two spectra to the target spectra. *Piecewise direct standardisation* (PDS)
  fits, for every point of the axis, a regression that gives the source value of the
  standards from a window of their target spectra; the window and the number of principal
  components are chosen by leave-one-out over the standards. PDS is also run with 16
  standards.

The table is for kernel ridge on the slopes. The tables for PLS and for the plain spectra
are in the result file.

| source to target | within the source | target as measured | each instrument centred | shift fitted | shift fitted, each instrument centred | mean difference of 8 standards | PDS, 8 standards | PDS, 16 standards | model fitted on the target |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corn, `m5` to `mp5` | 0.100 | 2.747 | 0.510 | 2.171 | 0.503 | 0.499 | 0.540 | 0.507 | 0.425 |
| corn, `m5` to `mp6` | 0.100 | 2.682 | 0.523 | 1.720 | 0.528 | 0.522 | 0.560 | 0.526 | 0.398 |
| corn, `mp5` to `m5` | 0.425 | 2.412 | 0.513 | 1.644 | 0.513 | 0.489 | 0.468 | 0.457 | 0.100 |
| corn, `mp5` to `mp6` | 0.425 | 0.988 | 0.492 | 0.600 | 0.493 | 0.453 | 0.446 | 0.446 | 0.398 |
| corn, `mp6` to `m5` | 0.398 | 2.636 | 0.518 | 1.355 | 0.522 | 0.502 | 0.456 | 0.441 | 0.100 |
| corn, `mp6` to `mp5` | 0.398 | 0.870 | 0.497 | 1.025 | 0.505 | 0.469 | 0.464 | 0.454 | 0.425 |
| tablets, 1 to 2 | 0.236 | 1.382 | 0.373 | 1.405 | 0.375 | 0.407 | 0.341 | 0.320 | 0.240 |
| tablets, 2 to 1 | 0.240 | 2.369 | 0.328 | 2.252 | 0.328 | 0.336 | 0.310 | 0.286 | 0.236 |

**What the table says.** Read as measured, the target spectra give an error of 0.9 to 2.7,
which is worse than predicting the mean in six of the eight crossings. The slopes do not
protect the model: the mean difference between two instruments is not a flat baseline.
Centring each instrument brings the error to 0.49 to 0.52 for corn and to 0.33 and 0.37 for
the tablets, without a standard. The fitted shift adds nothing, alone or with the centring.
PDS with 8 standards gives 0.45 to 0.56 for corn and 0.31 and 0.34 for the tablets, and the
plain mean difference of the same 8 standards is on average as good as PDS for corn. No treatment
reaches the model that was fitted on the target itself when the target is the precise
instrument `m5`: the model was fitted on spectra with four times the noise.

![Two instruments, simulated.
