The two sets of this section are fetched and are not in the repository, so the picture is made from the computed spectra of the 189 benzoic acids: the second instrument has a coarser resolution, an offset and a slope of its own. Left: one acid on both instruments. Middle: the same two spectra after the mean spectrum of each instrument is taken off; they now agree. Right: a ridge model fitted on the first instrument with two thirds of the acids predicts the Hammett constant of the other third from the second instrument, as measured and with each instrument centred. No acid is measured on both instruments. The centring assumes that the two sets of samples have the same mean, and the next paragraph says what that costs. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/instruments.svg)

**Centring has a cost of its own.** The centring assumes that the test samples have the
mean spectrum of the samples of the fit. They do not have it exactly, and the difference of
the two means is read as a difference in the property. This cost can be measured without
any second instrument: within one instrument, centring the test spectra raises the error of
`m5` from 0.100 to 0.221, of `mp5` from 0.425 to 0.471 and of tablet instrument 1 from 0.236
to 0.261. The cost falls with the number of samples on both sides (20 test samples for
corn, 500 for the tablets), and standards do not pay it. So most of what the centred
crossing loses against a model fitted on the target is this cost and not a remaining
difference between the instruments: `m5` to `mp5` gives 0.503, and `mp5` alone with its
test spectra centred gives 0.471.

**The gate of the plan item.** The item compares the kernel without standards (kernel ridge
on the slopes, the shift fitted, each instrument centred) with PLS on the plain spectra as
measured, and with PLS with PDS. A case is one crossing and one property: 24 for corn and 2
for the tablets. An interval is a 95 % bootstrap interval over the 20 splits; the splits
share the samples, so it says how much a result depends on the split.

| set | cases | below PLS as measured | within the interval of PLS with PDS, 8 standards | below it | above it | above PLS with PDS, 16 standards |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corn | 24 | 24 | 5 | 7 | 12 | 13 |
| tablets | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

The first half of the gate is met in all 26 cases, and it says little, because PLS on
spectra as measured is no serious reference. The second half is met for the tablets and for
half of the corn cases. On average over the cases the error without standards is 6 % above
PLS with PDS and 8 standards for corn and 1 % for the tablets, and 9 % and 11 % above PDS
with 16 standards. For corn the result depends on the property: for oil the error without
standards is below or equal to PDS in all six crossings, and for protein it is above in all
six.

**It is the treatment of the spectra, and not the model.** PLS on the same rows with the
same treatment gives the same errors as kernel ridge: the ratio is 0.98 for corn and 0.96
for the tablets on average, and 16 of the 26 cases are within the interval. What helps is
the centring. The two things that the item named, the widths and the shift, have nothing to
repair on these two sets.

**Part 3: a difference in resolution, simulated.** Since no pair of instruments differs in
resolution, the claim of equation (#eq:matched-widths) is tested on a simulated coarser
instrument: the target spectra are broadened by a Gaussian of 8, 16 or 32 nm. In the first
block the target is the source instrument itself, so the resolution is the only difference.
In the second block it is another instrument; there the shift is removed and each
instrument is centred in every column. The model is kernel ridge on the slopes.

| set and target | target broadened by, nm | read as measured | each instrument centred, widths not matched | widths matched, difference known | widths matched, difference fitted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corn, the source itself | 8 | 1.394 | 0.475 | 0.312 | 0.312 |
| corn, the source itself | 16 | 2.963 | 0.712 | 0.332 | 0.332 |
| corn, the source itself | 32 | 5.193 | 0.978 | 0.357 | 0.357 |
| tablets, the source itself | 8 | 1.444 | 0.392 | 0.236 | 0.236 |
| tablets, the source itself | 16 | 3.565 | 0.694 | 0.236 | 0.236 |
| tablets, the source itself | 32 | 5.569 | 1.017 | 0.241 | 0.241 |
| corn, another instrument | 8 | | 0.559 | 0.512 | 0.512 |
| corn, another instrument | 16 | | 0.764 | 0.527 | 0.527 |
| corn, another instrument | 32 | | 1.009 | 0.549 | 0.549 |
| tablets, another instrument | 8 | | 0.449 | 0.358 | 0.358 |
| tablets, another instrument | 16 | | 0.720 | 0.364 | 0.364 |
| tablets, another instrument | 32 | | 1.029 | 0.427 | 0.427 |

A loss of resolution that is not handled ruins the model: with a broadening of only 8 nm,
four steps of the grid, the error is 1.4 times the spread of the property. Centring removes
the part that is the same for all samples and leaves 0.39 to 1.02. Matching the widths
removes the rest. The error returns to that of the instrument itself (0.308 for corn on
average over the three instruments, 0.238 for the tablets) at 8 nm, and is 16 % above it for
corn at 32 nm, where the coarser spectra hold less. The difference in resolution is fitted
from the two mean spectra, which come from different samples, and the fit gives the true
value among nine candidates from 2 to 48 nm in every split and for every pair. PLS on the
same rows behaves in the same way (0.325, 0.344 and 0.376 for corn).

**Reading.** On the two sets that the literature uses, the instruments differ by a spectrum
that is the same for all samples, and not by resolution or by a shift. Centring each
instrument on its own mean removes that difference without a standard, at a cost that is
set by the number of samples and can be measured on one instrument. With 8 standards PDS is
6 % better for corn and equal for the tablets; with 16 standards it is about 10 % better for
both. Where a difference in resolution exists, matched widths repair it in full and need no
standard to find it; this is shown on simulated instruments only. The same rows serve PLS
as well as the kernel.

**What is not done.** No pair of real instruments that differ in resolution was tested; the
plan names Raman spectra at two gratings or powder patterns from two diffractometers. The
glass standards that the corn file holds for every instrument are not used. The published
division of the tablets into three parts is not used; the splits are random. The centring
was tried with one number of test samples per set, so its cost is measured at 20 and at 500
samples only. A nonlinear layer on the kernel was not tried on the tablets.

## Spectra with two axes: fluorescence maps and peak lists

This section is plan item SP4 (`cmfqsar/spectrum2d.py`, `benchmarks/run_fluorescence.py`,
`benchmarks/results/fluorescence/table.md`). Some measurements give an intensity over two
variables. A fluorescence *excitation-emission matrix* is a map of the emitted intensity
over the excitation wavelength and the emission wavelength. A 1H-13C HSQC spectrum is a list
of cross-peaks, each at a proton shift and a carbon shift. An LC-MS run is a list of ions,
each at a retention time and a mass. The usual treatment puts such data into bins and gives
the bins to PLS. The item treats the spectrum as a field on a plane.

**The kernel.** A peak list holds the places $(x_i, y_i)$ and the intensities $a_i$ of its
peaks. Every peak is replaced by a Gaussian with the width $\sigma_x$ along the first axis
and $\sigma_y$ along the second. The two axes have different units, so each has its own
width. The overlap of two broadened lists has a closed form,

$$
k(A, B) \;=\; \sum_i \sum_j a_i\, b_j\,
\exp\left(-\frac{(x_i - x_j)^2}{4\sigma_x^2} - \frac{(y_i - y_j)^2}{4\sigma_y^2}\right),
$$
<!-- #eq:peak-kernel -->

which is the spectrum kernel of equation (#eq:spectrum-kernel) with one more factor
(`spectrum2d.peak_overlap`, `spectrum2d.peak_kernel`). Its cost is the number of peaks of the
one list times that of the other, and no grid enters. With bins, two peaks on the two sides
of a bin border count as different and two peaks in one bin as the same; the width does what
the bin size does, without a border. A measured map enters as the same sum over its grid
points. For a set of maps it is cheaper to broaden every map on its grid
(`spectrum2d.smoothed`) and to take dot products of the maps (`spectrum2d.map_kernel`); the
two routes agree to rounding error when the grid step is well below the width. The weight of
a fitted model is a map over the two axes, the *co-map* (`spectrum2d.co_map`).

![A spectrum with two axes as a field on a plane, on simulated peak lists. Left: a list of fourteen peaks, and the same sample measured again with every peak moved by half a width. The area of a mark grows with the intensity, and the grey lines are the borders of a table of bins two widths wide. Middle: the first list as a field, one Gaussian on every peak. Right: the similarity of the list with a copy whose peaks have moved, against the size of the move: the cosine form of the kernel of Eq. (#eq:peak-kernel), and the same from the table of bins. The lines are means over forty copies, and the band is one standard deviation of the bins. The kernel falls smoothly; the bins fall faster and depend on where their borders are. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/peaklist.png)

A measured map has places without information about the sample. In a fluorescence map the
excitation light itself is scattered into the detector where the emission wavelength equals
the excitation wavelength, and again at twice that wavelength. `spectrum2d.scatter_mask`
marks these places, and `smoothed` broadens a map with missing values by taking, at every
place, the weighted mean of the measured values around it.

**The data.** A survey (`docs/public_3dqsar_datasets.md`) found two sets of fluorescence
maps that can be fetched, and no set of HSQC or LC-MS peak lists with a class for every
sample. `benchmarks/prepare_fluorescence.py` downloads both into the cache (77 MB); nothing
of them is in the repository.

- *Honey* (Lenhardt et al., Applied Spectroscopy 68, 557 (2014); data page of the
  chemometrics group of the University of Copenhagen, "available for public use"): 110
  honeys, of which 104 have one of four botanical origins (47 acacia, 30 meadow, 15
  sunflower, 12 linden) and six are "false" honeys from bees that were fed a sucrose
  solution. The scattered light is the largest signal of every map and is taken out.
- *Olive oil* (Venturini, Fluri and Baumgartner, Data 8, 81 (2023), CC BY 4.0): 24
  commercial extra virgin olive oils kept at 60 degrees C, three samples of every oil at each of 10
  steps of ageing, 720 maps. For one of the three samples the absorbance of the diluted oil
  at 232 and at 268 nm was measured. The regulation of the European Union grades an olive
  oil by these values; 168 of the 240 measured samples are within its limits for extra
  virgin oil.

```
python benchmarks/prepare_fluorescence.py   # once: downloads 77 MB
python benchmarks/run_fluorescence.py       # 33 minutes
```

**How the models are compared.** The reference is PLS on the map with its values in one row:
PLS regression for a measured value, and PLS discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) for a class,
with one model for each class against the others. The kernel models are kernel ridge
regression and the kernel Fisher discriminant of section *A classifier with a co-field*, one
for each class against the others. Both get the same descriptions: the map broadened by 0, 10 or
20 nm along the excitation axis and by 0, 4, 8 or 16 nm along the emission axis, as it is or
divided by its own length (the cosine form). The description and the setting of the model
are chosen by cross-validation inside the samples of the fit. "PLS on the map as measured"
has none of these choices but the number of components, and is what the literature reports.
The benchmark records how often a chosen setting is at the edge of its grid; it is 5 % of
the fits or less for both models.

**The kernel correlation, which the gate of the item asks for first.** The kernel of every
broadened description is compared with the kernel of the map as measured, over all pairs of
different samples. The correlation is 0.958 to 1.000 for the honeys and 0.993 to 1.000 for
the olive oils. A description whose kernel correlates this closely with the old one cannot
change a model much. So the prediction is that broadening gains nothing on these maps.

**Honey: the botanical origin.** Five folds with the classes in proportion, 20 repeats.

| model | right class, % | mean over the four classes of the share found, % |
|---|---|---|
| always the largest class | 45.2 | 25.0 |
| PLS-DA on the map as measured | 87.0 (3.1) | 86.3 (3.2) |
| PLS-DA, description chosen inside the fit | 86.3 (1.9) | 84.7 (2.4) |
| kernel Fisher discriminant, description chosen inside the fit | 87.9 (2.1) | 86.9 (2.0) |

The kernel Fisher discriminant finds the class of 87.9 % of the honeys. Against PLS-DA on
the map as measured the difference is +0.6 points (95 % bootstrap interval over the repeats
-0.7 to +2.0): the two are equal, as the kernel correlation said. Against PLS-DA with the
same choices it is +2.2 points (+0.7 to +3.6); the choices cost PLS-DA a little and do not
cost the discriminant. The description chosen most often is a broadening of 20 nm along the
excitation axis and none along the emission axis, in the cosine form. The honeys that are
put into a wrong class are mostly acacia and meadow honeys taken for each other, and linden
and sunflower honeys taken for meadow honeys; a meadow honey comes from many plants.

**Honey: real or false.** A description of one class is fitted on the real honeys of the
fit alone (`cmfqsar/oneclass.py`). The six false honeys are then scored against the real
honeys that the description has not seen. The number is the share of pairs of a real and a
false honey that are put in the right order.

| description of the class | maps as measured, cosine form | maps broadened by 20 and 16 nm |
|---|---|---|
| distance to the mean map | 0.909 | 0.884 |
| distance to the fifth nearest honey | 0.982 | 0.982 |
| distance from the main subspace (5 components) | 0.926 | 0.966 |
| Gaussian process on a constant | 0.965 | 0.848 |

A false honey is further from its fifth nearest real honey than a real honey in 98 % of the
pairs. There are six false honeys, so these numbers are a first reading and not a rate of
detection.

**Olive oil: the absorbance from the map.** The 30 samples of one oil are not independent,
so whole oils are held out: six folds of four oils, 10 repeats. The same with random folds is
given beside it. Root-mean-square errors in absorbance; the standard deviation of the
absorbance is 0.284 at 232 nm and 0.075 at 268 nm.

| model and input | 232 nm, whole oils held out | 232 nm, random folds | 268 nm, whole oils held out | 268 nm, random folds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the mean of the fit | 0.292 | 0.285 | 0.0756 | 0.0754 |
| linear regression on the sum of the intensities | 0.293 | 0.286 | 0.0733 | 0.0724 |
| PLS on the map as measured | 0.256 | 0.118 | 0.0409 | 0.0217 |
| PLS, description chosen inside the fit | 0.271 | 0.115 | 0.0376 | 0.0216 |
| kernel ridge, description chosen inside the fit | 0.269 | 0.111 | 0.0320 | 0.0207 |
| PLS, the mean of the three maps of a sample | 0.276 | | 0.0307 | |
| kernel ridge, the mean of the three maps | 0.261 | | 0.0279 | |

- *The absorbance at 268 nm can be read from the map of an oil that the model has not
  seen.* Kernel ridge has an error of 0.032, less than half of the error of the mean. It is
  22 % below PLS on the map as measured (difference -0.0089, interval -0.0168 to -0.0011)
  and within the interval of PLS with the same choices (-0.0056, -0.0132 to +0.0009).
- *The absorbance at 232 nm cannot.* With whole oils held out no model is more than 12 %
  below the mean of the fit. The oils differ in this value from the start, by more than
  ageing changes it, and the map does not show that difference.
- *Random folds overstate both.* With random folds the errors are 0.11 and 0.021, which is
  59 % and 35 % below the errors with whole oils held out. A model that has seen other
  samples of the same oil recognises the oil. A use of the set as its authors propose, to
  predict a chemical value from the map, has to hold out whole oils.
- *The sum of all intensities says nothing.* A linear regression on that one number is
  equal to the mean. What the map carries is in its shape.
- *The three maps of a sample as an ensemble.* The kernel of two ensembles is the mean of
  the kernels of their members, which for this kernel is the kernel of the mean maps. With
  the mean of the three maps the error at 268 nm falls from 0.0320 to 0.0279 (difference
  -0.0041, interval -0.0085 to -0.0001), and at 232 nm by 3 %.

The class "within the limits of the regulation" is found for 86.0 % of the samples by the
kernel Fisher discriminant with whole oils held out (mean over the two classes), for 85.5 %
by PLS-DA on the map as measured and for 84.7 % by PLS-DA with the same choices.

**Simulated peak lists: the case that the two sets do not hold.** The two measured sets are
smooth maps. The case that the item is about is a list of sharp peaks whose places move a
little from sample to sample. It is simulated: two classes of 50 lists with 40 peaks on a
square of side 100, six more peaks at random places in every list, and in one class four
peaks stronger by 60 %. The *jitter* is the standard deviation of the place of a peak along
each axis. The kernel of the peak lists (the width chosen inside the fit) is compared with
bins (the bin size chosen inside the fit), each with both models; 10 repeats.

| jitter | kernel of the peak lists, kernel Fisher discriminant | kernel of the peak lists, PLS-DA | bins, kernel Fisher discriminant | bins, PLS-DA | PLS-DA, bins of 1 | PLS-DA, bins of 16 | kernel correlation, peak lists against bins of 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 91.7 | 90.4 | 91.6 | 91.6 | 91.7 | 84.3 | 0.91 |
| 0.5 | 90.2 | 89.4 | 85.1 | 86.2 | 63.5 | 81.1 | 0.42 |
| 1 | 86.7 | 86.2 | 81.0 | 80.4 | 53.3 | 79.4 | 0.37 |
| 2 | 80.4 | 78.7 | 71.1 | 71.1 | 51.5 | 73.1 | 0.44 |
| 4 | 75.4 | 76.1 | 67.1 | 66.2 | 53.5 | 66.2 | 0.53 |

Without jitter every route finds 92 % of the classes. When the peaks move, the kernel of
the peak lists loses less than the bins do, although the best bin size is chosen inside the
fit: the difference to PLS-DA on bins is +4.0 points at a jitter of 0.5 (interval +0.5 to
+7.1), +6.3 at 1 (+3.9 to +8.4), and +9.3 and +9.2 at 2 and 4. Bins of the size of a peak
fall to chance at a jitter of 1. The model does not matter: PLS-DA on the kernel of the peak
lists equals the kernel Fisher discriminant on it, and the two models are equal on bins. The
kernel correlation between the two descriptions is 0.91 without jitter and 0.37 to 0.53 with
it, so here the test says that the descriptions differ, and they do.

**The gate of the plan item.** It has three parts. The kernel correlation is reported, and
it predicted both outcomes. The classifier on the kernel matches PLS-DA on the measured
maps, and beats PLS-DA on bins for simulated peak lists whose peaks move; on measured peak
lists it is not tested. The third part, that the co-map names the places that the paper of
the study names as its markers, is not checked: the result table lists the places of the
co-map of every honey class, and the paper has not been read against them.

**What is not done.** No measured peak list (HSQC, LC-MS) was fitted, because no set with a
class for every sample was verified. A third axis, as in a GC×GC-MS run, is not in the
module. The difference of two co-maps, which says what separates two classes and not one
class from the rest, was not computed. The inner filter effect of an undiluted oil, which
bends the relation between a concentration and the intensity, was not corrected.

## A migration path as the sample: the barrier of a Li hop

Ionic conductivity in a solid electrolyte is set by the barrier a mobile ion meets between two
sites, not by either site. That barrier is a field property in the sense of this program: the
ion moving from one site through the bottleneck to the next feels the electrostatic potential,
the repulsion and the polarisability of the framework around the path. In the language of the
rest of the manual the framework is the receptor, the ion is the ligand and the barrier is the
binding energy. Plan item BT7 makes the **hop** the sample (`cmfqsar/hops.py`), and everything
the per-atom sections above built carries over with three changes.

**The environment is cut from a periodic cell.** `point_environment` is the `environment` of the
local sections for a crystal: it collects every atom of the cell and every periodic image within
the reach of the envelope, measured from a *point* rather than from an atom, multiplies the
weights by $e^{-\rho d^2}$ and returns an ordinary field. The centre of a hop is the midpoint of
the two sites, the migrating ion is removed from both its positions, and the first atom of the
result is a weightless marker at the centre, so that the convention of the local modules that
the centre is atom 0 holds. The fields are the inorganic set of the crystal section: the
electrostatic field with oxidation states or, from a VASP run, net Bader charges
(`cmfqsar/vasp.py`, plan item M3, reads them from `ACF.dat` and the `OUTCAR` with nothing
written by hand), the steric field, the electronegativity, and one indicator field per element.

**The frame is the hop itself.** The origin is the midpoint and $z$ points from the first site to
the second, which is the direction the barrier is measured in; a hop and its reverse are two
samples with two barriers. What is left is the rotation about $z$, and the program does not
choose it: the kernel is **averaged over the whole rotation group about the hop axis**, which has
a closed form. For two Gaussians of widths $b_l$ and $b_m$ at $(\rho_l, z_l)$ and $(\rho_m, z_m)$
in cylindrical coordinates about the axis, the overlap at a relative angle $\theta$ is

$$
\left(\frac{2\pi}{b_l + b_m}\right)^{3/2}
\exp\!\left(-c\,[(z_l - z_m)^2 + \rho_l^2 + \rho_m^2 - 2\rho_l\rho_m\cos\theta]\right),
\qquad c = \frac{b_l b_m}{2(b_l + b_m)},
$$

and its mean over $\theta$ replaces the cosine term by the modified Bessel function
$I_0(2c\rho_l\rho_m)$:

$$
\bar k(l, m) = w_l w_m \left(\frac{2\pi}{b_l + b_m}\right)^{3/2}
\exp\!\left(-c\,[(z_l - z_m)^2 + (\rho_l - \rho_m)^2]\right)\, e^{-x} I_0(x),
\qquad x = 2c\rho_l\rho_m .
$$
<!-- #eq:hopkernel -->

This is the mean-map kernel over the rotation group, the device the local alignment uses for a
frame ambiguity, taken over a continuous group instead of a finite set of poses. The rotation
average is a projection, so the kernel of two averaged fields equals the kernel of one plain
field with one averaged field, and (#eq:hopkernel) costs one Bessel evaluation per atom pair,
the same as the plain overlap kernel; the finite poses of `posed_hop` cost the number of poses
squared and agree with it to machine precision at 96 poses. `HopModel` holds the kernel, one
block per field divided by its diagonal and summed with the mixing coefficients, and the ridge
regression on it; the rotation-invariant local kernel of the atom sections applies to the same
environments unchanged and is the frame-free comparison.

![A hop as the sample, for the hop of Li3PO4 the interface study computed with DFT, site 34 into site 0. Left: the environment cut from the cell, every atom within 6 Å of the midpoint with the two positions of the migrating ion removed (dashed circles), projected onto a plane through the hop axis, which is z; the dotted circles are where the envelope has fallen to 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01, and an atom is drawn fainter as its weight falls. The oxygen with the black edge forms the bottleneck, the point of least free space on the straight path. Right: the electrostatic field of the same environment averaged about the hop axis, as a function of the position along the hop and the distance from its axis, with the atoms at their (z, r) and the two sites on the axis; this is the view the rotation-averaged kernel of Eq. (#eq:hopkernel) and the co-field profile take.](docs/figures/hop.png)

**The co-field is a profile.** Averaged about the axis, the co-field depends on the position
along the hop and the distance from its axis, so `HopModel.profile` reads it as a table in
$(z, r)$: where along the path, and how far from it, an atom of a given field raises or lowers
the barrier. Its error follows the dual coefficients, whose covariance under independent noise of
level $\sigma$ in the barriers is $\sigma^2 (K + \lambda I)^{-2}$, and `atom_contributions`
splits a prediction over the atoms of the environment exactly, as the overlap model does.

**The sample index is a pair.** A hop is (structure, site $a$, site $b$, lattice offset of $b$).
`enumerate_hops` lists every pair of sites of the mobile species between 1.5 and 4.5 A apart,
periodic images included, both ways; `reduce_by_symmetry` keeps one of every set of hops with
the same fingerprint (the sorted symbols, distances from the midpoint and positions along the
hop of the atoms within 5 A), records the multiplicity, and `bottleneck` reports the point of
least free space on the straight path with the atoms that form it. `HopSet.targets` turns the
labelled hops into an `AtomTargets` whose "molecule" is the structure, so the folds hold out
whole structures and the bootstrap resamples structures, since the hops of one cell are not
independent.

**The labels.** `bvse_barriers` reads the barrier of every hop from the bond-valence site-energy
landscape of the softBV model (the `bvlain` package): the energy is evaluated on a box around
the path, the two sites are the lowest points within 0.6 A of them, and the barrier is the
lowest level at which the two are connected through the box, found by bisection with a
connected-components labelling at each step. That is a minimax path, which is what a migration
barrier on a grid is, and it is cheap, so it labels thousands of hops; under rule 1 of the plan
it is also the reference a model trained on DFT barriers has to beat. Measured or DFT barriers
come from a table (`read_hop_labels`): structure, the two site indices, the image of the second
site, the barrier and, if known, the reverse one.

**From hops to conduction.** The model predicts per hop. `percolation_thresholds` takes one energy
per hop of a structure, adds the hops in order of increasing energy to a union-find over the
sites that keeps the lattice offset of every site to its root, and reports the energy at which
the network first connects through the cell in one, two and three independent directions (a path
that comes back to a site at a different offset is a wrap, and the rank of the wraps is the
dimensionality). `structure_percolation` does this from the bond-valence saddles or from
predicted barriers, measured from the lowest site energy, which is what the effective activation
energy of a conductor is read from.

```bash
cmf hops examples/hops/phosphate.extxyz examples/hops/borophosphate.extxyz examples/hops/borate.extxyz \
    --charges file --bvse --reference --invariant --profile --percolate --out hops.csv
cmf hops structure.cif --labels barriers.csv --rho 0.05 0.1 0.25 --reference
cmf hops calcs/phosphate/pristine --charges file --list
```

The first command labels the hops of the three hosts of the Li interface study with the
bond-valence landscape, fits the count reference, the invariant kernel and the rotation-averaged
overlap kernel with folds that hold out whole structures, prints the co-field profile of the
best model and the percolation thresholds of each structure from the labels and from the
predictions, and writes every hop with its labels and out-of-fold prediction. The second takes
barriers from a table; the third reads a VASP run directory (`CONTCAR`, `ACF.dat`, `OUTCAR`)
and lists the distinct hops with their bottlenecks.

### What it is worth, measured

`benchmarks/run_hops.py` measures the hop model on a public set and on the three hosts of the
Li interface study (`benchmarks/results/hops/`).

**The public set.** 472 ternary compounds of lithium and oxygen (Li, O and one more element) of the Materials Project within
0.05 eV/atom of the convex hull, fetched through its OPTIMADE interface and prepared by
`benchmarks/prepare_hops.py`: 24004 Li hops of 1.5 to 4.5 A, of which
1732 are distinct by symmetry, labelled with the bond-valence barrier and kept as
the sample (at most six per structure, so that no structure dominates); 10 folds
holding out whole structures; environments within 6 A of the midpoint; the
fields are the electrostatic field with oxidation-state charges, the steric field, the
electronegativity and one indicator field per element. The bond-valence barrier is a known
function of the framework around the path, so the question is whether the kernel can learn such
a function across structure types, and which descriptor it needs. One of the descriptors is the
**two end sites** of the hop, each described the way plan item M5 describes a single site of a
cell: the row of the cell's periodic autocorrelation that belongs to that site
(`cmfqsar.sites.site_autocorrelation`), with the two rows combined as their sum and the absolute
value of their difference, so that the descriptor does not change when the hop is reversed. That
is the site-resolved model the gate of plan item BT7 asks the path model to beat. It is taken at
the three cutoffs of the site profile M5 chose between, 4, 6 and 8 A, where it gives
+0.439, +0.446 and +0.462; the row below is the one at 6 A, the radius the hop environments
themselves use.

| descriptor | envelope width (A) | q2 | error (eV) | against the counts | against length and bottleneck | against the two end sites |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| counts of atoms in shells about the midpoint | -- | +0.491 | 0.576 | -- | -- | -- |
| hop length and bottleneck distance | -- | +0.103 | 0.765 | -- | -- | -- |
| the two end sites, as item M5 describes a site (6 A) | -- | +0.446 | 0.601 | -0.045 [-0.142, +0.065] | +0.344 [+0.178, +0.452] | -- |
| invariant local kernel | 4.5 | +0.553 | 0.540 | +0.062 [-0.003, +0.170] | +0.451 [+0.321, +0.538] | +0.107 [+0.030, +0.218] |
| overlap kernel in the hop frame | 4.5 | +0.630 | 0.491 | +0.138 [+0.085, +0.219] | +0.527 [+0.402, +0.608] | +0.184 [+0.087, +0.298] |
| invariant local kernel | 3.2 | +0.624 | 0.495 | +0.133 [+0.066, +0.231] | +0.522 [+0.391, +0.609] | +0.178 [+0.082, +0.289] |
| overlap kernel in the hop frame | 3.2 | +0.649 | 0.478 | +0.158 [+0.096, +0.250] | +0.546 [+0.423, +0.628] | +0.203 [+0.102, +0.318] |
| invariant local kernel | 2.0 | +0.657 | 0.473 | +0.165 [+0.097, +0.266] | +0.554 [+0.421, +0.643] | +0.211 [+0.117, +0.329] |
| overlap kernel in the hop frame | 2.0 | +0.662 | 0.469 | +0.170 [+0.112, +0.265] | +0.559 [+0.432, +0.641] | +0.216 [+0.109, +0.334] |

Overlap in the hop frame against the invariant kernel at the same width: 4.5 A: +0.076 [-0.002, +0.145]; 3.2 A: +0.024 [-0.049, +0.099]; 2.0 A: +0.005 [-0.060, +0.071]. Learning curve
of the frame model, q2 against the number of training structures (three random draws each):
25: +0.078; 50: +0.153; 100: +0.441; 200: +0.498; 400: +0.660; 459: +0.662.

**The field beats the counts, and the frame pays only where the envelope is wide.** The
overlap kernel in the hop frame is ahead of the count reference by +0.170 [+0.112, +0.265] and
of the two chemist's numbers by +0.559 [+0.432, +0.641], so the barrier is not a function of the
hop length and the bottleneck width alone, nor of how many atoms of which kind surround the
midpoint; where they sit matters. Against the rotation-invariant kernel at the same width the
frame gains +0.076 [-0.002, +0.145] at 4.5 A, at the edge of the interval, and nothing at 3.2
and 2.0 A. That is the same picture the local alignment gave for the ring carbons: a wide
environment is nearly the same set of distances in every structure and the directions
separate it, while a narrow one is its first shell, which distances describe perfectly well.
The best width is the narrowest (2.0 A), so at this size of set the frame is not what limits
the model. The learning curve has not levelled off, +0.08 at 25 structures, +0.44 at 100 and
+0.66 at 400, which is the opposite of what the shift set showed in LP5: here the set, not the
representation, is the limit. The error of 0.47 eV on barriers whose quartiles are 0.34 and
1.13 eV is enough to rank hops and not to give a number; part of it is in the label, since a
rigid landscape and a box around the straight path give some hops barriers of several eV that a
relaxed path would not.

**The path is worth more than its two ends, which is the gate of plan item BT7.** The hop as an
object has to earn its place against the obvious alternative: describe the two sites the ion
moves between, each as well as the site-resolved model of item M5 describes a site, and let the
pair stand for the path. It does not reach the path model. The frame kernel is ahead of it by
+0.216 [+0.109, +0.334] at a site cutoff of 6 A, +0.222 [+0.134, +0.310] at 4 A and
+0.200 [+0.104, +0.322] at 8 A, clear of zero in all three, and the rotation-invariant kernel on
the same hop environments is ahead by +0.211 [+0.117, +0.329]. The two end sites are also no
better than the count of atoms in shells about the midpoint, -0.045 [-0.142, +0.065] at 6 A, so
describing the two sites well is worth about what counting the neighbours of the midpoint is
worth. The shortfall is not the descriptor confusing one hop with another: the two end sites
name 1195 distinct pairs for the 1732 hops and 923 hops share their pair with another hop, since
a hop and its reverse, and two hops through different images of the cell, get the same row, but
predicting the mean barrier of each such group would still reach q2 +0.950 at an error of
0.181 eV. The site description loses the barrier for want of the path between the sites, not for
want of a way to tell two paths apart. That is the reason the hop is a sample of its own: where
the bottleneck sits between the two sites is not a property of either of them.

**Three things stand above their error, and they are the rules a chemist would state.**
First, anything on the axis raises the barrier: the steric co-field is +1.5 to +2.8 along the
whole path at r = 0 (two to three standard deviations), the oxygen indicator +3.0 (1.1) and the
lithium indicator +5.2 (1.2) at the midpoint, because a path that runs through an atom is not a
path. The electrostatic co-field on the axis is negative, -1.2 to -2.6, for the same reason:
the atoms that lie on a straight line between two Li sites are oxygens, whose charge is
negative, and a negative co-field times a negative weight raises the barrier. Second, an oxygen
about 2 A from the axis at the midpoint **lowers** the barrier, -1.31 (0.31), four standard
deviations: that is the bottleneck rule, a wide ring of anions around the saddle makes a low
barrier and a narrow one a high barrier, and the co-field places the ring where the bottleneck
of a 3 A hop in an oxide sits. Third, lithium and cations beside the sites raise it: the
lithium indicator is +1.2 and +1.4 (0.25) at 3 A from the axis beside either site, five
standard deviations, and the electrostatic co-field is +0.8 (0.27) there, so a positive charge
within 3 A of a site repels the mobile ion out of it. The element indicators also separate
cobalt (+3.1 at the midpoint) and manganese (+1.8 beside a site) from nickel (-1.5 at the
midpoint), with the caution the local alignment section gives: the fields overlap in what they
describe, so the twelve co-fields are one effect decomposed over twelve bases and not twelve
statements, and an element read alone is partly the oxygen coordination that comes with it.

![The co-field of the public hop model as a profile in the hop frame: the position along the hop against the distance from its axis, for the electrostatic field, the steric field and the oxygen indicator, on a finer grid than the tables above. Red raises the barrier per unit of field, blue lowers it; inside the dashed line the value is more than two standard deviations from zero. Anything on the axis raises the barrier, an oxygen about 2 Å from the axis at the midpoint lowers it, and a positive charge about 3 Å from the axis beside a site raises it. Drawn from `benchmarks/results/hops/profile_fine.json`, written by `benchmarks/run_hops.py --fine-profile`.](docs/figures/hopcofield.png)

**From hops to conduction.** The out-of-fold barriers of every hop (the equivalent hops taking
their representative's value) were run through the percolation step and compared with the
thresholds of the labelled network, on the structures whose every distinct hop was labelled:

| direction | structures | correlation | mean absolute difference (eV) | finite or not agrees |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1D | 164 | +0.808 | 0.380 | 100% |
| 2D | 110 | +0.857 | 0.351 | 100% |
| 3D | 60 | +0.754 | 0.343 | 100% |

The predicted network agrees with the labelled one on whether a structure percolates in one,
two or three directions in every case, and gives the threshold to within 0.35 to 0.38 eV with a
correlation of 0.75 to 0.86. The difference is about the model's error on one hop, which is what
it should be, since a threshold is the barrier of one hop of the network. That is the step from
a per-hop model to a per-structure number, and it holds.

**The three hosts.** Applied unchanged to the 48 distinct hops of Li3PO4,
Li3BP2O8 and LiBO2 (`examples/hops/`, bond-valence labels, Bader charges on the atoms but the
public model's oxidation-state charges for the prediction), the public model gives
q2 -1.415, correlation +0.683 and an error of 0.279 eV. Within the
hosts, leaving one host out, the frame kernel gives -0.120 and the counts
-0.115; three structures cannot turn that into an interval, which is why the public
set exists. The two hops the study computed with DFT are listed next to the bond-valence value
and the prediction:

| host | hop | length (A) | DFT barrier (eV) | bond-valence (eV) | predicted (eV) | bottleneck (A) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| phosphate | 34 -> 0 | 2.98 | 0.287 | 0.732 | 0.798 | 1.26 (O) |
| borophosphate | 18 -> 8 | 2.64 | 0.003 | 0.393 | 0.561 | 1.48 (O O) |

The DFT values are plain elastic bands for a vacancy hop into a relaxed vacancy, so they are lower
bounds and include the relaxation the rigid landscape does not; the columns are not expected to
agree in value. The public model ranks the hops of Li3PO4 and Li3BP2O8 (correlations +0.84 and +0.78) and
fails on LiBO2, whose ten distinct hops span 0.03 eV, less than the error. The negative q2 says
it does not carry the scale over: the public barriers average 0.89 eV and the hosts' 0.46, and
the hosts are a phosphate, a borophosphate and a borate where the public set holds six
silicates, four borates and no phosphate. A model for these hosts wants a set of their own
chemistry, and the chemistry the public set has is that of the Materials Project, which is
cathodes. The DFT values are lower than the bond-valence ones by about 0.4 eV, as a relaxed
vacancy hop against a rigid landscape should be, and the order of the two hops is the same in
every column.

**The disordered conductors (plan item M2).** The thirteen structures of
`examples/hops/disordered/` are the families a solid-electrolyte study is about, read with the
partial occupancies their refinements report: 6408 hops between sites the Li ion can
hold, 298 distinct, 298 with a bond-valence barrier of the ordered
framework. The public model applied as it stands gives q2 -1.075, correlation
+0.273 and an error of 1.438 eV. A model cross-validated within the set, one
structure held out at a time, gives -0.064 for the frame kernel and +0.166
for the counts, -0.230 [-0.886, +0.143] between them.

**What the table says.** The percolation thresholds of the hop network agree with those of the
bond-valence grid wherever the Li sublattice is the disordered part: cubic LLZO 0.40 against
0.41 eV, LGPS 0.53 to 0.59 against 0.57 to 0.60, beta-Li3PS4 0.25 to 0.40 against 0.27 to 0.42,
Li2.92N 0.16 against 0.16, LISICON 0.45 to 0.49 against 0.47 to 0.52. That is the check that
the hops between 1.5 and 4.5 A are the paths the landscape uses, and it holds for the
families the item was built for. The ordered NASICON has no pair of Li sites in that window,
because its M2 sites are empty and not in the file, so it has no hops; the tetragonal garnet
and Li3PO4 differ from the grid because the network measures from the lowest site and the
grid from its own minimum. The model is a different matter. The public model does not carry
over (correlation +0.27 over all hops; +0.84 on the lithiated NASICON, +0.69 on Li3PO4, +0.52
on LGPS, nothing on the two cubic garnets whose eighteen distinct hops span 0.1 eV), and within
the set the frame kernel is behind the counts, inside an interval that reaches from -0.9 to
+0.1: twelve labelled structures, one of them with 98 distinct hops, and barriers up to 15 eV
where a straight path runs through an atom, are not a set a model can be measured on. What the
item delivers is the data model that lets these structures in, exact and at no cost; a result on
conductors needs the DFT-labelled set the previous section asks for.

### Against published numbers on the same labels

Everything above measures this program against references built inside it. One published
benchmark predicts the same quantity, so the models can be compared with other people's numbers:
the nebBVSE122k part of the LiTraj collection (Dembitskiy et al., *npj Computational Materials*
**11**, 131 (2025), MIT licence), which holds 122,421 bond-valence barriers of single Li hops in
11,290 structures of the Materials Project over 1,644 chemical systems. Its label is the barrier
of one hop on a rigid framework, as here, relaxed with the nudged elastic band method instead of
taken as the minimax path on a grid. Its split holds out whole structures, which was read from
its index rather than from the paper: none of its 1,172 test structures appears in its training
part. So the protocol is the one used here, and the numbers are comparable in kind.

Two differences remain. The collection covers every chemistry that holds lithium, so its barriers
spread 2.4 times as widely as those of the public set above (standard deviation 1.97 eV against
0.81 eV), and the same error in eV therefore gives a higher q2 on it. And a kernel holds one
number per pair of samples, so `benchmarks/run_litraj.py` reads a sample -- 400 structures with
at most six hops each, 1801 hops of 393 structures -- where the published models are fitted on
96,849 hops of 8,945 structures.

| model | q2 | error (eV) | mean absolute error (eV) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| counts about the midpoint (rule 1) | +0.468 | 1.389 | 0.812 |
| hop length and bottleneck | +0.179 | 1.725 | 1.050 |
| the two end sites, as item M5 describes a site (6 A) | +0.114 | 1.793 | 1.075 |
| rotation-invariant local kernel, rho 0.25 | +0.600 | 1.204 | 0.726 |
| overlap kernel in the hop frame, rho 0.25 | +0.580 | 1.234 | 0.730 |
| *published:* M3GNet, a graph network marking the midpoint | +0.95 | 0.44 | 0.21 |
| *published:* gradient-boosted forest on Voronoi features | +0.94 | 0.49 | 0.26 |
| *published:* nearest neighbours on the same features | +0.92 | 0.58 | 0.27 |

**Three things the table says.** The ordering inside this program holds on a chemistry it was not
built on: the field kernels are ahead of the count reference by +0.132 [+0.056, +0.209], so rule
1 is met here too. The size of the training set does not account for the distance to the
published models: between 200 and 393 training structures the model gains +0.028 in q2 for every
doubling, and the 4.5 doublings up to 8,945 structures carry it to about +0.71 at that rate, well
short of +0.95. And the two findings of the sections above hold on the new set as well. The hop
frame is again worth nothing in accuracy over the rotation-invariant kernel
(-0.020 [-0.073, +0.039] here, +0.005 [-0.060, +0.071] on the public set), so the frame earns its
place by the co-field it makes readable and not by its predictions. The site-resolved descriptor
falls from +0.446 on ternary lithium oxides to +0.114 here, so describing two end sites carries a
barrier only inside one chemistry.

#### What the distance to those numbers is made of

The two published models closest to the graph network are a random forest and a gradient-boosted
forest on hand-made features of the hop, not kernel models. The table above therefore mixes two
questions: is this program's **description** of a hop behind, or is fitting that description with
a **kernel**? They come apart by fitting both forests on this program's own descriptions, over
the same hops and the same folds. One care is needed first. Both kernels here rescale the feature
channels and then divide every row by its own length, so a kernel entry is the cosine of the
angle between two rows and the row length never reaches the model; a forest handed the raw rows
would be handed more than the kernel ever had. So each description is fitted twice, on the rows
the kernel is built from and on the raw rows.

| description | rows | fitted with | q2 | mean absolute error (eV) | against the kernel |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| counts about the midpoint | as the kernel | random forest | +0.559 | 0.643 | +0.091 [+0.024, +0.164] |
| hop length and bottleneck | as the kernel | boosted forest | +0.202 | 0.916 | +0.023 [-0.094, +0.119] |
| rotation-invariant local | as the kernel | random forest | +0.742 | 0.481 | +0.142 [+0.091, +0.198] |
| rotation-invariant local | as the kernel | boosted forest | +0.758 | 0.488 | +0.158 [+0.110, +0.212] |
| rotation-invariant local | raw | random forest | +0.844 | 0.374 | +0.243 [+0.188, +0.305] |
| rotation-invariant local | raw | boosted forest | +0.840 | 0.379 | +0.240 [+0.183, +0.305] |

The comparison favours the kernel, which is given the ridge that maximises the same out-of-fold
q2 it reports while the forests are fitted at fixed settings and search for nothing.

**The fitting method is worth a large part of the distance.** On exactly the rows the kernel is
built from -- the same description, nothing added -- a forest reaches q2 +0.758 where the kernel
reaches +0.600, and the mean absolute error falls from 0.726 to 0.488 eV. So the description of a
hop is not what was behind the published models here. Fitting it with a kernel ridge was.

**And the cosine normalisation throws away something that carries the barrier.** Adding the raw
row lengths back, so that the model can also see how large an environment's features are and not
only their direction, gains a further +0.086 and takes the mean absolute error to 0.374 eV. The
kernel cannot use that length by construction. This is a property of the invariant kernel of this
program and not of the hop models, so it bears on every kernel built on
`cmfqsar.invariant.autocorrelation_kernel`; the plan opens it as item M15, and nothing is changed
until it has been measured where that kernel is used. The same mechanism is already recorded as a
caution for particles, where the per-atom normalisation removes the particle size.

Set beside the published numbers: this program's description of a hop, fitted with a forest,
reaches a mean absolute error of 0.374 eV on 1801 hops, against 0.21 eV for the graph network and
0.26 eV for the published forest, both fitted on 96,849 hops. The forest also learns faster,
+0.053 in q2 for every doubling of the training set against +0.028 for the overlap kernel.

#### Can a kernel hold what the forest found?

The kernels here are **linear** kernels: `autocorrelation_kernel` rescales the channels, divides
every row by its own length and takes the inner product, so kernel ridge on one is a linear model
in the feature space, while a forest is not. The first guess is therefore that the barrier is not
a linear function of these features. A Gaussian kernel on the same rows tests that guess without
leaving the kernel framework: the rows are unit vectors, so the squared distance between rows $i$
and $j$ is $2 - 2K_{ij}$ and the whole family of widths is a function of the matrix already
computed, with no field touched again.

These arms are fitted more honestly than the table above. The width and the ridge are chosen
inside each training part, on an inner split that holds out whole structures, and the test fold is
touched once with the choice already made; the linear kernel is given the same treatment so the
two can be set beside each other. That is why the nested linear row scores below the same kernel
in the earlier table.

| description | kernel | q2 | mean absolute error (eV) | against the first table |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| counts about the midpoint | linear, nested | +0.445 | 0.818 | -0.024 [-0.070, +0.003] |
| counts about the midpoint | Gaussian, nested | +0.430 | 0.849 | -0.038 [-0.080, +0.000] |
| rotation-invariant local | linear, nested | +0.572 | 0.736 | -0.029 [-0.048, -0.006] |
| rotation-invariant local | Gaussian, nested | +0.623 | 0.653 | +0.023 [-0.002, +0.053] |

**The guess is the smaller part of the answer.** On the local description the width is worth
+0.052 [+0.023, +0.080] over the linear kernel given the same treatment. That is clear of zero,
but the whole distance from that kernel to the random forest on the very same rows is +0.171 in
q2, so a curved response to these features covers about 30 per cent of it, and the Gaussian
kernel is still -0.119 [-0.170, -0.071] behind the forest. On the counts the width is worth
nothing at all (-0.015 [-0.060, +0.032]), so this is not a general gain from curving a kernel; it
belongs to the description that has many columns.

**What the rest is more likely to be: the metric.** A Gaussian kernel measures one distance over
all 2601 columns at once, so the few columns that carry the barrier are diluted by the many that
do not, and no single width repairs that; a tree reads columns one at a time and ignores the rest.
On that reading the open question is which columns count and how they are weighted, which is a
different repair from putting a width on a kernel. It is a reading and not a measurement, and the
plan records it as the second half of item M15 -- together with the warning that learning weights
has already failed once, in the pooled mixing pilot on molecular sets, so this case has to say why
it differs before it claims anything.

One number came out in passing and applies to every kernel row of the earlier table. The nested
linear kernel scores -0.029 [-0.048, -0.006] against the same kernel fitted with the ridge chosen
on the folds it reports, which is what that search is worth. So the kernel rows above are
overstated by about that much and the forest rows by nothing.

#### The window the ion passes through

A barrier is set by the narrowest place along the path: a window of three or four framework atoms
the ion has to pass. The two-point description of an environment carries the distance between two
neighbours but not the two sides that meet at the centre, so it does not resolve the angle there,
and two different windows can leave the same distance histogram. The section on the SOAP gate
above measured what that costs on a carbon-shift model; here it is measured on a barrier.
`cmfqsar.triangles` resolves the triangle for an environment whose first atom is the centre, and
the first atom of a hop environment is a weightless marker at the midpoint, so its triangles are
exactly the midpoint with two framework atoms. The reach, the grid spacing, the exponent and
whether the row length is kept are all chosen inside each training part.

| description | q2 | error (eV) | mean absolute error (eV) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| two-point, nested, same environments | +0.572 | 1.246 | 0.736 |
| two-point with a Gaussian width, nested | +0.623 | 1.169 | 0.653 |
| random forest on the two-point rows | +0.742 | 0.967 | 0.481 |
| **three-distance, nested** | **+0.789** | **0.875** | **0.421** |

The three-distance kernel against the two-point description fitted the same way is
+0.217 [+0.159, +0.286] -- four times what a Gaussian width was worth -- and +0.209 [+0.145,
+0.274] against the overlap kernel in the hop frame, which was the best model of the sections
above. It passes the random forest on the two-point rows (+0.047 [-0.004, +0.096]) and the boosted
forest (+0.031 [-0.022, +0.083]), so on this task a kernel is no longer behind a forest given the
same description. **And it is still a linear kernel on fields, so the co-field survives**, which
neither a forest nor a Gaussian width offers.

Three further readings. The nested arm chose the setting that keeps the row length in every fold,
so resolving the angle and keeping the length are different pieces of information that add
together. Mixing the two-point kernel back in is worth -0.004 [-0.032, +0.028] and the arm chose
the pure three-distance kernel in every fold, so the two-point description adds nothing once the
three-distance one is there. And the gain does not rest on the grid: reaches of 3, 4 and 5
angstrom with spacings of 0.5 and 0.75 land within 0.003 of each other at the first power, and
only the exponent moves the figure.

Two cautions. A random forest on the raw two-point rows is still ahead of this kernel by
-0.055 [-0.090, -0.023], so a flexible learner finds something a linear kernel on triangles does
not; the second subsection below measures a forest on these same rows and says what that
something is. And the range of the three-distance grid was placed after a first look at this
same sample, so while nothing was chosen on a test fold, the grid is not independent of the
data.

#### A Voronoi volume is a ratio of fields

The published models' own feature ranking puts the **smallest volume of the Voronoi polyhedra**
around the three sites of a hop -- its start, its midpoint and its end -- first, and the largest
of the three fourth. A Voronoi cell is defined by a minimum over atoms, which looks unlike
anything this program computes, but it is the narrow-width limit of a ratio of fields. With
$d_i(\mathbf{r})=|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_i|^2-R_i^2$ the squared distance to atom $i$ less its squared
radius, the radical (power) Voronoi cell of a centre $c$ is where $d_c$ is the smallest, and

$$w_c(\mathbf{r})=\frac{e^{-\beta d_c(\mathbf{r})}}{\sum_i e^{-\beta d_i(\mathbf{r})}}$$

tends to the indicator function of that cell as $\beta$ grows, everywhere except its boundary. The
denominator is a steric field with unit weights and a Gaussian of width $1/\sqrt{2\beta}$, so the
volume is an integral of a ratio of fields and the Voronoi cell is its sharp limit.

Both are measured, on four columns from the three sites (their smallest, largest and mean volume,
and the midpoint alone):

| setting | q2 | mean absolute error (eV) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the Voronoi cell itself | +0.465 | 0.824 |
| the field version, $\beta$ = 32 | +0.465 | 0.823 |
| the field version, $\beta$ = 8 | +0.468 | 0.820 |
| the field version, $\beta$ = 2 | +0.467 | 0.817 |
| the field version, $\beta$ = 0.5 | +0.376 | 0.894 |

**A field carries the quantity with nothing to spare.** The cell and the field version are level,
and the nested arm chose a field over the cell in every fold. Only the widest setting fails, where
one point of space is shared between neighbours instead of belonging to the nearest.

**The feature is strong in few terms, and it adds nothing here.** Those four numbers are level
with the whole count reference (-0.000 [-0.074, +0.092]), which has hundreds of channels, and
ahead of the hop length with the bottleneck by +0.289 [+0.238, +0.338]; they remain behind the
whole two-point description (-0.103 [-0.168, -0.039]). But adding them to the three-distance
kernel is worth +0.010 [-0.005, +0.023], which does not clear zero: the triangles around the
midpoint already carry what the free volume says, as a description of those triangles should. That
mixture is the best kernel model of this section at q2 +0.799 and a mean absolute error of 0.418
eV, and it is still -0.045 [-0.080, -0.013] behind the random forest on the raw two-point rows. So
the published models' strongest feature is not what this program was missing; what the forest has
is accounted for by the next subsection.

#### The forest is the fitting method, not the description

Two things closed most of the distance in the sections above. One is the **description**: the
length of a row, which the kernel divides out, and the angle at the midpoint, which a two-point
description cannot resolve. The other is the **fitting method**: a forest instead of a linear
kernel on the same rows. The best model so far mixes the two -- it is a forest, and it is given the
raw two-point rows -- so it is not clear which of them it owes its lead to. The arm below separates
them by giving a forest the **three-distance** rows, with the same hops, the same folds and the
same forest settings as every other forest in this section. If the better description is worth to
a forest what it was worth to the kernel, the description side is still open; if it is worth
nothing, what is left is the fitting method alone.

| model | q2 | error (eV) | mean absolute error (eV) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| three-distance kernel, nested | +0.789 | 0.875 | 0.421 |
| three-distance kernel with the free volume | +0.799 | 0.854 | 0.418 |
| random forest on the two-point rows, raw | +0.844 | 0.753 | 0.374 |
| random forest on the three-distance rows | +0.842 | 0.758 | 0.356 |
| **boosted forest on the three-distance rows** | **+0.846** | **0.746** | **0.354** |

The reading is in two comparisons. Against the kernel on the same rows the two forests are
+0.053 [+0.015, +0.091] and +0.058 [+0.029, +0.089], both clear of zero, so a flexible learner
still finds something a linear kernel on this description does not. But against the random forest
on the raw two-point rows the best of them is +0.003 [-0.026, +0.028], which does not clear zero:
**the better description is worth nothing to a forest, while it was worth +0.217 to the kernel.**

So the description side of the distance is closed. What a forest has over this program on this
task is not a description of the hop that the fields cannot express. It is the fitting method: a
model that can combine the rows in ways a linear kernel cannot. The Gaussian width above had
already recovered about 30 per cent of that, and what is left is about +0.05 in q2, or 0.06 eV of
mean absolute error. For this program that is a trade rather than a loss, because the field kernel
keeps the co-field and a forest does not; and it says where to look next for accuracy on this
task, which is the fitting method and no longer the description.

One note on what was measured. The forests are given the rows the winning kernel is built from:
the channels scaled as that kernel scales them, with the row length left in, which is the setting
the nested arm chose in every fold. The normalised form of the same rows was not measured. It
would pair with a setting that was never chosen, and this feature matrix is 63,036 columns wide,
so one arm on it costs about half an hour.

**What this means for the program.** On this task a graph network fitted on a hundred thousand
barriers is still the most accurate model, and the published work shows a further step: a
machine-learned interatomic potential that runs the elastic band itself reaches a mean absolute
error of 0.07 to 0.08 eV against DFT barriers on structures without a transition metal, and 0.11
eV over the whole set once fine-tuned on it, which is a different kind of accuracy again. What
the field model offers on migration is not the lowest error. It is the cost -- no relaxation at
all, one field evaluation per hop -- and the co-field above, which says where along the path and
at what distance from its axis the barrier is decided. Those are reasons to use it for screening
and for reading, not for a number to quote.

What the measurements above add is where the distance to those numbers came from, and it was
mostly not the fields. Fitting the same description with a forest, keeping the row length the
kernel divides out, and resolving the angle at the midpoint take the mean absolute error from
0.726 eV to 0.354 eV; the one of those that keeps the model a linear kernel on fields, and so
keeps the co-field, takes it to 0.421 eV. The last arm says how the rest divides: the description
side is closed, and what a forest still has over the kernel is the fitting method. The published
graph network reaches 0.21 eV, on fifty-four times as many
hops, and it carries three-body terms of its own -- which is the same ingredient that moved this
model furthest.

### On barriers from density functional theory

Everything above is fitted on barriers from the bond-valence site-energy method, which is an
empirical energy landscape. The same collection holds a part with barriers from a quantum
calculation, `nebDFT2k`: 1,681 hops of a lithium ion into a vacancy in 867 structures, each
with the barrier of a path that was relaxed by the nudged elastic band method with density
functional theory (DFT, the PBE functional). Its index also gives the bond-valence barrier of
every hop. This subsection is the first fit of the hop models on DFT barriers
(`benchmarks/prepare_nebdft.py`, `benchmarks/run_nebdft.py`,
`benchmarks/results/nebdft/table.md`).

```
python benchmarks/prepare_nebdft.py --fetch    # once: downloads 69 MB
python benchmarks/run_nebdft.py                # 37 minutes
```

**The set as it is used.** A hop of the index is named by two atom indices in the structure
of the Materials Project. That reading is checked for every hop against the trajectory file
of the hop: the distance that the moving ion covers in the trajectory has to be the length
of the hop in the structure, within 0.5 A. Eight hops fail the check. 21 more hops belong to
12 structures that cannot be used: 8 that the interface of the Materials Project does not
return as an ordered cell, and 4 for which no oxidation states are found. 1,652 hops in
852 structures remain. The descriptions are built from the rigid structure, without a
vacancy and without any relaxation, as everywhere in this section.

**The two barriers.** The DFT barriers have a mean of 0.81 eV and a standard deviation of
0.79 eV. The bond-valence barriers of the same hops have a mean of 1.26 eV and a standard
deviation of 1.59 eV. The two correlate with r = 0.815. Taken as a prediction, the
bond-valence barrier is worse than the mean (a mean absolute error of 0.61 eV against
0.56 eV), because it is too high and too widely spread. As an input of a model it is useful,
and the best models of the paper use it so.

**The protocols.** The models are scored on the test part of the published split, where the
numbers of the paper are, after a fit on the training and the validation part (1,436 hops;
216 of the 220 test hops are among the hops that remain). And they are scored on ten folds
that hold out whole structures, over all hops, for the intervals. Every kernel model chooses
between the linear kernel and a Gaussian kernel on top of it, and its ridge, inside the
training part. An interval is a 95 % interval from a bootstrap that draws whole structures.

| model | published test part: mean absolute error, eV | RMSE, eV | R2 | ten folds: mean absolute error, eV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the mean of the fit | 0.546 | 0.824 | -0.01 | 0.557 |
| kernel ridge, the two end sites | 0.508 | 0.769 | 0.12 | 0.493 |
| kernel ridge, counts about the midpoint | 0.396 | 0.564 | 0.53 | 0.395 |
| kernel ridge, hop length and bottleneck | 0.352 | 0.557 | 0.54 | 0.362 |
| kernel ridge, invariant field about the midpoint | 0.326 | 0.486 | 0.65 | 0.289 |
| kernel ridge, fields in the frame of the hop (the model of this section) | 0.294 | 0.460 | 0.69 | 0.288 |
| kernel ridge on the bond-valence barrier alone | 0.300 | 0.435 | 0.72 | 0.302 |
| kernel ridge, fields in the frame of the hop, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.225 [0.187, 0.273] | 0.335 | 0.83 | 0.236 [0.220, 0.251] |
| random forest, invariant field about the midpoint | 0.212 [0.175, 0.259] | 0.310 | 0.86 | 0.228 [0.213, 0.245] |
| random forest, invariant field about the midpoint, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.203 [0.163, 0.253] | 0.313 | 0.85 | 0.222 [0.207, 0.237] |
| *the paper, best model without the bond-valence barrier (kernel ridge)* | 0.27 | 0.41 | 0.76 | |
| *the paper, random forest without it* | 0.29 | 0.48 | 0.68 | |
| *the paper, graph network without it* | 0.40 | 0.64 | 0.43 | |
| *the paper, best models with the bond-valence barrier* | 0.25 | 0.38 | 0.80 | |

- *The program's description of a hop, fitted with a random forest, is at or below every
  model of the paper that predicts a barrier from a structure.* On the test part its mean
  absolute error is 0.212 eV. The best number of the paper without the bond-valence
  barrier, 0.27 eV, is above the interval of this error; the best number with it, 0.25 eV,
  is inside. The forest does not need the bond-valence barrier: with it the error changes
  by -0.006 eV (-0.012 to -0.001) on the folds.
- *The kernel model of this section needs it.* Without the bond-valence barrier it has
  0.294 eV, near the forest of the paper. With the bond-valence barrier as a second kernel
  it has 0.225 eV; on the folds the gain is 0.052 eV (0.039 to 0.066).
- *The fitting method is again what separates the two.* On the same rows the kernel is
  0.061 eV above the forest (0.047 to 0.075). This is the finding of the subsection above,
  now on DFT barriers.
- *One number matches the field kernel.* Kernel ridge on the bond-valence barrier alone has
  0.302 eV on the folds, and the kernel on the fields in the frame of the hop has 0.288 eV;
  the difference is -0.014 eV (-0.033 to +0.006). The forest on the invariant rows is
  0.074 eV below the bond-valence barrier alone (0.057 to 0.090), so the fields hold more
  than that number, and the linear kernel does not bring it out.
- *The frame of the hop adds nothing here.* The overlap kernel and the invariant kernel
  differ by -0.001 eV (-0.016 to +0.013).
- *The two end sites say little* (0.49 eV against 0.56 eV for the mean): a barrier is
  decided between the sites and not at them.

**What the comparison can and cannot say.** The test part has 216 hops, so an error on it is
known to about 0.04 eV, and four of its hops are missing here. The models here are fitted on
the training and the validation part together, and the models of the paper on the training
part with the validation part for their settings. The numbers on the ten folds do not depend
on either choice. A random forest gives no co-field; the model that gives one is the kernel
with the bond-valence barrier, at 0.225 eV.

**What the number means.** A machine-learned potential that runs the elastic band itself
reaches 0.07 to 0.11 eV on this set, as the paper reports, and that remains another kind of
accuracy. At room temperature an error of 0.23 eV in a barrier is a factor of about 7,000
in the rate of a hop. A model that reads a barrier from the rigid structure is therefore a
tool to rank many candidates before a calculation, and not a replacement for the
calculation.

**Which hops need the calculation.** A model with this error does not have to answer
every hop. In a hierarchy of methods it has to say which hops it may answer and which have to
go to the DFT calculation; this is the tolerance rule of section *The model as the fast level
of a hierarchy*, here with a DFT barrier as the fine level
(`benchmarks/run_nebdft_rule.py`, `benchmarks/results/nebdft/rule.md`; 18 minutes after the
kernels are built). Every prediction gets a standard deviation in eV. For kernel ridge it is
that of the Gaussian process which matches the ridge fit. For the random forest it is the
spread of the predictions of its trees. A factor that is measured inside the training part
puts each on the right scale. Ten folds hold out whole structures.

| model | mean absolute error, eV | root mean square of error / standard deviation | inside two standard deviations | rank correlation of the standard deviation and the absolute error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kernel ridge on the bond-valence barrier alone | 0.301 | 1.01 | 94 % | +0.03 |
| kernel ridge, fields in the frame of the hop | 0.289 | 1.01 | 94 % | +0.16 |
| kernel ridge, fields in the frame of the hop, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.234 | 0.99 | 94 % | +0.11 |
| random forest, invariant field, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.222 | 0.99 | 97 % | +0.45 |

All four standard deviations have the right size: the errors divided by them have a root
mean square of one, and 94 to 97 % of the barriers are inside two standard deviations. The
size is not what a rule needs, though. A rule needs the standard deviation to be large where
the error is large, and only the spread of the trees is: its rank correlation with the
absolute error is +0.45, against +0.03 to +0.16 for the kernel models.

The table below sends the hops with the largest standard deviation to the calculation and
gives the mean absolute error of the hops that are left.

| model | none sent | 10 % sent | 20 % sent | 30 % sent | 50 % sent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| kernel ridge, fields in the frame of the hop, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.234 | 0.219 | 0.213 | 0.206 | 0.205 |
| random forest, invariant field, with the bond-valence barrier | 0.222 | 0.185 | 0.168 | 0.160 | 0.138 |
| the forest, the hops ordered by the predicted barrier | 0.222 | | 0.182 | | 0.154 |
| the kernel model, the hops ordered by the predicted barrier | 0.234 | | 0.192 | | 0.159 |
| the forest, the hops ordered by their true error (the best that any signal could do) | 0.222 | | 0.122 | | 0.064 |

- *With the forest the rule works.* One hop in five sent to the calculation lowers the
  error of the others from 0.222 to 0.168 eV, and one in two to 0.138 eV. With the
  tolerance at the error that the forest shows inside its training part (0.36 eV), it
  answers 68 % of the hops with a mean absolute error of 0.157 eV; the hops that it sends
  away would have had a root-mean-square error of 0.51 eV, against 0.24 eV for those it
  answers.
- *With the kernel models it does not.* Their standard deviation says how far a hop is
  from the hops of the fit, and it is the same for a low and for a high barrier. The errors
  grow with the barrier. So one number that costs nothing, the predicted barrier itself,
  orders the hops better than the standard deviation of the kernel model (0.192 against
  0.213 eV at one hop in five). For the forest the spread of the trees is better than that
  number (0.168 against 0.182 eV).
- *The disagreement between two cheap models is a weak signal.* Ordering the hops by the
  difference between the model and the model on the bond-valence barrier alone gives 0.195
  to 0.207 eV at one hop in five.
- *No signal halves the error at a useful price.* To halve the error of the forest, 76 %
  of the hops have to go to the calculation with its own standard deviation; an order by
  the true error would need 25 %.

So on DFT barriers the hierarchy saves a part of the calculations and not most of them, and
the model that makes it work is the forest. The calibrated Gaussian-process deviation, which
did its work on the bond-valence barriers of many chemistries, does not order hops whose
errors depend on the size of the barrier.

### From DFT barriers to the activation energy of a conductor

This subsection is the first half of plan item MS8 (`benchmarks/run_conductors.py`,
`benchmarks/results/conductors/table.md`; 10 minutes after the rows of the hops are built).
The item asks for one chain from DFT barriers to a measured quantity of a conductor, with
the error of the model carried through to the end. The chain stops at the activation energy.
A conductivity would also need the attempt frequency and the number of carriers, which this
program does not have.

**The chain.**

1. The model is the random forest on the invariant field about the midpoint of a hop,
   fitted on the 1,652 DFT barriers of the subsection above. On folds that hold out whole
   structures its mean absolute error is 0.228 eV. The spread of its trees, times 1.07, is
   the standard deviation of a prediction (96 % of the barriers are inside two standard
   deviations).
2. The model predicts the barrier of every hop of the thirteen disordered conductors of
   section *Partial occupancy* (`examples/hops/disordered`): 6,408 hops, 298 of them distinct
   by symmetry.
3. The hops of a structure form a network. Its *percolation barrier* is the lowest level
   that a lithium ion has to reach to cross the cell: the hops are opened in the order of
   their barriers until a path wraps around the cell. It is given for a path in one
   direction and for paths in all three directions.
4. The errors are carried through by drawing the barriers 400 times and taking the
   percolation barrier of each draw. The errors of the hops of one structure are not
   independent: on the folds 46 % of the squared error is common to the hops of a
   structure. A draw therefore gives every structure one common shift and every distinct
   hop its own shift, in these proportions.
5. The result is set beside measured activation energies of lithium conduction.

**Does the model carry over to the conductors?** No DFT barrier of a conductor is known,
so this cannot be measured directly. One check costs nothing. Inside the training set the
predictions for structures that the fit has not seen correlate with the bond-valence
barriers of the same hops with r = +0.84. For the conductors that correlation is +0.09.
The model was fitted on hops into a vacancy of an ordered structure. A conductor has partly
occupied sites, and four elements of these conductors (Ge, La, N, Zr) have no field of their
own in the training set. The standard deviation of a prediction says so in part: it is
0.50 eV on average for the conductors, against 0.35 eV inside the training set.

**The result for the six structures with a measured value.** All values in eV. An interval
is the 95 % interval over the draws, and the number before it is the median.

| structure | percolation barrier from the predicted barriers as they are, one / three directions | with the errors drawn, one direction | from bond-valence barriers, one / three directions | measured activation energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Li10GeP2S12 | 0.25 / 0.32 | 0.11 [0.00, 0.41] | 0.53 / 0.59 | 0.22 to 0.28 |
| beta-Li3PS4 | 0.28 / 0.37 | 0.07 [0.00, 0.52] | 0.25 / 0.40 | 0.36 |
| Li2.92N | 0.39 / 1.00 | 0.32 [0.00, 1.23] | 0.16 / 0.17 | 0.25 |
| La0.56Li0.33TiO3 | 0.70 / 0.82 | 0.49 [0.00, 1.24] | 0.82 / 15.17 | 0.40 |
| Li6.2La3Zr1.2Ta0.8O12, cubic garnet | 0.81 / 0.81 | 0.66 [0.00, 1.32] | 0.39 / 0.39 | 0.41 to 0.47 |
| Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12, cubic garnet | 0.99 / 0.99 | 0.63 [0.00, 1.43] | 0.40 / 0.40 | 0.41 to 0.47 |

- *The interval is about 1 eV wide.* The measured values of the six structures lie between
  0.25 and 0.44 eV. Every interval holds its measured value, and that says nothing.
- *Without the interval the values are no better than one number for all.* The mean
  absolute difference to the measured value is 0.24 eV for the forest (one direction) and
  0.16 eV for the bond-valence network. Giving every conductor the mean of the six measured
  values would be wrong by 0.07 eV.
- *The values divide by chemistry.* For the two sulfides the forest is within 0.08 eV. For
  the garnets it is too high by a factor of two, where the bond-valence network is right
  within 0.05 eV. The garnets hold two of the elements without a field of their own.
- *The median of the draws is below the value without draws.* The lowest of several
  uncertain barriers is on average lower than the lowest of their means, so a network of
  uncertain barriers looks easier to cross than it is.

**How the error of one barrier moves the result.** This is what the plan item asks for by
name. The standard deviations of the barriers are made smaller, and the width of the
interval of the percolation barrier (one direction, the mean over the twelve structures
with hops) is taken again:

| standard deviation of a barrier, eV | width of the 95 % interval of the percolation barrier, eV |
|---|---|
| 0.50 (the model) | 1.12 |
| 0.25 | 0.66 |
| 0.13 | 0.36 |
| 0.05 | 0.15 |

The interval is two to three times as wide as the standard deviation of one barrier. For an
interval of 0.15 eV a barrier has to be known to 0.05 eV, which is the accuracy of the DFT
calculation itself. A model that reads a barrier from the rigid structure does not reach
it, here or in the paper of the set.

**What this subsection does not show.** Only the value for Li10GeP2S12 was read on the page
of its source; the other five measured values come from the summaries of a search and are
marked so in the result table. A percolation barrier is compared with an activation energy
from impedance, which also holds the energy to form a carrier where carriers have to be
formed. The intervals come from errors that were measured inside the training set, so they
are a lower bound.

## Reading the model from another program

Everything above reads a model from inside this program: the window, the command line, the library.
A multiscale scheme needs it the other way round -- the model as a component of somebody else's
calculation, the fast level between an electronic-structure method and a coarse model. Three
interfaces are what the other programs ask for, and they are in `cmfqsar.interfaces` (plan item
MS7). None of them is a new model. Each is a way in to the one that is already fitted, and the
measurement at the end of this chapter is the check that nothing changes on the way.

### A model as an ASE calculator

The Atomic Simulation Environment is how a structure reaches most of the atomistic tools in use.
`CMFCalculator` makes a fitted model one of its calculators:

```python
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from cmfqsar.interfaces import CMFCalculator

atoms.calc = CMFCalculator(model, sign=-1.0)   # -1: move towards a *higher* prediction
BFGS(atoms).run(fmax=0.02, steps=50)
```

What the calculator calls the energy is `sign` times the prediction, in the units of the activity
and not in eV. An ASE optimiser minimises, so `sign=+1` drives the structure towards a lower
prediction and `sign=-1` towards a higher one, which is the direction a design loop wants. Nothing
converts units, because a predicted activity has no energy scale: the step sizes of the optimiser
have to be chosen for the numbers the model gives.

The forces are minus the gradient of the prediction, from the analytic derivative of the chapter
*The gradient of a prediction*. They exist for the two kernels that derivative covers -- the
overlap integral and the rotation-invariant autocorrelation -- and the calculator says so when
they do not: it reports `energies only`, drops `forces` from the properties it offers, and the
refusal names the kernel and the reason. A model with no gradient is still useful through this
interface, because a single-point screen needs energies alone.

One caution carries over from the gradient chapter, and it is the reason this is a component and
