not a force field: the gradient knows nothing about valence, and following it alone pulls bonds out
of shape. Added to a force field, or used to turn a rigid body, it moves a structure towards what
the model calls active. Used on its own, it will break the molecule and raise the number.

A periodic model answers energies and refuses forces, and writing this interface is what found the
reason. The periodic **overlap** kernel evaluates the ordinary overlap against an image-expanded
table, so moving one atom moves every image of it, and that term is not in the derivative. It had
not been refused before, because the refusals of the gradient chapter are written per kernel source
and the periodic overlap carries the ordinary one. It is refused now, by name and with the reason,
rather than answering with a number nobody has checked.

### A barrier per migration path

The hop model of the chapter above answers for a path, not for a structure, and a kinetic Monte
Carlo or a percolation analysis asks about a structure. `HopBarriers` closes that gap: it
enumerates the symmetry-distinct paths of the mobile ion, builds each environment the way the
training set was built, predicts, and hands back a table.

```python
from cmfqsar.interfaces import HopBarriers

reader = HopBarriers(model, fieldset, rho=0.25, r_max=6.0, mobile="Li")
table = reader.table(atoms, name="Li3PO4")
table.write_table("barriers.csv")        # one row per path, with where it is
print(table.percolation())               # E_1D, E_2D, E_3D under the predicted barriers
```

The settings are arguments and not guesses. An environment built with another envelope width or
another reach is a different descriptor, so the width, the reach, the mobile element and the path
length limits have to be the ones the model was fitted with. The table carries each path's two end
sites, its length, its midpoint, how many paths of the structure it stands for, and its predicted
barrier; `barriers` maps every path of the structure, not only the distinct ones, because a
percolation step needs the whole network. A caller who already has the network -- this program's
own benchmark does -- passes it as `hopset=` and only the environments and the prediction are done
here.

### A field on a grid

`write_cofield_cube` writes the co-field as a Gaussian cube file, which is what a visualiser or a
grid-based code reads. For a molecular model this is the export the command line already had. What
is new is the periodic case: for a model on one lattice the cube is one cell, with the **lattice
vectors as the cube's own axes**, so the file is the periodic field itself and tiles to as much of
the crystal as a viewer is asked for. The earlier export could only write a cubic cell, because a
cube file was built from one spacing and three counts; a general cell needs general axes, which
this writes. On the command line it is `cmf cofield MODEL --cell STRUCTURE`.

The rotation-invariant kernels have no co-field at all -- their channels know no place -- and are
refused by name rather than drawn. The map of `cmf sites` is what such a model offers instead.

### Does the measurement survive the journey out?

This is the gate of item MS7, and it is a reproduction rather than a new number: the public hop
model is rebuilt at its stored width and ridge, and then read twice. Once by the route the
benchmark script uses -- environments built in the script and handed to the model -- and once
through `HopBarriers`, which is given a structure and does the rest itself. The structures are the
three hosts of the lithium interface study, which the public model has never seen.

| Paths of the hosts | Distinct by symmetry | Compared by both routes | Largest difference |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1040 | 48 | 48 | 1.2e-11 eV |

The two routes agree to 1.2e-11 eV, which is round-off: the interface is a way in and not
another model. The two paths the benchmark lists against a DFT elastic-band barrier come back as
the stored table has them:

| Host | Path | Stored | Through the interface |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| phosphate | 34 -> 0 | 0.7979 | 0.7979 |
| borophosphate | 18 -> 8 | 0.5610 | 0.5610 |

And so do the percolation thresholds, which is what a conductivity estimate starts from -- the
lowest barrier at which the paths form a connected network in one, two and three dimensions:

| Host | E_1D | E_2D | E_3D |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| phosphate | 0.403 / 0.403 | 0.452 / 0.452 | 0.798 / 0.798 |
| borophosphate | 0.528 / 0.528 | 0.654 / 0.654 | 1.571 / 1.571 |
| borate | 0.281 / 0.281 | 0.437 / 0.437 | none / none |

In eV above the lowest site, by the script's route / through the interface. The full table is in
`benchmarks/results/hops/table.md` (`benchmarks/run_hops.py --interfaces`).

What this does not show is a faster calculation. Both routes pay for the same two things, the
environments and the kernel against the training set, and the interface pays a little more because
it works one structure at a time. What it shows is that the number a coarse model reads through the
interface is the number this program measured, which is the only property a component of somebody
else's calculation has to have.

## Feeding a cell model: a parameter set with its deviations

A continuum battery model -- the Doyle-Fuller-Newman model and its single-particle reductions,
as the PyBaMM package implements them -- predicts the capacity of a cell from cycle to cycle. It
is a set of partial differential equations, with time and transport in them. This program has
neither, so it cannot be such a model. It can feed one. Several of the cell model's material
parameters are quantities that benchmarks here predict, and each prediction comes with a
standard deviation in the parameter's own unit (plan item MS1). Plan item MS9 is the interface
for that, and a measurement of what it is worth.

**The scheme.** A multiscale model of a cell joins descriptions on different length scales, from
one ion that hops between two sites of a crystal to the whole cell. No single method covers all
of them, so each level passes a few numbers to the level above it. The fine level is an
electronic-structure calculation or a measurement, and it gives labels for a few hundred
structures. A model of this program learns the labels and answers for any other structure, with
a standard deviation. A conversion turns the answer into a material parameter of the cell
model, and the cell model gives the capacity. The figure shows the four channels that were
built, and under them what was measured.

![Multiscale modelling of a battery cell and the place of this program in it. Each row is one channel on its own length scale: the data of the fine level (grey), the model of this program that learns them and returns a value with its standard deviation (green), and the parameter of the cell model that the value becomes (yellow). The exchange-current density is not predicted and enters with a stated spread. The continuum cell model (blue) is run once for every draw of a parameter from its deviation, so the deviation reaches the capacity. Below: the measurement of `benchmarks/run_cellmodel.py` on the cell of the Chen 2020 parameter set. A bar is the 95 % interval of the capacity when one parameter is drawn and the others keep their published values. Red marks the interval that misses the capacity of the published parameters. The numbers beside the bars are the shares of the variance of the capacity. Two parameters decide the capacity, and the subsections below say why neither interval is narrow enough to use. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py` from the stored results.](docs/figures/multiscale.svg)

### The parameter set and its conversions

`cmfqsar.interfaces.CellParameter` holds one parameter. It carries the cell model's own name for
the parameter, the value, the standard deviation, and what the number does to the published
value: it **replaces** it, **multiplies** it or is **added** to it. A conductivity or an
exchange-current density is a function of concentration or of state of charge in a cell model,
and one number cannot replace a function, so a prediction for such a parameter is a factor or a
shift. The record also says where the number comes from, whether the model's deviation is
calibrated (the root mean square of the standardised residual on held-out data between 0.8 and
1.25, the rule of MS1), and whether the material lies inside what the model was fitted on.
`CellParameterSet` writes the set as JSON and CSV, one record per parameter, and reads it back.

Five functions do the conversions:

| Function | What it takes | What the cell model receives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `diffusivity_from_barrier` | a migration barrier, or a set of drawn barriers | a solid diffusion coefficient |
| `conductivity_scale_from_log10` | a predicted conductivity, as a logarithm | a factor on the published conductivity |
| `ocp_shift` | a predicted average voltage | a shift of the published open-circuit voltage |
| `ladder_to_ocp_curve` | an insertion ladder of two-phase steps | a voltage-against-stoichiometry staircase |
| `bruggeman_from_conductivity_ratio` | the effective conductivity of a porous electrode | a Bruggeman exponent |

The diffusion coefficient is that of a random walk: $D = a^2 \nu \exp(-E/kT) / (2d)$, with $a$ the
hop length, $\nu$ the attempt frequency (10^13 per second; this program does not predict it), $E$
the barrier and $d$ the number of directions the ion can move in. The deviation of $\ln D$ is the
deviation of the barrier divided by $kT$, which is 0.0257 eV at room temperature: a barrier
known to 0.1 eV gives a diffusion coefficient known only to a factor of 50. When the barriers
were drawn already, the diffusion coefficients of the draws are carried over one by one, which
keeps the shape the exponential gives them. The Bruggeman exponent $b$ is defined by
$\sigma_\mathrm{eff} = \sigma \varepsilon^b$, where $\varepsilon$ is the porosity, so
$b = \ln(\sigma_\mathrm{eff}/\sigma) / \ln \varepsilon$.

### The sampler and the report

`cmfqsar.cellmodel` runs the cell model; PyBaMM is an optional dependency, as pymatgen is.
`sample` draws one parameter from its deviation, keeps the others at their published values, and
runs the cell model once per draw. `band` turns the runs into an interval of the capacity per
cycle, and says what share of the draws the cell model refused. `variance_shares` gives the share
of the variance of the last cycle's capacity that each parameter explains when it is drawn alone.
`local_sensitivity` gives the reading that does not depend on this program: the elasticity, the
relative change of the capacity for a change of one tenth in the parameter around its published
value. `tolerance_for_capacity` makes a deviation smaller step by step and reports, for each step,
whether the interval is **narrow** and whether it still **holds** the capacity the published value
gives. An interval is worth using only if it is both.

### What it is worth, measured

The cell is the graphite / nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide cell of the Chen 2020 parameter set,
which PyBaMM ships. The cell model is the single-particle model with electrolyte, with the growth
of the passivating layer on the negative electrode. One cycle is a discharge at the one-hour rate
to 2.5 V, a charge to 4.2 V and a hold. At the published values the cell gives 4.992 A.h and loses
0.023 % of it over ten cycles. Four parameters are predicted, each by a benchmark of this
repository with its deviation measured on held-out groups, and a fifth carries a stated spread:

| Parameter | Predicted by | Value | 95 % interval | z rms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Positive particle diffusivity | the forest on 1,652 DFT barriers (BT7), percolation barrier of layered LiNiO2 | 4.8e-22 m²/s (published 4e-15) | 3.8e-30 to 8.2e-14 | 1.07 |
| Positive electrode open-circuit voltage | the kernel on the composition of 303 insertion pairs (BT3) | shift +0.28 V | -1.64 to +2.20 V | 0.98 |
| Electrolyte conductivity | the kernel on the composition of 62 measured electrolytes (BT5) | factor 0.987 | 0.76 to 1.28 | 1.01 |
| Positive electrode Bruggeman exponent | the kernel on 200 generated two-phase structures | 1.91 (published 1.5) | 1.59 to 2.22 | 1.04 |
| Positive electrode exchange-current density | not predicted: a stated spread | factor 1 | 0.10 to 9.9 | -- |

All four deviations are calibrated: z rms between 0.98 and 1.07, and 95 or 96 % of the held-out
activities inside two standard deviations. The values are another matter. Each parameter is drawn
200 times from its own deviation while the others stay published:

| Parameter | Capacity of the last cycle, A.h | Holds the published curve? | Share of the variance | Elasticity |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Open-circuit voltage | 0.04 to 5.42 | yes | 72.8 % | -2.426 |
| Positive particle diffusivity | 0.61 to 5.01 | yes | 27.2 % | +0.004 |
| Exchange-current density | 4.958 to 4.998 | yes | 0.0 % | +0.002 |
| Bruggeman exponent | 4.983 to 4.990 | **no** | 0.0 % | -0.002 |
| Electrolyte conductivity | 4.989 to 4.992 | yes | 0.0 % | +0.001 |

**The electrolyte conductivity is the one channel predicted for the cell's own material under its
own conditions**: lithium hexafluorophosphate in ethylene carbonate and ethyl methyl carbonate, 3
to 7, with that solvent mixture held out of the fit. It agrees with the published parameter set
to 1.3 %, and the cell does not care: its whole interval moves the capacity by 0.003 A.h.

**The diffusion coefficient holds the published curve for a reason that is no credit.** Its
interval spans sixteen orders of magnitude and covers almost every capacity the cell can give,
from 0.61 A.h (the solid stops taking lithium) to 5.01 A.h (it never limits). The layered oxide's
hop network percolates in two of three directions, which is the two-dimensional diffusion such an
oxide is known for, at a median barrier of 0.87 eV. Through the same Arrhenius law and the same
prefactor, the published diffusion coefficient corresponds to a barrier of 0.46 eV. The
prediction is 0.41 eV too high, as the garnets of MS8 were. The tolerance rule shows what kind of
error this is:

| The barrier known to, eV | Interval of the capacity, A.h | Narrow? | Holds the published capacity? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.254 (as predicted) | 0.611 to 5.010 | no | yes |
| 0.127 | 0.611 to 1.186 | no | no |
| 0.064 | 0.611 to 0.614 | yes | no |
| 0.025 | 0.611 to 0.611 | yes | no |

No row is both narrow and right. A smaller deviation narrows the interval towards the capacity of
the median prediction, and that prediction is wrong. The error of this channel is a **bias and
not a spread**, and no tolerance rule can repair a bias. This parameter needs a better prediction,
which for this cathode means the barrier from the fine level itself.

**The Bruggeman exponent fails the gate** although its deviation is calibrated. The generated
structures are more tortuous than the exponent of 1.5 the authors of the cell fitted, and the
interval misses the published curve by 0.0006 A.h. The record marks the channel as outside
what its model was fitted on, because the structures are generated and not the cell's own.

**The ranking is not the one the item expected.** The cell-model literature ranks the solid
diffusion coefficient and the exchange current ahead of the open-circuit voltage. Here the voltage
comes first under both readings. A tenth of a voltage is 0.38 V, which empties a cell, while a
tenth of a diffusion coefficient changes almost nothing. And this program's deviation on a voltage
is about one volt, where a measured open-circuit curve is known to millivolts. The literature's
ranking is for a cell whose voltage curve has been measured. Between the two transport parameters
the expected order does come out: the diffusion coefficient is ahead of the exchange current under
both readings.

**The deviations move the level of the curve and not its slope.** Over 100 cycles the cell loses
0.18 to 0.20 % of its capacity at either edge of every interval that leaves it running, against
0.18 % at the published values. The slope is set by the parameters of the passivating layer,
which no channel touches.

So the gate is not met in either of its parts. What does carry over is the interface: the
deviation reaches the cell model in its own units, the report says which parameter to measure
better, and the tolerance rule separates a prediction that is too uncertain from one that is
wrong. The table is in `benchmarks/results/cellmodel/table.md` and the parameter set, as the cell
model reads it, in `benchmarks/results/cellmodel/parameters.json`.

### The electrolyte at faster discharge and in the cold

At the one-hour rate the cell hardly responds to its electrolyte: the whole interval of the
predicted conductivity moves the capacity by 0.003 A.h. So the 1.3 % agreement above is real but
untested by the cell. Two conditions make the electrolyte matter, and the stage
`--stage stress` draws its parameters again under both, with the full Doyle-Fuller-Newman model,
since the single-particle model approximates the electrolyte and is not meant for high rates.

* **Faster discharge** at room temperature: 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 times the one-hour rate.
* **A colder cell**: 263 and 253 K. The published electrolyte functions have **no temperature
  dependence**; of the whole parameter set only the two exchange-current densities depend on
  temperature. A cold run of the published set is therefore a cold cell with a warm
  electrolyte. The composition model of item BT5 predicts the activation energy of the
  conductivity too, with the solvent mixture held out: 13.56 +/- 0.91 kJ/mol against 13.68
  measured, over the 62 electrolytes a mean absolute error of 1.47 kJ/mol against 3.54 for the
  mean, z rms 1.13. `conductivity_scale_at_temperature` carries the predicted conductivity to
  the cell's temperature with it, drawing both predictions.

The curve a prediction is judged against is the **measured electrolyte**: the cell model with its
conductivity replaced by the one CALiSol-23 measured for this electrolyte, carried to the cell's
temperature by the measured activation energy.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Published, A.h | Measured electrolyte, A.h | From the conductivity, A.h | From the Bruggeman exponent, A.h |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 298 | 1C | 4.991 | 4.991 | 4.990 to 4.993 | 4.983 to 4.990 |
| 298 | 1.5C | 4.905 | 4.904 | 4.901 to 4.908 | 4.837 to 4.900 |
| 298 | 2C | 4.783 | 4.779 | 4.771 to 4.793 | 3.053 to 4.706 |
| 298 | 2.5C | 3.675 | 3.662 | 3.640 to 3.715 | 1.692 to 3.144 |
| 263 | 1C | 4.960 | 4.949 | 4.943 to 4.956 | -- |
| 263 | 1.5C | 4.863 | 4.833 | 4.814 to 4.852 | -- |
| 253 | 1C | 4.949 | 4.930 | 4.921 to 4.940 | -- |
| 253 | 1.5C | 4.848 | 4.793 | 4.756 to 4.824 | -- |

**The conductivity is right, now that the cell can see it.** The predicted interval holds the
capacity of this measured electrolyte under all eight conditions (the second reference below
qualifies this for the coldest cells). In the cold it also excludes the
published curve under all four: the published set, whose electrolyte does not get colder, gives
too much capacity (0.055 A.h too much at 253 K and 1.5C), and the predicted activation energy
corrects it by about as much as the measured one does. The effect is modest, at most about 1 %,
because the conductivity is the only electrolyte property carried to the cold here; the
electrolyte diffusivity and the two solid diffusivities stay at their room values in this
parameter set, so a real cold cell loses more.

**The tortuosity takes over at faster discharge, and its error grows with it.** At 2C and 2.5C the
Bruggeman exponent explains all but a fraction of a per cent of the variance, against the
conductivity. Its interval misses the published curve under every rate, by 0.0015 A.h at 1C and
by 0.53 A.h at 2.5C, where the published cell gives 3.675 A.h and the interval ends at 3.144. The
generated structures are more tortuous than the 1.5 the cell's authors fitted. How much that
costs at a fast discharge depends on the electrolyte the cell is given: with a measured
electrolyte in place, most of this miss goes away (see the second reference below).

**What stays open on the electrolyte side.** The cell model holds four electrolyte transport
parameters, and only the conductivity is predicted. The electrolyte diffusivity, the cation
transference number (0.2594 in the published set) and the thermodynamic factor (1.0) have no
prediction here, because the measured series of item BT5 holds conductivities and activation
energies only; the second reference below supplies measured values for them, but not a
prediction. The prediction is also one point, at 1.11 mol/kg and 298 K, and the
cell model keeps its own dependence on concentration; the measured point is a molality and the
cell starts at one mole per litre, which is not converted (near the maximum of the conductivity,
where this electrolyte is, the difference is small: 7.00, 8.83 and 6.99 mS/cm at 0.44, 1.11 and
2.01 mol/kg). And the value comes from the composition model, not from the shell fields of item
BT5, which were less accurate on this target.

#### A second reference: all four transport parameters measured

The published cell takes its conductivity and electrolyte diffusivity from one study at room
temperature, and holds the transference number and the thermodynamic factor constant.
Landesfeind and Gasteiger (*J. Electrochem. Soc.* 166 (2019) A3079, open access) measured all
four for the same electrolyte, LiPF6 in EC:EMC 3:7 by weight, between 263 and 323 K and between
0.1 and 3.0 mol/L. PyBaMM ships their fitted functions in its `ORegan2022` parameter set, and
`cmfqsar.cellmodel.measured_electrolyte` returns them as replacements for the cell model, so
nothing has to be downloaded. The stress stage runs two more curves under every condition:

* **Conductivity only**: their conductivity alone in the cell. This is the fair reference for the
  predicted conductivity, which is the only one of the four that is predicted.
* **All four**: every transport parameter from the study. At 1 mol/L and 298 K their diffusivity
  is 1.6 times the published one, their transference number 0.22 instead of 0.26, and their
  thermodynamic factor 2.2 instead of 1.0. In colder cells the transference number and the
  thermodynamic factor are read at +20 degrees Celsius (293 K). The study says these two are less
  precise below +20 degrees, its -10 degree values have large errors and are negative, and its
  fitted transference number is negative at 0 degrees from 0.5 mol/L up, which a model with two
  kinds of ion cannot use.

At room temperature the Bruggeman exponent is drawn again with all four in place.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Published, A.h | Measured conductivity only, A.h | From the predicted conductivity, A.h | All four measured, A.h | From the Bruggeman exponent with all four measured, A.h |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | --- |
| 298 | 1C | 4.991 | 4.991 | 4.990 to 4.993 | 4.987 | 4.978 to 4.985 |
| 298 | 1.5C | 4.905 | 4.904 | 4.901 to 4.908 | 4.899 | 4.878 to 4.896 |
| 298 | 2C | 4.783 | 4.778 | 4.771 to 4.793 | 4.789 | 4.704 to 4.779 |
| 298 | 2.5C | 3.675 | 3.699 | 3.640 to 3.715 | 4.609 | 3.873 to 4.574 |
| 263 | 1C | 4.960 | 4.948 | 4.943 to 4.956 | 4.755 | -- |
| 263 | 1.5C | 4.863 | 4.804 | 4.814 to 4.852 | 3.512 | -- |
| 253 (below the measured range) | 1C | 4.949 | 4.921 | 4.921 to 4.940 | 3.788 | -- |
| 253 (below the measured range) | 1.5C | 4.848 | 4.427 | 4.756 to 4.824 | 2.409 | -- |

**The predicted conductivity holds near room temperature and misses in the coldest cells.** Its
interval holds the capacity of the measured conductivity under 6 of 8 conditions. It misses at
263 K and 1.5C by 0.010 A.h, and at 253 K and 1.5C by 0.33 A.h, which is below the coldest
temperature the study measured. The prediction carries the conductivity to the cold with one
activation energy, and the measured conductivity falls faster the colder it gets: its apparent
activation energy at 1 mol/L is 14.6 kJ/mol between 298 and 263 K, close to the predicted 13.6,
and 20.7 kJ/mol between 263 and 253 K. One activation energy is a fair description from room
temperature down to about 263 K, and not below.

**At fast discharge the published electrolyte decided the verdict on the tortuosity.** At 2.5C
the cell with all four measured parameters gives 4.609 A.h, against the published 3.675, mostly
because the measured diffusivity is larger. With the measured electrolyte in place, the interval
of the Bruggeman exponent runs from 3.873 to 4.574 A.h and misses by 0.035 A.h, where it missed
the published curve by 0.53. It still misses under every rate (by 0.002 A.h at 1C), so the
generated structures are still too tortuous. But most of the earlier miss came from the
published electrolyte, not from the tortuosity.

**In the cold the parameters that are not predicted decide the capacity.** At 253 K and 1.5C the
measured conductivity alone gives 4.427 A.h, all four measured parameters give 2.409, and the
published cell gives 4.848. The difference between the two measured capacities comes from the
diffusivity, the transference number and the thermodynamic factor. This program predicts none
of these three, so in a cold cell its conductivity prediction settles only a small part of the
capacity.

#### How accurate the three parameters without a prediction have to be

The salt diffusion coefficient, the cation transference number and the thermodynamic factor of
the electrolyte have a measured reference and no prediction (plan items BT9, BT10 and BT11).
Before any of them is simulated, `--stage tolerance` asks a question that needs no prediction:
how accurate would a prediction have to be?

The cell holds the electrolyte with all four transport parameters as measured. One parameter at
a time is then changed over a fixed set of points. The diffusion coefficient is multiplied by
19 factors between 0.05 and 20, and the thermodynamic factor by 15 factors between 0.2 and 5.
The transference number is shifted by 15 constants between -0.4 and +0.4. The full
Doyle-Fuller-Newman model is run once per point, under the eight conditions of the stress stage.
The result is the **response curve** of the cell to that parameter
(`cmfqsar.cellmodel.response`). Nothing is drawn. A drawn sample says what one stated deviation
does to the capacity. A response curve says it for every deviation at once, because the capacity
for any spread of the parameter can be read from the curve.

Two quantities are read from each curve (`cmfqsar.cellmodel.tolerated_range`):

* The **tolerated range** is the connected range around the measured function inside which the
  discharge capacity stays within a stated share of the capacity with the measured function. Its
  ends are found by linear interpolation between neighbouring points, on the logarithm of a
  factor.
* The **tolerated deviation** is the largest standard deviation of an error whose 95 % interval
  stays inside that range: of the natural logarithm for a factor, of the number itself for a
  shift. The nearer end of the range sets it.

A run counts only if its discharge ended at the lower voltage limit;
`run_cell(..., details=True)` records why a discharge ended and the lowest and highest
concentration of the electrolyte during it. The table below is for a capacity that may move by
5 %; the result table of the benchmark also holds the one for 1 %. An end written with < or >
is the outermost point that was run, so the range is at least that wide, and a deviation written
with >= is a lower bound for the same reason.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Capacity with the measured electrolyte, A.h | Diffusion coefficient: tolerated factor | Deviation of its logarithm | Transference number: tolerated shift | Deviation | Thermodynamic factor: tolerated factor | Deviation of its logarithm |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| 298 | 1C | 4.987 | 0.32 to > 20.00 | 0.585 | < -0.40 to > +0.40 | >= 0.204 | < 0.20 to > 5.00 | >= 0.821 |
| 298 | 1.5C | 4.899 | 0.49 to > 20.00 | 0.367 | < -0.40 to > +0.40 | >= 0.204 | < 0.20 to 3.34 | 0.616 |
| 298 | 2C | 4.789 | 0.67 to > 20.00 | 0.206 | -0.28 to > +0.40 | 0.143 | < 0.20 to 2.20 | 0.403 |
| 298 | 2.5C | 4.609 | 0.83 to > 20.00 | 0.098 | -0.13 to > +0.40 | 0.064 | < 0.20 to 1.58 | 0.233 |
| 263 | 1C | 4.755 | 0.85 to > 20.00 | 0.086 | -0.10 to > +0.40 | 0.053 | < 0.20 to 1.41 | 0.174 |
| 263 | 1.5C | 3.512 | 0.96 to 1.05 | 0.023 | -0.03 to +0.03 | 0.017 | 0.48 to 1.37 | 0.160 |
| 253 | 1C | 3.788 | 0.93 to 1.10 | 0.040 | -0.05 to +0.06 | 0.027 | 0.67 to 1.35 | 0.154 |
| 253 | 1.5C | 2.409 | 0.96 to 1.04 | 0.020 | -0.03 to +0.03 | 0.014 | < 0.20 to 1.55 | 0.224 |

At 1 mol/L and 298 K the measured diffusion coefficient is 2.89e-10 m2/s, the measured
transference number 0.221 and the measured thermodynamic factor 2.18.

**At room temperature only a diffusion coefficient that is too small is punished.** A larger one
costs less than 5 % of the capacity at every factor that was tried, up to 20. The lower end of
the tolerated factor rises with the rate: 0.32 at 1C, 0.49 at 1.5C, 0.67 at 2C and 0.83 at 2.5C.
A prediction of this parameter should therefore err on the high side.

**In a cold cell the tolerance is narrower than the agreement of two measurements.** At 263 K and
1.5C and at both rates at 253 K the tolerated factor of the diffusion coefficient lies between
0.93 and 1.10, and the tolerated shift of the transference number is 0.03 to 0.06 either way. The
two measurements of this electrolyte that the repository holds, the function of the published
set and the function of the second reference, differ by a factor of 1.6 at 1 mol/L and 298 K.
Under these three conditions the electrolyte is exhausted somewhere in the cell, which is what
ends the discharge early, and a small change of a transport parameter moves the point where that
happens.

**What the cheapest reference of each item costs.** Each of the three plan items names a value
that needs no new data. For the diffusion coefficient it is the Nernst-Einstein value from the
measured conductivity $\kappa$ and the transference number $t$ of the published set, which is
the coefficient of an ideal solution of fully dissociated ions
(`cmfqsar.cellmodel.nernst_einstein_diffusivity`):

$$
D = \frac{2\,t\,(1-t)\,\kappa R T}{F^2 c}
$$

For the other two it is the constant of the published set. Each value is put in place of the
measured function, with the other three parameters as measured. The table gives the difference
of the capacity as a share of the capacity with the measured electrolyte. Two more values of the
diffusion coefficient are run to say where the error of the first comes from.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Diffusion coefficient: Nernst-Einstein value | Diffusion coefficient: Nernst-Einstein value times the measured thermodynamic factor | Diffusion coefficient: function of the published set | Transference number: the constant 0.2594 | Thermodynamic factor: the constant 1 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 298 | 1C | no usable discharge | -0.2 % | -0.4 % | +0.0 % | +0.2 % |
| 298 | 1.5C | -36.0 % | -0.6 % | -1.1 % | +0.1 % | +0.4 % |
| 298 | 2C | -56.9 % | -15.8 % | -3.1 % | +0.3 % | +0.8 % |
| 298 | 2.5C | -71.3 % | -40.4 % | -19.6 % | +0.8 % | +2.2 % |
| 263 | 1C | -68.9 % | -48.8 % | +3.1 % | +2.4 % | +3.3 % |
| 263 | 1.5C | -83.8 % | -70.0 % | +27.5 % | +9.5 % | +4.5 % |
| 253 | 1C | -81.7 % | -70.3 % | +26.9 % | +8.0 % | +10.3 % |
| 253 | 1.5C | -91.0 % | -82.6 % | +61.8 % | +9.1 % | +0.3 % |

* **The diffusion coefficient needs a prediction under every condition.** The Nernst-Einstein
  value is 3.1 times below the measured coefficient at 1 mol/L and 298 K. With it the cell loses
  36 % of its capacity at 1.5C and more under every faster or colder condition, and at 1C the
  discharge does not end at the voltage limit, so there is no capacity to compare. Multiplied by
  the measured thermodynamic factor the value is 1.4 times below the measured one, and costs
  0.2 % at 1C and 0.6 % at 1.5C, but 16 % at 2C and 40 % at 2.5C.
* **The published constant of the transference number is enough at room temperature.** It costs
  at most 0.8 % of the capacity at 298 K. In the colder cells it costs 2.4 % at 263 K and 1C and
  8.0 to 9.5 % under the other three conditions.
* **The thermodynamic factor matters more as an input of the diffusion coefficient than for its
  own term.** The constant 1 costs at most 2.2 % at 298 K, 3.3 to 4.5 % at 263 K, and 10.3 % at
  253 K and 1C. But it is the difference between a Nernst-Einstein value 3.1 times too low and
  one 1.4 times too low.

Two limits of this reading are stated with it. First, the reference itself leaves the measured
range: the study measured between 100 and 3000 mol/m3, and with the measured electrolyte in
place the concentration somewhere in the cell goes outside that range under 5 of the 8
conditions, up to 4673 mol/m3 at 263 K and 1C. There the fitted functions are read outside the
measurements they were fitted to, so the capacity called measured is the capacity of an
extrapolation. Second, in the colder cells the transference number and the thermodynamic factor
called measured are the values at 293 K, as in the second reference. A verdict on these two in
the cold therefore compares two assumed values.

**The reading of the curve was checked by drawing.** A tolerance is read from a curve of a few
points, with straight lines between them. At 298 K and 2.5C each parameter was drawn 100 times
with the deviation tolerated at 5 %, and the cell was run once per draw. The capacity the curve
gives at a drawn value differs from the run at the same value by at most 0.019 A.h, which is
8 % of the 5 % limit of 0.230 A.h. The runs left the limit in 2 %, 2 % and 0 % of the draws,
where about 2.5 % is expected, because the deviation is set by the nearer end of the range.

#### How accurate the exchange-current densities and their activation energies have to be

The exchange-current density is the rate of the charge-transfer reaction at the surface of an
electrode particle at equilibrium, per unit of area. The Butler-Volmer equation of the cell
model takes it as an input. This program does not predict it for either electrode (plan item
BT12), so `--stage exchange` asks the question of the section above for it. The cell holds the
measured electrolyte. The exchange-current density of one electrode at a time is multiplied by
17 factors between 0.001 and 100, and the full model is run once per factor under the same
eight conditions. The table is for a capacity that may move by 5 %; the result table of the
benchmark also holds the one for 1 %.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Capacity with the published exchange-current densities, A.h | Negative electrode: tolerated factor | Deviation of its logarithm | Positive electrode: tolerated factor | Deviation of its logarithm |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| 298 | 1C | 4.987 | 0.01* to > 100 | 2.350 | < 0.001 to > 100 | >= 2.350 |
| 298 | 1.5C | 4.899 | 0.01* to > 100 | 2.350 | 0.0013 to > 100 | >= 2.350 |
| 298 | 2C | 4.789 | 0.02* to > 100 | 1.996 | 0.0067 to > 100 | >= 2.350 |
| 298 | 2.5C | 4.609 | 0.035 to > 100 | 1.712 | 0.035 to > 100 | 1.713 |
| 263 | 1C | 4.755 | 0.05* to > 100 | 1.528 | 0.031 to > 100 | 1.769 |
| 263 | 1.5C | 3.512 | 0.05* to > 100 | 1.528 | 0.048 to > 100 | 1.552 |
| 253 | 1C | 3.788 | 0.1* to > 100 | 1.175 | 0.036 to > 100 | 1.695 |
| 253 | 1.5C | 2.409 | 0.1* to > 100 | 1.175 | 0.032 to > 100 | 1.764 |

An end written with * is not a point where the capacity left the limit. At the next smaller
factor the cell model did not start the discharge, because its solver failed at the first step.
The range is therefore at least that wide.

**The discharge capacity tolerates a factor of 10 on the exchange-current density.** The
parameter set of this benchmark states a spread of a factor of 10 either way for this
parameter. With a factor of 0.1 on one electrode the capacity changes by -3.6 to -0.7 % over
the eight conditions, and with a factor of 10 by +0.1 to +2.8 %. For a capacity that may move
by only 1 %, the tolerated factor is about one half to two in the cold cells and at 2.5C. The
same cold cells need the salt diffusion coefficient within 4 to 10 %, so for the discharge
capacity the exchange-current density is the less sensitive of the two parameters by a wide
margin.

**A tolerated factor is also a tolerated shift of the activation energy.** In the published set
each exchange-current density follows an Arrhenius law that equals 1 at 298.15 K. Its
activation energy is 35.0 kJ/mol for the negative electrode and 17.8 kJ/mol for the positive
one (`cmfqsar.cellmodel.activation_energy_of` reads it from the function). The cell model is
run at one temperature $T$. A shift $\Delta E$ of the activation energy is then the same as a
factor on the exchange-current density (`cmfqsar.cellmodel.arrhenius_factor`):

$$
f = \exp\!\left[\frac{\Delta E}{R}\left(\frac{1}{298.15\ \mathrm{K}} - \frac{1}{T}\right)\right]
$$

In a cell colder than 298.15 K a higher activation energy gives a slower reaction. At 298 K
the activation energy changes nothing, so the table holds the four cold conditions. The column
*published law* is the factor that the published activation energy puts on the
exchange-current density at that temperature.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Negative electrode: published law | Tolerated shift, kJ/mol | Tolerated deviation, kJ/mol | Positive electrode: published law | Tolerated shift, kJ/mol | Tolerated deviation, kJ/mol |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| 263 | 1C | 0.153 | < -85.8 to +55.8* | 28.5 | 0.385 | < -85.8 to +64.6 | 33.0 |
| 263 | 1.5C | 0.153 | < -85.8 to +55.8* | 28.5 | 0.385 | < -85.8 to +56.7 | 28.9 |
| 253 | 1C | 0.081 | < -64.2 to +32.1* | 16.4 | 0.279 | < -64.2 to +46.3 | 23.6 |
| 253 | 1.5C | 0.081 | < -64.2 to +32.1* | 16.4 | 0.279 | < -64.2 to +48.2 | 24.6 |

For a capacity that may move by 1 % the tolerated shift is 9 to 15 kJ/mol upwards, and the
tolerated deviation is 5 to 8 kJ/mol.

**Stated activation energies in place of the published ones.** The cold cells were also run with
an activation energy of 20 to 70 kJ/mol on one electrode or on both
(`cmfqsar.cellmodel.ActivationEnergy`). The numbers are the difference of the capacity, in per
cent of the capacity with the published activation energies.

| Temperature, K | Rate | Electrode | 20 kJ/mol | 30 kJ/mol | 40 kJ/mol | 50 kJ/mol | 60 kJ/mol | 70 kJ/mol |
| ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 263 | 1C | negative | +0.9 % | +0.3 % | -0.3 % | -1.0 % | -1.8 % | -2.5 % |
| 263 | 1C | positive | -0.1 % | -0.8 % | -1.5 % | -2.2 % | -3.0 % | -3.9 % |
| 263 | 1C | both | +0.8 % | -0.5 % | -1.9 % | -3.4 % | -5.2 % | -7.1 % |
| 263 | 1.5C | negative | +0.8 % | +0.3 % | -0.3 % | -1.1 % | -1.9 % | -2.8 % |
| 263 | 1.5C | positive | -0.2 % | -0.9 % | -1.7 % | -2.6 % | -3.5 % | -4.5 % |
| 263 | 1.5C | both | +0.7 % | -0.5 % | -2.1 % | -4.0 % | -6.1 % | -8.4 % |
| 253 | 1C | negative | +1.4 % | +0.5 % | -0.5 % | -1.6 % | -2.6 % | -3.7 % |
| 253 | 1C | positive | -0.2 % | -1.3 % | -2.4 % | -3.4 % | -4.5 % | -5.7 % |
| 253 | 1C | both | +1.1 % | -0.8 % | -2.9 % | -5.1 % | -7.7 % | -10.4 % |
| 253 | 1.5C | negative | +0.7 % | +0.3 % | -0.3 % | -1.1 % | -2.1 % | no usable discharge |
| 253 | 1.5C | positive | -0.1 % | -0.9 % | -1.8 % | -2.9 % | -4.2 % | -5.5 % |
| 253 | 1.5C | both | +0.6 % | -0.5 % | -2.3 % | -4.8 % | -7.8 % | no usable discharge |

One electrode alone stays inside 5 % up to 60 kJ/mol. The two electrodes together leave it at
about 50 to 60 kJ/mol. Whether a cold cell needs better values than the published ones therefore
depends on the measured activation energies, which plan item BT12 collects from the literature.
The requirement is not strict: an activation energy known to about 15 kJ/mol for each electrode
is enough for a capacity within 5 %.

Two limits belong to this reading. The stage reads the discharge capacity down to 2.5 V and
nothing else. Charge transfer lowers the voltage of the cell, so it changes the energy and the
power more than the capacity, and it is one of the things that decide whether lithium is plated
when a cold cell is charged. None of these was run. And in three of the four cold conditions a
factor of 100 on the negative electrode lowers the capacity by 0.9 to 3.2 %, where a faster
reaction was expected to raise it. This was not examined.

```bash
python benchmarks/run_cellmodel.py      # 54 minutes, after run_nebdft.py
```

The run is in stages -- `--stage channels`, `reference`, `sample`, `stress`, `tolerance`, `exchange`, `finish` -- and each stage
writes its own file, so a run that stops is continued and not repeated. One parameter is drawn
with `--stage sample --parameter NAME`.

## The voltage of an insertion electrode: the cell against its composition

A cathode is judged by its **average voltage**: the work per electron of taking the working ion
out of the host. For the insertion of $(y-x)$ lithium into $\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Host}$ the
average voltage over that interval is the change in energy per electron, referred to lithium
metal,

$$
V = -\frac{E(\mathrm{Li}_y\mathrm{Host}) - E(\mathrm{Li}_x\mathrm{Host})
 - (y-x)\,E(\mathrm{Li})}{y-x},
$$

with the energies per host formula unit and in electronvolts. Plan item BT3 makes that pair the
sample (`cmfqsar/battery.py`), and the benchmark asks what an electrode paper asks: does the
**arrangement** of the atoms say anything about the voltage that the **composition** does not
already say? Composition is a strong baseline here, because the voltage is mostly decided by
which metal is reduced and by how much.

**The data need no account.** The Materials Project serves its structures and their formation
energies through OPTIMADE without an API key, and a formation energy already carries the
elemental reference: it is the energy of the cell minus the energies of the elements it is made
of. Elemental lithium is one of those elements, so it cancels in the difference above and the
voltage follows from the two formation energies alone. One query per chemical system, the phases
within 0.03 eV per atom of the convex hull kept, each cell reduced to its **host
framework** (its composition with the lithium removed, divided by the common factor) and its
**lithium content per host formula unit**, and neighbouring steps of one framework's ladder
paired. The official insertion-electrode documents, with topotactic pairs and the corrections a
battery database applies, need a free key and the `mp-api` package; `insertion_electrodes`
fetches them when a key is given.

**The reconstruction is checked before it is used** (`python benchmarks/run_battery.py --stage
check`). Over the first insertion, up to one lithium per host formula unit:

| cathode | published, V | reconstructed, V |
|---|---:|---:|
| LiCoO2, layered | 4.10 | 3.77 |
| LiFePO4, olivine | 3.45 | 3.33 |
| LiMn2O4, spinel | 4.00 | 3.23 |
| LiNiO2, layered | 3.80 | 3.47 |

The reconstruction is **0.39 V low on average, and low every
time**. Both reasons are limits of the data and not of the kernel: the energies are the published
GGA/GGA+U ones without the corrections a battery database applies, and the average here runs over
the intermediate phases of the ladder, which a two-phase measurement does not see. The window
above the hull was chosen on that table. At 0.01, 0.02 and 0.03 eV per atom the agreement is the
same, 0.39 V, while the set grows from 83 to
303 pairs; at 0.08 it is worse, 0.57 V. So
0.03 is the default, and the table is in `results/battery/table.md` so the choice can be read
rather than taken on trust.

**The protocol.** 303 insertion pairs over 157 host frameworks, the discharged cell
describing the pair, 23 fields. Five folds keep a framework together: two steps of
one ladder share a framework, a chemistry and most of their structure, so a model that has seen
one of them has been told most of the answer for the other. The ridge and the width of the
Gaussians are chosen inside the training part by ten-fold cross-validation. The composition model
is a linear kernel on the element fractions of the cell and the crystal descriptors of item BT2.

| model | mean absolute error, V | spread over the folds | R² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| the mean voltage of the set | 1.203 | - | 0.000 |
| composition | 0.569 | 0.115 | +0.728 |
| fields | 0.650 | 0.146 | +0.624 |
| fields and composition | 0.582 | 0.117 | +0.684 |

The voltages of the set average 2.77 V and predicting that mean costs
1.203 V, so every model here is well inside the question.

**What the numbers say.** **The composition decides this property and the arrangement adds
nothing.** The field kernel is 0.081 V worse than the composition baseline and the two together
0.013 V worse, both inside the fold-to-fold spread of 0.146 V, which under rule 4 is not a result.
That is the answer the data support for an average voltage: it is a thermodynamic quantity of a
composition, and the geometry enters only through which phase that composition takes. The item is
kept under rule 5 because it is the loader and the baseline every other battery item needs, and
because a negative result measured against a baseline is worth more than an unmeasured kernel.

By family of hosts, for the model that uses both kernels:

| family | pairs | mean absolute error, V | mean voltage, V |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| phosphate | 113 | 0.509 | 3.61 |
| oxide | 105 | 0.664 | 2.83 |
| other | 51 | 0.603 | 0.34 |
| fluoride | 21 | 0.678 | 4.23 |
| sulfide | 10 | 0.466 | 1.86 |
| silicate | 3 | 0.178 | 2.81 |

The family called *other* is the lithium alloys: Li-Mg, Li-Sn, Li-Ag, Li-Ga, Li-Si, Li-Pb, Li-Zn
and Li-Al, whose voltages run from -0.25 to 1.18 V with a mean of 0.34 V. They are anode materials
rather than cathodes, and they are kept because the voltage of an alloying reaction is the same
quantity measured the same way. They are also most of what makes the set wide, and so most of the
reason that predicting its mean costs 1.203 V.

**The difference of the two cells, as a field (item BT6).** A voltage is a property of a pair and
not of a structure, and the fields are linear in the atoms, so the difference of the two cells'
fields is itself an ordinary field in the cell: the atoms of the lithiated cell with their weights,
and the atoms of the delithiated one with their weights negated (`cmfqsar/celldiff.py`). Where the
two cells agree -- most of the host -- the two contributions cancel, and what is left is the
inserted ions and the relaxation their arrival caused. Two things do not cancel, and neither is a
fault: the formal charge of the metal, which item BT1 makes Co(+3.5) at half lithiation and Co(+3)
at full, and the electronegativity proxy, which is a deviation from the mean over the cell and so
moves when lithium enters it. Because a field difference is a field, every kernel takes it
unchanged; it is bilinear in the weights and nothing has to be re-derived for signed ones.

**What the construction costs.** A difference is defined only when the two cells stand on one
lattice and hold the same host atoms, and two cells relaxed separately do not: their lattice
constants differ by the volume change of the insertion, which is a quantity a battery paper reports
in its own right. Of the 303 pairs, **42 have cell lengths within 5% of each other and the same
host atoms**, over 33 frameworks; the other 261 are refused, with the reason recorded for each, so
what the frame costs is reported and not hidden.

**What it gives, and what it does not.** The reading the item asked for comes out of the
construction rather than out of a model: over the 42 pairs the inserted ion sits in **5.0 +/- 1.1
oxygens at 2.22 +/- 0.13 angstrom**, which is the first shell of a lithium in an oxide. The model
is another matter. On the same five folds, grouped by framework:

| model | mean absolute error, V | spread over the folds | R² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| the mean voltage of these pairs | 0.791 | - | 0.000 |
| composition | 0.656 | 0.100 | +0.228 |
| the discharged cell alone | 0.699 | 0.143 | +0.138 |
| the difference field | 0.797 | 0.083 | +0.014 |
| the difference field and the composition | 0.680 | 0.118 | +0.250 |

**The gate the item set itself is not met.** Paired over the same samples, the difference field is
+0.090 V against the discharged cell alone, with an interval of [-0.034, +0.216] that contains
zero, so the two are indistinguishable here; against the composition it is +0.134 V [+0.004,
+0.273], which does not contain zero, so on this set the difference field is **worse** than the
element fractions. The set is the reason to be careful either way: 42 pairs over 33 frameworks
leave about eight pairs per fold, and every model sits within 0.135 V of simply predicting the mean
voltage. What the numbers do support is the conclusion of the stage before them, now with the pair
itself as the sample: the voltage follows the composition, and the arrangement does not add to it.

The co-field in the cell the item promised is not here, and the reason is worth stating. A co-field
needs every sample in one frame, which for cells means one parent lattice for the whole set; 33
different hosts do not have one, so the kernel used here is the autocorrelation, whose reading is a
co-pattern over distance channels rather than a map. With R² +0.014 that co-pattern has nothing to
say, and the channels it names are element indicators of single frameworks, which means the model
is recognising hosts and not geometry. The map needs a ladder of one host on one lattice -- which
is the beta-Li3PO4 vacancy series the conductivity literature argues about, and the one case this
program still has to compute for itself.

**The limits.** The pairs are matched by host *composition* and not by host *structure*: two cells
with the same framework formula and different frameworks can be paired, which a topotactic
criterion would refuse. The target carries the 0.39 V offset of the
check above, so an error below that is not a claim about measured voltages but about reproducing
these energies. And 303 pairs is a large set for this program and a small one for a materials
benchmark: the same code reaches 528 pairs at a hull window of 0.05 eV per atom,
at the cost of a worse agreement with the published values.

## An ion as the probe: where a cation sits, and what it gains

A probe field answers "what would this group gain by sitting here?". With an ion as the probe the
answer is the quantity an electrolyte or an ionophore is designed for, and it can be checked
against a number that was computed rather than fitted. `examples/ether/` holds the set that makes
the check possible: 1,085 saturated acyclic ethers -- glymes and their branched relatives -- with
the binding energy of Li⁺, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ at wB97X-D3/def2-TZVP, and 1,050 of them in the relaxed
geometry of the lithium complex, from the distribution of Wang et al. (Chem. Commun. 56 (2020)
8920). `examples/make_ether_examples.py --fetch` downloads it and checks the hashes; the
distributor states no licence, so the status of the copy is *unclear* in the sense of
[public_3dqsar_datasets.md](docs/public_3dqsar_datasets.md). `benchmarks/run_ether.py` is the
measurement (plan item EC7).

**Where the ion sits.** A probe field is a map of an energy, so its deepest point is a prediction
of where the ion goes, and it needs no model and no fitting at all. On the 1,050 relaxed
complexes, with the ion removed and its position kept, the deepest point of the lithium probe
field lies 0.36 ± 0.55 Å from the lithium the DFT relaxation placed, and within 1.0 Å in 97 % of
the complexes. Two references that also need no model: the centroid of the molecule's oxygens is
0.65 ± 0.74 Å away (86 % within 1.0 Å) and the centroid of its heavy atoms 0.67 ± 0.80 Å (82 %).
The probe field is thus a usable guess of the binding site in a flexible chain, which is the one
thing a docking program would otherwise be needed for.

![The lithium probe field of triglyme, in the geometry of its lithium complex with the ion taken out. The plane passes through the place of the ion and along the two directions in which the four oxygens, the red dots, spread most. Left: the electrostatic field, which is lowest on the oxygens. Right: the lithium probe field, the energy of a lithium ion at each place, which is lowest between them. The star is the ion as the published relaxation placed it, and the cross is the lowest point of the field of each panel in this plane. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/ionprobe.png)

**The binding energy.** Nested cross-validation, five outer folds, the ridge and the field width
chosen inside each fold, no frame anywhere (the alignment-free kernel). Mean absolute error in eV,
folds drawn at random:

| model | Li⁺ (1048) | Na⁺ (980) | Mg²⁺ (982) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| predicting the mean of the set | 0.454 | 0.449 | 1.235 |
| oxygen count, C:O ratio, heavy atoms | 0.296 | 0.279 | 0.505 |
| the same with the molecule's HOMO energy | 0.254 | 0.246 | 0.444 |
| the electrostatic field alone | 0.209 | 0.248 | 0.557 |
| the five fields | **0.124** | **0.181** | **0.266** |
| the matching ion probe field alone | 0.140 | 0.193 | 0.321 |
| the five fields and the probe field | **0.117** | **0.171** | **0.254** |

Paired over the same molecules, with a bootstrap interval: the ion probe beats the counts by
0.156 eV [0.139, 0.175] on lithium, and it beats *the electrostatic field alone* -- which is the
comparison the plan item names -- by 0.069 eV [0.060, 0.078] on lithium, 0.055 on sodium and
0.236 on magnesium, every interval clear of zero. The probe field is slightly behind the five
fields together (+0.015 eV [+0.009, +0.022] on lithium) and the two together are ahead of either.
With one oxygen count held out at a time, which asks for a chain length the model has not seen,
the five fields and the probe reach 0.129, 0.204 and 0.279 eV against 0.284, 0.291 and 0.571 for
the counts. **This is the first measurement in this part of the manual where the arrangement of
the atoms beats what the formula already says**, and by about a factor of two: the voltage of an
insertion electrode went the other way.

**The selectivity between two ions is a much harder quantity.** The difference between the
lithium and the sodium energy is what an ionophore is designed for. Over the 980 molecules that
carry both it has a mean of −1.07 eV and a spread of 0.36, and the oxygen count tells one nothing
about it (correlation −0.05, q² +0.01). Predicting its mean costs 0.190 eV; the five fields and
the probe together reach 0.171 eV (q² +0.22) and the two ion probes 0.176. The field models are
ahead of the counts by 0.012 eV [0.003, 0.022], which is a real difference and a small one. Adding
the sodium probe to the lithium probe changes nothing at all (+0.001 eV [−0.000, +0.003]), which
is what the probe definitions predict: two singly charged probes report the same potential at two
distances, and that is not enough to separate two ions. **Selectivity needs what a fixed probe
charge cannot carry**, namely the polarisation of the ion and of the donor atoms.

**Three ions as three endpoints.** The three columns are the multi-task problem of plan item E1
with descriptors of the endpoint rather than a label: 3,010 measurements over 1,048 molecules, one
kernel, and the covariance between the endpoints taken from the ion's radius, charge and
polarisability. Fitting the endpoints independently costs 0.204 eV; one shared correlation of 0.5
gives 0.198 and the descriptor covariance 0.188, with q² +0.893, +0.698 and +0.852 for Li⁺, Na⁺
and Mg²⁺. The covariance it chooses is worth reading: lithium is more closely related to
magnesium (0.46) than to sodium (0.27), and sodium and magnesium least of all (0.20). What decides
which endpoint helps another is therefore the size of the ion -- Li⁺ 0.76 Å, Mg²⁺ 0.72, Na⁺ 1.02 --
and not its charge.

**An ion that was never measured cannot be predicted here.** Each ion in turn was removed
entirely and predicted from the other two. Magnesium is refused before any arithmetic: the mean
of an endpoint is a linear function of the charge, and with two monovalent ions left that function
cannot be evaluated at charge +2, so the design matrix has two identical rows. Lithium and sodium
can be evaluated and both fail: 1.484 eV and 0.539 eV against their own means of 0.454 and 0.449.
They are far better than every reference a model that never saw the ion has -- the mean of the
measured ions is 3.5 and 4.7 eV away -- and still much worse than knowing the removed ion's own
average. The part that fails is the mean: lithium's is −3.84 eV and the model, which may use only
the charge to place it, predicts −2.36. Three endpoints are too few for more than one descriptor
column, so this is a limit of the set and not of the method.

**The limits.** The coordinates are the relaxed *lithium* complexes, so the sodium and magnesium
models are built on a lithium-shaped conformation; the three energies correlate (+0.80 and +0.85),
which hides the error in a single-ion model but limits what the selectivity may be read as. The
targets are computed energies of a one-to-one complex in the gas phase, not solvation free
energies, so nothing here is a statement about a real electrolyte, where a lithium ion is
surrounded by four or five molecules. And the published model of this set is a neural network
potential trained by active learning, which is a different object from a kernel on a field: the
comparison made here is against the formula and against the electrostatic field, not against it.

## The ion with its shell as the molecule: a solvation complex

The section above models the solvent molecule. For almost every property of an electrolyte the
object that carries the property is not the solvent but the complex: the ion together with the
molecules that touch it. `cmfqsar/solvation.py` builds one (plan item BT4), and it does three
separate things so that each can be checked on its own.

**It places.** A donor atom is an oxygen or a nitrogen with a lone pair, and the direction of that
lone pair is the reverse of the sum of the atom's bond directions — the bisector for an ether
oxygen, the C=O axis for a carbonyl. `place_shell` puts the ion at the origin, takes as many
directions as there are molecules from the polyhedron of that coordination number (linear,
trigonal, tetrahedral, and the bipyramid and octahedron above that), turns each molecule so its
lone pair points back at the ion, and sets the donor at the coordination distance — 2.01 Å for
Li⁺ and oxygen, the distance measured in the relaxed complexes of `examples/ether/`. Each molecule
is then spun about its own ion–donor axis to the angle that leaves the most room. An anion may
join the shell, which makes a contact ion pair, and the total charge follows from the fragments.
`wrap_ion` is the other case: one molecule that wraps the ion with several of its own oxygens, as
a glyme does.

**It optimises.** GFN2-xTB through `cmfqsar.xtb`, which caches by molecule, charge, method and
starting geometry, so a run resumes where it stopped. A complex of fifty atoms takes under a
second. The binding energy is E(complex) − E(ion) − ΣE(solvent) and the desolvation energy
E(n−1) + E(solvent) − E(n), both written out in the functions that compute them.

**It frames.** This is what the complex gives that the free solvent cannot. A series of glymes has
no scaffold to superimpose, but a series of complexes has one atom in common, and the polyhedron
of its donors fixes the orientation: `cation_frame` puts the origin on the ion, the axes along the
principal axes of the donor set, and resolves the four proper sign choices by the third moments of
the donors. Where two moments are equal — a regular polyhedron — the axes inside that plane are
taken from the heavy atoms of the whole complex instead, and `frame_quality` reports the moment
ratios so that a caller can see when the frame still leaves a rotation free. With a frame there is
an overlap kernel, and with an overlap kernel there is a co-field.

### What the builder is worth, measured against a published relaxation

`benchmarks/run_solvation.py` measures the builder on 150 of the 1,050 Li⁺–ether complexes of
`examples/ether/`, which were relaxed with density functional theory. Three runs per molecule: the
free solvent, the published complex re-optimised with xTB, and the complex the builder makes from
five generated starting conformers, each optimised, the lowest kept.

| Quantity | The published relaxation | xTB from that geometry | The builder's own complex |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| oxygens reaching the ion | 4.24 ± 0.87 | 4.38 | 3.81 ± 0.84 |
| nearest oxygen (Å) | 1.935 | 1.874 | 1.856 |
| mean oxygen distance (Å) | 1.995 ± 0.068 | — | 1.926 ± 0.088 |
| binding energy, correlation with the published one | — | **+0.907** | +0.555 |
| binding energy, mean error (eV) | — | −1.323 | −0.919 |

Two statements follow, and they are about different things. **The method overbinds**: GFN2-xTB
puts a lithium ion about 1.3 eV deeper into an ether than wB97X-D3 does, and gets the ordering
right while doing it (+0.91). It ranks and it must not be quoted as an absolute number.
**The builder loses the longer chains**: it reaches 3.81 of the 4.24 oxygens and its correlation
with the published energy is +0.555, not +0.907. The reason is measured rather than guessed: the
five starting conformers of one molecule spread 1.52 ± 0.71 eV, so which conformer the builder
starts from decides the answer, and five of them are not enough for a chain with five oxygens.
What the builder lacks is a conformational search, not a better placing rule.

### The gate: does the shell carry what the solvent alone does not

Item BT4 asks that question, and the 1,048 complexes with a published binding energy answer it.
Five outer folds, the ridge and the field width chosen inside each fold. Predicting the mean of
the set costs 0.454 eV.

| Model | MAE (eV) | R² |
|---|---:|---:|
| the solvent alone, alignment-free kernel (the model of the section above) | 0.124 ± 0.016 | +0.894 |
| the complex, alignment-free kernel | **0.114 ± 0.013** | **+0.914** |
| the complex, overlap kernel in the cation frame | 0.145 ± 0.018 | +0.868 |
| the solvent again, overlap kernel in the same frame | 0.143 ± 0.009 | +0.886 |

**The gate is met, and by a small margin.** Paired over the same molecules, putting the ion back
gains 0.010 eV [0.004, 0.016], an interval clear of zero and eight per cent of the error. The
shell does carry something the solvent alone does not, and it is not much: the solvent in the
geometry it holds in the complex already says most of what there is to say.

**The frame costs accuracy.** The overlap kernel in the cation frame is 0.018 eV [0.010, 0.027]
worse than the alignment-free kernel on the same molecules, and inside that frame the ion adds
nothing at all (+0.002 eV [−0.003, +0.008]). The two models were run precisely to separate the
ion from the frame, and the separation says the gain above belongs to the ion. The frame is not
useless, but what it buys is not accuracy.

**What it buys is the co-field**, which the alignment-free kernel cannot have at all. Fitted on
every complex and evaluated on a grid, the largest magnitude of the electrostatic co-field lies
1.37 Å from the ion and 1.37 Å from the nearest donor oxygen, and that of the hydrogen-bond
acceptor field 1.03 Å from the ion. Both sit inside the first shell, which is where the chemistry
is, so the item's reading gate is met. The hydrogen-bond donor field is the control that costs
nothing: an ether has no donor, that field carries no weight anywhere, and its largest magnitude
lands 12.5 Å away, in the corner of the box.

### The series computed here: carbonates, ethers and fluorinated ethers

Nineteen solvents with one to four molecules around Li⁺, every complex placed and optimised by
this module (75 complexes, one failure). At one solvent molecule the carbonates bind
−2.49 ± 0.12 eV, the ethers −3.01 ± 1.08 and the fluorinated ethers −2.91 ± 0.61. The wide spread
of the ethers is not noise: twelve of the nineteen solvents give a complex in which the ion
touches one oxygen, and those twelve agree closely (−2.36 ± 0.18 eV), while the other seven are
chains that fold and donate two or three oxygens at once, so their "one molecule" is already a
three-coordinate complex. Two numbers from the table are worth reading on their own.
**Fluorination weakens the donor**: FEC binds 0.29 eV less than EC, which is the effect those
additives are used for. **The fluorinated ethers hold the fourth molecule weakly**: the
desolvation energy at four solvents is 0.92 to 1.35 eV for the carbonates and 0.02 to 0.33 eV for
the fluorinated ethers, which is what a diluent is chosen to do. Two of the 56 desolvation
energies are negative, meaning the optimiser did not find a bound complex at that size, and the
table names them.

## A distribution of shells instead of one: sampling a bulk electrolyte

The section above builds one complex and optimises it. A liquid electrolyte does not hold one
complex. At any moment every lithium ion in the box has a different set of neighbours, and the
property an experiment measures — a conductivity, a transference number, a diffusion coefficient —
is an average over that distribution. Plan item BT5 asks whether the distribution is worth
sampling: does a model built on shells cut out of a bulk simulation predict better than the same
model built on item BT4's single optimised complex? Two modules answer it.
`cmfqsar/electrolyte.py` builds and runs the box. `cmfqsar/shells.py` cuts the shells out of the
trajectory and turns them into one field.

### Why a distribution of shells is still one field

This is the reason the route needs little new code. A CMF field is a sum of Gaussian functions
centred on atoms, and the kernel between two fields is bilinear: linear in each of them. So the
weighted mean field of a set of shells is itself a field of the same kind. Its atoms are all the
atoms of all the shells, and each atom keeps its own weight multiplied by the weight of the shell
it came from. Nothing new has to be defined, and three statements follow at once.

* The kernel between two such mean fields is exactly the weighted mean of the shell-to-shell
  kernels. No pairwise sum has to be written out, and a 16-member ensemble costs one kernel
  evaluation on a larger atom list, not 256 of them.
* The kernel matrix stays positive definite, because a mean of fields is a field and the kernel is
  the same kernel.
* The model is still linear in that mean field, so the co-field and the Shapley decomposition keep
  their meaning. The co-field of an ensemble is the weight function that the average shell is
  integrated against.

`combine_members` in `cmfqsar/fields.py`, written for plan item D4, needed no change for this.
It already accepted members that carry their own atoms, and that is what shells are: two shells of
the same electrolyte need not even hold the same molecules.

![A distribution of solvation shells as one field, for lithium hexafluorophosphate in ethylene carbonate and ethyl methyl carbonate, 3 to 7 by weight, at 1.11 mol/kg. Every shell is drawn in the frame of its lithium ion, which is the star, and seen along the third axis of that frame. The dashed circle has a radius of 2 Å, about the distance of an oxygen that coordinates the ion. Top left: the representative shell with the largest weight; oxygen is red, fluorine green and phosphorus orange, and hydrogens are not drawn. Top right: all sixteen representative shells of this electrolyte, each drawn the darker the larger its weight, with the oxygen and fluorine atoms within 2.6 Å of the ion. The frame puts the anion on the same side in most shells. Bottom left: the electrostatic field of the one shell, summed along the direction of view, red positive and blue negative. Bottom right: the mean field of the sixteen shells with their weights, which is the sample the kernel is given. What the shells have in common stays sharp, and what differs from shell to shell is spread out. Drawn by `docs/make_figures.py`.](docs/figures/shells.png)

The per-atom reading needs one decision, because a per-atom contribution has to point at *an*
atom. `atom_maps` sends the ion to the ion, and every solvent atom to the matching atom of the
first molecule of its own species in the first member. A per-atom number is therefore per atom of
a species, summed over however many molecules of that species the shell happens to hold. That is
the only reading the geometry supports: "the second ethylene carbonate" is not a well-defined
object in a liquid.

### The box: what is simulated, and with what

A `Formulation` is a salt, a set of solvent weight fractions and a molality. From those three
`counts` works out the exact number of molecules of each species: 250 solvent molecules in the
proportions asked for, and the number of ion pairs that reproduces the molality, with at least
four pairs so that the shells are not all cut from one ion. The arithmetic needs no density,
which is why molality and weight fractions are the only concentration units accepted. A molarity
or a volume fraction would require a density to be assumed, and the simulation is supposed to
produce the density, not to be given it.

The rest is an ordinary molecular-dynamics protocol, and every part of it is a stated setting of
`Settings` rather than a default buried in a script:

| Step | What is done |
|---|---|
| Starting geometry | packmol packs the molecules into a cube whose side comes from the pure-component densities, loosened by ten per cent |
| Topology | assembled from the same RDKit templates packmol was given, in a fixed species order; the packed file supplies coordinates only, because packmol writes no bond records |
| Solvent and anion parameters | GAFF-2.11 through `openmmforcefields`, with atom types from `antechamber` |
| Charges | the OpenFF NAGL graph-network AM1-BCC model, which gives AM1-BCC charges without a semi-empirical calculation per molecule |
| Cation parameters | the Amber monovalent ion set in `amber14/tip3p.xml`, because GAFF has no lithium |
| Electrostatics | particle-mesh Ewald, 1.0 nm real-space cutoff |
| Integration | Langevin middle integrator, 2 fs steps, hydrogen bonds constrained |
| Ensemble | 298.15 K, Monte Carlo barostat at 1 bar |
| Equilibration | 150 ps, during which the box finds its own density |
| Production | 1,000 ps, one frame every 2 ps |

The net charge of the assembled system is checked against zero before the run starts, since a
wrong anion template would otherwise give a silently charged box. The versions used for the series
below are OpenMM 8.3.1, `openmmforcefields` 0.15.1, OpenFF Toolkit 0.18.0, OpenFF NAGL 0.5.5,
AmberTools 24.8, packmol 20.14.3 and MDTraj 1.11.1, run on a CUDA device inside WSL.

The reach of the force field decides which electrolytes can be in the series at all, and the
module makes that a refusal rather than an approximation. GAFF has no boron, so `SALTS` holds no
borate: asking for LiBF₄ or LiBOB raises an error that names the reason. This matters for the
series below, because those two salts are a large part of the open conductivity table it is drawn
from.

### Cutting a shell out of a periodic box

A shell is every molecule with at least one donor atom — oxygen, nitrogen, fluorine, sulfur or
chlorine — within a cutoff of the ion. The cutoff is 1.3 times the ion–donor coordination distance
measured in item BT4's relaxed complexes, which is 2.613 Å for Li⁺ and oxygen. The ion's own
counter-ion is not excluded: a shell that holds the anion is a contact ion pair, and whether one
forms is exactly what changes with concentration.

Two faults of a periodic box have to be repaired, and both of them produce a wrong geometry rather
than an error, so neither announces itself:

* **A molecule split across a face of the box.** Half its atoms are at one edge and half at the
  other. `trajectory.make_whole`, written for item D7, puts it back together by following bonds.
* **A shell on the far side of the box from its ion.** The molecule is whole but it sits a box
  length away. `trajectory.reimage` moves it to the image nearest the ion.

The selection itself is written for speed, because a single electrolyte here needs 3,500 to 31,000
shells. All donor atoms of the frame are screened at once: one array of distances to the ion under
the minimum-image convention, which is a matrix product and a rounding. Only the residues that
pass are then made whole and reimaged. The first version repaired every residue before measuring
any distance, which meant about half a million repairs for one electrolyte, and it was too slow to
use.

Each shell records what it is made of: the species and the number of molecules of each, the
distances of the donor atoms that reached the ion, and a `fingerprint` that does not depend on the
order the molecules were found in, so that two shells of the same shape are recognised as the same
shape.

### Thinning, and the two numbers that say whether it converged

Twelve thousand shells cannot all be carried into a kernel. `cluster_shells` keeps a limited
number of representatives — 16 by default — by grouping the shells whose fingerprints lie within
0.75 of each other and taking one shell from each group. The weight of a representative is the
share of all sampled shells in its group.

Those weights are populations, not Boltzmann factors. This is item D7's rule and it is worth
repeating here: an equilibrated trajectory has already sampled the distribution, so a shell that
is common appears often. Weighting those occurrences again by a Boltzmann factor would raise the
distribution to a power and count the energy twice.

Item D8 requires a sampling error next to any accuracy figure obtained from a trajectory, and
`convergence` reports two separate numbers. Both are computed exactly from one shell-to-shell
overlap matrix, with no model fitted and no grid involved, as one minus the normalised overlap of
two mean fields:

* **The block error of the mean field.** The frames are split into blocks, the mean field of each
  block is formed from an equal number of shells, and the error reported is how far those block
  means lie from the mean of the whole run. This is the sampling error the item asks for: it falls
  as the trajectory grows.
* **The cost of keeping 16 members.** How far the thinned ensemble's mean field lies from the mean
  field of all the shells. This is not a sampling error. It is the price of the thinning, and it
  does not fall when the trajectory grows.

The first version mixed the two, by measuring the block error on the thinned ensembles. It rose
with more sampling, from 0.055 at 40 frames to 0.145 at 500, because thinning noise is larger than
sampling noise and more frames give more distinct shapes to throw away. A diagnostic that gets
worse as the data get better is reporting the wrong quantity. Measured separately on the same
trajectory the two numbers are 0.00008 and 0.00496, and they mean different things.

### The series: 62 measured electrolytes from an open table

The item allows simulated or measured transport data. Measured data is the better choice here,
because taking the target and the descriptor from the same trajectory would test the force field
against itself. CALiSol-23 is an open collection of 13,825 measured ionic conductivities of
lithium electrolytes, published under CC BY 4.0, and `examples/make_electrolyte_shells.py` fetches
it, checks its hash, and selects a series from it by stated rules.

Two targets are read off each formulation, not one. A fit of log₁₀ k = a + b/T + c/T² to that
formulation's own measurements gives **log₁₀ of the conductivity at 298.15 K**, which is what an
electrolyte is chosen for, and **the activation energy at 298.15 K**, which is its temperature
dependence. The second is the quantity a solvation shell has the better claim on: an ion moves by
leaving one shell and entering the next, so the barrier should depend on how tightly the shell
holds it. The fit is an interpolation and is never extrapolated.

Every selection rule is in the script, and each is there for a reason that can be checked:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| LiPF₆ only | GAFF has no boron, so LiBF₄ and LiBOB cannot be simulated here |
| molality and weight fractions only | those two units fix the molecule counts exactly, with no density assumed |
| solvents the module can parameterise | eleven carbonates, esters, ethers and acetonitrile |
| at least four temperatures, spanning at least 20 K and containing 298.15 K | so that both targets are interpolated |
| fit residual at most 0.03 in log₁₀ k, activation energy between 0 and 40 kJ/mol | drops formulations whose measurements do not follow one smooth curve |
| a source paper whose conductivity scale is below a tenth of the collection's is dropped | one paper's values are 0.019 of everyone else's at the same salt, solvent and temperature, which is a unit error in the source, not a property of an electrolyte |
| at most three molalities per solvent composition | keeps the concentration axis without letting one well-measured mixture dominate |

What comes out is **62 formulations over 22 solvent compositions** of six solvents, from 0.245 to
2.373 mol/kg. The conductivity at 298 K spans 0.169 to 1.172 in log₁₀ mS/cm, where predicting the
mean of the set costs 0.146, and the activation energy spans 5.5 to 37.8 kJ/mol, where predicting
the mean costs 3.535 kJ/mol.

The concentration axis is kept on purpose, because that is where a sampled shell can say something
an optimised complex cannot. The share of shells that hold the anion rises with the molality
(correlation +0.729), from 0.222 in the most dilute box to 0.978 in the most concentrated. A single
four-molecule complex has no way to express that: the 22 compositions give only 12 distinct
complexes, because rounding a mixture to four molecules makes several compositions identical, and 9
of those 12 are shared by more than one composition. Two of them, DEC/PC at 50:50 and at 60:40,
round to two molecules of each and so give the same geometry and the same energy to six figures.

### What the simulations cost, and what they produced

| Quantity | Over the 62 boxes |
|---|---|
| atoms in a box | 3,500 ± 398 (2,853 to 4,285) |
| simulation rate | 456 ± 49 ns per day |
| time per box, including the shell extraction | 191 ± 17 s (139 to 223) |
| failures | none |
| density the barostat settled at, g/cm³ | 1.205 ± 0.081 (1.058 to 1.445) |
| molecules in a shell | 4.26 ± 0.35 (3.72 to 4.98) |
| donor atoms reaching the ion | 6.95 ± 0.40 (5.83 to 7.43) |
| shells cut per electrolyte | 13,427 ± 7,716 (3,500 to 31,000) |
| block error of the mean field | 0.00019 ± 0.00037 (0.00003 to 0.00253) |
| cost of keeping 16 members | 0.0065 ± 0.0070 (0.0010 to 0.0394) |

The whole series takes about three and a half hours on one CUDA device. The trajectories are 1.2
GB and are not kept in the repository; what is kept is one small structure file of 16 shells per
electrolyte, which is all a model needs.

One number here is a statement about the force field rather than about the electrolytes. The 6.95
donor atoms at the ion is far above the 4.24 oxygens item BT4 measured on complexes relaxed with
density functional theory. Part of the difference is that anion fluorine atoms count as donors
here, and the donor count also rises with the molality (+0.769). The rest is the missing
